title: ADRs & Roadmapping
description: A preview of the Planning & Communication toolkit's decision and narrative artifacts.
body: In the full toolkit Named artifacts this page previews Four specific templates, beyond the general practice described below. Architecture Decision Record Template , a durable format for hard-to-reverse decisions plus the conventions that keep the practice alive rather than decorative Target-State Narrative Template , a prose-first structure for describing a future operating model to executive audiences, built on the principle that diagrams illustrate clear writing and cannot replace it Capability-Driven Roadmap Method , building multi-year roadmaps rooted in capability gaps rather than technology initiatives, with traceability from strategy to initiative Business Case Template and Narrative , a financial model paired with the narrative structure that makes it defensible to executives and finance reviewers, including a candid options analysis and named benefit owners Framework What a good ADR contains An Architecture Decision Record exists to answer one question well after the fact: why did we decide this, given what we knew at the time. Most ADR templates fail at exactly that. Section What it should contain Context The situation and constraints as understood at decision time, written before hindsight sets in. This section goes stale fastest and matters most. Decision What was decided, stated in a single clear sentence rather than buried in a paragraph of qualifications. Alternatives considered What else was on the table and why it was rejected. Absence of this section is the most common ADR failure; it's what lets someone later ask "why didn't we just do X" and get a real answer instead of a re-litigation. Consequences What this decision makes harder later. Every architecture decision has a cost; an ADR that lists only benefits is incomplete. 1 When a decision needs an ADR Not every choice. Writing one for every minor decision produces the same fatigue problem as over-gating architecture review. Write one When the decision is expensive to reverse, when it affects more than one team, or when you can already predict someone will ask "why did we do it this way" in six months. What counts as expensive to reverse scales with the team, a change that's a quick fix for a three-person startup might be a multi-quarter migration for a five-hundred-engineer org, so weigh it against your own team's capacity rather than a fixed unit of time. Skip it Reversible implementation choices scoped entirely within one team, where the cost of writing the record exceeds the cost of just trying something and changing it later if it's wrong. 2 Roadmaps for two different audiences The most common roadmap mistake is one document trying to serve both an engineering audience and a business audience, and serving neither well. Engineering roadmap Organized by system or capability, includes technical sequencing dependencies, appropriately detailed about implementation approach, timeframes expressed as sprints or quarters. Business roadmap Organized by customer or business outcome, no implementation detail, timeframes expressed as calendar dates tied to business events (a renewal cycle, a fiscal year), directly reusable in the board reporting format described on the Board Reporting page. Maintain one underlying plan and generate both views from it, rather than maintaining two documents that inevitably drift out of sync with each other within a quarter or two. 3 The business case, stripped to what gets funded What separates a business case that gets approved from one that gets deferred indefinitely. What gets funded A specific, falsifiable claim (this reduces X by Y amount, measured how, by when) tied to a number the approver already tracks, with the cost of not doing it stated as explicitly as the cost of doing it. What gets deferred A business case built entirely around technical merit ("this reduces technical debt") with no connection to a business metric anyone outside engineering tracks. Technical merit is necessary justification, rarely sufficient justification on its own. 4 ADR conventions that keep the practice alive The template is the easy part. These conventions are what turn a folder of documents into a resource people consult. Numbers are never reused , even for deprecated or superseded ADRs. The number identifies the record; it says nothing about priority. Once accepted, the decision is immutable. Circumstances change, a new ADR supersedes it. Editing the original to reflect current understanding destroys the record. One decision per ADR. A compound ADR is a sign the team is avoiding the harder work of separating decisions. One to two pages. Longer usually means design work leaking in that belongs elsewhere; shorter usually means the alternatives section is missing. Author by role as well as name. "Lead Architect, Payments" carries context that survives staff changes. Signals of a healthy practice: new engineers read old ADRs during onboarding and find them useful, debates reference specific ADRs by number, superseded ADRs exist and are traceable. Signals of a failing one: ADRs only get written when leadership asks to see one, the alternatives section always contains only the chosen path with strawman alternatives dismissed, no ADR has ever been superseded. 5 A worked roadmap example A compressed real example showing the method end to end: strategic priority through capability gaps through sequenced initiatives. Strategic priority: reduce customer acquisition cost 25 percent within 36 months while maintaining conversion on qualified leads. Capability Gap Initiative Sequence Customer Insight Prospect scoring is rule-based, updated quarterly, limited signal integration Prospect Scoring Modernization Starts first; outputs feed the other two Campaign Management Execution is batch-oriented, attribution manual Campaign Operations Overhaul Starts month 3, overlapping Digital Engagement First response to leads requires human effort, capacity-constrained Early-Stage Engagement Automation Starts month 6, once upstream work is stable What the example demonstrates: three initiatives, all traceable to one strategic priority, sequenced by real dependency rather than organizational convenience, each owned by a named business sponsor. The technology choices support the story; they don't constitute it. Download ADR template A ready-to-use starting point for the format described above: context, decision, alternatives considered, consequences. Markdown for pasting into your own docs system, or a formatted Word doc. Download .md Download .docx

title: Agile and SAFe
description: What agile requires versus what most transformations install instead, and where SAFe specifically earns its overhead at scale versus where it becomes its own kind of theater.
body: Reference The four values, and what commonly gets installed instead Each value in the agile manifesto asks for a concrete change in how a team works. Most organizations install a process substitute that satisfies the ritual and skips the substance. Value What it requires What commonly gets installed instead Individuals and interactions over processes and tools Trust, and a team empowered to change its own process A fixed ceremony calendar treated as the definition of agile itself Working software over comprehensive documentation Frequent, real integration and deployment Sprint demos of work that has not been deployed Customer collaboration over contract negotiation Direct, frequent contact between the team and the people using what they build A product owner as the sole interface, recreating the exact handoff agile was meant to remove Responding to change over following a plan A backlog re-prioritized as new information arrives A locked sprint commitment defended against any change, optimizing for predictability over responsiveness 1 Why "doing agile" and "being agile" diverge The gap that determines whether the ceremonies are earning their keep. Being agile The team changes what it does based on what it learns, mid-sprint if warranted, and treats each ceremony as a tool it owns and can modify or drop the moment it stops earning its keep. Doing agile Standup, retro, planning, and review run on schedule whether or not they produce anything, treated as compliance requirements rather than tools the team controls. The tell: ask when the team last changed its own process because of a retro. Silence answers the question. 2 Where SAFe helps A real coordination problem exists at scale, and SAFe was built to address it, whatever else gets said about the framework. The problem it addresses Coordinating dependencies across many teams building toward a shared release or shared platform, where informal coordination breaks down past a certain team count and someone has to own cross-team sequencing explicitly rather than leaving it to hope. Roughly where it starts to matter Often cited around 50 to 125 people, five to twelve teams, though the trigger that matters is dependency density between teams, and headcount is only a proxy for it. Ten independent teams with no shared release need none of this; four teams shipping one product together might. 3 Where SAFe becomes its own theater The same framework, installed for a coordination problem the organization doesn't have. The failure mode The framework's ceremonies, PI planning, the various sync meetings, the layered roles, get installed wholesale regardless of whether the organization's coordination problem matches what SAFe was built to solve, producing ceremony overhead that outweighs the coordination it buys. The tell Ask what specific coordination failure a given SAFe ceremony prevents. If the answer is "we don't know, this is just what SAFe says to do," the ceremony is cargo cult and can go. 4 Scaling down deliberately, as well as up The adoption decision most organizations skip: choosing which pieces to install and which to leave out. Practice Apply only the specific mechanisms that address a named coordination problem, and skip the rest. A framework adopted partially and deliberately produces less overhead than either the full framework or no coordination structure at all. Common failure mode Adopting the framework "properly" because partial adoption feels like doing it wrong, which installs overhead for coordination problems the organization doesn't have, simply because the framework bundles them together with the ones it does. 5 The main frameworks, compared plainly Every framework below solves a real problem. The mistake is choosing one by reputation instead of by the coordination problem you actually have. Framework Scale and shape Fits when Costs Scrum (Scrum Guide 2020) One team of typically ten or fewer, fixed-length sprints A single team building one product increment at a time Sprint ceremonies; weak on cross-team dependencies Kanban Continuous flow with limits on work in progress Ops, platform, and support teams with unpredictable arrival of work Needs discipline on limits or it becomes a to-do list SAFe 6.0 Agile Release Trains of about 50 to 125 people in 5 to 12 teams, planning increments of 8 to 12 weeks Many teams with dense dependencies toward shared releases The heaviest role and ceremony set; easy to over-install LeSS Up to about eight teams on one product with one product owner and one backlog; LeSS Huge beyond that One large product where splitting ownership would create handoffs Demands deep structural change and removal of roles Nexus (Scrum.org) Three to nine Scrum teams with an integration team Organizations already running Scrum that need light scaling Limited guidance beyond integration Team Topologies (Skelton and Pais) Not a process: team types and interaction modes that reduce the need for coordination Dependency problems are structural and should be designed away Requires reorganizing teams, not just adding meetings 6 Measure flow and outcomes, not ceremony What gets reported upward determines what the framework becomes. Report the things agility is supposed to change. Measure Source Replaces Deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate, failed deployment recovery time, rework rate DORA metrics, per Engineering Metrics Velocity reported upward as if comparable across teams Flow time, flow load, flow efficiency, and the mix of features, defects, risk, and debt The Flow Framework (Mik Kersten, Project to Product, 2018) Story points completed Planned versus delivered objectives, with business value assessed after the fact SAFe program predictability measure, used honestly Ceremony attendance and on-time PI events Customer and business outcomes for shipped work Your own product analytics Output counts of any kind 7 A worked example: right-sizing PI planning A nine-team train ran full two-day PI planning every quarter with about 90 people in the room. A dependency map showed the dependencies were real but clustered. Figures are illustrative. Before Change After Two days, about 90 people, every quarter: roughly 180 person-days of planning Mapped actual cross-team dependencies from the previous two increments Two clusters of three and four teams with dense dependencies; two teams nearly independent Program predictability around 70 percent Replaced full-train planning with one planning day per cluster, plus a monthly 60-minute dependency review About 60 person-days of planning per quarter; predictability unchanged Independent teams sitting through two days of other teams' planning The two independent teams moved to their own quarterly planning Those teams reported the most improvement in focus time Checklist Signs agile or SAFe has become theater Patterns that show up when process is running on schedule but no longer producing what it's meant to. Ceremonies run on schedule regardless of whether the team can name what each one is currently producing The team has never changed its own process based on a retrospective Story points or velocity get reported upward as if comparable across different teams SAFe ceremonies are followed without anyone able to name the specific coordination failure each one prevents "Being agile" and "following the ceremony calendar" are treated as the same thing by leadership The framework was chosen without first mapping which teams actually depend on each other

title: AI Architecture Map
description: Pipeline stage by pipeline stage, from raw documents to a grounded, human-supervised, secured response.
body: Reference Managed platform equivalents, all four clouds The same six capabilities the toggle below covers in full depth, summarized here across all four providers at a glance. Use it as a rosetta stone for translating a design conversation across clouds. The depth is in the stages that follow. Managed model access AWS Bedrock, unified Converse API across model families (Claude, Titan, Llama, Mistral) Azure Microsoft Foundry (formerly Azure AI Foundry), Azure OpenAI models plus the Foundry Model Catalog's open-weight options GCP Vertex AI, Gemini-first with third-party and open-weight models via Model Garden OCI OCI Generative AI, native and third-party models Managed RAG / knowledge base AWS Bedrock Knowledge Bases (S3, Confluence, SharePoint sources) Azure AI Search with integrated vectorization, hybrid vector, keyword, and semantic ranking built into the index itself GCP Vertex AI Search (Google Drive, Cloud Storage sources) OCI Generative AI Agents RAG service, integrated vector store and ingestion pipeline built in Agent orchestration AWS Bedrock Agents, AgentCore, and Flows Azure Foundry Agent Service, built-in tool calling GCP Vertex AI Agent Builder OCI Generative AI Agents, tool and API orchestration built into the same service as RAG Native vector search AWS pgvector on RDS, or OpenSearch at larger scale Azure AI Search's HNSW vector index, hybrid query mode built in GCP Vertex AI Vector Search, or vector functions inside BigQuery OCI AI Vector Search built into Oracle Database 23ai, or HeatWave GenAI for the MySQL side Custom / self-managed training AWS SageMaker Azure Azure Machine Learning GCP Vertex AI custom training OCI OCI Data Science, paired with GPU-backed AI infrastructure instances Guardrails / content safety AWS Bedrock Guardrails, content filtering and PII redaction built in Azure AI Content Safety, prompt shields and content filtering built in GCP Gemini Safety Settings for content filtering, plus Model Armor as a separate service for prompt injection and sensitive data protection OCI OCI Guardrails: content moderation, prompt injection defense, and PII detection, in Inform or Block mode Model family availability by provider changes fast, and sources published a few months apart often disagree. Confirm the current model catalog and licensing directly with the provider rather than trusting a cached comparison, including this one. AWS Azure GCP OCI Self-hosted Stage 1 Document intelligence / ingestion Turning raw PDFs, scans, forms, and images into machine-readable structured content: OCR, layout analysis, table and key-value extraction. AWS Textract for OCR, layout, table, and key-value extraction; pair with Comprehend for downstream entity extraction on the recovered text. Azure AI Document Intelligence for OCR, layout, table, and key-value extraction using prebuilt or custom-trained models. AI Content Understanding covers multimodal parsing (image, audio, video) as a Foundry service when documents aren't purely text/table. GCP Document AI, with prebuilt processors for common document types (invoices, IDs, contracts) and a general OCR processor for everything else. OCI Document Understanding for OCR, table, and key-value extraction through prebuilt AI models, customizable for industry-specific extraction needs. Self-hosted / open-weight The unstructured library or docling for parsing, paired with Tesseract or PaddleOCR for text recognition. For layout-aware extraction, a locally served vision-language model (Qwen-VL, InternVL, or a comparable open-weight multimodal model) handles document QA-style extraction where prebuilt OCR alone isn't enough. Stage 2 Chunking Splitting extracted content into retrieval-sized units without breaking semantic units apart. Same across every environment Chunking is orchestration-layer logic that runs in your own code, so this one doesn't change when you switch the toggle above. LangChain's RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter , embedding-similarity-based semantic chunking, or a managed index's built-in chunking step (Azure AI Search's integrated vectorization skillset is one example) all run identically regardless of which provider or self-hosted stack sits downstream. The choice of algorithm matters far more than the choice of cloud. Stage 3 Embeddings Converting chunks into vectors for semantic retrieval. AWS Titan Text Embeddings via Bedrock, or Cohere Embed for multilingual needs, billed per token with no separate deployment step. Azure OpenAI embedding models ( text-embedding-3-large / small ) via Foundry, pay-as-you-go per token or reserved via provisioned throughput for predictable latency at volume. GCP Vertex AI text embedding models, billed per character, with native integration into BigQuery for embedding data already living there. OCI OCI Generative AI embedding models, callable through the same API surface as OCI's generation models. Self-hosted / open-weight Open-weight embedding models (BGE-large, E5-mistral, Nomic Embed, GTE) served on owned GPUs via Hugging Face Text Embeddings Inference (TEI) or an Infinity server. No per-token bill; cost is amortized GPU time. Stage 4 Vector indexing & retrieval Storing embeddings for fast approximate nearest-neighbor search, typically combined with keyword search for hybrid retrieval. AWS OpenSearch Service for large-scale ANN search with hybrid BM25 support, or pgvector on RDS/Aurora for teams staying inside an existing Postgres footprint. Azure AI Search: HNSW vector index, hybrid (vector + keyword + semantic ranking) query mode, metadata filters, and ACL-aware secure access baked into the index itself. GCP Vertex AI Vector Search for dedicated ANN at scale, or vector functions inside BigQuery when the data already lives there and a separate index is overhead. OCI AI Vector Search built directly into Oracle Database 23ai, keeping vectors and relational data in one system rather than a separate store. Self-hosted / open-weight pgvector if you want to stay inside an existing Postgres footprint, or a dedicated vector database (Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus) for larger-scale ANN search with metadata filtering. Hybrid search typically pairs the vector store with OpenSearch/Elasticsearch for BM25, or uses a store with native hybrid support. Stage 5 Reranking & context assembly Re-scoring initial retrieval results with a more precise (and more expensive) model before assembling the final context window. AWS Bedrock's Rerank API offers Amazon Rerank 1.0 and Cohere Rerank 3.5 as managed models, and Bedrock Knowledge Bases can apply reranking inside the retrieval call. Outside Knowledge Bases it's an explicit extra step in your retrieval code, the same pattern as self-hosting one. Azure AI Search's semantic ranker applies a Microsoft-trained cross-encoder as an L2 re-ranking pass over the initial hybrid results, exposed as a query-type option, no separate deployment required. GCP Vertex AI Search includes a ranking API as part of its managed search stack, applying a similar L2 re-ranking pass over initial results. OCI Cohere Rerank models built into the Generative AI service itself, called directly through the RerankText API, available both on-demand and through dedicated clusters. Check the service's current model list for which Rerank version is offered in your region. Self-hosted / open-weight An open cross-encoder reranker (BGE-reranker, Jina Reranker) served alongside the embedding model, typically on the same TEI/Infinity serving stack, called as an explicit extra step in your retrieval code. Stage 6 Generation / model serving Running the language model itself against the assembled, grounded context. AWS Bedrock model deployment: unified Converse API across Claude, Titan, Llama, and Mistral. Provisioned Throughput for predictable latency at volume, on-demand for variable load, plus a batch tier at a discount for non-interactive workloads. Azure Microsoft Foundry model deployment: Azure OpenAI models or the Foundry Model Catalog's open-weight options, on managed online endpoints. Provisioned Throughput Units (PTU) for predictable latency and cost at volume, or pay-as-you-go token billing for variable load. GCP Vertex AI model deployment: Gemini-first, with third-party and open-weight models available through Model Garden. Provisioned throughput and pay-as-you-go both available, same shape as the other two. OCI OCI Generative AI model deployment, native and third-party models, callable through the same managed endpoint pattern as the rest of the OCI Generative AI service. Self-hosted / open-weight vLLM or TGI serving an open-weight model (Llama, Qwen, Mistral, DeepSeek-class) on owned or leased GPUs, with continuous batching and paged KV-cache for throughput. Ollama for smaller-scale or development use; llama.cpp for CPU/edge deployment. Stage 7 Agent tool layer (MCP) Giving the model controlled access to enterprise systems and external data through defined tools. AWS Bedrock Agents, AgentCore, and Flows for managed tool-use orchestration, or a self-built MCP server fronting enterprise systems, called from a Bedrock-hosted agent. Azure Foundry Agent Service with built-in tool calling, or a self-built MCP server fronting enterprise systems, called from a Foundry-hosted agent. GCP Vertex AI Agent Builder for managed tool orchestration, or a self-built MCP server called from a Vertex AI-hosted agent. OCI OCI Generative AI Agents, with tool and API orchestration built into the same service that handles RAG. Self-hosted / open-weight Identical MCP server code across every environment, since MCP is a protocol rather than a cloud service. The dependency that bites is whether your serving stack (vLLM, TGI) supports the model's native tool-calling chat template, so verify per model rather than assuming. The protocol layer is the same everywhere. What changes across all five environments is only whether the serving stack in question has tool-calling support wired up for the specific model you chose. Stage 8 Human-in-the-loop Routing outputs by risk and reversibility to a review queue, notification layer, and durable orchestration that can pause and resume a process for hours or days. AWS DynamoDB for the review queue/state table, SNS or SQS plus EventBridge for notification and escalation timers, Step Functions for the durable orchestration that survives a pause spanning hours or days. Azure Cosmos DB or Azure SQL for the review queue/state table, Teams webhook plus Power Automate for notification and escalation timers, Azure Durable Functions for the durable orchestration that survives a pause spanning hours or days. GCP Firestore for the review queue/state table, Pub/Sub for notification, Cloud Workflows for the durable orchestration spanning the pause. OCI Autonomous Database for the review queue/state table, Notifications service for alerts, OCI Functions chained via Events for the durable orchestration. Self-hosted / open-weight Postgres for the queue, Slack webhook for notification, Temporal (self-hostable) for durable orchestration. Functionally the same architecture as every column above, different concrete products. This entire stage sits above the model, at the application layer. The tiering logic (route by reversibility and blast radius, with model confidence as a secondary input) and the queue-overload failure mode are identical across all five environments. The full HITL design detail sits outside this page. Stage 9 · cross-cutting Security & threat model Prompt injection, tool-call authorization, and the model supply chain. Data doesn't pass through this once; it applies to every stage above. AWS Bedrock Guardrails runs as a pre-processing gate for content filtering and PII redaction on both input and retrieved content. Tool calls run under IAM roles scoped per agent; Bedrock endpoints sit behind VPC endpoints with public access disabled. Azure AI Content Safety's prompt shields run as a pre-processing gate on both user input and any retrieved or tool-returned content before it reaches the model, since an injected instruction can arrive through a poisoned document just as easily as through the chat box. Tool calls run under managed identities with least-privilege RBAC scoped per agent through Entra ID. Foundry deployments sit behind private endpoints and VNet integration; AI Search restricted to private link with public network access disabled. GCP Two layers: Gemini's built-in Safety Settings for per-request content filtering (hate speech, harassment, sexually explicit, dangerous content, configurable thresholds), plus Model Armor as a separate dedicated service for prompt injection and jailbreak detection, sensitive data protection, and malware scanning. IAM and VPC Service Controls provide the network and identity isolation layer underneath both. OCI OCI Guardrails, a named, documented feature with three protections: content moderation (hate speech, harassment, violence, explicit material), prompt injection defense (binary risk scoring on embedded ma

title: AI and the Engineering Operating Model
description: What AI-assisted coding is doing to how engineering work gets done: skill development, code review, and how to measure productivity when the tool itself is part of the output. Distinct from deciding which AI initiatives to build.
body: Reference What changes, and what doesn't AI-assisted coding shifts specific parts of the job and leaves others alone. Treating it as a uniform speedup misreads what's happening. Changes Doesn't change Speed of first-draft code and boilerplate generation The cost of a wrong architectural decision What code review has to look for Who's accountable for what ships How junior engineers first encounter patterns The need for architectural judgment on anything non-routine Where the bottleneck in the delivery pipeline sits The value of debugging intuition built through direct repetition 1 AI productivity does not automatically equal more story points The most common measurement mistake, and the one most likely to produce a plan that breaks on contact with reality. What happens AI-assisted coding speeds up the mechanical parts, boilerplate, first drafts, syntax, which moves the bottleneck to review, architectural judgment, and testing. Those were never the slow part for a senior engineer, and they were close to the entire job for a junior one. The naive read Treating a rise in lines of code or pull request volume as productivity, then setting headcount or delivery expectations against that number. The plan breaks the moment the team hits the bottleneck AI never touched: review capacity and architectural decision-making. 2 Code review changes shape Reviewing AI-generated code is a different skill than reviewing human-written code, and most engineers were never trained on the difference. What's different Reviewing AI-generated code means checking for plausible-but-wrong patterns, code that looks idiomatic and compiles cleanly but embeds a subtly incorrect assumption, more than checking for the kind of mistake a human engineer is likely to make. That's a distinct reviewing skill. The risk Review fatigue from higher volume, combined with AI-generated code's tendency to look confident and clean, produces a false sense of safety. Reviewers approve faster because the code reads well, without having verified it any more rigorously. 3 What happens to junior engineer development The concern most tempting to dismiss, because it doesn't show up as a problem until much later. The concern A junior engineer who leans on AI for the mechanical work skips the repetition that used to build pattern recognition and debugging intuition the slow way. That intuition doesn't obviously appear missing until a novel problem requires it and it isn't there. What to do about it Deliberately assign some work without AI assistance specifically for skill-building, framed as a training decision rather than a productivity one, the same way a pilot still trains on manual flight even though autopilot handles most of the flying. 4 Measuring productivity when the tool is part of the output The measurement question every other section on this page eventually points back to. What doesn't work Raw output volume: lines of code, pull requests merged, AI suggestions accepted. All of these can rise while the team ships less correct, maintained value, since none of them measure whether the output was right. What holds up The outcome measures already covered on Engineering Metrics, cycle time, change failure rate, and ultimately business outcomes, tracked specifically before and after AI tooling adoption, rather than assuming adoption itself is automatically the win. 5 What the evidence says, as of September 2026 The research is mixed in ways that matter. Gains are real on bounded tasks and harder to find on complex, familiar codebases, and quality and security do not improve on their own. Source Finding GitHub controlled experiment (Peng and colleagues, 2023) Developers finished a bounded, well-specified task about 55 percent faster with an AI assistant [1] DORA, 2024 Higher AI adoption was associated with slightly lower delivery throughput and noticeably lower delivery stability [2] DORA, 2025 State of AI-assisted Software Development About 90 percent of respondents use AI and over 80 percent report productivity gains [3] ; AI adoption was now associated with higher throughput, but instability persisted, and only about a quarter reported high trust in AI output. The report's central finding is that AI amplifies a team's existing strengths and weaknesses METR randomized trial (July 2025) Experienced open-source maintainers working in their own large repositories took about 19 percent longer with AI tools, while believing they were faster [4] METR update (February 2026) A follow-up could not produce a reliable new estimate because developers increasingly declined to work without AI; the authors think gains have likely grown since early 2025 but could not measure how much [5] Veracode GenAI Code Security Report (2025) About 45 percent of AI-generated code samples failed security tests, with no material improvement from newer models; syntax correctness rose while security did not [6] Sources Peng and colleagues, The Impact of AI on Developer Productivity, 2023 DORA, 2024 Accelerate State of DevOps Report DORA, 2025 State of AI-assisted Software Development METR, early-2025 AI and experienced open-source developer productivity, July 2025 METR, changes to the developer productivity experiment design, February 2026 Veracode, 2025 GenAI Code Security Report 6 The DORA AI Capabilities Model DORA's 2025 research identified seven capabilities that determine whether AI helps or hurts. [3] Most are not about AI at all, which is the point. Capability What to do about it A clear, communicated AI stance Publish which tools are approved, what data may be used, and what is expected of engineers A healthy data ecosystem Quality, accessible internal data, per Data Strategy AI-accessible internal data Connect assistants to internal documentation, code, and decision records, with access controls Strong version control practices Frequent commits, small reviewable changes, and the ability to roll back quickly Working in small batches Keep AI-generated changes small enough to review properly A user-centric focus Anchor work on user outcomes so faster output goes to the right things A quality internal platform Golden paths, fast pipelines, and guardrails, per Platform Engineering Sources DORA, 2025 State of AI-assisted Software Development 7 An AI coding policy engineers will actually follow Short, specific, and enforced by tooling where possible. Anything that relies only on memory will not survive the first deadline. Topic Policy Tools and data Only approved tools under enterprise terms that exclude training on your code; no customer data, secrets, or regulated data in prompts to unapproved tools Review AI-assisted changes meet the same review bar as any other; very large generated diffs are split before review Security Secret scanning, dependency scanning, and static analysis run on every change, because roughly half of generated code fails security checks Licensing Use tools with duplicate-code filtering and IP indemnity; flag generated code that reproduces recognizable open-source code Agents Coding agents run with least privilege in sandboxed environments, never hold production credentials, and need human approval to merge or deploy Measurement Track change failure rate, rework rate, and review time before and after adoption, per Engineering Metrics 8 A worked example: the first six months A 40-engineer product organization adopts AI coding assistants. Figures are illustrative but follow the pattern DORA describes. Point What the numbers showed What the team did Baseline Change failure rate 12 percent; median review wait 6 hours Recorded the baseline before rollout, the step most teams skip Month 3 Pull requests up 35 percent; review wait up to 9 hours; change failure rate 16 percent Capped change size, made security scanning blocking, added a review rotation Month 6 Change failure rate 11 percent; lead time down about 20 percent from baseline Kept the controls; moved freed capacity to the backlog of tests nobody had time to write Checklist Signs AI adoption is being measured or managed naively Patterns that show up when AI tooling gets adopted enthusiastically but without adjusting how the organization measures or trains around it. Productivity claims rest on lines of code, PR volume, or AI suggestion acceptance rate rather than outcome measures Code review practice hasn't been adjusted for the specific failure modes of AI-generated code No deliberate mechanism exists for junior engineers to build skills without AI assistance Change failure rate or defect rate hasn't been tracked before and after AI tooling adoption Headcount or timeline plans assume a productivity multiplier that was asserted rather than measured There is no written AI coding policy, or it exists but nothing in the pipeline enforces it Coding agents run with credentials that can reach production

title: AI FinOps Map
description: Cost modeling stage by stage across AWS, Azure, GCP, OCI, and self-hosted, the same environments the Architecture Map covers in depth.
body: AWS Azure GCP OCI Self-hosted 1 Pricing model: tokens vs amortized hardware The fundamental cost shape differs before any workload-specific decisions get made. AWS Bedrock is billed per token, input and output priced separately, output typically several times more expensive than input, with per-model rates ranging from a few cents per million input tokens for the smallest models to several dollars for frontier models, a spread of more than a hundredfold. [2] Cost scales directly and immediately with usage, unpredictable at the account level until volume stabilizes. Azure Pay-as-you-go is billed per token, input and output priced separately, output typically several times more expensive than input. Cost scales directly and immediately with usage, visible per-call, but unpredictable at the account level until volume stabilizes. GCP Vertex AI bills current Gemini models per token, input and output metered separately; older model generations were metered per character, so check which meter applies to the model you pick. An easy-to-miss cost multiplier: Gemini's internal reasoning (thinking) tokens are billed as output, and on reasoning-heavy requests they can inflate cost several times beyond what the visible response length suggests. OCI On-demand OCI Generative AI is billed per transaction (character-based) for on-demand inference, separate from the per-unit-hour rate that applies once you move to a dedicated cluster. Consumption draws against an existing Universal Credits commitment rather than a standalone bill. Self-hosted / open-weight Cost is amortized GPU time (purchase or lease depreciation, power, cooling, ops staff), largely fixed regardless of query volume until you hit a capacity ceiling and need to add hardware. Marginal cost per additional query approaches zero until that ceiling, then jumps in a large step when you provision another node. The break-even point is a number you can calculate, so calculate it: (fixed self-hosted cost per month) divided by (per-query managed cost) gives the query volume where self-hosting starts winning. Below that volume, pay-as-you-go almost always wins on total cost. Sources AWS, Amazon Bedrock pricing Interactive Find your own break-even point The break-even formula above, projected forward. Enter the fixed monthly cost of self-hosting, the managed price per query, today's volume, and how fast volume grows. The tool finds the break-even volume, the month self-hosting starts to win, and the cumulative cost of each option over 24 months, with a price sensitivity check. Runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere. Fixed self-hosted cost per month ($) Managed cost per query ($) Actual or expected queries per month Calculate 2 Reserved capacity vs GPU procurement Committing ahead of time to guarantee throughput and control cost variance. AWS Provisioned Throughput reserves dedicated capacity in model units, billed hourly whether used or not, with no-commitment, 1-month, and 6-month terms. [2] Only pays off above sustained utilization; buying a 6-month commitment before traffic is stable is the single fastest way to overspend here. Some custom and fine-tuned models still require Provisioned Throughput rather than on-demand billing; check the deployment options for the specific model before assuming pay-as-you-go is available. Azure Provisioned Throughput Units (PTU) reserve dedicated capacity at a flat monthly rate, converting variable token cost into a predictable fixed cost, but only pays off above a specific utilization threshold; idle PTU capacity is money spent on nothing. GCP Provisioned throughput, priced per PTU per hour rather than per token, with Azure Reservations for 1-month or 1-year terms at a discount that varies by model family and term. Hourly billing suits short or variable use; for sustained production volume a reservation is usually cheaper. Compare against the pay-as-you-go bill at your actual volume before reserving. [3] OCI Dedicated AI clusters bill per unit-hour, but the distinctive gotcha here is the minimum commitment: hosting clusters require at least 744 unit-hours, roughly a full month, even if actual usage is far lower. That minimum doesn't exist on the other three clouds' reserved-capacity tiers. Self-hosted / open-weight Owning or leasing GPUs is the hardware equivalent of a reserved-capacity commitment: a large fixed cost that only pays off at sustained utilization. Renting from a GPU cloud (on-demand) is the hardware equivalent of pay-as-you-go, more expensive per hour but no idle-capacity risk. Sources AWS, Amazon Bedrock pricing Microsoft Learn, provisioned throughput billing and cost management 3 Chargeback & unit economics Making AI spend attributable to the team or product that generated it instead of leaving it as one opaque line item. AWS Cost Explorer's tagging and cost allocation tags attribute Bedrock spend to a team, product, or environment tag, feeding a per-team chargeback model the same way any other AWS resource would. Azure Cost Management's tagging and scope hierarchy lets you attribute Foundry deployment spend to a subscription, resource group, or tag, feeding a per-team or per-product chargeback model the same way any other Azure resource would. GCP Cloud Billing labels plus BigQuery billing export let you attribute Vertex AI spend down to the label or project level, queryable alongside the rest of the GCP bill rather than as an isolated line item. OCI Compartment structure plus tag-based attribution in OCI Cost Analysis, with FOCUS-format billing exports increasingly the default pipeline for feeding a chargeback model. Cost Analysis falls back to a tagless view when tag coverage is incomplete. Self-hosted / open-weight No managed billing hierarchy to lean on; attribution requires your own request-tagging at the application layer (which team or product initiated the call) correlated against GPU-hour cost allocated proportionally to usage. This is meaningfully more engineering work to build. The metric that matters across every environment is cost per unit of business value: cost per resolved support ticket, cost per underwriting decision. Cost per token and cost per GPU-hour are inputs to that number and poor substitutes for it. Build the unit economics dashboard around the business metric first and let infrastructure cost roll up into it. 4 Cost observability & budget alerting Catching a cost anomaly (a runaway agent loop, a misconfigured retry, a prompt that ballooned in size) before the monthly bill does. AWS AWS Budgets with configurable thresholds and Cost Anomaly Detection using machine learning to flag unusual spend patterns automatically, without a manually defined rule for every scenario. Azure Cost Management budgets with action-group-triggered alerts at defined thresholds; Monitor can alert on token consumption rate directly if instrumented, catching an anomaly within the billing period rather than after it closes. GCP Budgets & Alerts plus Cost Anomaly Detection at the billing-account level; the reasoning-token cost multiplier from Stage 1 is exactly the kind of anomaly this catches before it compounds across a month of traffic. OCI OCI Cost Analysis with budget-based alerts, increasingly paired with FOCUS-format billing exports for teams that have moved off the native dashboard onto a broader FinOps pipeline. Self-hosted / open-weight No native billing-anomaly alerting since there's no per-token bill to watch. The equivalent signal is GPU utilization and request-rate anomalies via Prometheus alerting. An unusual spike in request volume or output length is the leading indicator you have. 5 Model selection as a cost lever The single highest-leverage FinOps decision, made once per use case, before any of the above matters. AWS Bedrock's catalog spans a more than hundredfold price range across model tiers; [2] routing simple classification or extraction tasks to a cheaper model (Nova Micro or Haiku-class) and reserving the frontier model for complex reasoning is often a larger lever than any reservation optimization. Azure Foundry's model catalog spans a wide price-performance range; routing simple classification or extraction tasks to a smaller, cheaper model and reserving the frontier model for complex reasoning is often a larger cost lever than any PTU or reservation optimization. GCP Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite at $0.10 input and $0.40 output per million tokens on Vertex AI, against $1.25 input for Gemini 2.5 Pro; [4] the same routing principle applies, with the added wrinkle that reasoning tokens make the effective cost gap between tiers larger than the sticker price alone suggests. OCI OCI's catalog spans Oracle-curated and partner models (Cohere, Llama, xAI Grok) at meaningfully different price points; the same routing principle applies, and dedicated-cluster pricing tiers differ enough by model family that the choice compounds with the reserved-capacity decision from Stage 2. Self-hosted / open-weight Same principle, and arguably higher stakes: a smaller open-weight model (7B to 14B class) served efficiently can handle a large share of production traffic at a fraction of the GPU footprint a frontier-class open-weight model requires, if the task doesn't need frontier reasoning. This is the FinOps decision most teams skip because it requires an evaluation harness to prove the cheaper model is good enough, and building that harness feels like overhead. It almost always pays for itself faster than infrastructure optimization does. Sources AWS, Amazon Bedrock pricing Google Cloud, Vertex AI generative AI pricing 6 Waste: idle reservations and orphaned capacity The unglamorous but highest-frequency cost leak across every environment. AWS Provisioned Throughput reserved for peak load sitting idle most of the day; forgotten Knowledge Bases vector storage (OpenSearch Serverless bills a minimum of about $350 a month for a standard collection even at zero query traffic; dev-test collections cost about half that, and newer collection types scale to zero when idle) [5] left running after a project ends. Both invisible unless someone is specifically auditing deployed resources against active use cases. Azure PTU reservations sized for peak load sitting idle most of the day; forgotten dev/test Foundry deployments left running after the project using them ended. Both invisible unless someone is specifically auditing deployed resources against actual active use cases. GCP Online prediction endpoints, Vector Search nodes, and Workbench instances all bill per hour regardless of traffic; a forgotten deployed endpoint is one of the most common GCP AI cost surprises, silently running up thousands a month for zero real usage. OCI Idle dedicated AI clusters are described directly in Oracle's own licensing guidance as the top cost trap: a reserved cluster bills around the clock, and under-utilized, can cost many times what on-demand inference would for the same volume, compounded by the 744-hour minimum commitment from Stage 2. Self-hosted / open-weight GPU nodes provisioned for a launch that never reached expected volume, or a dev cluster left running after the project wound down. Same failure mode, higher absolute cost per incident since GPU hardware commitments are larger and stickier than a cloud service you can just delete. Run a quarterly audit matching every deployed model endpoint or reserved capacity allocation, on any provider, against an active, named use case. Anything without one gets decommissioned. Flagging it and moving on is how the next audit finds the same list. Sources AWS, Amazon OpenSearch Service pricing 7 Prompt caching A cost lever specific to how LLMs are billed, with no equivalent in traditional cloud FinOps. AWS Prompt caching on Bedrock caches a stable prefix (system prompt, long reference document) and bills cache reads at 10 percent of the standard input rate for Anthropic models, up to 90 percent savings on context-heavy applications. [2] Same architectural discipline as every provider here: stable content first, dynamic content last, or the cache never hits. Azure Prompts of 1,024 tokens or more are cached automatically on supported models, with no opt-in, and cached input tokens are billed at a discount on Standard deployments (up to 100 percent on provisioned deployments). The exact rate depends on the model, so check the pricing page. [6] The architectural work is keeping the cacheable part of the prompt byte-identical and in the same position on every request; dynamic content has to move to the end, after the cacheable prefix, or the cache never hits. GCP Context caching bills cached input at a fraction of the normal rate (75 percent off for Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite at this review) plus a storage charge per million tokens per hour the cache is held. The discount differs by model, so check the pricing page for the model you use. [4] OCI As of this review, OCI does not document a general-purpose prompt caching discount comparable

title: AI Governance Map
description: Four layers, from data foundation to responsible AI oversight, each with concrete controls mapped to what breaks without them and which regulatory frameworks.
body: Layer 1 · data foundation Data foundation Before anything else, know what the model uses. If you cannot answer where a piece of training or retrieval data came from, nothing above this layer holds up. Control Source registry covering every system feeding the AI pipeline Data dictionary defining what each field means and where it originated Lineage and provenance tracking from source document to retrieved chunk Clear data ownership assigned per source system Driver & failure mode NIST AI RMF's Map function starts here: you cannot assess risk in a system whose inputs you cannot trace. Without this layer, an incident investigation cannot answer "where did this bad output come from," which is usually the first question an investigation asks. Layer 2 · governance layer Governance layer Once the data foundation is solid, decide who decides what. Definition locks, retrieval boundaries, input validation, and a named data steward give the system clear lines of accountability. Control Definition locks: agreed, versioned definitions for terms the system reasons about, so they stop drifting between teams Retrieval boundaries: which sources an agent or index is allowed to draw from for a given use case Input validation on both user prompts and any document entering the ingestion pipeline A named data steward with the authority to change what's retrievable Driver & failure mode Without a data steward, retrieval boundaries erode silently as new sources get connected for convenience, and the system starts answering from data nobody approved for that use case. This is the layer that turns "we have a RAG pipeline" into "we have a RAG pipeline someone is accountable for." Layer 3 · trusted outputs Trusted outputs With governance in place, you can start defending your answers. Confidence thresholds, output guardrails, and bias checks turn "the AI said so" into something you can stand behind to a customer, auditor, or regulator. Control Confidence thresholds tied to the human-in-the-loop tiering model (see the Architecture Map ) Output guardrails: schema validation, citation requirements, forbidden-content checks before a response ships Bias and fairness checks on outputs for any use case touching people (hiring, credit, care recommendations) Explainability sufficient to answer "why did it say that" after the fact, as well as at design time Driver & failure mode A confidence score without a documented threshold policy is a number nobody acts on consistently, and no auditor will accept it as a control. This layer is what regulators and auditors ask to see evidence of, so it has to produce artifacts (logs, rubric scores) rather than exist only as a design intention. Layer 4 · responsible AI Responsible AI & high-risk oversight The outer layer: autonomous agents, high-risk decisions, and regulated use cases. This only works because everything underneath it is already solid. Control Formal classification of which use cases count as high-risk under applicable frameworks Documented incident response plan specific to AI failures, separate from the generic IT incident process Human oversight for high-risk decisions, implemented as the Tier 2 gate described on the Architecture Map and enforced in code rather than by policy statement alone Hallucination and groundedness checks running continuously in production, beyond the initial launch evaluation Driver & failure mode Credit scoring, employment screening, and medical decisioning fall within the EU AI Act's Annex III high-risk use cases when the specific system matches the criteria listed there; operating in one of those domains does not by itself make a system high-risk. Article 14 requires human oversight for systems that do qualify. [1] The high-risk obligations were deferred by the Digital Omnibus on AI, adopted in June 2026 and in force from 27 July 2026: Annex III stand-alone systems, including employment and credit uses, now apply from 2 December 2027, and AI embedded in Annex I regulated products from 2 August 2028. Article 50 transparency duties still apply from 2 August 2026. The final text set fixed dates and dropped the Commission's earlier proposal to tie them to the readiness of harmonised standards, so confirm the current date for your specific use case against the published regulation. Sources Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act) Cross-cutting Model risk management Treating the model itself, and not only its outputs, as something with a lifecycle that needs governing. Control A model inventory listing every deployed model, its version, what it's used for, and who owns the decision to keep using it. Pre-deployment evaluation against a defined rubric before a new model version replaces an old one. Ongoing drift monitoring in production, tied to the observability stage on the Architecture Map , in place of a one-time evaluation at launch. Driver & failure mode The single most common gap: a team can name the model they deployed in January but not confirm what's running in production today after three silent provider-side updates. If you cannot answer "which exact model version produced this output," you cannot investigate an incident or defend a decision. Reference The standards and credentials landscape Four different things people mean when they say "AI governance," easy to conflate and different in what they certify, who holds them, and what they cost. Name What it is Who or what it applies to AIGP (IAPP) An individual professional credential, the AI-governance equivalent of IAPP's CIPP privacy certifications. 100-question exam across four domains: AI governance foundations, applicable laws and standards, governing AI development, governing AI deployment and use. A person. Validates that someone can run an AI governance program; doesn't certify the organization or any specific system. ISO/IEC 42001 A certifiable AI management system standard, the AI equivalent of ISO 27001 for information security. Third-party audited (Stage 1 and Stage 2), valid three years with annual surveillance audits, 38 Annex A controls selected and justified against your own risk assessment rather than applied as a fixed checklist. An organization's AI management system. Already held by AWS, Anthropic, and Microsoft. Doesn't by itself satisfy EU AI Act obligations, but the risk assessment and governance structure it requires feeds directly into the technical documentation the Act does require. NIST AI RMF A voluntary US framework (Govern, Map, Measure, Manage). It is guidance to structure a program against; nobody audits you to it. An organization's practice, self-assessed. Already referenced throughout this page's layer structure. ISO/IEC 23894 Risk management guidance specific to AI, meant to be used alongside ISO 31000's general risk management approach. An organization's risk process. Guidance rather than a certifiable standard on its own. OECD AI Principles High-level international principles (inclusive growth, human-centered values, transparency, robustness, accountability), adopted by dozens of governments as policy language. National policy and regulation that draws on these principles; not something an organization implements or gets certified against directly. The practical distinction that matters most: AIGP tells you something about a person you might hire or promote into an AI governance role. ISO 42001 tells a customer or regulator something about your organization, backed by an independent audit. Neither substitutes for the other, and neither substitutes for the technical controls described in the four layers above; a certified management system with no enforced technical controls underneath it is a common failure pattern. Judgment call Is ISO 42001 certification worth pursuing A decision with a cost attached. Don't default into it because the standard exists. Worth it Enterprise customers or regulators are asking for independent evidence of AI governance maturity and a policy document no longer satisfies them. Selling into procurement processes where a competitor's ISO 42001 badge is becoming a checkbox. The organization already holds ISO 27001, since the incremental cost and timeline drop substantially when the management-system muscle already exists. Not worth it yet A small AI footprint with a handful of internal use cases and no customer demanding third-party evidence. The four layers above aren't solidly in place yet. Certifying a management system before the underlying technical controls exist produces a certificate that doesn't reflect reality, and an auditor will eventually find that gap. NIST AI RMF, applied seriously and evidenced internally, covers most of the same ground without the $20,000 to $60,000 audit cost and multi-year commitment. Reference Regulatory framework mapping Which control layer above satisfies which framework's requirement. Not legal advice; confirm applicability with counsel for your specific use case and jurisdiction. Framework What it requires Which layer covers it HIPAA Minimum necessary access, immutable audit trail for PHI access Layer 2 (retrieval boundaries) plus the PHI/PII stage on the Architecture Map EU AI Act, Article 14 Human oversight for high-risk AI systems Layer 4, enforced technically via the HITL tiering model NIST AI RMF Govern, Map, Measure, Manage functions across the AI lifecycle All four layers plus model risk management, roughly one NIST function per layer ISO/IEC 42001 An auditable AI management system: policy, risk assessment, selected Annex A controls, continuous improvement All four layers plus the accountability and model risk management sections provide the evidence an auditor asks for SOC 2 (if applicable to the AI system) Access controls, change management, monitoring evidence Layer 2 for access, model risk management for change control, Layer 3 for monitoring evidence Accountability Accountability & audit trail Who signs off on an AI system going live, and what gets logged so that decision can be reconstructed later. Control A named accountable owner per AI use case. A committee with no single decision-maker does not count. Decision logging: every promotion of a new model or index version recorded with who approved it and what evaluation evidence supported the approval. Driver & failure mode Diffuse accountability is a recurring AI governance failure pattern behind headline incidents. It's rarely that no one thought about the risk; it's that no single person owned the decision to accept it. Incident response AI-specific incident response Different from a general IT incident: a hallucinated answer causing harm, a bias incident, or a model behaving unexpectedly needs its own triage path. Control A defined severity classification specific to AI failures (harmful hallucination, biased output, data leakage through a response, agent taking an unauthorized action). A rollback path that can revert to a prior model or index version quickly, which depends directly on the versioning discipline described in model risk management above. Driver & failure mode A general incident response process (see Incident Response ) usually isn't built to ask "was this the model's fault, the retrieval's fault, or the underlying data's fault," and that triage question determines the fix. Build this as an extension of the general process rather than a replacement for it.

title: AI Portfolio Management
description: Which AI initiatives should get built, scored and classified with the same discipline applied to the rest of the application estate.
body: Reference Scoring dimensions and classification Nine dimensions feed the score; four classifications follow from it. The value is in forcing the same questions to be asked of every initiative, so the loudest pitch can't skip the screen. Precision in the score itself matters less. Dimension What it asks Business value What outcome does this move, and how much Feasibility Can this be built with current capability and technology Data readiness Does the required data exist, at the needed quality, with clear rights to use it Risk Regulatory, reputational, and model-behavior risk if this goes wrong Adoption likelihood Will the people this is built for use it Time to value How long until the outcome in row one is realized, which is a later date than launch Operating cost The ongoing cost to run this, on top of the cost to build it Differentiation Does this create an advantage competitors can't quickly copy Reversibility How expensive is it to unwind this if it doesn't work out Classification Meaning Scale Proven value and feasibility; fund it fully and remove obstacles Incubate Promising but unproven on one or more dimensions; fund a bounded pilot with a defined checkpoint Watch Not ready to fund, but conditions could change; revisit on a set schedule rather than forgetting about it Kill Fails on a gating dimension or has passed its own kill criteria; stop funding it explicitly and say so 1 Feasibility and data readiness gate the score before anything else contributes to it Averaging all nine dimensions into one number lets a high-value, technically infeasible idea pass through if it scores generously elsewhere. The right sequence Screen on feasibility and data readiness first. If the data doesn't exist at usable quality, or the model risk is unacceptable regardless of upside, the initiative doesn't reach a business-value conversation at all. Gating dimensions eliminate; they don't get averaged away. What a single blended score hides A compelling business case with a fatal data gap can still produce a respectable average score if the other eight dimensions are strong, which is exactly how organizations end up funding pilots that were never going to work, discovered only after real money and credibility were spent. 2 Reversibility deserves its own weight Not all AI bets carry the same downside if they fail, and the classification should reflect that. Why it matters A pilot built on a vendor API is cheap to unwind. A model embedded into a core workflow customers now depend on is expensive to unwind. Two initiatives with identical business-value scores warrant different treatment if one is trivially reversible and the other isn't. Where this gets missed Treating an irreversible bet with the same enthusiasm as a reversible pilot because both scored well on value, without ever separately asking what it costs to walk away if the initial results don't hold up at scale. 3 Kill criteria set before the bet starts AI initiatives are unusually prone to surviving on prestige rather than results, which makes advance kill criteria more important here than almost anywhere else in the portfolio. Practice Define, before funding, the specific result that would trigger a move to Watch or Kill, a metric, a threshold, a date. Write it down where it can't be quietly renegotiated once the team is emotionally invested in the outcome. Common failure mode An initiative that's been "six months from proving itself" for over a year, kept alive because killing an AI project carries a different kind of organizational embarrassment than killing an ordinary feature, independent of what the results show. Interactive Score an initiative Score every initiative competing for AI investment, one row each, on the nine dimensions. Feasibility and data readiness are hard gates: a score below 3 on either kills the initiative regardless of everything else. The tool classifies each one as Scale, Incubate, Watch, or Kill, says why, and ranks the portfolio. Runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere. Classify it 4 Stage gates with evidence, not enthusiasm Each gate asks for evidence that did not exist at the previous one. Durations are typical, not rules. Gate Evidence required to pass Typical kill signal 1. Feasibility spike, 2 to 6 weeks An offline evaluation on real, representative data with a written rubric; confirmed rights to use the data; a rough cost per task Quality cannot beat the current manual baseline on the evaluation set 2. Pilot, 8 to 12 weeks Real users on real work; measured outcome against a baseline; cost per successful task including human review; a named business owner Users route around it, or the review burden eats the time saved 3. Scale Service levels, monitoring for quality drift, a human escalation path, incident runbook, unit economics inside target Cost per task grows with volume instead of falling 4. Operate and revisit Quarterly re-scoring against the same nine dimensions; model and vendor changes re-evaluated A cheaper or better option makes the build redundant 5 Rules and standards that change the score The Risk dimension is where most scoring goes wrong, because the rules moved quickly. Status as of September 2026. Source What applies Effect on the score EU AI Act General-purpose AI obligations have applied since August 2, 2025. The AI Omnibus, in force since July 27, 2026, moved obligations for high-risk systems in Annex III, such as hiring and credit, to December 2, 2027, and for AI in regulated products to August 2, 2028 [1] [2] Deferred, not removed; a high-risk use case still needs the conformity work planned into its cost Colorado SB 26-189 Replaced the 2024 Colorado AI Act; from January 1, 2027 it requires notice, adverse-decision explanations, appeal, and human review for automated decisions in consequential areas including employment [3] Raises operating cost for AI in hiring, lending, housing, insurance, and similar decisions NYC Local Law 144 Independent bias audits and candidate notice for automated employment decision tools used in New York City Adds an annual audit cost to any hiring tool in scope NIST AI Risk Management Framework and its Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1, 2024) [4] A voluntary structure for mapping, measuring, and managing AI risk A ready-made checklist for the Risk dimension ISO/IEC 42001:2023 A certifiable AI management system standard [5] Increasingly asked for by enterprise buyers of AI products Healthcare: FDA guidance on predetermined change control plans for AI-enabled device software (final, December 2024) [6] and ONC's HTI-1 rule on decision support transparency Rules for how AI in clinical and medical-device settings may change after clearance and what must be disclosed to users Clinical-facing initiatives need regulatory review as a gate, not a later step Sources European Commission, AI Omnibus enters into force, July 2026 Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act) Seyfarth Shaw, Colorado enacts AI replacement law (SB 26-189), May 2026 NIST AI 600-1, Generative AI Profile, July 2024 ISO/IEC 42001:2023, AI management system FDA, predetermined change control plan guidance for AI-enabled device software 6 Measure value, not usage The most common way AI portfolios lie to themselves is by reporting activity as if it were outcome. What to measure Outcome per task against the pre-AI baseline, such as minutes per claim, first-contact resolution, or error rate, and the fully loaded cost per successful task, including human review, retries, and model spend. Report both monthly for anything past gate 2. What misleads Seats licensed, prompts sent, or share of employees who tried the tool. All of them rise while the outcome stays flat, and they are what most dashboards show by default. Checklist Signs AI portfolio governance isn't real Patterns that show up when AI initiatives are being funded by momentum rather than by the same discipline applied elsewhere in the technology portfolio. No AI initiative has ever been formally moved to Kill despite some producing no measurable result Feasibility and data readiness were never checked before funding, only the business case The same initiative has been described as close to proving itself for well over a year No one can name what's currently in Watch status or when it's due for reassessment AI investment decisions bypass the standard capital allocation process applied to everything else Initiatives pass from pilot to scale without a measured outcome against a pre-AI baseline The Risk score was set before checking which rules apply to the use case, including the revised EU AI Act dates and US state laws

title: Application Portfolio Management
description: How to look at an entire application estate at once, rather than one system at a time, and decide where to invest, where to hold, where to modernize, and where to retire. Built on the Gartner TIME model, layered with risk scoring and a technical debt backlog.
body: In the full toolkit What exists behind this preview A working spreadsheet instrument rather than a static framework: three linked sheets feeding one dashboard, with the same scoring logic reused for standing portfolio governance and for scoring an acquisition target's stack under diligence. 3 linked sheets · 1 live dashboard · standing portfolio and M&A variants Technical debt backlog Every known debt item scored on severity, business impact, confidence, and remediation effort, rolled up to a priority ranking. Direct remediation, annual carry, and contingent risk cost per item, each carrying its own confidence rating Status and aging tracked against a target remediation window, so stale items surface instead of hiding Rolls into portfolio-level totals: active items by severity, cost by confidence tier, overdue count Application risk register A five-factor risk score per application, independent of how valuable or well-built the system is. Cybersecurity, compliance, operational resilience, vendor, and knowledge-concentration risk scored separately, then composited Surfaces the application that's fine on paper but one departure or one vendor lapse from a bad quarter Portfolio classification (TIME) Every application placed on the Gartner TIME grid using a Business Value score and a Technical Health score. Business Value built from five factors: strategic alignment, business criticality, user reach, differentiation, regulatory necessity Technical Health built from five factors: technology currency, architecture quality, integration complexity, data architecture fit, technical debt Composite Portfolio Score, cost score, and risk score sit alongside the classification as informational overlays and are kept out of its inputs M&A-specific variant The same instrument, repointed at a target company's application estate during diligence or the first 100 days. Same scoring mechanics, framed around acquisition-specific questions: what's redundant with the acquirer's stack, what's a hidden Eliminate candidate the seller never flagged Feeds directly into the Integration Architecture Decision Tree's merge, integrate, or coexist call per system 1 The Gartner TIME model, applied Every application lands in one of four quadrants based on two independent scores: how much the business needs it, and how healthy it is technically. The four quadrants Invest : high value, high health. Fund it. Tolerate : low value, high health. Leave it alone and don't over-invest. Migrate : high value, low health. This is the modernization backlog, ranked by value at risk. Eliminate : low value, low health. These are the retirement candidates most portfolios carry more of than anyone admits. Where it breaks down Business Value gets inflated when the scorer is the system's own owner. Score it with someone outside the owning team in the room, or the whole portfolio drifts toward Invest and the model stops doing its job. Technical Health is the opposite failure: engineers score their own systems harshly relative to peers they haven't had to maintain, which skews Migrate counts up. 2 Risk as an independent axis, kept out of the TIME inputs A system can be a clean Invest on the TIME grid and still be the one that takes the company down. Risk is scored and reported separately on purpose. Why it's kept separate Folding risk into Technical Health hides exactly the applications that need visibility: strategically critical, well-funded, actively developed, and sitting on a single unreplaceable engineer or an end-of-life dependency no one has scheduled work against. Reporting risk on its own axis keeps that combination visible instead of averaging it away. What to do with a high-risk Invest These get remediation budget ahead of Migrate-quadrant systems, even though they score well overall, because the downside is asymmetric: a breach or a key-person departure on a high-value system costs more than slow modernization debt on a low-value one. 3 Turning individual scores into a portfolio signal One application's score is a data point. The value is in the aggregate: how many Eliminate candidates are still costing money, how concentrated the high-risk applications are, whether Migrate is growing or shrinking quarter over quarter. What to track over time Average Composite Portfolio Score by quadrant, count of high-risk applications, count of high-cost applications relative to their Business Value, and the ratio of Eliminate-classified applications still consuming a meaningful share of total run cost. Movement in these over two or three quarters tells you whether governance is changing behavior or only producing a nicer chart. The trap Treating this as a one-time inventory exercise. A TIME classification from eighteen months ago is closer to fiction than to data; technical health decays continuously even when business value hasn't moved, so the cadence matters as much as the scoring model itself. Worked example Five applications, classified and acted on Scores are 1 to 5. Thresholds match the downloadable workbook: high business value and high technical health both start at 3.0. Application Business value Technical health Run cost / yr TIME Decision with a date Customer portal 4.6 2.1 $1.4M Migrate Re-platform funded in next year's plan; freeze new features after Q2 Order management 4.2 3.8 $0.9M Invest Extend to the new channel; owner named Legacy reporting server 1.8 1.9 $0.3M Eliminate Retire by Q3 once two remaining reports move to the warehouse Partner API gateway 3.4 4.1 $0.2M Invest Keep; add usage metering Internal wiki 2.2 3.6 $0.05M Tolerate No investment; review at renewal Reading it The portfolio signal, not the single score The useful output is the share of run cost sitting in Migrate and Eliminate. In this example $1.7M of $2.85M, about 60 percent of run cost, sits in applications the organization has decided not to keep as they are. That figure belongs in the budget conversation with the CFO. Common mistake Treating the quadrant as the decision. A Migrate label with no funded plan and no date is a list of worries, and the same application appears on it next year. Download Debt, risk, and application portfolio simulator One workbook for the three registers this page describes: a debt backlog with severity, impact, confidence, and effort scoring plus direct, carry, and contingent cost; a risk register across cybersecurity, compliance, resilience, vendor, and knowledge concentration; and an application portfolio that scores business value, cost, and technical health, classifies each application on the TIME quadrant, and rolls up to an overview dashboard. Room for a thousand rows in each, with sample data loaded. Download simulator (.xlsx) Scoring weights are on the Lists sheet at even defaults so you can see and change them. The calibrated weights by industry and the M&A target-scoring variant are part of the full simulator, available through direct engagement. Interactive TIME quadrant classifier Score one application on the same five-factor Business Value and Technical Health axes the full instrument uses. The tool shows which factors drive the result, how far the application sits from each threshold, what single change would move it to another quadrant, and produces a short decision record. Runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere. Risk and cost scoring, and the multi-application portfolio view, are part of the full simulator. Score key Every slider below works the same way: 1 is always low (low value, or low health, or lots of debt / a highly complex, brittle integration), 5 is always high (high value, or high health, or minimal debt / a clean, well-abstracted integration). Business value Technical health Classify it Migrate High value, low health Invest High value, high health Eliminate Low value, low health Tolerate Low value, high health

title: Architecture Principles Library
description: Fifteen principles with the reasoning, the trade-off it forces, a worked example of how it shows up in a decision, and the signs it's being misapplied.
body: Framework What makes a principle worth having Most architecture principles are bad: generic ("we will be agile"), self-serving ("we prefer our favorite technology"), or untestable ("we will deliver business value"). A useful principle has four properties. Names a specific trade-off the organization has chosen Is defensible against its opposite Produces different decisions than its absence would Comes with examples of when it was applied and what was given up as a result Strategic P1 Buy before build, build only where differentiation justifies the cost Rationale: Most software the organization needs has already been built by someone else. Building it again produces ongoing maintenance costs for software that doesn't differentiate the business. Trade-off: Loss of control over roadmap and feature set. Accepted for commodity capabilities, rejected for differentiating ones. Worked example: Customer identity management is commodity, adopt a commercial platform. Fraud detection for a specific transaction pattern is differentiating, build it. Signs of misapplication: Everything gets classified as differentiating to justify building. The cure is making someone name the differentiation concretely. P2 Pay down technical debt continuously instead of in campaigns Rationale: Debt accumulates continuously.
