Campaigns to address it are always disruptive, under-scoped, and insufficient. Trade-off: Feature velocity appears lower in the short term because capacity is visibly allocated away from new work. Worked example: Delivery teams allocate 15 to 20 percent of sprint capacity to debt items, owned by engineering, informed to product. Signs of misapplication: The allocation becomes theoretical; sprint reviews consistently show 100 percent feature work. P3 Make reversible decisions quickly; reserve slow deliberation for the irreversible Rationale: Treating all decisions with the same process produces either dangerous speed on the irreversible or pointless bureaucracy on the reversible. Trade-off: Some decisions are harder to classify than the principle implies; the organization has to develop judgment about what's reversible in its context. Worked example: A logging library choice is reversible, the team picks and moves. A primary data platform can't be reversed within a reasonable timeframe, so it goes through review with ADR documentation. Signs of misapplication: Teams classify inconvenient decisions as irreversible to defer them, or reversible to avoid oversight. The test: what does it cost in time and money to change this in 18 months? P4 Prefer loose coupling between autonomous teams over tight integration Rationale: Tight coupling between systems produces tight coupling between the teams that own them, and destroys both the system's and the team's autonomy over time. Trade-off: Loose coupling costs more to build initially; interfaces take design effort that a shared database doesn't. Worked example: The Order team calls the Customer service's API rather than reading the Customer database directly. The Customer team can refactor storage without coordinating with Order. Signs of misapplication: Teams paper over coupling with facades that still expose the underlying structure. Test: if the upstream team changes its implementation, does the downstream code break? Technical P5 Failure is the default state; design for it Rationale: At any non-trivial scale, something is always failing. Systems designed on the assumption that components work experience their first failure as an outage. Trade-off: Upfront complexity; designing for failure takes thought and adds code paths. Worked example: The order placement service, when the fraud service is unavailable, falls back to rule-based scoring rather than refusing orders. Flagged orders get deferred review. Signs of misapplication: Retries and fallbacks added without thinking through cascade effects; retry storms that take down dependencies are worse than the original failure. P6 Observability is a first-class concern Rationale: Systems not designed to be observed are systems whose behavior is a mystery in production, and the cost of instrumenting retroactively is higher than instrumenting from the start. Trade-off: Instrumentation is code that must be maintained; noisy instrumentation is worse than none. Worked example: Every service produces request logs with correlation IDs, metrics on the operations that matter most, and traces covering cross-service flows, specified alongside functional requirements. Signs of misapplication: Teams log everything, measure nothing, and produce dashboards nobody reads. The cure: for each piece of instrumentation, ask what decision it supports. P7 Prefer convention over configuration; prefer explicit over implicit Rationale: Configuration without convention produces infinite surface area. Convention without explicit seams produces invisible magic. Trade-off: The organization must invest in establishing and evolving conventions, ongoing work that drifts into inconsistency without it. Worked example: All services log in a common format and expose health/metrics on conventional paths. A service deviating for regulatory reasons documents why, explicitly. Signs of misapplication: Conventions are stated but not enforced; new services do whatever their authors prefer. P8 Automate what gets done more than twice Rationale: Manual work is error-prone, non-repeatable, and invisible. The person doing it is a bottleneck and a knowledge concentration point. Trade-off: Automation costs more than doing the thing once; the 'more than twice' rule calibrates when that cost is worth paying. Worked example: New developer environment setup was a 3-day manual process. After the second hire it became a script; after the fifth, a one-click pipeline. Signs of misapplication: Automation becomes an end in itself; teams automate one-off work and produce scripts no one else uses. Data P9 Data has one authoritative source; every other copy is derived from it Rationale: Parallel sources of truth always diverge, usually not discovered until a reconciliation problem surfaces in production. Trade-off: The authoritative source becomes a hard dependency for every downstream consumer; its availability matters more than in a distributed-truth design. Worked example: Customer contact information is authoritative in the CRM; Marketing receives it via streaming replica; Billing queries CRM directly. Nobody has their own editable copy. Signs of misapplication: Two teams claim authoritative ownership of overlapping data; reconciliation scripts appear. The cure is naming a single owner and migrating the other to consumer status. P10 Data models reflect domain reality rather than system convenience Rationale: Data outlives systems. A model shaped by today's storage technology will be wrong when the technology changes, which it will. Trade-off: Domain-driven models are sometimes less efficient for the current storage technology than technology-optimized ones would be. Worked example: The order model captures business concepts, order, line item, party, event, because those concepts are stable, regardless of the underlying storage engine. Signs of misapplication: The model has fields named for technical conventions (is_deleted, legacy_status_code) that pollute the domain. The cure is separating domain model from storage model. P11 Classify data by sensitivity before any other decision Rationale: Retrofitting sensitivity controls is more expensive than building them in; systems that move data without awareness of sensitivity produce the gaps that show up in breach postmortems. Trade-off: Classification requires ongoing organizational discipline, every system handling data must know what classification applies. Worked example: Customer purchase history is classified Restricted. A log entry including purchase history is subject to Restricted-level controls even if the producing system wouldn't otherwise be. Signs of misapplication: Classification exists on paper but isn't wired into any control. The cure is instrumenting classification into specific enforcement (encryption, access logging). People & process P12 The team that builds runs, or the runbook doesn't exist Rationale: Build-only teams produce systems that are hard to operate because they don't experience the operational cost; run-only teams receive systems they can't confidently change. Trade-off: Asking build teams to operate adds ongoing work. The cost of operational-ownership confusion is larger, but this is still a cost. Worked example: A product team building a customer-facing service is on-call for it. If responsibility transfers to a central ops team, the transfer includes validated runbooks and paired on-call for 90 days. Signs of misapplication: Teams claim to operate but delegate incidents upward constantly. The cure is staffing and training to the operational responsibility. Softening the principle only hides the gap. P13 Decisions are recorded; rationale is part of the decision Rationale: The reasoning behind a decision is usually the most valuable artifact, and the one most frequently lost. Trade-off: Writing a good rationale takes effort, and most teams underestimate how much. Worked example: An event-driven integration decision is recorded as an ADR including alternatives considered, why the chosen path won, and what would trigger revisiting it. Signs of misapplication: ADRs exist but are written as announcements rather than reasoning. 'We will use X' with no explanation of what was rejected is a memo. P14 Small, stable teams outperform large, dynamic ones for complex work Rationale: Architectural work compounds on team context. A team that's operated a system for two years makes better decisions about it than one assembled three weeks ago. Trade-off: Stable teams are harder to scale up rapidly for new initiatives; the organization has to plan for this rather than throwing people at problems. Worked example: The team owning customer identity has a core of four engineers with two-plus years on it. New engineers onboard over three to six months rather than three weeks. Signs of misapplication: Team composition changes frequently, no one's been on the team more than six months. The cure is slowing the churn. Asking teams to document more treats the symptom. P15 Measure what matters; do not optimize what is merely easy to measure Rationale: Goodhart's law applies to architecture: when a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. Easy proxies produce organizations that look healthy while failing at what matters. Trade-off: Measures that matter are harder to collect and slower to move; the temptation to substitute easy proxies is constant. Worked example: Instead of 'reviews conducted,' measure 'percentage of significant initiatives with early architecture engagement,' which requires judgment but reflects reality. Signs of misapplication: Dashboards show green metrics while the function is widely considered unhelpful. The cure: ask what consumers of the work would say is getting better or worse. When principles conflict Conflict is expected Principles conflict. The conflict surfaces a trade-off the organization has to make; three approaches help resolve it in practice. State the specific conflict. "These sometimes conflict" is useless; "P1 conflicts with P4 here because the commercial product creates tight coupling with our existing systems" is resolvable. Identify which principle the context prioritizes. A regulatory system might privilege data classification over decision speed; a greenfield product might privilege the reverse. Neither is wrong; the context decides. Record the resolution in the ADR. Future decisions in similar contexts have precedent to draw on.

title: Architecture Review Board
description: How to stand up a review board that examines evidence from engineering work already done, rather than diagrams produced for the meeting, and how to keep it working as a forcing function for years after the founding energy fades.
body: Reference What belongs in front of the board, and what doesn't The most common way a review board fails is reviewing everything, which turns it into a bottleneck and trains teams to route around it. The same filter used to decide when a decision needs an ADR applies here. Goes to the board Doesn't need the board A new external dependency or a shared service other teams will depend on A team's fully contained internal implementation detail A decision that affects more than one team's roadmap A reversible, single-team decision costing less than a day to undo A new system of record or data store other systems will read from Adding a field to a schema the team already owns exclusively A deliberate deviation from an established architecture principle Following a pattern the board has already approved elsewhere 1 Evidence over drawings The distinction that separates a review with teeth from a rubber stamp with a diagram attached. What a working review looks at The running system, observed traffic patterns, incident history, a working prototype or spike, existing code. Evidence produced by doing the engineering work rather than evidence produced to satisfy the meeting. The theater version A polished architecture diagram produced in the days before the review, disconnected from the codebase, that nobody consults again once the meeting ends. The tell: check the diagram file's last-modified date six months later. If it's the review date, it was never a working artifact. 2 Setting it up: composition and authority Two decisions made once, at founding, that determine whether the board has standing or only a name. Composition A small standing group, four to six people, spanning the systems most likely to be affected by cross-cutting decisions. Rotate membership on a defined cycle so it doesn't calcify into the same five people's opinions indefinitely. The proposing team's own senior engineer is always in the room, never reviewed in absentia. Authority, stated explicitly See Technology Decision Rights : the board should be Consulted, rarely Accountable. A named individual, the CTO or a delegate, is accountable for architecture standards and can be persuaded by a strong board recommendation, but the board's vote is input to that person's decision and can be overridden. 3 The review itself What makes a specific session evidence-based rather than theater, independent of how well the board was set up. Practice The proposing team walks through the tradeoffs they considered and rejected, the same alternatives-considered discipline covered on the ADR page, with numbers behind claims (this handles X load, this costs Y) rather than assertions. The review produces a decision and its reasoning captured in an ADR. A verbal thumbs-up disappears when the meeting ends. Common failure mode The review becomes a presentation the team already knows how to pass: confident language and a clean diagram calibrated to satisfy the audience rather than stress-test the reasoning. At that point the board is a rubber stamp with theater added, arguably worse than no review, since it spends time producing a false signal of scrutiny. 4 Running it long-term without decaying into theater A board that works well in its first year and quietly stops working in its third is the most common lifecycle, and it's predictable enough to design against. What sustains it A standing cadence, biweekly is common, that runs whether or not there's a full docket. A public backlog of upcoming reviews so teams plan around it instead of being surprised. Periodic retrospectives on the board's own past decisions: did what it approved work out, was what it blocked right to block. How it decays The board approves the same rubber-stamp pattern for months. Membership never rotates, so the room's authority rests on tenure rather than current context. No one checks whether a past decision held up, so the board never learns whether its own judgment is any good, and keeps operating on the same instincts regardless of outcomes. 5 Empty slots: turn them into innovation salons instead of canceling What to do with a scheduled review slot that has nothing queued for it, which happens regularly once a board is running well and teams aren't manufacturing proposals just to fill the docket. The idea Instead of canceling the slot, which trains people to deprioritize the cadence, or filling it with a low-stakes item just to have something on the agenda, open it up: anyone can bring an early-stage idea, a technical curiosity, or a "here's something I've been thinking about" for informal discussion. No funding decision required, no ADR required, just structured space for ideas that aren't ready for a formal pitch yet. Why this works better than canceling It keeps the room's habit and rhythm intact, the same people, the same regular slot, the same expectation of showing up prepared to think carefully, without wasting the time when nothing formal needs review. It also creates a low-stakes on-ramp: an idea that draws interest in a salon session is the kind of thing ready to become a formal pitch at the next innovation tournament . The board and the tournament are the same room used two different ways: one evaluates evidence against a decision that needs to be made, the other surfaces ideas that don't have evidence yet. Keeping both on the same cadence, in the same room, with the same people, is what makes the salon slot feel like a natural extension rather than a separate initiative competing for calendar space. 6 Review tiers and turnaround commitments A board earns trust by being fast on the routine and thorough on the consequential. Publishing turnaround commitments is what stops teams from routing around it. Times are suggested starting points. Tier Triggers Process Turnaround 0. Self-serve Uses a pattern the board already approved Team writes a short ADR referencing the approved pattern; no meeting None; the ADR is the record 1. Async review New dependency, moderate cross-team impact, reversible within a quarter Written ADR reviewed by two board members in the document itself Three business days 2. Full board New system of record, shared platform, principle deviation, or hard-to-reverse spend Live session with evidence: prototype, load data, cost model, alternatives rejected Scheduled within ten business days of request Emergency A production incident forced an unreviewed change Change ships; the ADR and review follow Retrospective review within two weeks Diagram Routing a change to the right tier Most changes should never reach a meeting. Published turnaround times are what keep teams from routing around the board. Routing a proposed change to the right review tier Proposed change Tier 0: self-serve uses an approved pattern ADR only, no meeting no wait Tier 1: async review new dependency, reversible two members review the ADR 3 business days Tier 2: full board system of record, hard to reverse live session with evidence within 10 business days Emergency incident forced the change ship now, ADR follows review within 2 weeks Tiers and turnaround times from the table above; treat them as starting points. Every tier ends in a decision record. 7 Standards and practices worth borrowing Most of what makes a board work is already written down elsewhere. Borrow deliberately rather than inventing a process. Source What it contributes Architecture Decision Records (Michael Nygard, 2011) [1] The short, immutable record of context, decision, and consequences that every review should produce ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010:2022 [2] A precise vocabulary for architecture descriptions: stakeholders, their concerns, and the viewpoints that address them. Useful for deciding what a proposal must show C4 model (Simon Brown) Four levels of diagram, context, containers, components, code, so reviewers see the right level of detail instead of one crowded picture arc42 A free, widely used template for documenting a system; a good default for the evidence pack on tier 2 reviews Architecture fitness functions (Ford, Parsons, Kua, Sadalage, Building Evolutionary Architectures, 2nd ed., 2022) Turning an architecture decision into an automated check so it stays true after the meeting The architecture advice process (Andrew Harmel-Law, Facilitating Software Architecture, 2024) A decentralized alternative in which teams decide after seeking advice, with the board acting as an advisory forum and keeper of the decision log TOGAF Standard, 10th Edition The formal Architecture Board and compliance review concepts, useful for regulated enterprises that need an auditable governance trail Sources Michael Nygard, Documenting Architecture Decisions, November 2011 ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010:2022, Architecture description 8 Fitness functions: keep the decision true after the meeting A decision that exists only in an ADR decays as soon as the next deadline arrives. Encode the important ones. Practice For each tier 2 decision, ask what automated check would fail if the decision were violated, then put it in the pipeline. Examples: Dependency rules that stop one domain calling another's database directly A latency budget checked in a performance test A cost ceiling alarm on a new service A policy-as-code rule that blocks public storage buckets Common failure mode Treating the board's approval as the control. Six months later the system has drifted, nobody noticed, and the next review argues about a design that no longer exists in production. 9 Measure the board itself A board that never measures its own performance cannot tell whether it adds value or delay. These five numbers, reviewed quarterly, are enough. Metric What healthy looks like What it warns about Median days from request to decision Within the published turnaround for each tier Rising numbers mean teams will start routing around the board Share of proposals changed by review Somewhere between a fifth and a half Near zero is a rubber stamp; very high means teams arrive unprepared or the principles are unclear Decisions with a written ADR All tier 1 and tier 2 decisions Anything lower means the board's reasoning is lost when members rotate Decisions revisited after 6 to 12 months A sample reviewed every quarter, with a verdict on whether each held up No review of outcomes means the board never learns whether its judgment is good Bypass rate Few or no systems in production that should have come to the board and did not A high bypass rate is the clearest sign the board is seen as an obstacle Checklist Signs the board has become theater Patterns that show up when a review board exists on the calendar but has stopped functioning as a forcing function. Reviews consistently approve with no pushback or requested changes No one can name a decision the board changed its mind about after seeing how it played out Board membership hasn't rotated in over a year Decisions aren't captured anywhere durable, no ADR, no written record, once the meeting ends Teams prepare a specific "board-ready" version of their architecture that differs from what's running in production Nobody can say the median time from review request to decision Important decisions exist only in ADRs, with no automated check to catch drift

title: Board Reporting
description: A preview of the Technology Board Reporting Framework: what works reporting technology, security, and AI posture to a board.
body: 1 Cadence & format How often the board hears from technology, and in what form, before a single word of content is decided. What works A consistent one-page technology summary attached to every board meeting, regardless of whether anything dramatic happened, plus a deeper technology review quarterly or semi-annually. Consistency builds the board's pattern recognition for what normal looks like, so they notice when something isn't. What backfires Technology only showing up on the agenda when something has gone wrong. This trains the board to associate a CTO presentation with bad news, which makes every appearance feel like a confession rather than a normal operating rhythm. 2 The out-of-cycle escalation path The specific mechanism that makes a promise like "the quarterly report never contains a surprise" true, rather than aspirational. What works A pre-agreed threshold for what triggers a call to the board chair or committee lead outside the normal cadence, a confirmed material breach, a regulatory filing obligation, a decision that can't wait until the next scheduled meeting, defined before an incident happens rather than improvised during one. What backfires No defined threshold, which means every incident becomes a judgment call about whether it's board-worthy, made under pressure by whoever's closest to it. That's how a material issue ends up sitting until the next quarterly meeting for no reason other than nobody decided to escalate it sooner. 3 Two clocks: internal escalation versus external disclosure For a public company, the out-of-cycle path above and the regulatory disclosure deadline are related but distinct, and conflating them creates legal exposure. The internal clock The board should hear about a likely-material incident within roughly 24 hours, well ahead of any external deadline, so there's time to prepare a proper disclosure and align on the facts before anyone outside the company sees them. The external clock Under current SEC rules, a public company must disclose a cybersecurity incident determined to be material on Form 8-K within four business days of that materiality determination. The clock starts when materiality is decided rather than at discovery, which is why the internal escalation path needs to run well ahead of it rather than up against it. This is a compliance question. Confirm the exact disclosure obligations, timing, and materiality process for your company with counsel; don't rely on this page for the legal determination. 4 Translating technical risk into business risk The single most common failure mode in board reporting: reporting the risk in the language it was diagnosed in rather than the language the board makes decisions in. What works "A vulnerability in our authentication system could allow unauthorized account access, affecting an estimated 40,000 customer accounts and carrying breach notification obligations in three states" states the business consequence first and the technical detail second, for anyone who wants it. What backfires "We have a CVSS 9.1 vulnerability in our OAuth implementation" is accurate and unusable by a board that isn't going to look up what CVSS 9.1 means mid-meeting. If a board member has to ask "what does that mean for us," the report failed before the discussion even starts. For more than one or two risks, a single narrative paragraph stops working. A heat map, top risks plotted by likelihood and impact, gives the board a portfolio view in one glance, with the highest-priority item then unpacked in business language the way the example above does. 5 Investment & roadmap tied to outcomes Connecting engineering spend and roadmap decisions to something the board governs: capital allocation and strategic risk. What works Framing a platform investment as "this reduces our customer onboarding time from six weeks to two, which our sales pipeline data shows is currently costing us an estimated 15 percent of qualified leads" ties the spend to a number the board already tracks. What backfires A roadmap slide organized by internal team names and sprint numbers. It's accurate to how the work is organized internally and meaningless to a board trying to understand what changes for the business and when. 6 Security & compliance posture What a board needs to know here, distinct from an operational security review the CISO or security team runs separately. What works A small, stable set of metrics tracked over time: mean time to detect, mean time to remediate critical vulnerabilities, percentage of the environment covered by current compliance certifications, third-party and vendor posture (percentage of vendors with a current SOC 2 or equivalent), and current cyber insurance coverage, with any material incidents since the last meeting and the incident response postmortem attached if one occurred. What backfires A wall of green checkmarks with no trend line, no incident history, and no sense of how the organization compares to industry peers. A board cannot distinguish "consistently secure" from "we've never measured this rigorously enough to find a problem" without a track record and an external reference point to compare against. 7 Reporting on AI specifically An increasingly standard board expectation, and one most technology leaders haven't built a repeatable format for yet. What works A short standing section covering what AI systems are in production, what's spent on them, and what governance controls are in place, referencing the AI Governance Map's control layers directly rather than reinventing the language each quarter. Boards are increasingly asking about this whether or not it's offered, and forward-looking boards are starting to ask about emerging technology risk more broadly, post-quantum cryptography readiness, for example, is now a live board discussion topic at some companies. What backfires Treating an AI pilot as not board-relevant because it's "still experimental." If it touches customer data or a regulated decision, the board's risk oversight duty applies well before the system reaches full production, and finding out about it after an incident is worse than a modest early mention. 8 Common mistakes, named directly Patterns that show up repeatedly enough to call out specifically rather than leave implicit in the sections above. The mistake Reporting activity (story points completed, deployments shipped) instead of outcomes (what changed for the business) Surprising the board with bad news in the meeting instead of a pre-brief to the chair or committee lead beforehand Treating every board update as a status report instead of occasionally using the time to ask the board for something specific: a decision, a resource, air cover for a hard tradeoff The fix Before every board meeting, write one sentence per section: "what do I want the board to know, feel, or decide because of this." If a section doesn't have a clear answer to that, cut it or rework it. A board deck is a decision-support tool. Documentation belongs elsewhere. Download Sample board deck A seven-slide illustrative example applying every section above: at-a-glance metrics, business outcomes, security and AI posture, a risk heat map plus one risk translated into business terms, investment tied to outcomes, and a specific ask. Figures are synthetic; adapt the structure with your own numbers. Download .pptx

title: Build vs Buy
description: The criteria that decide a build-versus-buy debate, the differentiation test people misapply most often.
body: Framework The criteria that decide it Most build-versus-buy debates get stuck arguing cost in isolation. Cost matters, but it's rarely the deciding factor once these have been answered. Question Leans build Leans buy Is this a differentiator? Yes, this is part of what customers pay for versus competitors No, it's necessary but customers don't choose you for it Does a mature vendor solution exist? No, or existing options are a poor fit for the requirement Yes, and it's been production-hardened by many other customers already Time to value You have runway to spend months getting it right You need it working in weeks rather than quarters Ongoing maintenance capacity You have, or are willing to build, a team that will own this indefinitely You don't want a permanent internal team dedicated to this domain Vendor lock-in risk if you buy Switching cost would be unacceptably high later Data portability and exit path are reasonable if the vendor relationship sours Interactive Score your own decision Score each criterion from the table above, 1 to 5, high meaning it leans build, and weight them for this decision. Then compare five-year cost for Build, Buy, and Extend (buy the platform and build a thin custom layer); the defaults reproduce the worked example below. The tool tells you when the criteria and the cost point in different directions. Runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere. Score it 1 The differentiation test The single most misapplied criterion, usually stretched to justify a decision already made for other reasons. Differentiation A capability customers explicitly cite as why they chose you over an alternative, or one that materially changes your unit economics versus using a vendor. If you removed it, you'd lose deals or margin specifically because of its absence. Preference dressed as differentiation "We want more control" or "the vendor's roadmap doesn't match ours exactly" are legitimate preferences. They aren't differentiation, and building an entire internal system to solve a preference is usually a worse trade than living with 90 percent fit from a vendor. 2 The maintenance question people skip Build decisions are evaluated on initial build cost far more often than on the ongoing cost of owning it for the next five years. What gets counted Initial development time, initial infrastructure cost, time to first working version, the numbers that show up in a project proposal and are easy to estimate. What gets missed Security patching indefinitely, keeping pace with a changing regulatory or integration landscape, the bus-factor risk when the one engineer who deeply understands it leaves, and the opportunity cost of the team's attention being split across build-and-maintain instead of focused on the differentiator. Maintenance is the dominant cost of owned software. The research summarized by Robert Glass in Facts and Fallacies of Software Engineering puts it at 40 to 80 percent of lifecycle cost, around 60 percent on average. [1] A build proposal whose five-year view shows maintenance as a small line has left out most of the cost; the worked example below shows the effect. Sources Robert L. Glass, Facts and Fallacies of Software Engineering, Addison-Wesley, 2002 3 The middle option nobody names: partner or extend Build-versus-buy is usually presented as binary. A frequently better third option gets skipped. What it looks like Buying a vendor platform for the undifferentiated 80 percent and building a thin, differentiated layer on top of it via the vendor's API or extension points, rather than building the whole stack from scratch or accepting 100 percent of the vendor's opinion. When to reach for it When the differentiation is narrow and specific (a particular workflow, a particular integration, a particular scoring model) rather than the whole domain. This is very often the right answer and gets dismissed early because the binary framing never surfaced it as an option. 4 Reversing the decision later Build-versus-buy isn't necessarily a permanent choice. The sequencing of which comes first matters as much as the eventual answer. Buy first, build later if it proves out Start with a vendor to get to market fast. If the capability proves out as differentiation worth owning, build a deliberate replacement once you understand the requirements from having lived with the vendor's version, rather than guessing at them upfront. The trap of building first to keep optionality Building something in-house "to stay flexible" before you know whether it's a differentiator usually produces a worse version of what a mature vendor already built, at a cost that vendor already amortized across many customers instead of just you. 5 Vendor risk beyond lock-in The framework above asks whether you can leave a vendor. It's an incomplete question on its own. The fuller question Lock-in asks "can I leave." It's worth also asking what happens if the vendor leaves you: acquisition risk, a pricing change once you're dependent, a wind-down of the specific product you rely on. See Vendor Evaluation for scoring this directly. Where this bites A string of individually reasonable buy decisions, each cleared on its own lock-in and exit-cost merits, that quietly concentrate several important capabilities behind the same vendor. A single vendor's bad quarter becomes every one of those capabilities' bad quarter at once. 6 A worked five-year cost of ownership A customer notification platform: email, SMS, and in-app messages with templates, preferences, and delivery tracking. Figures are illustrative, in thousands of dollars, loaded engineer cost of $200K a year. Cost line Build Buy Extend (platform plus thin custom layer) Initial 900: six engineers for nine months 150: implementation and integration 250: platform setup plus a custom preference engine Licensing over five years None 1,035: $180K a year rising 7 percent annually 690: $120K a year rising 7 percent annually People over five years 2,500: 2.5 engineers maintaining, patching, on call 500: half an engineer on integration 1,000: one engineer on the custom layer Infrastructure and compliance 500 Included Included Five-year total 3,900 1,685 1,940 When it wins Only if notifications are a differentiator customers pay for The default for undifferentiated capability When one narrow piece, here the preference engine, is genuinely differentiating Diagram Where the five-year cost goes The worked example above as bars. Figures in thousands of dollars. Five-year cost of ownership for build, buy, and extend Build 900 2,500 500 $3,900K Buy 1,035 500 $1,685K Extend 690 1,000 $1,940K Initial Licensing People Infrastructure People cost over five years, not the initial build, is what makes building expensive: 2.5 engineers maintaining it for five years. Illustrative figures from the worked example. The calculator above lets you enter your own and compares them with the criteria score. 7 Exit terms to negotiate before signing The cost of leaving is set at signature, when you have the most leverage and the least motivation to think about it. See SaaS Contract & Renewal Negotiation for the full clause set. Term What to ask for Data export Complete export in a documented, machine-readable format, on request and at termination, at no additional fee Transition assistance A defined period after termination, commonly 30 to 90 days, with continued access and support at existing rates Renewal price protection A cap on renewal increases, tied to an index or a fixed percentage Product end of life Written notice well in advance, 12 months is common, if the product or a feature you depend on is discontinued Change of control The right to terminate or renegotiate if the vendor is acquired Escrow Source code escrow for self-hosted software that is critical to operations Checklist Signs the decision wasn't tested Patterns that show up when a build-versus-buy call was made to justify a preference rather than worked through. Differentiation was asserted rather than tested against "would we lose deals or margin without this" No five-year total cost of ownership estimate exists for the build option, only the initial build cost The partner-or-extend middle option was never evaluated, only a binary build-or-buy framing No plan exists for reversing the decision later if the underlying assumption turns out wrong Vendor concentration across other decisions wasn't considered, only this one decision's lock-in risk in isolation The buy option was evaluated without negotiating exit terms: data export, transition assistance, and renewal caps

title: Business Case Calculator
description: A working NPV, IRR, and payback calculator for a multi-year technology investment, built on the same mechanics as the full business case workbook.
body: 1 What the model produces Roll-up numbers from year-by-year cost and benefit inputs, the same structure as the full business case workbook: net present value, benefit-to-cost ratio, internal rate of return, and payback period. The five outputs NPV: sum of discounted after-tax net cashflow across the analysis period. The tax rate is applied to each year's net cashflow, which assumes costs are deductible against other taxable income; capitalized costs are deducted on a different schedule, see Working with the CFO Benefit-to-cost ratio: present value of benefits divided by present value of costs, on the same discounted basis as NPV IRR: the discount rate at which NPV equals zero Payback period: when cumulative after-tax cashflow turns positive Verdict: a plain-language read on whether the case is strong, acceptable, or fragile Reading it NPV positive and B/C above roughly 1.5x reads as a strong case. NPV positive with B/C under 1.5x is worth funding, with the sensitivity checked before committing. These are illustrative reference points; your organization's bar depends on its cost of capital and risk appetite and should be set deliberately rather than borrowed from this page. NPV negative at base case doesn't automatically kill an initiative with strategic value that doesn't show up in the numbers, but it does mean the strategic argument has to carry the case explicitly instead of hiding behind an inflated financial one. Interactive Run the numbers Enter total costs and benefits per year. The tool runs the base case and a pessimistic case side by side (benefits cut and costs raised by the percentages you set), because a case that only works at the base numbers is a weaker case than it looks. Defaults are pre-filled with a representative example. Runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere. Year 1 Year 2 Year 3 Year 4 Year 5 Costs ($) Benefits ($) Discount rate (WACC) % Tax rate % Calculate 2 What the pre-filled example represents The default numbers loaded above are a representative modernization program. They are there to show the shape, so replace them with your own. Shape of the numbers Front-loaded implementation cost in Years 1 and 2, tapering to steady-state run cost by Year 3. Benefits ramp in behind it, typically 30 percent of steady-state value in Year 1, 70 percent in Year 2, full value from Year 3 onward, since adoption and realization lag the investment. Why that ramp matters A business case that assumes full benefit realization starting Year 1 is either describing a trivial change or overstating the case. Reviewers who've seen enough of these will discount an unramped benefit projection on sight. 3 Sensitivity: what happens if you're wrong The most common gap between a business case that survives scrutiny and one that only looks solid under one set of assumptions. Practice Run the same model at a pessimistic case, benefits 20 to 30 percent lower, costs 10 to 15 percent higher, before presenting the base case. If NPV still clears positive under the pessimistic scenario, the case is robust. If it only works at the base case, say so explicitly rather than letting the base case stand in for more confidence than the analysis supports. Common failure mode Presenting only the base case with no sensitivity shown. Either it was never tested, or it was tested, the pessimistic case failed, and it quietly got left out of the deck, which a CFO who's seen enough of these will assume by default even without being told. 4 Choosing a discount rate The single input most likely to be pulled from thin air, and the one most likely to quietly determine the verdict. What it represents The return the capital could earn elsewhere, the company's cost of capital if it tracks one, or a hurdle rate leadership has explicitly agreed represents good enough for a technology investment. 8 percent shows up often as an illustrative default for an established company, but it is only a placeholder. Your own cost of capital is company-specific and should replace it. A deliberately higher rate, 15 percent or more, is often used for early-stage or higher-risk bets specifically because the higher bar forces only the strongest cases through. The trap Picking a lower discount rate because it makes more initiatives clear the bar, which quietly inflates the entire portfolio's apparent quality without anyone deciding to lower the standard. If the rate changes between two business cases with no stated reason, that's worth questioning before either number gets trusted. 5 How business cases get gamed, and how to catch it A handful of specific patterns account for most inflated cases. Worth knowing what to look for, whether reviewing someone else's case or checking your own. Double-counted benefits. The same cost saving claimed by two different initiatives' business cases, each one looking stronger on its own than the two deliver combined. A skipped ramp. Full benefit value assumed from Year 1, which is either describing a trivial change or quietly overstating the case, covered above. Costs that stop at go-live. The build cost is modeled carefully; the run cost the initiative adds afterward, ongoing licensing, additional on-call load, incremental support burden, never makes it into the model at all. A quietly adjusted discount rate. The rate shifts from the standard used elsewhere in the portfolio, with no stated reason, until the number clears the bar. Download Business case one-pager template Drop the NPV, IRR, benefit-to-cost, and payback numbers from the calculator above straight into this one-pager, alongside the problem statement, strategic rationale, and risks a pure financial model doesn't capture. Markdown for pasting into your own docs system, or a formatted Word doc. Download .md Download .docx

title: Working with the CEO
description: The relationship that determines whether everything else in this toolkit gets funded, listened to, or quietly ignored. The single most consequential relationship a CTO manages, and the one least often discussed explicitly.
body: Reference What the CEO needs from a CTO Four things a CEO can't get from anyone else on the team. Technical competence is assumed; none of these are about it. Need What it looks like What it isn't Translation Business strategy translated into its technology consequences, in language a non-technical executive can act on Technology strategy explained in a way that requires the CEO to already understand the technology Protection Technology risk surfaced while there's still time to do something about it Risk explained for the first time during the incident it caused Judgment A clear recommendation with the tradeoff stated plainly A menu of options with no point of view, leaving the decision entirely to someone without the context to make it well Predictability Commitments that hold, or an early, honest flag when they won't Optimistic timelines that quietly slip without anyone hearing about it until the deadline arrives 1 Telling the CEO no The moment that defines the relationship more than any status update ever will. How it works Arrive with the tradeoff already worked out alongside the refusal: "we can hit that date if we cut X, or hit full scope two weeks later, which do you want." A no with a stated alternative reads as judgment. A no with nothing behind it reads as an obstacle. Where it goes wrong A flat no delivered late, often after the CEO has already committed to the date externally, which turns a technical disagreement into a credibility problem for both people, and makes the next no much harder to deliver and to hear. 2 A worked example What the mechanics above look like against a common scenario. The CEO wants to announce a launch date publicly at a conference six weeks out. The CTO's engineering estimate is ten weeks for the full feature set. Rather than a flat "we can't hit that," the CTO brings the tradeoff already worked out: a limited beta with three core features ships in six weeks, the full launch stays on the ten-week timeline. The CEO announces the beta at the conference instead of the full launch. Engineering hits the beta date. The full launch ships on the timeline that was true from the start. Nobody's public credibility gets damaged, because what got promised matched what was deliverable, and the CEO had a positive announcement to make either way. 3 Founder CEO versus professional CEO The same relationship, shaped very differently depending on who's in the role. Founder CEO Often has deep intuitive product and technical instincts even without a formal technical background, and personal identity tied closely to the company. Disagreements can feel personal in a way they don't with a professional CEO. Technical credibility gets earned through demonstrated judgment over time; the title alone buys none. Professional or hired CEO Usually more process-oriented, expecting the same structured decision-rights model and reporting cadence used at previous companies. The relationship starts more transactional and earns trust faster through consistent, predictable execution rather than through personal rapport built up over years. 4 When technology should be invisible, and when it's the strategy Getting this posture wrong in either direction costs credibility. Invisible For most companies, most of the time, technology is an enabler. The goal is for the CEO to rarely have to think about it, and that quiet is a sign of health as long as it isn't masking a risk building underneath. The strategic differentiator When the technology is the competitive edge, what customers are buying is the technical capability, invisibility is the wrong posture. The CTO needs to be actively pushing technology into the CEO's strategic conversations instead of staying quietly out of them. 5 Handling a CEO who's miscalibrated in either direction Two opposite failure modes, requiring opposite corrections. Over-indexes on technology Treats every technical detail as something worth personally weighing in on. Give them a small, explicit set of decisions that warrant their attention, rather than either blocking them out entirely or letting them relitigate implementation details that don't. Treats technology as a cost center Treat this as a translation failure rather than a values failure. Find the specific business metric technology investment moves, and lead every conversation with that number. Technical merit on its own gives the CEO nothing to evaluate it against. 6 Building trust before you need it The high-stakes moments described above draw on a trust balance that has to be built somewhere else first. Practice Regular, low-stakes contact, the weekly touchpoint described below, builds the trust that a high-stakes "telling the CEO no" moment later draws on. A CEO who's watched a CTO be right about smaller things repeatedly extends more benefit of the doubt when it matters most. Common failure mode The CTO only appears in the CEO's calendar when something's wrong, which means every interaction the CEO has with the CTO is colored by a problem, and trust never gets the chance to compound the way it does with regular, unremarkable contact. 7 Escalation and cadence, stated explicitly What should reach the CEO, and on what rhythm, shouldn't be reinvented every time something comes up. Escalate: a material change in risk, anything crossing a stated board-visibility threshold, and any commitment at risk of slipping, as early as it's known. Handle independently: implementation approach, internal architecture decisions, and day-to-day engineering management. A regular weekly touchpoint covers the practical items; a deeper monthly or quarterly conversation, tied to the broader operating cadence, covers strategy and portfolio; anything crossing an escalation threshold gets raised immediately rather than saved for the next scheduled meeting. The full decision-rights model this escalation guidance points to lives on its own page: Technology Decision Rights . 8 The monthly one-page technology narrative The single artifact that does most of the trust-building work, because it replaces ad hoc status with a predictable, readable account. One page, written, sent before the monthly one-on-one, no acronyms. Five sections, always in the same order: What changed in the business that affects technology. A new market, a lost deal, a regulator's letter, and what it means for the plan Three commitments, on or off track. Each with a date and a number, and for anything off track the recovery option already worked out Risk movement. What moved relative to the stated risk appetite , in either direction Decisions needed from the CEO. Two at most, each with a recommendation and the tradeoff stated plainly What I am not worried about, and why. The section CEOs value most, because it tells them where they can stop spending attention The format matters less than the consistency. After three months the CEO knows where to look, and a surprise is rare enough that when it does come, it is taken seriously. 9 Translate the CEO's metrics into technology levers A CEO evaluates technology through a handful of business numbers. Knowing which technology levers move each one is most of what translation means in practice. What the CEO tracks Technology lever Leading indicator to report Revenue growth and net revenue retention Roadmap delivery, availability of revenue-critical paths Committed roadmap items shipped on time; customer-facing incident minutes Gross margin Cloud and hosting unit cost, support automation Infrastructure cost per transaction or per customer, trended monthly Enterprise sales cycle Security posture and evidence Security questionnaire turnaround in days; current SOC 2, ISO 27001, or HITRUST status Operating expense Headcount mix, vendor portfolio, commitment discounts Engineering cost as a share of revenue; vendor spend under active management Exit or financing readiness Diligence hygiene Open diligence red flags: IP assignments, key-person concentration, unremediated critical findings 10 The first 90 days with a new CEO A new CEO, or a new CTO joining an existing CEO, resets the relationship to zero. The first quarter decides whether it compounds or stalls. Window What to do What to avoid Weeks 1 to 2 Learn their top three priorities, how they like to receive information, and what they were told about technology before arriving Presenting the technology strategy before understanding theirs Weeks 3 to 6 Agree the escalation rules and cadence explicitly, in writing; send the first one-page narrative Assuming the previous CEO's norms carry over Weeks 7 to 12 Bring one well-framed recommendation with a real tradeoff; review the risk appetite together Saving every hard conversation until trust feels established; trust is built by having them well Checklist Signs the relationship is unhealthy Patterns that show up when the CEO-CTO relationship has drifted, regardless of how well either person would describe it individually. The CEO learns about a material technology risk from someone other than the CTO Every technology conversation with the CEO is either a routine status update or a crisis, nothing in between The CTO can't name the one or two business metrics the CEO tracks Disagreements get resolved by whoever escalates loudest rather than by a stated decision-rights model The CEO has stopped asking the CTO's opinion before making technology-adjacent decisions Most contact between the two only happens when something is already wrong There is no regular written account of technology from the CTO; the CEO's picture is assembled from meetings and hallway updates The CEO's top business metrics have never been explicitly mapped to the technology levers that move them

title: Cloud FinOps
description: Managing general infrastructure spend as a standing discipline rather than a quarterly panic when finance asks why the cloud bill jumped.
body: Framework Phases: one building block of a larger framework These are the FinOps Foundation's own Phases. The Foundation is the industry body (under the Linux Foundation) that maintains the full FinOps Framework and the FOCUS billing specification referenced throughout this page. The complete framework also includes Principles, Personas, Domains and Capabilities, Technology Categories, and Scopes, and the Foundation's current definition centers on maximizing the business value of technology spend broadly rather than cloud alone. The 2026 framework names five Technology Categories, public cloud, SaaS, data center, data cloud platforms, and AI, and treats a Scope as a business-defined slice of spend across those categories, started because a business question needs answering. [1] This page covers public cloud infrastructure, which is why AI cost modeling gets its own page rather than folding into this one. Phase Focus Typical activities Inform Visibility and allocation Tagging, showback, budgets, forecasting, benchmarking spend against peers Optimize Reducing waste and improving rates Rightsizing, reserved capacity and commitment discounts, workload rearchitecture for cost efficiency Operate Continuous governance Automated policies, anomaly detection, aligning engineering and finance around cost as a shared, ongoing metric Sources FinOps Foundation, FinOps Framework 2026, March 2026 Diagram The phases are a loop, not a sequence Organizations cycle through all three repeatedly, at different maturity for different parts of the estate. FinOps phases as a continuous loop Inform visibility and allocation tagging, showback, budgets Optimize reduce waste, improve rates rightsizing, commitments Operate continuous governance policies, anomaly alerts Each pass is driven by a business question Most programs stall between Inform and Optimize: savings are found but nobody owns the spend they sit in. Phase names and focus areas are the FinOps Foundation's, as summarized in the table above. Reference Where cost hides The categories that consistently account for the largest share of avoidable spend, in roughly the order worth checking first. This is the Optimize phase in practice. Category What to look for Idle and oversized compute Instances provisioned for a peak load that rarely occurs, running at 10-15 percent utilization around the clock Non-production environments Dev, staging, and QA environments running 24/7 when they're only used during business hours Orphaned resources Volumes, snapshots, and load balancers left behind after the workload that used them was decommissioned Untagged spend Cost with no owning team attached, which nobody feels accountable for reducing because nobody's dashboard shows it Storage tiering Data sitting in a hot storage tier years after it stopped being accessed regularly Data egress Cross-region or cross-cloud transfer that could be avoided with different architecture, often invisible until the bill arrives 1 Rightsizing and idle elimination The fastest money on the table, and the easiest to let slide once the first sweep is done. Practice Automated shutdown for non-production environments outside business hours, utilization-based rightsizing recommendations reviewed monthly, and a default assumption that any resource untouched for 90 days gets flagged for a decommission decision rather than left alone indefinitely. Common failure mode Treating this as a one-time cleanup sprint instead of an ongoing practice. Six months after the sweep, utilization has drifted again and nobody's watching, because the tooling that found the savings the first time was never left running. 2 Reserved capacity and commitment strategy Committing to reserved instances or savings plans locks in a discount and locks in a bet about future usage. Both halves matter. Practice Commit only on the stable baseline, the usage level that's been consistent for at least six months, and use on-demand or short-term commitments for anything still growing or shrinking. Ladder commitment terms so not everything renews at once, which avoids a cliff where the whole discount structure needs renegotiating simultaneously. Common failure mode Overcommitting based on a growth projection that doesn't materialize, then paying for reserved capacity that sits unused, which is a worse outcome than paying on-demand rates for the same idle resource would have been. 3 Tagging, showback, and chargeback Cost visibility changes behavior. Cost invisibility guarantees nobody optimizes anything they can't see themselves accountable for. Practice A mandatory tagging policy enforced at resource creation rather than applied retroactively by a cleanup script, with showback reporting that puts each team's spend in front of that team monthly. Chargeback, where teams' budgets are directly debited, is a stronger lever but works only once tagging discipline is already solid. Common failure mode Rolling out chargeback before tagging is reliable, which produces disputed, inaccurate bills that teams learn to ignore rather than a credible signal they act on. Trust in the numbers has to come before the numbers carry financial weight. 4 Governance without becoming a bottleneck The tension every cost program eventually hits: enough control to prevent waste, without so much that provisioning something new takes a week of approvals. Practice Guardrails over gatekeeping: budget alerts that trigger automatically, instance-size policies enforced by infrastructure-as-code rather than a manual review, and approval requirements reserved for large or unusual spend rather than every new resource. Most cost control should be invisible to an engineer working within normal bounds. Common failure mode An approval queue that becomes the default path for routine provisioning, which teaches engineers to over-request once to avoid asking twice, producing the exact oversizing the governance process was meant to prevent. 5 FOCUS: a shared billing language across clouds The FinOps Foundation's second major contribution beyond the phase model, and the reason cross-cloud cost comparison stopped being a manual exercise. What it solves Before FOCUS (the FinOps Open Cost and Usage Specification), comparing a dollar of AWS spend to a dollar of Azure spend meant manually normalizing wildly different billing export formats, column names, and units. FOCUS is an open, vendor-neutral spec, now adopted by AWS, Microsoft, Google, and others, that puts every provider's billing data into the same shape. What it doesn't solve FOCUS standardizes the data format and leaves the underlying pricing and discount structures untouched. A normalized bill still requires the same rightsizing and commitment discipline covered above. FOCUS removes the translation tax from the reporting layer; the practice itself still has to happen. 6 Crawl, Walk, Run, applied practically The FinOps Foundation's maturity model, stated concretely enough to assess against rather than claim. What distinguishes each stage Crawl: tagging exists but is inconsistent, cost visibility is monthly and reactive, no forecasting. Walk: tagging enforced at creation, showback running, budgets set proactively, rightsizing is a recurring practice with an owner. Run: chargeback in place, unit economics tracked (cost per customer or transaction), anomaly detection automated, cost is a first-class input to architecture decisions rather than an afterthought. The trap Treating maturity as a label to claim rather than a description of what's happening. An organization that calls itself "Run" but can't answer what a single team spent last month is Crawl with better branding. Interactive Score your own FinOps maturity Six of the FinOps Framework's capabilities, the ones that most reliably separate stages of maturity, scored now and at target. The tool maps each score to Crawl, Walk, or Run, applies this page's rule that allocation caps everything else, and gives a next step for every gap. Runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere. Calculate maturity score 7 Allocation methods for multi-account, multi-BU estates Section 3 covers tagging discipline as the prerequisite. Once tagging is reliable, the question becomes which allocation method to run on top of it, and shared infrastructure that no single team's tags can attribute cleanly is where most multi-BU chargeback programs stall. Method How it splits shared cost Where it fits Direct allocation Cost attributed to the team or BU whose tag is on the resource, no splitting required Dedicated compute, storage, and services with clean tagging; the majority of spend in a mature program Even split Shared cost (a common network egress bill, a shared database cluster) divided equally across consuming teams regardless of actual usage A fast starting point when metering shared usage isn't built yet; crude, and worth replacing with proportional splitting once the metering exists Proportional (metered) Shared cost split by actual measured consumption, requests served, data volume, compute-seconds against the shared resource The target state for anything shared and material; requires usage metering per consumer, which is the real cost of running this method rather than even split Fixed or negotiated A pre-agreed percentage split, set by governance rather than derived from either headcount or metered usage Joint infrastructure where no consumption metric fairly represents the benefit each BU gets, decided once by the same forum that owns the funding model on Technology Capital Allocation The FinOps Foundation's own Allocation capability, under the Inform phase, covers this same problem in more depth; treat the table above as the working version rather than a substitute for reading it at finops.org when the shared-cost picture gets complicated. 8 What changed in the FinOps Framework, 2025 to 2026 Worth knowing because tooling vendors, certifications, and job descriptions now use this vocabulary. Change What it means in practice Scopes (2025, refined 2026) Spend is analyzed in business-defined segments, a product line, an acquisition, an AI program, rather than only by account or service Technology Categories (2026) Dedicated guidance for public cloud, SaaS, data center, data cloud platforms such as Snowflake and Databricks, and AI Executive Strategy Alignment (2026) [1] A new capability recognizing that technology value is a board-level conversation; FinOps output feeds strategy and capital allocation, not only engineering Intersecting Disciplines (2026) Formal overlap with IT asset management, IT financial management, sustainability, and security, which often own adjacent data FOCUS 1.3 (December 2025) The billing specification added a contract commitments dataset, columns that expose how shared costs such as Kubernetes are split, and metadata stating whether data is final or still subject to revision [2] Sources FinOps Foundation, FinOps Framework 2026, March 2026 FinOps Foundation, Introducing FOCUS 1.3, December 2025 9 Unit economics, worked The measure that turns a rising bill from a spending question into an efficiency question. Figures are illustrative for a B2B SaaS product. Quarter Cloud spend Active customers Cost per customer per month Reading Q1 $1.20M 4,000 $100 Baseline Q2 $1.38M 4,800 $96 Spend up 15 percent, efficiency improving: growth, not waste Q3 $1.52M 4,900 $103 Spend up 10 percent on flat customers: investigate before the next commitment purchase Q4 $1.45M 5,300 $91 Rightsizing and a savings plan on the stable baseline brought unit cost below Q1 Checklist Signs cost governance isn't working Not exhaustive, but the patterns that show up consistently when a cost program looks good on paper and isn't changing behavior. The last optimization effort was a one-time project with no recurring owner Untagged or misattributed spend is a growing percentage of the bill rather than shrinking Reserved capacity utilization is below 80 percent, meaning committed spend is going unused Non-production environments run around the clock with no automated schedule No one outside the finance or platform team can say what their own team's monthly cloud spend is The organization describes itself as FinOps "mature" but can't answer what a single team spent last month Cost is reported only as total spend, with no unit cost agreed with finance The program still uses pre-2025 FinOps vocabulary and cannot map spend to business-defined scopes Download Cloud FinOps workbook Six linked tabs: instructions, a rightsizing tracker, a reserved capacity break-even calculator, showback and chargeback allocation, the maturity assessment above made live, and a savings opportunity log. Every formula recalculates when you change an input. Download .xlsx

title: Cloud Service Mapper
description: A working reference for translating capabilities and services across AWS, Azure, GCP, and OCI, plus a side-by-side landing zone and foundational best-practices guide. Naming and feature parity shift as providers evolve their catalogs; treat this as a starting point for a conversation rather than a guarantee of equivalence.
body: The building blocks every cloud foundation needs before workloads land on it: how accounts are structured, how identity and network are established, and how guardrails get enforced from day one. This is the layer landing zone automation (Control Tower, Landing Zones, blueprints, or a hand-rolled equivalent) is meant to stand up before a single application team gets access.

title: Working with the CFO
description: The relationship where every capital allocation debate gets litigated. Distinct from the CEO relationship in what it requires: the CEO extends trust to judgment, while the CFO needs numbers that hold up under scrutiny.
body: Reference What the CFO needs from a CTO Different from what the CEO needs. The CEO wants judgment and a point of view; the CFO wants numbers that survive scrutiny. Need What it looks like What it isn't Predictable numbers A forecast that holds, or an early, honest flag the moment it won't A number that moves without warning and gets explained after the fact Defensible logic A stated method for how a figure was derived, so disagreement is about one assumption A number asserted with confidence but no visible derivation Honest framing ROI language where it fits, risk language where it doesn't ROI language forced onto every investment regardless of whether it applies No budget-meeting surprises Priorities shared before the formal cycle, so the CFO's first exposure isn't in a contentious room A ranked list revealed for the first time in front of other executives 1 Defending a number the CFO doesn't like The moment that determines whether the relationship is adversarial or productive going forward. How it works Show the derivation along with the conclusion. Walk through the specific assumption that, if changed, would change the number. Disagreement then becomes a conversation about one assumption, which is productive, instead of a vague sense that the number feels wrong, which goes nowhere. Where it goes wrong Presenting a number as settled fact with no visible derivation. Any pushback then becomes a credibility fight rather than a disagreement about a specific input, and credibility fights are much harder to walk back than assumption disagreements. 2 When ROI framing doesn't fit, and saying so Forcing every investment into ROI language is a common, well-intentioned mistake that costs credibility over time. What's ROI-shaped Infrastructure consolidation, a specific automation replacing manual work, a feature with a modeled revenue impact. These reduce cleanly to a number, and the CFO relationship is healthiest when that number is presented as exactly what it is. What isn't, and shouldn't be forced Security investment, reliability investment, and technical debt remediation reduce risk and avoid future cost; they rarely produce a clean, defensible ROI figure. Forcing one produces a number nobody believes, which costs more credibility than justifying the investment on risk grounds instead. 3 The budget conversation before the budget conversation Where most CFO relationships go wrong: the timing of when the CFO first sees the numbers, more than the numbers themselves. Practice Bring the CFO the pre-ranked capital allocation priorities before the formal budget cycle starts, in a one-on-one setting. The CFO should never see the logic behind technology priorities for the first time in a room with other executives present. Common failure mode The CFO's first exposure to how priorities were ranked happens live in the budget meeting itself, which makes every question feel adversarial even when it's just first contact with the reasoning. 4 Capitalization and accounting realities worth understanding A CFO thinks in capex versus opex and amortization schedules. A CTO who understands the basics speaks the CFO's language instead of translating everything through an interpreter. Software development costs that qualify for capitalization, versus costs that must be expensed immediately, materially change how a project's cost looks in a given quarter, independent of the project's actual value. Understanding this distinction, even at a high level, prevents a CTO from being caught off guard when a CFO cares more about the timing of a cost than its total, or pushes back on a schedule change that seems purely technical but carries a real capitalization consequence on the books. The rules themselves changed in 2025 on both the book and the tax side; the next section sets out what applies now. 5 The rules that change how a project looks, as of September 2026 Book accounting and tax treatment are separate systems with separate rules. A CTO does not need to apply them, but does need to know which one a CFO is talking about. Area Current rule Why the CTO should care Internal-use software, US GAAP (ASC 350-40) ASU 2025-06, issued September 2025 [1] , removes the old preliminary, development, and post-implementation stages. Capitalization starts once management has authorized and committed funding and completion is probable, and cannot start while significant development uncertainty remains. Effective for annual periods beginning after December 15, 2027; early adoption is permitted Agile teams no longer have to force work into waterfall stages to support capitalization, but novel or unproven work stays expensed until the uncertainty is resolved through coding and testing Software sold or licensed to customers (ASC 985-20) Costs are capitalized only after technological feasibility is established, which in practice leaves most development expensed Hosted SaaS generally follows the internal-use guidance instead; confirm with finance which model applies to your product Implementing SaaS you buy (ASU 2018-15) Implementation costs of a cloud computing arrangement are capitalized and amortized over the hosting term [2] , presented with the hosting fees as operating expense A large SaaS implementation can be spread over the contract rather than hitting one quarter, which changes how a CFO views the timing IFRS (IAS 38) Research is expensed; development is capitalized only when six criteria are met, including technical feasibility and a reliable measure of cost. Configuration and customization of SaaS is generally expensed unless it creates a separate asset Multinationals may report the same project differently under IFRS and US GAAP US tax: research and experimental costs (Sections 174 and 174A) The 2025 budget reconciliation law restored immediate deduction of domestic research costs, which include software development, for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024. Foreign research is still amortized over 15 years. [3] Smaller businesses, with average gross receipts of $31M or less, could elect to apply it retroactively to 2022 through 2024 Where the engineering work is done now changes the tax cost: domestic development is deductible at once, offshore development is not Sources FASB, ASU 2025-06, Internal-Use Software, September 2025 FASB, ASU 2018-15, cloud computing implementation costs, August 2018 IRS, Rev. Proc. 2025-28, Section 174A guidance Diagram The capitalization test, as three questions Why the same engineering work can hit the P&L in one quarter or be spread over several years. When internal-use software cost can be capitalized under ASU 2025-06 Internal-use software cost Funding authorized and committed? Completion probable? Significant development uncertainty resolved? Yes Yes Capitalize and amortize Yes Expense as incurred novel or unproven work stays here until coding and testing resolve the uncertainty No No No ASU 2025-06 replaces the old project-stage test. Effective for annual periods beginning after December 15, 2027; early adoption permitted. A summary for orientation, not accounting advice. Finance decides the treatment; the CTO's job is to know which question is holding a project in expense. 6 What to do with that as a CTO The practical consequences sit in how engineering tracks its work, not in the accounting itself. Practice Track time by project or initiative in the tool the team already uses, so finance can support capitalization and tax positions without a quarterly scramble. Tell the CFO early when a capitalized project is likely to be cancelled or fundamentally rescoped, because that can mean an impairment charge that has to be planned for, not discovered. Common failure mode A capitalized project is quietly abandoned, and finance learns about it at quarter close. The write-off is a surprise, the CFO concludes engineering does not understand the numbers, and every future capitalization request gets more scrutiny. 7 A worked example: defending a cloud forecast The derivation made visible, so the disagreement lands on one assumption instead of on the total. Line Figure Derivation Current run rate $4.20M a year 200M transactions a year at $0.021 each Volume next year 236M transactions Sales plan of 18 percent transaction growth, the assumption finance owns Unit cost next year $0.018 Commitment discounts on the stable baseline plus rightsizing already identified Forecast $4.25M 236M at $0.018; without the unit-cost work it would be $4.96M Sensitivity About $180K per 5 points of growth The one number to hand the CFO: if the growth assumption moves, this is how the forecast moves with it 8 Unit economics as the shared language The single change that most improves a CTO-CFO relationship is agreeing one or two unit costs and reporting them every month. Practice Pick a unit the business already counts: cost per transaction, per active customer, per claim processed, per patient encounter. Report infrastructure and tooling cost against it monthly. The FinOps Framework treats this as a core capability because it turns a growing bill into a question about efficiency rather than a question about spend. The failure mode Reporting total cloud spend alone. Total spend rises with success, so the CFO sees a number going up and the CTO argues it is fine, and neither can show who is right without a unit to divide by. Checklist Signs the relationship is unhealthy Patterns that show up when the CTO-CFO relationship has drifted into friction, regardless of how either person would describe it individually. Technology budget numbers get revised after the CFO has already committed them upward, more than once Every investment gets forced into ROI language regardless of whether it fits The CFO's first exposure to a priority ranking happens in a contentious budget meeting rather than before it The CTO can't explain, at a basic level, why a project's cost is phased the way it is on the books Disagreements about a number become personal rather than staying focused on a specific stated assumption The CTO cannot say which current projects are capitalized or what happens to the books if one is cancelled No unit cost has been agreed with finance, so every budget discussion is about total spend

title: The CTO Operating System
description: A concrete operating rhythm, what belongs at the daily, weekly, monthly, quarterly, and annual tier, plus a map of the areas of responsibility and how time allocation across them shifts as the organization scales.
body: Reference The five tiers Each tier exists to protect a different kind of work from being displaced by the others. The failure mode at each tier is different too. Tier What belongs here The failure mode Daily Active critical incidents, a risk that just became material, an executive blocker, a staffing emergency Anything that isn't time-sensitive creeps in, training the organization to escalate everything Weekly Engineering leadership sync, architecture and risk review, delivery health, recruiting, vendor issues Becomes a status-reporting ritual instead of a decision-making one Monthly Portfolio health, financials, security posture, reliability, people metrics Gets skipped under deadline pressure, exactly when it's most needed Quarterly Strategy reassessment, portfolio reallocation, board preparation, organizational health, technical debt review Treated as a report-out instead of a reallocation decision Annual Strategy reset, operating model, budget, org design, succession, architecture evolution, risk appetite Compressed into a single offsite instead of multi-week preparation Reference Areas of responsibility The five tiers above answer when. This answers what, and where to go on this site for the full depth on each.
