Area What it covers Depth on this site Technology strategy & direction The three-horizon investment split, tradeoffs, competitive positioning Technology Strategy Architecture & technical standards Capability models, principles, review governance Enterprise Architecture , Architecture Principles , Architecture Review Board Team & organization Structure, hiring, leveling, culture Org Design , Technical Hiring & Leveling , Engineering Culture Capital allocation & budget Portfolio-level investment decisions and the standing budget process Technology Capital Allocation , Running the Technology Budget Risk & security Stated risk appetite, security program, resilience Technology Risk Appetite , Security Program , Disaster Recovery Executive & board relationships The relationships that determine whether anything above gets funded or heard Working with the CEO , Working with the CFO , Board Reporting Delivery oversight Whether the organization is shipping, reliably, and knows it Engineering Metrics , Platform Engineering , Incident Response Hands-on technical work Direct coding, architecture deep-dives, code review No dedicated page; this is the category with the steepest decline as the organization scales, covered in the allocation table below M&A & diligence Applies only during an active transaction; there is no steady-state allocation Technology Diligence , Technology M&A Integration Reference Time allocation by company stage Illustrative rather than measured. The direction of the shift is the point, and no single number is precise; treat these as a starting frame to check your own calendar against rather than a target to hit exactly. Area Early-stage (under 50 eng) Scale-stage (50-500 eng) Enterprise (500+ eng) Technology strategy & direction 8% 15% 20% Architecture & technical standards 12% 15% 10% Team & organization 20% 20% 15% Capital allocation & budget 3% 8% 13% Risk & security 2% 7% 8% Executive & board relationships 10% 15% 22% Delivery oversight 15% 12% 10% Hands-on technical work 30% 8% 2% M&A and diligence isn't in the table because it isn't a steady-state allocation; it spikes heavily during an active transaction regardless of stage and returns to near-zero afterward. Diagram The same table, as the shape of the job Each bar is one stage; each segment is a share of the CTO's time. How a CTO's time shifts across areas as the company scales Early-stage (under 50 eng) 8% 12% 20% 10% 15% 30% Scale-stage (50 to 500) 15% 15% 20% 8% 7% 15% 12% 8% Enterprise (500+) 20% 10% 15% 13% 8% 22% 10% Strategy Architecture Team and org Capital and budget Risk and security Executive and board Delivery oversight Hands-on technical Hands-on work falls from 30 to 2 percent while executive, board, and capital work more than doubles. The shift is the point; the exact numbers are illustrative. Illustrative figures from the table above. Check your own calendar against the bar for your stage, not against the numbers. 1 Why cadence beats reactive prioritization The alternative to a stated cadence is an implicit one where whoever's loudest wins. What a working cadence does Separates urgent from important by giving each its own guaranteed slot, so a crisis doesn't consume the time that should go to the quarterly reallocation decision, and a quarterly review doesn't get treated with an urgency it doesn't warrant. What happens without one Everything competes for attention at the same priority, and daily fires win every time by default. Long-horizon work, technical debt, succession planning, architecture evolution, never gets protected time because nothing forces it onto the calendar. 2 Why allocation should shift over time The table above is one trajectory rather than three unrelated snapshots, and the shift itself has to be managed deliberately. What works Deliberately renegotiating your own time allocation at each scaling milestone (a new engineering VP hired, an architecture function stood up, a CFO relationship established), rather than letting the shift happen passively or resisting it out of habit. Common failure mode, in both directions A CTO who keeps writing code and reviewing every pull request well past the point the org has outgrown that involvement becomes the bottleneck they used to prevent. A CTO who delegates architecture and technical judgment before the org has anyone ready to hold it leaves a capability gap disguised as "scaling the team." 3 Intended versus actual: where the time really goes Most CTOs, asked to describe their allocation, would sketch something close to the table above. Their calendar usually disagrees. The gap An audited calendar usually shows meetings and reactive interruptions consuming twenty to thirty percentage points more than intended, almost always stolen from technology strategy and hands-on deep work, the two categories with no urgent deadline forcing their own defense. The fix The Thursday deep-work block described later on this page is the mechanism that defends strategy time from being silently eaten by whatever's urgent that particular week. Audit the calendar quarterly against the intended allocation; a gut sense of how the time is going is usually wrong in the same direction. 4 The daily tier is smaller than it feels Daily access to the CTO is available, which is exactly why the daily tier is the one most prone to creep. What belongs Only what can't wait: an active Sev1 or Sev2, a risk that just crossed a material threshold, an executive blocker stopping other work, a staffing emergency. If it could wait a week without cost, it isn't a daily item. The creep Status updates, routine decisions, and anything convenient get pulled into daily attention simply because the CTO is reachable. Once this starts, the daily tier stops protecting anything and becomes the default channel for everything. 5 The quarterly reset is a reallocation decision The tier most likely to exist on the calendar and produce nothing. What it should produce A change: capital moved between horizons, a strategic assumption revisited and possibly overturned, an initiative killed. If nothing changed, the review didn't do its job, regardless of how thorough the discussion was. What it becomes without discipline A calendar ritual summarizing the quarter that already happened, with no mechanism forcing a reallocation decision. The portfolio mix persists by inertia rather than by choice, and everyone leaves the room having confirmed what they already believed. 6 The weekly tier: sync rather than status The tier that runs most often and is therefore most at risk of becoming ritual rather than function. What works The weekly sync exists to make decisions that can't wait for the monthly review but don't rise to daily urgency: a hiring tradeoff, a scope cut, a risk needing more than one function's input. Attendees arrive having already read written updates, so the room's time goes to discussion and decisions rather than readout. What it becomes without discipline A round-robin status update where each function reports what it already reported in writing, consuming an hour that produces no decision. The decisions then happen in a separate, smaller, unscheduled conversation right after the official meeting ends, which quietly tells everyone where the work happens. 7 The annual tier, done properly The tier most often compressed, and the one where compression costs the most. What preparation looks like Weeks of groundwork before the offsite itself: the capital allocation review already run, the succession heatmap already updated, input already gathered from the people who'll be in the room. The offsite is for decisions and alignment; nobody should be seeing the material for the first time there. The compressed version A two-day offsite where strategy, budget, and org design all get worked out live in the room for the first time, producing decisions made on the spot that get quietly revisited and often reversed in the following weeks, once people have had time to think about material they were seeing for the first time under pressure. 8 A worked week, illustrative What the tiers look like assembled into one calendar, for a CTO at roughly a 150-engineer organization. Day What's on it Monday Weekly engineering leadership sync (60 min), written updates read in advance, agenda limited to decisions needed this week Tuesday 1:1s with direct reports, protected time for a Horizon 3 review if one is scheduled that month Wednesday Architecture Review Board slot (biweekly), CFO or CEO touchpoint if one is due this week Thursday Deep work block, no standing meetings, reserved for whatever the quarterly or annual tier currently needs preparation time for Friday Monthly portfolio and financial review (when due), otherwise a lighter day absorbing whatever the week's daily-tier items turned out to be The specific days don't matter. What matters is that Thursday's block exists at all: without a protected slot for the work that isn't urgent this week, it never happens, because something urgent is always available to fill the time instead. Checklist Signs the operating cadence has decayed The cadence can exist on a calendar and still not be functioning. These patterns show up when it's decayed into performance rather than practice. Daily conversations routinely include topics that could have waited a week The monthly portfolio or financial review has been skipped or shortened for three or more consecutive months Quarterly reviews haven't produced a capital reallocation in over a year No one outside the CTO could describe what happens at each cadence tier Annual strategy work gets compressed into a single offsite with little preparation beforehand The weekly sync consistently produces no decisions, and the decisions happen in a separate, unscheduled conversation afterward The calendar hasn't been audited against an intended time allocation in over a year, or ever Hands-on technical work hasn't declined as a share of time despite the organization scaling well past the stage where that made sense

title: CTO Leadership & Succession
description: Who runs things if the CTO disappears for ninety days, and more broadly, where institutional knowledge and leadership readiness sit versus where the org chart says they sit.
body: Reference The questions a succession plan has to answer If any of these has no answer, that is the finding, and it matters more than the document. Who can run engineering if the CTO is out for ninety days? Who can represent technology to the board? Who can run a major incident from start to finish? Who owns architecture, in practice rather than by title? Who is willing to challenge the CTO's thinking, and does the CTO listen to them? Where is institutional knowledge concentrated, and what happens to it if that person leaves? 1 The bus-factor question, applied to leadership The same discipline already applied to code ownership, extended to people in leadership roles. Practice Name the specific individuals whose departure would create a multi-month gap in a specific capability. A generic sense that "the team is strong" names nobody. Bus-factor analysis works the same way for leadership as it does for a codebase: identify where there's exactly one person who can do something critical. Common failure mode Assuming seniority or title implies succession readiness. A VP title doesn't mean that person could credibly represent technology to the board tomorrow if asked to do it without warning. 2 Building the bench deliberately A bench that exists by accident usually turns out not to exist at all when it's tested. Practice Give a successor candidate exposure before they need it: board attendance, incident command rotation, ownership of an architecture review. The first time someone does something this consequential shouldn't be during an emergency. Common failure mode Protecting a strong deputy from visibility because delegating feels slower than doing it yourself in the moment, which guarantees the organization has no bench when it's tested. 3 The leadership succession heatmap A small artifact that makes the state of succession visible instead of assumed. For each critical leadership function, name the current owner, the identified successor, and their readiness: ready now, six to twelve months out, or not yet started. A "none identified" in several rows is the finding the exercise exists to surface. It does not mean the document was filled out incorrectly. 4 The heatmap, worked What a filled-in version looks like, including the gaps most organizations would rather not write down. Function Current owner Identified successor Readiness Represent technology to the board CTO VP Engineering 6 to 12 months out Run engineering day-to-day CTO Director of Engineering Ready now Own architecture decisions Principal Architect None identified Not started Run a major incident end to end Head of SRE Senior SRE Lead Ready now Represent technology in an M&A conversation CTO None identified Not started The two "none identified" rows are the output of this exercise. An organization that fills every row in green either has an exceptional bench or went easy on itself; both are worth double-checking. 5 Emergency versus planned succession are different playbooks Confusing the two produces a plan that works for neither scenario. Emergency, no notice The interim owner named on the heatmap steps in immediately. Communication goes out within 24 to 48 hours, framed around continuity. The board is looped in the same day. The goal is stability. Naming a permanent replacement can wait weeks; the stability signal can't. Planned, with notice Use the notice period deliberately. The successor takes on visible responsibility gradually across the transition window rather than all at once on the last day. The departing CTO makes introductions, to the board, key customers, key vendors, personally, rather than leaving the successor to build those relationships cold after the fact. 6 What the board needs to know, and when Enough to avoid surprise. The detailed heatmap stays internal. Standing awareness The board should know a succession plan exists and who the interim contact would be, discussed at least annually as part of a broader risk conversation, the same cadence as the risk appetite review, rather than sprung on them during a departure. Common failure mode The board's first exposure to "who runs technology if the CTO leaves" is the day the CTO leaves, which is exactly the worst moment to be building consensus on an interim leader while also managing the departure itself. 7 Measure key-person concentration from evidence A bus-factor conversation based on impressions misses the concentrations nobody talks about. These sources show them directly. Where to look What to measure A red flag Version control history The truck factor: the fewest people whose departure would leave most of a codebase without anyone who has worked in it recently. Avelino and colleagues published a practical method in 2016 [1] A revenue-critical service where one person authored most recent changes Incident records Who commanded each Sev1 and Sev2 over the last year One person commanded more than half of major incidents Privileged access Holders of root, break-glass, domain registrar, and cloud organization owner credentials A single holder, which is a security finding as well as a succession one External relationships Who the key customers, vendors, auditors, and board members actually call Relationships that exist only through the CTO Runbooks and documentation Authorship and last-edit dates of operational documentation Critical procedures written by one person and never exercised by anyone else Sources Avelino and colleagues, A Novel Approach for Estimating Truck Factors, ICPC 2016 8 The emergency succession pack Prepared in advance, held by the CEO and general counsel, reviewed annually. It exists so the first 48 hours of an unplanned absence are execution, not discovery. Interim authority letter. The named interim leader and the scope of decisions they can make, pre-approved by the CEO Access continuity. How break-glass credentials are recovered, with at least two authorized holders and a tested procedure In-flight commitments. The top ten commitments with owners and dates: launches, contract renewals, audits, regulatory deadlines Relationship map. Key customers, vendors, auditors, and board members, with who should contact each and what they need to hear Top risks. The current top risks from the risk register and their owners Communication drafts. A holding message for the team, key customers, and the board, framed around continuity 9 Stretch assignments that actually build readiness Readiness is demonstrated, not declared. Each capability has an assignment that produces evidence. Capability Stretch assignment Evidence of readiness Represent technology to the board Present one section at two consecutive board meetings Board members ask the successor follow-up questions directly Run a major incident Command two Sev1 or Sev2 incidents with the incumbent shadowing, not leading Clean timeline, decisive calls, a postmortem the team trusts Own a budget Own one portfolio line through a full planning cycle, including the CFO review The number held, or the variance was flagged early with a derivation Handle a transaction Join the diligence or integration team for one deal Findings written up that the deal team acted on Hold external relationships Lead an executive briefing with a key customer The customer contacts the successor directly afterward Checklist Signs succession is assumed rather than planned Patterns that show up when succession planning exists as an idea but not as a tested plan. No one has been identified who could run engineering for ninety days without the CTO The people who could represent technology to the board have never done it Succession candidates have title and tenure but no exposure to the responsibilities they'd inherit The heatmap, if it exists, hasn't been updated since the last reorg A single individual's departure would create a gap the organization has no plan for The board has never heard the succession plan discussed outside of a departure Break-glass or organization-owner credentials have a single holder No emergency succession pack exists, so an unplanned absence starts with a search for passwords and commitments

title: Data Governance & Privacy
description: The regulatory and stewardship side of data: who owns it, what protects it, and what happens when a regulator or a customer asks what's held about them. Distinct from the architecture question of how data is stored and modeled.
body: Reference Which regulation applies, and when A starting map rather than a legal determination. Applicability depends on where customers are located, what data is collected, and industry-specific rules; confirm with counsel. Framework Triggers when Core obligation GDPR Processing personal data of individuals in the EU/EEA, regardless of where the company is based Lawful basis for processing, subject access and deletion rights, breach notification within 72 hours CCPA / CPRA Processing personal data of California residents above certain revenue or volume thresholds Disclosure of data collected, opt-out of sale/sharing, deletion rights HIPAA Handling protected health information as a covered entity or business associate Safeguards on PHI, breach notification, business associate agreements with vendors Sector and state-specific Financial services, children's data, and a growing list of individual state privacy laws Varies; often layered on top of the frameworks above rather than replacing them 1 Data classification as the foundation Every governance obligation downstream depends on first knowing what data exists and how sensitive it is. Practice A classification scheme with a small number of clear tiers, public, internal, confidential, restricted or regulated, applied at the point data is created or collected rather than retrofitted later through an audit. Every system holding data above the lowest tier has a named owner accountable for it. Common failure mode A classification policy that exists on paper but was never applied to the systems in production, so nobody can answer a basic question like "where does our customer PII live" without a multi-week investigation. 2 Subject access and deletion requests, operationally The rights GDPR and similar frameworks grant individuals are only real if the organization can fulfill them within the required window. Practice A documented, at least partially automated process for locating and exporting or deleting an individual's data across every system that holds it, tested against a live request rather than assumed to work. A tracked SLA against the regulatory deadline, with an owner accountable for meeting it. Common failure mode Fulfillment handled manually by whichever engineer is available, searching system by system with no authoritative list of where personal data lives, which routinely blows past the regulatory response window on anything beyond the simplest request. 3 A worked example: a request end to end What the practice above looks like against an incoming request, including where it commonly breaks. A request arrives through a web form and gets logged against the SLA clock immediately. The response process checks it against the data inventory: CRM, product database, support ticketing, and email marketing tool are all on the list, get queried, and the results get compiled into a portable export within the regulatory window. Where it commonly breaks: the analytics warehouse isn't on the inventory, because nobody classified it as holding personal data even though it has user IDs joinable back to an identity through the product database. The request gets marked complete while a meaningful chunk of what the organization holds on that person was never touched. This is why the inventory in section 1 has to be built by mapping data flows rather than by asking each team what they think they hold. 4 Ownership versus stewardship Two different roles that get conflated, and the conflation is where accountability gaps live. The distinction A data owner is accountable for the business decisions around a dataset, retention, access policy, whether it should exist at all. A data steward implements those decisions day to day, quality checks, access provisioning, pipeline maintenance. The same person can hold both roles, but the accountability should be explicit either way. Common failure mode Data that's used operationally by several teams but formally owned by none of them, so retention and access decisions never get made deliberately, they just accumulate as whatever the default happened to be. 5 Privacy by design rather than privacy as a review gate Where privacy consideration enters the development process changes how much friction it creates and how much risk it catches. Practice A lightweight privacy impact assessment built into the design phase for any feature touching personal data, before implementation starts, so decisions about what to collect and how long to keep it are made deliberately rather than defaulted to "collect everything, figure out retention later." Common failure mode Privacy review as a gate right before launch, which arrives too late to change the data model, so findings either get overridden under deadline pressure or become expensive retrofits after the feature is already live and being used. 6 Breach notification, the mechanics The 72-hour clock most people have heard of, and the specific way organizations usually miss it despite meaning to comply. What has to happen The 72-hour window starts when the organization becomes aware of a breach, well before it's fully understood. A preliminary notification with known facts, followed by updates as the investigation progresses, is compliant. Waiting for a complete picture before notifying anyone is a violation. Common failure mode Treating the deadline as something to hit only once the full scope is understood, which routinely blows past 72 hours since an investigation almost always takes longer than that, when a partial, updated notification would have been compliant from day one. 7 Cross-border data transfer, briefly A specific, common gap that surfaces during customer security reviews more often than during an internal audit. What's required Standard Contractual Clauses or an equivalent mechanism for transferring EU personal data outside the EEA, documented per vendor. A vendor's general terms of service do not cover it by default. Common failure mode Discovering during a customer security questionnaire that data has been flowing to a vendor or a region with no transfer mechanism in place, sometimes for years, because nobody mapped where data goes once it leaves the primary system. Checklist Governance red flags Patterns that show up when data governance exists as policy and stops there. No single, current inventory of where personal or regulated data lives across the estate Subject access or deletion requests handled manually with no tracked SLA against the regulatory deadline Data retained indefinitely by default because no one made an active decision to delete it Third-party vendors processing personal data with no data processing agreement or business associate agreement on file Privacy consideration enters the process only as a pre-launch review, never during design No documented transfer mechanism exists for personal data moving to vendors or regions outside its origin

title: Data Strategy
description: Beyond the storage architecture question: the operating model behind who owns data, self-service and literacy for the rest of the organization, metadata and lineage, real-time versus batch as an economic decision, build versus buy for the data stack, and whether the data itself is a product worth monetizing, alongside warehouse versus lakehouse versus mesh, master data management, and data quality as an AI prerequisite.
body: Framework Warehouse, lakehouse, or mesh The architectural choice most data strategy conversations start with. It is one of eleven topics on this page, and far from the whole strategy. Definitions first, then the tradeoff. Pattern What it is Fits when Struggles when Data warehouse A central repository holding structured, pre-cleaned data, modeled and indexed for fast BI and reporting queries. Structured, well-understood reporting needs, a single team can reasonably own data quality centrally Data sources are highly heterogeneous or domain ownership needs to be distributed Data lakehouse Cheap, flexible storage for raw data in any format, with a warehouse-style query and schema layer built on top of it. Mixed structured and unstructured data, need for both BI and ML workloads on the same underlying data Organizational discipline around schema and quality is weak; a lakehouse without governance becomes a swamp fast Data mesh A decentralized operating model: each business domain owns, publishes, and is accountable for its own data as a product, instead of one central team owning all of it. Large organization with independent domains, each with the capacity to own their own data product Applied to an organization too small to staff domain-level data ownership; the coordination overhead exceeds the benefit 1 Data as a product rather than a project The mindset shift underneath data mesh, applicable even in organizations not adopting the full mesh architecture. Project mindset A data pipeline gets built once to answer a specific question, then quietly rots as the source system changes underneath it, with no owner responsible for noticing or fixing the drift until a report breaks and someone escalates. Product mindset A dataset has a named owner, a defined quality bar, a consumer-facing contract (schema, freshness, meaning of each field), and a deprecation process, the same discipline applied to an internal API, applied to data instead. 2 The operating model: centralized versus federated data teams The organizational question underneath data mesh. Mesh describes how data is structured and owned technically; this is who's staffed, and where they report. Centralized One team owns data infrastructure, pipelines, and quality end to end across the whole company. Consistent standards and a single point of accountability, but becomes a bottleneck as the number of data-consuming teams grows past what one team can service responsively. Federated Data engineers embedded within each domain team, closer to the business context and faster to respond to that domain's needs. Standards and quality drift apart across domains without a strong central platform layer underneath providing shared tooling and governance. Most organizations land somewhere between the two: a central platform team providing shared infrastructure and standards, with domain-embedded engineers applying them locally. The failure mode is picking neither deliberately and ending up with an accidental, undocumented mix of both. 3 Data literacy and self-service for everyone beyond engineering Most data strategies are written for the people building the pipelines. This is about everyone else. What works A defined, curated set of self-service tools and pre-modeled datasets a non-technical analyst can query directly with guardrails, paired with training investment. A BI tool license handed out on its own is access, and access alone is not self-service. Common failure mode Self-service rolled out as tool access alone, which produces a proliferation of inconsistent, ungoverned dashboards each answering the same business question slightly differently, worse for decision-making than the centralized bottleneck it was meant to fix. 4 The golden record problem Master data management's central challenge: the same real-world entity represented differently across systems, with no single system holding the authoritative version. Why it's hard Customer data alone commonly lives in a CRM, a billing system, a support tool, and a product database, each with its own ID, its own update cadence, and its own partial view. Picking one as automatically authoritative is rarely right for every field. What works A defined source-of-truth mapping at the field level rather than the entity level: billing system is authoritative for payment status, CRM is authoritative for account ownership, product database is authoritative for usage data. Merge logic follows the mapping rather than picking one system to trust for everything. 5 Metadata, catalog, and lineage The layer that answers "what data do we have, what does it mean, and what breaks if I change it," consistently the weakest layer in organizations that otherwise have their data strategy in order. Why it's easy to skip A catalog and lineage graph don't show up in a quarterly roadmap the way a new pipeline or dashboard does, and the pain of not having them is diffuse: a slow, five-hop manual trace when a report breaks, a schema change shipped without knowing which six downstream jobs depend on it, an analyst who can't tell if a dataset is still owned or safe to trust. None of that shows up as a single dramatic incident, so it stays permanently below the cutline. What it buys you A catalog makes data discoverable and answers who owns it and whether it's still trustworthy. Lineage traces the path from source system to final dashboard or model, so a schema change or a broken pipeline can be traced to every downstream consumer in minutes instead of hours of tribal-knowledge archaeology. Both compound directly into the migration work further down this page (you can't safely run old and new in parallel if you don't know what depends on what) and into the AI grounding problem below (an agent that can't see schema, lineage, and ownership will guess). Buy here almost without exception; this is the same mature, competitive market referenced in Build versus buy below. The strategic decision is how to make metadata active from day one (tagged, enforced, and surfaced where people already work) instead of a static wiki page that's stale within a quarter. 6 Data quality as an AI prerequisite Why this page and the AI Governance Map 's data foundation layer are describing the same underlying problem from two different altitudes. The connection An AI system retrieving from or trained on poor-quality, poorly owned data inherits every one of that data's problems, at scale and with less visibility into the failure than a human analyst working the same data manually would have had. The practical implication Data quality and ownership work is the same foundational investment whether or not AI is on the roadmap, so it doesn't need to be framed as a prerequisite project to finish first. An organization with strong data product discipline has most of what AI governance's Layer 1 requires already in place. 7 Real-time versus batch, as a strategic decision An implementation detail on the surface, and an economic decision underneath, the same shape as the argument on Reliability as an Economic Decision , applied to data freshness instead of system uptime. When real-time earns its cost Fraud detection, live personalization, operational alerting, use cases where the value of the insight decays to near-zero within minutes or seconds, justifying real-time infrastructure's higher operational complexity and cost. The overengineering trap Building real-time streaming infrastructure for a report that gets looked at once a week. The freshness nobody needed doesn't add value; it just adds an ongoing operational tax the same way an unneeded ninth of availability does. 8 Build versus buy for the data stack See Build vs Buy for the general framework. Data tooling is one of the clearest places it applies. Where buying usually wins ETL and ELT tooling, data catalogs, and BI platforms are mature, competitive markets. Building these in-house rarely produces a competitive advantage and usually recreates a worse version of what's commercially available. Where building can be justified A novel data product that is itself the company's competitive differentiation. The infrastructure underneath it still gets bought. The same differentiation test from Build vs Buy applies directly: would the company lose deals or margin without owning this specifically. 9 Migrating between patterns without a rewrite Almost no organization starts on the right pattern and stays there forever. How the migration happens matters as much as which pattern is the eventual target. What works Run the new pattern alongside the old one for specific domains first, proving value on a bounded scope before cutting anything over globally. The same strangler-fig discipline covered on Legacy Modernization Execution applies directly here: incremental migration instead of a single rip-and-replace event. What backfires Announcing a full data platform migration as a single multi-quarter program with no intermediate value delivered along the way. Executive patience for a program with no visible output runs out well before a data platform migration typically finishes. 10 Data contracts, made concrete "Data contract" gets used loosely. A contract that doesn't specify these things isn't one. What a usable contract specifies The schema, a freshness commitment (how current the data is guaranteed to be), the meaning of each field in plain language, and a deprecation policy for breaking changes, published somewhere consumers can find and reference it rather than carried in a single engineer's memory. What passes for a contract but isn't A schema definition with no freshness commitment and no deprecation process. Consumers build against it anyway, because it's the only documentation available, and get broken silently the first time the upstream schema changes without warning. 11 Data as a product to external customers A question worth asking explicitly, even for organizations that will answer no. For some organizations, the data itself, aggregated, anonymized, or offered directly, is a monetization opportunity distinct from its internal analytical use. This isn't relevant to every company, but it's worth asking deliberately: does this organization sit on data that would be valuable to someone else, and if so, is productizing it worth the privacy, security, and packaging investment that would require. The answer for most companies is no, but it should be a considered no rather than a question nobody asked. 12 Standards and open formats worth knowing The data stack has converged on a few open standards in the last three years. Choosing them lowers switching cost later, which is the build-versus-buy argument applied to formats. Standard What it is Why it matters Open table formats: Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake, Apache Hudi Table layers over files in object storage that add transactions, schema evolution, and time travel The same tables can be read by several engines, so the lakehouse is no longer tied to one vendor's compute Open Data Contract Standard (ODCS), maintained by Bitol under the Linux Foundation A YAML standard for data contracts: schema, quality rules, service levels, ownership, and terms Makes section 10's contract definition machine-checkable in CI instead of a document nobody reads OpenLineage An open specification for emitting lineage events from pipelines and tools Lineage collected from many tools into one graph without per-vendor integrations DAMA-DMBOK (DAMA International) The reference body of knowledge for data management disciplines A shared vocabulary for governance, quality, metadata, and master data roles DCAM (EDM Council) A data management capability assessment model A way to benchmark maturity that regulators and auditors in financial services recognize Checklist Signs the data strategy isn't working Patterns that show up when a data strategy exists on a slide but isn't shaping how data gets built and maintained. No dataset has a named owner accountable for its quality A migration between patterns has stalled in an expensive middle state, both old and new running indefinitely with no plan to finish Data contracts, where they exist, specify a schema but no freshness or deprecation commitment The same real-world entity holds conflicting values across systems with no field-level source-of-truth mapping to resolve it AI initiatives are blocked by data quality issues that were already flagged as a data strategy risk before the AI initiative started Self-service access was granted with no curation or training, producing multiple dashboards that answer the same question differently Real-time infrastructure exists for a use case nobody has ever needed the data faster than daily for The centralized-versus-federated data team question was never decided deliberately, it just happened by accident of hiring

title: Decision ArchitectureSix stages from strategy to measurement, with the loop back to strategy
description: The actual shape underneath the 52 pages: six interconnected domains, a feedback loop, and a foundational layer that doesn't fit a sequence.
body: Where Six interconnected domains below: which page applies to which part of running the function, from setting direction to measuring whether it worked. How PrOACT: the process for making one decision well, run inside whichever of the six domains that decision currently sits in. Lens Foundational: standing habits of mind, evaluating evidence, seeing interconnection, managing key relationships, active regardless of domain or decision. Where · six interconnected domains 1 Strategy → 2 Operating Model → 3 Architecture → 4 Governance → 5 Execution → 6 Measurement ↻ Measurement feeds back into Strategy. The line is a loop. Lens · Foundational and cross-cutting, outside the sequence Epistemology & Research Methods Systems Thinking for CTOs Seeing the System Before Changing It Working with the CEO Working with the CFO Stakeholder Engagement Diagram The shape, drawn Six stages in sequence, one loop, one separation. Every page on this site sits in one of the six boxes, in the loop, or in the two bands underneath. Six stages from strategy to measurement, with the loop back to strategy 1 Strategy direction, priority 2 Operating model how decisions get made 3 Architecture what gets built 4 Governance constraints, control 5 Execution where it happens 6 Measurement did it work feedback: measurement re-opens strategy (plan, do, check, act) managing (operating model) is separated from governing (governance) HOW PrOACT: the process for making one decision well, inside any stage LENS Foundational: evidence, systems, relationships; active in every stage The green loop is Deming's plan-do-check-act applied to the whole function: measurement is the input to the next strategy rather than the end of the sequence. The dashed bracket is COBIT's separation of governing from managing, which is why operating model and governance are different stages. 1 · Strategy What are we trying to do Direction and priority, before anything gets built or governed. Technology Strategy Technology Strategy During a Downturn Data Strategy Innovation Portfolio Management Transformation and Innovation AI Portfolio Management Build vs Buy Business Case Calculator Vendor Evaluation Technology Diligence Technology Portfolio Management Technology Risk Appetite Technology Capital Allocation Highlighted links are hybrid: listed here and in a second domain below, on purpose. 2 · Operating Model How decisions get made, and by whom Turning direction into a functioning system: roles, rhythms, decision rights. The CTO Operating System Technology Decision Rights Role Boundaries Org Design Technology Governance Across Business Units Enterprise Architecture EA Maturity Assessment Governance, Risk & Compliance Building a Security Program CTO Leadership & Succession Running the Technology Budget Platform Engineering Architecture Review Board Technology Capital Allocation 3 · Architecture What gets built, and how it's structured The technical shape: systems, platforms, the application estate. AI Architecture Architecture Principles Library Cloud Service Mapper Application Portfolio Management Zero-Trust Maturity Identity & Access Architecture Integration & API Patterns Global Technology Operations Technical Debt Economics Cloud FinOps 4 · Governance Where the constraints and control mechanisms live The specific decisions worth constraining and why. Centralization for its own sake is a different thing. AI Governance Data Governance & Privacy Security & Compliance Maturity Regulatory Map Technology Risk Appetite ADRs & Roadmapping Disaster Recovery & Business Continuity Architecture Review Board Board Reporting 5 · Execution Where it happens, day to day Delivery, incidents, people, the work itself once direction and constraints are set. Agile and SAFe Engineering Culture Technical Hiring & Leveling AI and the Engineering Operating Model Incident Response Observability & SRE Operating Model Legacy Modernization Execution Disaster Recovery & Business Continuity Technology M&A Integration M&A Diligence Kit SaaS Contract & Renewal Negotiation Vendor Contract Lifecycle Management ADRs & Roadmapping 6 · Measurement Whether any of it worked The evidence that feeds back into Strategy, closing the loop rather than ending it. Engineering Metrics Reliability as an Economic Decision AI FinOps Board Reporting Technology M&A Integration M&A Diligence Kit SaaS Contract & Renewal Negotiation Cloud FinOps How · PrOACT Making one decision well Hammond, Keeney, and Raiffa's PrOACT framework ( Smart Choices , 1999, building on Howard Raiffa's earlier decision analysis work) provides a structured sequence for making a decision well, run inside whichever of the six domains the decision currently sits in. PrOACT step What it looks like Where it lives here Frame the Problem State what's being decided, and what's explicitly out of scope Strategy, Technology Strategy Objectives State what you're optimizing for before you look at options, so the options don't retroactively define the goal Strategy, Business Case Calculator Alternatives Options that could each win, rather than the one you already prefer plus a straw man Governance, ADRs & Roadmapping Consequences Confidence-graded evidence for what each alternative produces Foundational, Epistemology & Research Methods Tradeoffs Explicit scoring against the same criteria, so the tradeoff is visible instead of hidden inside a gut call Strategy, Vendor Evaluation Choose A named, accountable owner makes the call Operating Model, Technology Decision Rights Implement and monitor Ship it, then check whether it produced what the objectives step said it should Execution and Measurement, Engineering Metrics The six domains above answer where a decision's supporting content lives. PrOACT answers how you make any one decision well, regardless of which domain it's in. A CTO doing both, using the domain map to find the right page and the PrOACT sequence to reason through the call, is the difference this page exists to make explicit. Lens · Foundational What doesn't fit the sequence, and why forcing it would mislead Six pages that are never a step you pass through once. They sit underneath every domain or run continuously alongside all of them. Epistemology & Research Methods Systems Thinking for CTOs Seeing the System Before Changing It Working with the CEO Working with the CFO Stakeholder Engagement Epistemology is about how you evaluate claims across every domain above. Systems Thinking is the lens, and Seeing the System Before Changing It is the diagnostic that lens produces; both apply regardless of which domain the decision sits in. The relationship pages are never a phase you complete. They stay active regardless of which domain the work is in.

title: Disaster Recovery & Business Continuity
description: What happens when a primary system, region, or data center becomes unavailable. Distinct from day-to-day incident response: this is about surviving the loss of something whole rather than degrading gracefully around a partial failure.
body: Reference RTO and RPO, defined by tier Recovery Time Objective is how long the business can tolerate a system being down. Recovery Point Objective is how much data loss is acceptable. Both should be set by business impact rather than by what's technically easy. Tier Example systems Typical RTO Typical RPO Tier 1: Revenue-critical Payment processing, core transaction systems, customer-facing platform Minutes to under 1 hour Near-zero, seconds to minutes Tier 2: Operationally important Internal tools, reporting, secondary customer channels 4 to 24 hours Minutes to hours Tier 3: Deferred impact Archival systems, non-urgent internal tools Days Up to 24 hours 1 Setting RTO and RPO The most common DR failure is a target that was never realistic in the first place; the bad recovery only exposes it. Practice Ask the business owner what happens at 1 hour, 4 hours, and 24 hours of downtime for each system, in dollars or customer impact, then set the target from that answer. The target should hurt to miss; if missing it wouldn't matter, the system is probably a lower tier than it's currently classified. Common failure mode An RTO of 4 hours written into a policy document, never tested, while the infrastructure would take 2 days to recover. The number on paper and the number that's true are different, and nobody finds out which one is real until a disaster. 2 Backup testing discipline A backup that has never been restored is a hypothesis. Practice Scheduled, automated restore tests, rather than manual ones someone remembers to run occasionally, with the restore time measured and compared against the stated RTO every time. A backup that restores successfully but takes 3x longer than the RTO promises is a finding. Common failure mode Backups that run successfully and are never restored until the day they're needed, at which point corruption, missing dependencies, or forgotten configuration steps turn a routine recovery into an extended outage. 3 Tabletop exercises Rehearsing the decision-making as well as the technical recovery steps. Practice A scheduled exercise, at least annually for Tier 1 systems, that walks a realistic scenario end to end: who declares the disaster, who has authority to fail over, how customers get notified, and how the team knows recovery is complete rather than just visually normal again. Common failure mode A DR plan that's technically sound but has never been rehearsed by the humans who'd execute it, so the event itself surfaces confusion about authority and sequencing that the document assumed away. 4 Multi-region versus single-region, costed Multi-region resilience is expensive, and the expense is often invisible until someone prices it out. Practice Cost the multi-region architecture (data replication, cross-region networking, the operational overhead of maintaining two live environments) against the quantified cost of the downtime it prevents. For revenue-critical systems, this usually clears the bar. For everything else, it often doesn't. Common failure mode Multi-region architecture applied uniformly across the whole estate because it feels like the responsible default, without anyone pricing whether the systems getting that treatment warrant it. 5 Answering the board question "What's our recovery time if we lose a region" is a standard board question. The credible answer is specific rather than reassuring. A credible answer names the tier, states the tested RTO with the date it was last verified, and states which systems don't yet meet target. "We're covered" without those specifics is the answer of someone who hasn't tested it recently, and board members who've heard that answer before know the difference. Interactive Is the faster recovery time worth its cost? List the systems you are deciding on. For each, the tool compares the expected annual value of a faster recovery (probability of an event, times hours saved, times downtime cost) with what the faster RTO costs, then ranks the systems. It is the same expected-value logic as before, applied across the estate. Runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere. Cost of downtime, per hour ($) Current RTO (hours) Target RTO (hours) Probability of a disaster event this year (%) Annual cost to reach the faster RTO ($) Calculate 6 Communicating DR investment as insurance See Working with the CFO for the general argument about when ROI framing doesn't fit. DR spend is one of the clearest examples. Practice Frame DR investment the way an insurance purchase gets framed: an expected-value calculation across many possible years rather than a promised return in any single year. The probability input in the calculator above is an estimate, and saying so out loud is more credible than pretending it is precise. Common failure mode Presenting a DR business case with the same confident ROI language used for a revenue-generating feature, which invites exactly the wrong question, "did we get that return this year," when the true answer is that a well-run DR program often means the disaster didn't happen to test it. 7 Standards and regulatory expectations Obligations differ by sector; this is where most auditors and examiners start. Source What it expects ISO 22301:2019 A certifiable business continuity management system: impact analysis, strategies, exercises, and improvement [1] EU Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) For EU financial entities since January 2025: tested ICT continuity and recovery plans, and threat-led penetration testing at least every three years for entities designated as significant [2] HIPAA Security Rule, 45 CFR 164.308(a)(7) A contingency plan with data backup, disaster recovery, emergency mode operation, and testing [3] FFIEC Business Continuity Management booklet (2019) US financial institutions: resilience across the whole organization, including third parties [4] NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Contingency planning guide for information systems; widely used outside government [5] Sources ISO 22301:2019, Business continuity management systems Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 (Digital Operational Resilience Act) 45 CFR 164.308(a)(7), contingency plan FFIEC, revised Business Continuity Management booklet, November 2019 NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide 8 Ransomware changes the recovery design Most DR plans assume the failure is an outage. Ransomware assumes the attacker has already reached the backups. Design for it Keep at least one backup copy immutable or offline, restore into an isolated clean environment, and rebuild identity systems first, since a compromised identity provider re-infects everything restored after it. The 3-2-1-1-0 rule summarizes it: three copies, two media, one offsite, one immutable or offline, zero errors on test restores. Test for it A tabletop that assumes backups are encrypted, and a timed restore of a critical system from the immutable copy alone. The time measured there, not the replication lag, is the realistic recovery time. Checklist DR red flags Patterns that show up consistently when a disaster recovery program looks complete on paper and isn't. RTO and RPO targets exist in a document but have never been tested against measured recovery time The last full-scale restore test or tabletop exercise was more than a year ago, or has never happened Recovery depends on a single person's institutional knowledge rather than a documented, rehearsed runbook Backup and primary infrastructure share a failure domain, same region, same provider account, same network path, undermining the recovery they're meant to enable Tier classification hasn't been revisited since the systems it covers changed significantly DR investment gets pitched with certain-return ROI language rather than framed as insurance against a probabilistic event

title: EA Maturity Assessment
description: A structured baseline across six dimensions of enterprise architecture maturity, with a working scoring calculator and the diagnostic patterns that show up when specific dimensions diverge from each other.
body: 1 What this assessment is for Produces two things and nothing more: a defensible baseline across six dimensions, and a starting position for a twelve-month improvement plan. It doesn't produce a grade. Most useful when A new EA leader takes over the function An organization is deciding whether to invest in EA at all An established function has plateaued and needs a structured look at why The scoring scale 1, Absent: no recognizable version exists 2, Emerging: exists in pockets, driven by specific individuals, unreliable beyond them 3, Defined: named, documented, applied consistently in most cases 4, Managed: measured, reviewed, improves in response to data 5, Optimized: integrated into business decision-making with evidence of enterprise-wide impact Most functions should target 3 to 4 across all six. A 5 in every dimension usually signals over-investment relative to risk rather than excellence. Framework The six dimensions Each answers a different question about the function. A function can be strong in one and weak in another; that unevenness is the useful signal, and averaging it away loses it. Dimension What it asks Strategy Alignment Does EA's work connect to the strategy the enterprise is pursuing? The dimension most commonly rated optimistically. Governance Are architectural decisions made through a process that scales, with exceptions tracked and reviews credible to delivery teams? Domain Coverage Does the function cover the domains EA should cover, or is it a strong application-architecture function playing above its weight class? Delivery Integration Does EA produce better decisions in delivery, or operate as a parallel track delivery works around? Talent & Operating Model Is the function organized to be sustainable: roles, succession, sponsor relationships, demand management? Artifacts & Tooling Does the function maintain what it produces, at a cost proportionate to the value? Scored last and carefully; the easiest dimension to over-invest in. Interactive Score your own function Score each dimension now and at target, and record the overall score you expected before you started. The tool flags the diagnostic patterns below, ranks the gaps, and shows the self-perception gap the worked example describes. For a full assessment, score independently across 2 to 4 scorers before reconciling, per the facilitator guidance below; this tool is a single scorer's pass. Runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere. Calculate maturity score 2 Running it as a full assessment This page's calculator is a single-scorer pass. A full assessment is deliberately multi-evaluator, same principle as the vendor scorecard, for the same reason. Select scorers The EA leader scores, plus two to four others selected for angle of view rather than seniority: a senior delivery leader, a business sponsor who consumes EA output, an outside solution architect, optionally a prior EA leader. Avoid scorers who have a position to defend. Score, then reconcile Each scorer completes the assessment independently, same briefing, same scale, no discussion, forty-five minutes. Then a ninety-minute session, dimension by dimension: where scores diverge by more than one point, discuss it. The discussion is the data, and persistent divergence is itself a finding worth preserving rather than averaging away. The overall average is the least interesting number in the assessment, useful for trending year over year and useless for conclusions in any single pass. Individual indicators scored 1 or 2 are what a roadmap should be built around. Reference Diagnostic patterns the calculator flags The average hides the finding. These are the score shapes that recur, what each usually means, and what to do about it before building a roadmap. Pattern What it usually means First move Artifacts & Tooling high, Delivery Integration low A documentation function. The models are beautiful and delivery teams do not consult them Stop producing artifacts for a quarter; embed architects in the two most important delivery streams and measure whether decisions change Strategy Alignment high, everything else low The EA leader is trusted by executives and the function has no machinery beneath that trust Governance first: a lightweight review path with a written exception process, so the trust converts into decisions that stick Governance high, Delivery Integration low A gate. Reviews happen, delivery teams route around them, and the exception log is where the architecture that ships gets decided Move review earlier and make it evidence-based; see Architecture Review Board Domain Coverage low, all else moderate A strong application architecture group called EA. Data, security, and business architecture are uncovered Name the uncovered domains explicitly and decide whether to staff them, partner for them, or state that they are out of scope Talent & Operating Model at 1 or 2 with anything at 4 Key-person risk. The function's maturity is one resignation away from a 2 Succession and demand management before any further capability investment Uniform 3s Either a balanced, mid-maturity function or a single scorer who did not want to commit. The multi-scorer process tells you which Run the reconciliation session before drawing any conclusion Worked example Reading one score pattern The score that most often surprises the EA leader who runs it on their own function. The scores Strategy Alignment 2, Governance 3, Domain Coverage 3, Delivery Integration 2, Talent & Operating Model 2, Artifacts & Tooling 4. Average 2.7. The EA leader's own pre-assessment estimate was 3.5. The function has a mature capability model, a current application catalog, and a well-maintained standards library. Delivery leaders, asked in the reconciliation session, could not name a decision the function had changed in the past year. The reading This is the library pattern: the highest-scoring dimension is the one that is easiest to over-invest in, and the two lowest are the ones that determine whether the function matters. The artifacts are fine as they are; the next dollar should go elsewhere. The twelve-month roadmap that came out of it moved one architect into the payments modernization program full time, replaced the monthly architecture forum with a review attached to live design work, and set one measurable target: three documented decisions per quarter where a delivery team changed course because of an EA input. A year later the artifact score had not moved and the function's budget had been protected in a cost cut, which is the outcome that matters. Method Turning the result into a twelve-month roadmap The assessment produces a baseline. The roadmap is what justifies having run it. Quarter Focus Evidence at quarter end Q1 The single lowest-scoring dimension that determines relevance, almost always Delivery Integration or Strategy Alignment One delivery stream with an architect embedded; one strategic initiative with an EA-authored options paper that executives used Q2 Governance that delivery teams experience as help: review path, exception process, decision records Reviews happening on live design work, exception log with owners, first ADRs published Q3 Operating model: demand intake, roles, succession, sponsor cadence A written demand process, a named successor for the EA lead, a quarterly sponsor review on the calendar Q4 Domain coverage decision and re-score with the same scorers An explicit statement of which domains EA covers; a second assessment showing movement in the dimensions targeted and, ideally, no movement in Artifacts Re-score annually with the same scorers where possible. The trend across two or three years is the first point at which the average becomes meaningful; in any single year, the individual indicators at 1 and 2 are the whole story. Common pitfall Scoring on intent The assessment is only as good as the scoring, and the scorer with the most at stake is usually the EA leader. What it looks like Governance is scored a 4 because a review process is documented and a board meets monthly. Nobody checks how many designs went through it, how many exceptions were granted, or whether any decision was ever reversed by it. The score reflects the process that exists on paper, and the roadmap built on it fixes the wrong dimension. The counter-move Every score of 3 or above needs an artifact: the review log, the exception register, the decision that changed, the sponsor's own words. If the artifact cannot be produced in the reconciliation session, the score drops to a 2 and the missing artifact becomes a roadmap item. This is the same discipline the Zero-Trust Maturity and Security & Compliance Maturity assessments apply, for the same reason.

title: Engineering Culture
description: What shapes how an engineering organization behaves day to day, beyond org charts and values decks. The thing every other page under building the organization quietly assumes is healthy underneath it.
body: Reference Symbol versus substance The gap between what an organization says its culture is and what determines behavior is where most culture work fails. Symbol What determines behavior Stated values on a wall or a slide What gets rewarded in promotion and compensation decisions A culture deck What happens in the room when a deadline and a quality standard conflict Perks and amenities Whether people ship work they're proud to put their name on "We value work-life balance" Whether anyone leaves on time without guilt or a backlog of resentment 1 Culture is whatever gets rewarded The clearest predictor of the culture you have is what a high performer gets away with that no one else would. What shapes it Promotion criteria, what leadership visibly celebrates in public forums, and what gets quietly tolerated from a top performer that would draw a consequence for anyone else. These three things are the culture, regardless of what the values document says. The trap Writing a values document and treating the exercise as complete, without ever auditing whether promotion decisions, performance reviews, and day-to-day tolerance reflect those stated values. The gap between the two is usually visible to everyone except leadership. 2 A worked example: diagnosing a gap What the audit in section 1 looks like run against data instead of impressions. A company's values deck states "we value work-life balance and sustainable pace." Nobody has ever written a rule contradicting that. But a look at the last two promotion cycles against work-pattern data shows every engineer promoted to senior had a visible pattern of late-night and weekend Slack activity; nobody promoted in that window kept a strictly nine-to-six pattern. No survey would have caught this, since a pulse survey asks about stated values rather than revealed behavior. Cross-referencing promotion outcomes against a specific behavioral signal (hours of activity rather than self-reported sentiment) made the reward function visible immediately. The stated value and what gets rewarded had diverged completely, and the gap stayed invisible until someone looked at the right data instead of asking the right question. 3 Blameless is a practice See Incident Response for the mechanics of a blameless postmortem. This is about what determines whether the practice survives contact with a bad outage. What sustains it Leadership visibly not punishing the engineer who caused a serious incident, in front of the team, repeatedly, until it's trusted rather than merely declared in a policy document. Trust here is built slowly, one incident at a time. What kills it One visible instance of blame after a sufficiently bad incident erases months of stated blameless culture instantly. The trust is asymmetric: it takes a long series of consistent restraint to build and one data point to destroy. 4 Whose culture wins in a merger or a scaling moment Two cultures rarely blend into something new. One absorbs the other, and which one wins is more predictable than most leaders expect. What determines dominance The size of the surviving organization, which leadership team's members remain in place after the transition, and which systems and processes get adopted as the combined standard. All three tend to point the same direction. The mistake Assuming a merger or rapid scaling event will produce a neutral, blended culture through goodwill alone, rather than deliberately deciding what's worth preserving from the smaller or absorbed side and building that preservation explicitly into the integration plan. 5 Remote and hybrid culture specifically The core mechanism doesn't change with location. What changes is how much deliberate effort it takes to make it visible. What stays the same Culture is still whatever gets rewarded. If anything, it becomes more visible remotely, since behavior happens in trackable channels, Slack timestamps, meeting attendance, async response times, rather than the more ambiguous signal physical presence in an office used to provide. What changes The blameless-culture trust described above depends on visible, repeated leadership behavior. Remote teams see far less of that by default, no hallway conversations, no visible body language during a tense moment, so leadership has to be far more deliberate about making the same restraint visible through explicit written communication rather than trusting it'll simply be felt. 6 Burnout as a distinct signal from attrition Someone burned out and still employed is a worse leading indicator than someone who already left. Why it's distinct Declining output and a rising error rate in a burned-out but still-employed engineer often get misread as a performance problem rather than a culture symptom, precisely because they haven't yet generated the attrition data point that would trigger an investigation. What to watch A sudden change in someone's own baseline, working hours, response time, output quality, is a more reliable signal than a static threshold. A chronically overworked culture normalizes a baseline that looks fine compared to itself but wouldn't compare well to a healthy organization. 7 Measuring culture without gaming it See Engineering Metrics for the trust problem that determines whether any metrics program survives; culture measurement has the identical problem. What to track Voluntary attrition, especially regretted attrition among senior or high-performing people, pulse survey trends over time rather than a single point-in-time score, and whether people internally refer friends for open roles, a strong revealed-preference signal that's hard to fake. What doesn't work A single annual engagement survey score treated as the complete picture, gamed the same way any metric gets gamed once it's tied to a leader's own performance review and that leader controls how the survey gets framed and followed up on. 8 What the research actually says Culture is one of the few areas where the evidence is consistent across many years of studies. Leaning on it moves the conversation away from opinion. Source Finding worth using Ron Westrum's typology of organizational cultures (2004) Organizations fall into pathological, bureaucratic, or generative patterns, distinguished mainly by how information flows and how messengers are treated [1] DORA research program (Google Cloud, annual since 2014) Generative culture, in Westrum's sense, repeatedly predicts better software delivery and organizational performance. The 2025 report found AI amplifies whatever culture and practices a team already has [2] Amy Edmondson on psychological safety (1999 onward) Teams that feel safe to raise problems report more errors early and learn faster, which looks worse on a dashboard in the short run and better in outcomes [3] Google's Project Aristotle (2015 to 2016) Psychological safety was the strongest of the factors that distinguished effective teams, ahead of team composition [4] SPACE framework (Forsgren, Storey, and others, 2021) Productivity has several dimensions, including satisfaction and wellbeing; measuring output alone misreads it [5] DevEx research (Noda, Storey, Forsgren, Greiler, 2023) Developer experience comes down to three things leaders can change: fast feedback loops, manageable cognitive load, and protected flow time [6] Sources Westrum, A typology of organisational cultures, 2004 DORA, 2025 State of AI-assisted Software Development Edmondson, Psychological Safety and Learning Behavior in Work Teams, 1999 Google re:Work, Understand team effectiveness Forsgren and colleagues, The SPACE of Developer Productivity, ACM Queue, 2021 Noda, Storey, Forsgren, Greiler, DevEx, ACM Queue, 2023 9 Measuring it: a short team-level pulse A small, repeatable instrument beats an annual engagement survey for spotting drift. Run it quarterly at team level, report trends, and never tie it to an individual manager's rating. Ask each engineer to rate agreement from 1 to 7 with six statements built on Westrum's dimensions, paraphrased here: People on my team actively seek out the information they need, and get it People who bring bad news or raise problems are not punished for it Responsibilities are shared rather than pushed onto others Working across team boundaries is encouraged When something fails, the response is inquiry into the system, not a search for someone to blame New ideas are welcomed, including from junior people Add two DevEx items, how often work is blocked waiting on someone else and how often the engineer gets two uninterrupted hours, and pair the results with regretted attrition and internal referral rates. The single most useful reading is the item that moved most since last quarter, not the average. 10 A worked example: reading the pulse after a reorg Three teams, the same quarter, the same reorg. The averages look similar; the pattern underneath does not. Team Average before Average after Largest single change What it pointed to Payments 5.6 5.4 Cross-team work, down 0.4 Normal adjustment to a new neighbor team; no action beyond a joint planning session Platform 5.8 4.1 Messengers not punished, down 2.3 A new manager had criticized an engineer in public for flagging a launch risk. Addressed directly with the manager within the week Mobile 4.9 5.3 New ideas welcomed, up 1.1 The reorg removed an approval layer; worth protecting in the next org change Checklist Signs culture is deteriorating beneath a healthy-looking surface Patterns that show up before the problem is visible in a survey score or an exit interview. Voluntary attrition among senior or high-performing engineers is elevated, even if overall attrition looks acceptable Employees have quietly stopped referring friends for open roles The stated values and the working promotion criteria have diverged, and most people already know it Blameless postmortems exist as a stated policy, but the last serious incident produced visible blame anyway Pulse survey trends are flat or declining while leadership continues describing culture as strong in the same conversation Someone's individual work baseline has shifted noticeably and it's being treated as a performance issue rather than investigated as a possible culture symptom Culture is measured only by an annual engagement score, never by team-level items on information flow and psychological safety

title: Engineering Metrics
description: The five DORA metrics and their benchmark bands, why story points and lines of code persist despite being poor proxies.
body: Framework The five DORA metrics The closest thing the industry has to a validated, research-backed set of engineering performance metrics. They are an incomplete picture on their own, and still the right starting point before inventing something else. Metric What it measures Elite (2024 cluster) Low (2024 cluster) Deployment frequency How often code reaches production On demand, multiple times a day Between once per month and once every six months Change lead time Time from commit to running in production Under one day Between one month and six months Change fail rate Percentage of deployments requiring immediate intervention Around 5 percent Around 40 percent Failed deployment recovery time How long it takes to recover from a failed deployment Under one hour Between one week and one month Deployment rework rate Percentage of deployments that are unplanned rework fixing a previous release rather than new feature work No standardized industry band yet; track your own trend for this one Deployment rework rate was added to the model in 2024 [1] as a third stability signal alongside change fail rate. It's newer, and unlike the first four metrics, the industry hasn't converged on performance bands for it. That is a useful reminder that even a well-established framework keeps evolving, and that the confidence attached to a number should match how long it's been tested rather than how official it sounds. Sources DORA, 2024 Accelerate State of DevOps Report Interactive Classify your own numbers Enter one row per team. Each metric is banded against the table above: Elite means daily or more frequent deploys, lead time under a day, change fail rate of 5 percent or less, and recovery under an hour. Low means deploying less than about once a month, lead time over a month, change fail rate of 30 percent or more, or recovery over a week. Anything between is reported as Medium here; the 2024 report split that middle into High and Medium clusters. The tool also flags teams whose speed is not matched by stability. Runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere. Deployment frequency (deploys per week) Change lead time (hours, commit to production) Change fail rate (%) Failed deployment recovery time (hours) Deployment rework rate (%, informational only) Classify 1 What not to measure, and why it persists anyway Story points, lines of code, and commit count remain common despite being well understood as poor proxies. Worth naming why they persist. Why they're wrong Story points measure estimation rather than output, and are calibrated differently per team, making cross-team comparison meaningless. Lines of code rewards verbosity over good design. Commit count rewards small, frequent commits over meaningful ones, and is trivially gamed the moment someone knows it's being watched. Why they persist They're easy to pull from existing tools with no new instrumentation, and they produce a number, which satisfies a reporting requirement even when the number means very little. Replacing them requires investing in DORA-style instrumentation that most orgs haven't built yet. 2 Distribution over average The most common mistake in reading engineering metrics: reporting a mean when the distribution is what matters. Why the average lies A team with a median lead time of two hours and a long tail of three-week outliers has a very different problem than a team with a consistent two-day lead time across the board, but both can produce the same average. The fix rarely looks the same for both. What to look at instead Report the median and the 90th percentile together. The median tells you what's typical; the gap between median and p90 tells you how bad the worst case gets, and that gap is usually where the operational risk lives. 3 Using metrics without weaponizing them The trust problem that kills a metrics program faster than any technical flaw in the metrics themselves. What works Metrics owned and reviewed at the team level first, with the team using them to improve their own process, before any number rolls up to a leadership dashboard. People who see a metric being used to improve their own work engage with it in good faith. What backfires Individual-level metrics tied to performance review, or a leadership dashboard that ranks teams against each other. Both produce the same response: people optimize for the number instead of the outcome the number was supposed to represent, and the metric stops meaning anything. 4 Beyond DORA: what the five metrics don't capture DORA measures delivery. It says nothing about the team's health or whether the work being delivered is sustainable. Signal What it catches that DORA misses Code review turnaround time A team can deploy frequently while pull requests sit unreviewed for days; this is often the bottleneck DORA's lead time number is quietly absorbing Pages per on-call rotation Elite change fail rate and failed deployment recovery time can coexist with an on-call rotation that's burning people out through sheer volume of low-severity noise Technical debt ratio (tracked debt items versus new feature work merged) Delivery metrics can look healthy for months while debt accumulates invisibly until it surfaces as a sudden change fail rate spike Time-to-first-commit for new hires A slow, painful onboarding process doesn't show up in any DORA number until the new hire's productivity ramp is already six weeks behind where it should be 5 The conversation is the point, and the dashboard is only the prompt A metrics program that produces a dashboard nobody discusses has produced nothing. Where metrics earn their keep In a team retro, where the team itself asks why lead time crept up this sprint and proposes a change to test next sprint, or in a 1:1 where a manager notices a specific engineer's review turnaround has quietly doubled and asks what's going on before it becomes a pattern. The number is a prompt for a conversation rather than the output. Where they don't A dashboard displayed in a wiki that gets glanced at during a monthly all-hands and never referenced between updates.
