Building the dashboard is the easy 20 percent; making it something a team uses to change a decision is the hard 80 percent, and most metrics programs stop at the easy part. 6 A worked example What reading distribution instead of average looks like against concrete numbers. The team: eight engineers, reports a median lead time of 4 hours (inside the Elite band) and a change fail rate of 12 percent (between the High and Medium clusters). On paper, a strong team. The distribution check: p90 lead time is 11 days. Roughly one deployment in ten is taking over a week and a half, dragging against a median that looks fine. Digging in, the p90 outliers cluster around one specific service with a manual, undocumented deployment step that only two engineers know how to run. What the average would have hidden: a leadership dashboard reporting only the median would show this team as healthy indefinitely, right up until both engineers who know the manual step are unavailable during an incident on that specific service, at which point failed deployment recovery time, the metric that matters most in the moment, blows well past any benchmark band. The fix that came out of the conversation: the team automated the manual step as a two-week investment, dropping p90 lead time to under two days within the next reporting cycle. The median barely moved, because the median was never the problem.

title: Enterprise Architecture
description: Enterprise architecture end to end: what it is and is not, the artifact chain from strategy to a buildable decision, how to build and use a capability model and operating model canvas, writing a target state executives finish, capability-driven roadmaps, portfolio and modernization calls, assessing an inherited architecture, EA in M&A, and how the EA function itself should run, relate, fail, and be measured.
body: 1 What enterprise architecture is The discipline of shaping how an organization operates: translating strategy into the capabilities, processes, information, and technology required to execute it, and governing how those elements evolve together. Is The unit of analysis is the enterprise as an operating system. Business capabilities define what the organization does; the operating model defines how those capabilities are delivered; technology exists to support that operating model. When EA works, technology decisions follow from capability decisions, and capability decisions follow from strategy. Is not A documentation function; the goal is future-state decisions, and a current-state inventory is at most an input to them A technology review board; approving individual selections is narrow governance and a small slice of the discipline A framework exercise; TOGAF and Zachman are vocabularies for the work rather than the work itself A tool implementation; choosing and populating a repository supports the work but will not, on its own, produce a better decision A long-range planning department; EA is distinct in owning the linkage between strategic intent and operational reality across domains Every EA output is judged by what it changes. A capability model earns its place when it moves an investment decision, a reference architecture when variance across teams falls, and a roadmap when the organization can actually absorb the sequence it proposes. 2 Enterprise, domain, and solution architecture Three disciplines answering different questions at different scopes. Work done at the wrong scope either stalls (too broad for the problem) or creates debt (too narrow for the implication). Enterprise Domain Solution Scope The organization as a whole A specific capability or technology domain A single initiative, product, or system Primary question How should the organization operate and evolve to deliver on strategy? How should this domain be structured and advanced over time? How do we design and deliver this specific solution? Time horizon Three to five years, rolling One to three years Weeks to months Typical outputs Capability model, operating model, target state, investment roadmap, governance Reference architecture, standards, patterns, domain roadmap Solution design, implementation plan, technical specifications Value shows up when Cross-domain investments compound and the operating model keeps pace with strategy Variance across solutions falls and the domain becomes predictable to consume The system ships on scope, schedule, and quality Failure mode Drifts into abstraction, loses connection to delivery Becomes a rubber-stamp review function rather than a design discipline Optimizes locally at the expense of the broader portfolio Treating all architecture as one thing fails in three predictable ways. Enterprise trade-offs get delegated to solution architects, so each team optimizes its own delivery and the portfolio fills with overlapping capabilities nobody chose on purpose. Domain architecture, with no enterprise view to anchor it, follows whichever project is loudest and writes standards after the decisions are made. And solution teams end up reasoning from first principles on every initiative, carrying risk a working architecture function should have taken off them. Diagram The EA artifact chain Strategy reaches a buildable decision through six artifacts, each one feeding the next. Most EA functions build several of these well and never connect them, which is why the output reads as shelfware. The upward arrow matters as much as the forward ones. When solutions, ADRs, and portfolio moves are traced back to the capabilities they change, the capability model stays current without anyone rewriting it. Artifact Question it answers Owned by Go deeper Strategy decomposition Which five to seven priorities matter, and how will we know they were met? Executive team Technology Strategy Business capability model What does this organization do, independent of structure, process, or system? Business leadership, EA facilitates Sections 4 and 5 below Operating model canvas How is one capability actually delivered today? Capability owner Sections 6 and 7 below Target-state narrative What does the organization look like when the change is done, and why this target? Named authors, sponsor approves Section 8 below Capability-driven roadmap Which gaps close, through which initiatives, in what order? Business sponsors per priority Section 9 below; ADRs & Roadmapping Portfolio decisions Which applications to invest in, tolerate, migrate, or eliminate? Portfolio governance board Section 11 below; Application Portfolio Solution design and ADRs What gets built, and why was it built this way? Delivery teams, EA advises Architecture Review Board 3 Business Capability Model: the structural rules A hierarchical, business-led view of what the organization does, independent of process or technology. Violating these rules loses credibility quickly; treat them as rules rather than style preferences. The rules Capabilities are nouns: Customer Onboarding rather than Onboard Customers . Verb phrases slide toward process, which varies by business unit and time. MECE (mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive) at each level: no capability overlaps with its siblings, and together they cover everything the parent capability includes, with nothing left out Three levels is usually enough, four is the ceiling; Level 1 is 8 to 12 capabilities, Level 2 decomposes each into 3 to 8 The business owns the model; EA facilitates. A model that can't survive a conversation with the COO is an IT artifact with capability labels Common failure modes The model that's really an org chart, and breaks the next time the org restructures The model that reads like a process map, verb phrases and sequential flow The model nobody owns, drifting from reality within two reorganizations The model used only for IT planning, never referenced in a business investment conversation A capability also describes what, never how, where, or who. Customer Identity Verification is a capability; verifying identity through a third-party service at the call center is an implementation that belongs in another view and traces back to it. 4 Building the capability model, and putting it to work A defensible Level 1 and Level 2 takes six to eight weeks for an organization of moderate complexity. Larger or multi-segment enterprises take longer, and the extra time goes to validation, not construction. Reference structure, three families Family Level 1 starting points Customer-facing: what customers experience directly Market Development, Customer Acquisition, Customer Engagement, Product and Service Delivery, Customer Support Operational: running the core business Product Management, Supply and Sourcing, Operations, Risk and Compliance Enabling: keeping the organization itself running Finance and Treasury, Human Capital, Information and Technology, Corporate Services Adapt it: B2B: Customer Acquisition decomposes further than Market Development Regulated industries: Risk and Compliance grows at Level 2 and often needs Level 3 Asset-heavy businesses: Operations and Supply and Sourcing carry the weight Platforms and marketplaces: Product Management and Operations effectively merge at Level 1 Level 2 example: Customer Engagement Channel Management: which channels exist and how they relate Interaction Handling: receiving, routing, and responding within service levels Customer Identity and Profile: one coherent view of the customer Communication and Outreach: transactional, relationship, and campaign contact Self-Service Enablement: customers reaching outcomes without staff Engagement Analytics: measuring whether the five above are working A reference pattern, not an answer. The test is whether every activity under the parent lands in exactly one child. When Work The rule that keeps it honest Week 1 Gather strategy documents and prior architecture work; name the sponsor and a working group with a senior business leader per segment; write a one-paragraph charter Architects facilitate; they do not vote Week 2 Adapt a reference structure in a half-day workshop until Level 1 reads like this organization Never attempt Level 2 in the same session Weeks 3 to 4 One two-to-three hour workshop per Level 1 area with its business owners Run the MECE test at the end of each session; failures go to a parking list, and overlaps are resolved at the boundary Weeks 5 to 6 Walk the draft through each owner, then the sponsor; publish with a version and a named owner Changes at this stage are language, not structure Week 7 onward Put it to work immediately: heat-map current pain by capability, map the top ten in-flight initiatives, map the application portfolio at Level 2 or 3 Plan these three uses before publishing; an unused model loses credibility within a quarter Maintenance is light once built: confirm Levels 1 and 2 with the sponsor annually (most years nothing changes), review proposed changes quarterly against the MECE test, and keep traceability from initiatives, applications, and data current continuously. That last part is where the model earns its keep. And if there is no executive who will cite the model in their own communication, no business owner willing to be named, and no appetite for capability-anchored funding conversations, do not build it yet. Build those conditions first, or it becomes a wall poster. 5 Operating Model Canvas: six dimensions A one-page view of how a capability is delivered. Makes an operating model that's normally invisible, living in heads and habits, explicit enough to reason about in one conversation. Dimension Question Accountability Who is accountable for the outcomes this capability produces? A small number of named roles, tied to outcomes rather than activity. Workflow How does work flow from initiation to completion? Main path and significant variants. Decision rights What decisions get made here, and who makes them? The dimension most often left underspecified. Information What does the capability consume, produce, and rely on? Where is the authoritative source? Technology What systems enable the capability? Where are the load-bearing manual workarounds? Locations Where is work performed, by whom, under what arrangement? Internal vs. external, geographic distribution. Five diagnostic patterns show up repeatedly once a canvas is complete: accountability-workflow mismatch (the accountable role doesn't control the critical path), decision rights vacuum (significant decisions have no clear owner), information authority ambiguity (two systems both claim to be the source of truth), technology-workflow inversion (process steps exist because the system requires them rather than because they add value), and location-decision rights mismatch (decisions made where the work can't be observed). 6 Running a canvas, and the four ways it goes wrong Leaders with line accountability plus a few practitioners who do the work, two sessions, architecture facilitating. The canvas sits on top of process maps, RACI, and the application portfolio; it summarizes them and points to them. Use it Before a transformation, to baseline how work really happens After an acquisition, one canvas per side for each capability being combined Before centralizing, decentralizing, or creating shared services As the unit of design in a capability-led target state Skip it For a capability no one has ever described, unless you are ready to surface that no two leaders agree on it As a substitute for process or data modeling when depth is needed To grade an operating model with nothing to compare it against Session What happens Session 1, 90 minutes: draft Agree the boundary first; thirty minutes on scope saves two hours of dispute. Work the six dimensions in order. Everyone writes before anyone debates, so disagreement surfaces instead of deferring to whoever speaks first. Close by naming the three biggest disagreements and who resolves each before session 2. Session 2, 90 minutes: stress-test Clarifications only, no structural rewrites. Then three tests: trace the last real exception through the canvas; take the last real change and check which dimensions moved; describe a plausible future change and see whether the canvas predicts what would have to move. Publish with the working group named, a version, and a review date. The four errors: a wishful current state that describes how the capability should work and fails the stress tests; overloading, where any dimension with more than five to seven elements means the scope is too broad; boxes and arrows standing in for statements, when a finished canvas should read aloud as sensible prose; and no named owner, so it goes stale within a year. 7 The target-state narrative: prose first, diagrams second Executives read a target-state diagram for ten seconds, ask two questions, and move on. A narrative that stands on

title: Epistemology & Research Methods
description: How we know what we know, and how to know enough, fast enough, to make a decision that has a deadline. This is the discipline sitting underneath every diligence finding, postmortem root cause, and portfolio score elsewhere on this site, made explicit here instead of left implicit.
body: Reference Academic concept, translated into practice Epistemology is the study of what counts as knowledge and how it's justified. None of these ideas require a philosophy background to use; they're already implicit in good discovery work. Concept Practical translation Where it shows up Justified true belief A finding needs stated evidence and reasoning behind it; confident assertion on its own doesn't qualify Every "Evidence Requirements" list across the diligence frameworks Degrees of belief State how sure you are along with what you think is true. Certainty is rarely binary. Confidence tags (High/Medium/Low) on every dollar figure in technical debt assessment Falsifiability A claim only means something if some piece of evidence could have proven it wrong Red-flag pattern libraries naming what specifically would change a finding Evidence hierarchy Sources deserve unequal trust; rank them before you rely on them Management representation ranked below direct system access in every diligence checklist Bounded rationality Perfect information isn't available; the goal is the best decision achievable within the constraints you have Time-boxed diligence phases, quick-win prioritization in the 100-day assessment 1 Why the research window should be bounded The instinct that more research is always better is wrong for organizational decisions in a way it isn't for a dissertation. The question that matters "Have we learned enough to decide better than we would with no research at all, relative to what more research costs in time and opportunity." That is a different question from "have we learned everything." Confidence gains follow a diminishing curve: the fifth independent data point usually moves a conclusion more than the fiftieth does, once the pattern has already stabilized. Where open-ended research fails Academic research optimizes for near-total certainty over a timeframe measured in years, because the currency is being right rather than being timely. A business decision has a clock the underlying situation doesn't wait for. A diligence report finished after the deal has already closed has close to zero value, no matter how thorough it is. This is why confirmatory diligence runs 2-4 weeks and exclusivity diligence runs 4-8 weeks elsewhere on this site. More time would produce marginally more certainty, but the decision has a deadline, and every framework here separates "what was assessed" from "what wasn't" rather than pretending the boundary doesn't exist. 2 Research methods, the working toolkit None of these require formal training. They're habits of checking a claim before treating it as settled. Method What it does Where it applies Triangulation Cross-check a claim against at least two independent sources before treating it as fact A claim made in one interview versus the same claim confirmed by system access or a second interviewee who wasn't in the room for the first Primary versus secondary evidence Direct observation outranks a secondhand account of the observation Reviewing the codebase itself versus accepting a description of the codebase's quality Sampling logic A convenience sample, whoever happens to be available and willing, is rarely a representative sample Interview subject selection; reference customers a vendor hand-picks versus a broader, independently chosen set Disconfirmation-seeking Actively look for evidence against the working conclusion, and weigh it at least as heavily as the evidence for it Testing whether an alternative explanation survives contact with the same evidence Correlation versus causation A pattern in the data isn't automatically an explanation of the pattern Distinguishing a triggering event from the underlying condition it merely exposed, in incident root-cause analysis What correlation shows Two things moved together, or one happened right before the other. That's an observation, and an explanation still has to be found. The pattern could come from a causal link, a third factor driving both, plain coincidence in a small sample, or a pattern noticed after the fact and mistaken for meaningful because someone went looking for one. What causation requires A mechanism: if the first thing had been different, the second thing would have been different as a direct result, rather than merely less likely to appear alongside it. Establishing that usually takes more than the one data point that prompted the question, ideally a case where the suspected cause was absent and the effect still didn't happen. Worked example. A deployment goes out at 2:14pm. Error rates spike five minutes later. The natural read: the deploy caused the spike, since it's the thing sitting right next to it in time. Rolling the deploy back doesn't fix anything. Investigation finds a database connection pool that had been slowly exhausting for three days because of a slow query introduced earlier that week; the deploy's restart briefly reset open connections, masking the problem for a few minutes before the pool hit its ceiling anyway, on a schedule that had nothing to do with the deploy. The deploy correlates with the spike. The slow query, running unnoticed for three days, is what caused it. 3 Confirmation bias is structural in discovery work Treating it as an occasional character flaw misses the point. The shape of discovery work invites it by default. Why discovery invites it A working hypothesis usually forms early, often within the first interview or the first system walkthrough, and every subsequent finding then gets unconsciously filtered through it. A compressed collection window raises the temptation to stop looking the moment a plausible story has assembled, since a plausible story feels like an answer. Practice Before writing the finding down, state the working conclusion explicitly and deliberately argue the opposite for a few minutes, even alone. It's a small, cheap step compared to the cost of a wrong root cause or a wrong severity rating that resurfaces the same problem next quarter. 4 Calibrated confidence beats false precision A number presented as fact when it's a best estimate is a small dishonesty that compounds into bad decisions downstream. Practice Pair every material number with a confidence tag and a one-line reason: what would need to be true, or what evidence would need to arrive, for that confidence to move up or down. A range with a stated confidence level is more useful than a single unqualified figure, and easier to defend later. Common failure mode Dropping the confidence tag because an unqualified number feels more authoritative in a report or a board deck. This trades accuracy for the appearance of certainty, and the decision built on top of it inherits precision the underlying research never supported. Applied Where this already lives across the toolkit None of this is new to this site; it's the pattern underneath several pages, named explicitly here for the first time. Technology Diligence : evidence-requirements lists and the discipline of separating what was confirmed from what was taken on management's word Technical Debt Assessment : a five-level severity scale and a confidence rating (High/Medium/Low) attached to every dollar figure, so a report never travels with more certainty than the underlying work supports Application Portfolio Management : the explicit caution that Business Value scores drift toward inflation when the scorer is the system's own owner, a direct application of source bias Incident Response : the distinction between a triggering event and the underlying condition it exposed, which is the correlation-versus-causation problem applied to postmortems Vendor Evaluation : the caution against accepting only the references a vendor's sales team hand-picked, a direct sampling-bias correction Checklist Signs research quality is weak, regardless of how long it took Time spent and rigor are different things. These patterns show up in reports that took weeks and reports that took an afternoon alike. Findings state conclusions with no evidence source attached A single interview or a single document is treated with the same confidence as a cross-referenced, triangulated finding No visible effort was made to find evidence against the working conclusion before it was written down Numbers are presented without a confidence range or a stated basis The research window kept extending without anyone asking whether the additional time was buying more confidence, or just more pages

title: Governance, Risk & Compliance
description: The GRC layer this site doesn't already cover: mapping controls once across multiple frameworks, centralized versus distributed GRC, and continuous compliance tooling.
body: Reference Where the rest of GRC already lives on this site Read this page for the layer above these. Read these for the individual pieces themselves. Piece Where it lives Risk tiers and acceptance Technology Risk Appetite Security program sequencing and governance Security Program NIST CSF maturity, evidence over policy Security & Compliance Maturity Architectural security posture Zero-Trust Maturity Privacy regulation, data lifecycle, breach notification Data Governance & Privacy AI-specific governance, EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF AI Governance Map Decision governance for architecture Architecture Review Board Decision rights and escalation generally Technology Decision Rights 1 Common controls: map once, satisfy many The current practice, and the reason a dedicated GRC layer earns its keep once an organization is answering to more than one framework. Practice Build one internal control set, then map each control to every external framework it satisfies, SOC 2, ISO 27001, HIPAA, PCI-DSS, GDPR. One access review, one screenshot, one policy document gets reused everywhere it's relevant, collected once and referenced by every audit that needs it instead of re-produced fresh for each one. Common failure mode Treating each framework as its own separate project with its own evidence collection cycle, so the same access review gets re-screenshotted three times a year for three different auditors, and the organization never builds a control library that compounds in value as more frameworks get added. This is what most current GRC and compliance automation tooling is built around: automating the reuse of evidence across all the frameworks, rather than automating any single one. 2 Centralized versus distributed GRC An organizational design question that usually gets decided by accident rather than on purpose. Centralized One function owns governance, risk, and compliance end to end: a single risk register, one consistent methodology, one team an auditor talks to. The risk: that function can drift distant from the technical and threat context each domain needs to assess its own risk accurately. Distributed Security owns security compliance, legal owns privacy compliance, finance owns financial controls, each close to its own domain's context. The risk: findings don't reliably reach each other, and a cross-cutting risk, AI governance is the clearest current example, can fall through every function's boundary at once because it isn't fully owned by any of them. Most organizations land somewhere in between: a small central function owning the common control library and the risk register, with domain owners responsible for implementing controls within their own area against it. The failure mode is landing there by accident rather than deciding it deliberately, the same distinction Role Boundaries makes for CTO, CIO, CISO, and CPO scope generally. 3 Continuous compliance tooling, briefly What this category of tool changes. No specific product is recommended here. A newer category of GRC tooling automates evidence collection and control monitoring continuously, connected directly to the underlying systems, rather than producing a point-in-time snapshot assembled by hand in the weeks before an audit. The practical shift: compliance posture becomes something the organization already knows on any given day, instead of something it scrambles to reconstruct once a year. This doesn't remove the need for judgment (validating evidence, handling exceptions, and talking to an auditor still require a person), but it removes most of the repetitive manual collection that used to consume the weeks before every audit cycle. Interactive What a common control library saves List the frameworks you maintain and the controls in scope for each. The tool compares evidence collection run as separate projects with one mapped control library, in hours, full-time equivalents, and cost per audit cycle. Control counts in the example are illustrative; use your own scoping. Runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere. Frameworks you maintain Controls per framework (average) Overlap across frameworks (%) Hours to collect evidence, per control Calculate 4 The frameworks most organizations end up mapping Who is asking determines what you need. Status reflects September 2026. Framework Who asks for it Notes SOC 2 US business customers Type II report, renewed annually ISO/IEC 27001:2022 International and enterprise customers Three-year certificate with annual surveillance audits; the 2013 version is no longer certifiable [1] HIPAA Security Rule Regulators, and health system customers through business associate agreements A major update was proposed in January 2025 (mandatory MFA and encryption, asset inventory, annual audits); HHS now expects to finalize it no earlier than 2027 [2] [3] . Build toward it now HITRUST CSF Health systems and payers Often requested in place of, or on top of, SOC 2 in healthcare PCI DSS v4.0.1 Card brands and acquiring banks Scope reduction through tokenization is usually cheaper than broad compliance NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, FedRAMP US federal agencies The most control-heavy baseline; FedRAMP authorization is a multi-quarter program CMMC 2.0 US Department of Defense Phased into contracts from November 10, 2025 [4] GDPR and US state privacy laws Regulators and customers See Data Governance & Privacy and Regulatory Map ISO/IEC 42001:2023, EU AI Act Customers and EU regulators for AI systems See AI Governance Sources IAF MD 26:2022, transition requirements for ISO/IEC 27001:2022 HHS, HIPAA Security Rule proposed rule, Federal Register, January 6, 2025 Unified Agenda, RIN 0945-AA22 (final action listed for 2027) DFARS final rule on CMMC, Federal Register, September 10, 2025 5 Where to start the common control library Nobody should build a control library from a blank page. Start from a published metaframework and trim. Starting point What it gives you Tradeoff Secure Controls Framework (SCF) A free metaframework already mapped to hundreds of laws, standards, and frameworks Large; most organizations adopt a subset NIST CSF 2.0 with NIST's online informative references Official mappings from CSF outcomes to 800-53, ISO 27001, CIS, and others Outcome-level, so you still write your own control statements HITRUST CSF A harmonized control set already mapped across healthcare-relevant frameworks Licensed, and assessment is through HITRUST's own program Unified Compliance Framework A commercial, continuously updated mapping database Subscription cost; strongest for heavily regulated multinationals Your compliance automation vendor's library Controls pre-mapped to the frameworks the tool supports Convenient, but ties your control set to one vendor's structure 6 Continuous control monitoring, done honestly Automation changes how often you know your posture. It does not change whether the controls are effective. What automation does well Machine-checkable configuration controls: MFA enforced, encryption on, logging enabled, public storage blocked, departed staff deprovisioned. Checked daily rather than sampled once a year, with drift raised as a ticket to the owning team. What it cannot do Judge whether a human control happened well: an access review that rubber-stamped every entitlement, a risk assessment copied from last year. A fully green dashboard over hollow human controls is the modern version of the audit-window control described in section 1. 7 A worked example: adding HITRUST to an existing SOC 2 program A healthcare SaaS company with a clean SOC 2 Type II is asked by two health system customers for HITRUST. Figures are illustrative. Step What happened Effect Map Existing SOC 2 controls mapped to the HITRUST i1 requirement set Roughly two thirds of requirements covered by controls already running Gap Remaining gaps concentrated in formal risk assessment, media handling, and a documented business continuity test Three owners, one quarter of work Evidence Evidence stored once in the common library and referenced by both audits The annual access review and vulnerability scans now serve both reports Result HITRUST i1 achieved within about six months of starting The sales cycle for both health systems resumed; the next framework will cost less again Checklist Signs GRC is fragmented rather than functioning Patterns that show up when governance, risk, and compliance exist as activities without a coordinated function behind them. The same evidence gets collected fresh for each separate audit instead of drawn from a reusable control library A risk finding from one function, security, never reaches another function that needed to know about it, privacy, legal No single risk register exists; each function tracks its own risks in its own spreadsheet with no shared view Compliance posture is only known in the weeks right before an audit, never on an ordinary day Whether GRC is centralized or distributed was never deliberately decided; it's whatever happened as the organization grew The control library was built from scratch rather than from a published metaframework, and nobody maintains its mappings Automated monitoring shows all green while human controls such as access reviews are not checked for quality

title: Incident Response
description: A blameless, repeatable incident process from detection through postmortem follow-through: the roles, the severity scale, the communication cadence, the resolution bar, the postmortem method, and the metrics that tell you whether any of it is working. Two worked incidents run end to end, one availability and one security, because the two diverge in ways a single process document usually hides.
body: Reference Severity classification Defined ahead of time rather than decided in the moment, when judgment is already under pressure. The definitions below are a starting point; the table that matters is the one your on-call engineers can recite. Severity Definition Response Who is told, and when SEV1 Full outage, data loss, or confirmed breach affecting all or most customers, or any incident with regulatory or public-disclosure consequence Incident commander within 5 minutes, all relevant responders paged, dedicated bridge and channel opened CTO and CEO immediately; counsel and CISO if data is involved; customers within 30 minutes via status page SEV2 Significant degradation, a subset of customers fully affected, or a core internal system down during business hours Incident commander assigned, core responders paged, channel opened CTO within the hour; customers when impact is confirmed customer-visible SEV3 Minor degradation with a workaround, limited customer impact, or elevated error rates below the SLO threshold Owning team handles it in business hours; tracked as an incident, no command structure Engineering leadership in the weekly review SEV4 No customer impact; an internal issue caught before it mattered, or a near miss worth recording Logged and addressed in normal workflow Nobody outside the team, but it goes in the incident log so near-miss patterns are visible Two rules that keep the scale useful. First, severity is set by impact rather than by cause, so a one-line config error that takes down checkout is a SEV1. Second, when in doubt, declare high and downgrade later. Downgrading costs nothing; upgrading an hour late costs the hour. Reference How this maps to the published standards The process on this page is a working synthesis of three sources most auditors, insurers, and enterprise customers will recognize by name. Knowing the mapping matters when a customer questionnaire or a regulator asks which framework you follow. Source What it contributes Where it appears on this page NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 (2025), Incident Response Recommendations The lifecycle: preparation; detection and analysis; containment, eradication and recovery; post-incident activity. Rev. 3 aligns the lifecycle to the CSF 2.0 functions [1] , so a security incident program can be evidenced against the same ladder as Security & Compliance Maturity Preparation (final reference card), detection and triage (1), containment and recovery (4 and the security variant), post-incident (5 and 6) Incident Command System, via Google SRE (2016) and PagerDuty's published response process A single commander, defined roles, span of control, and a fixed communication cadence, adapted from emergency services to software The four roles, incident command (2), communication cadence (3) Blameless postmortems (Etsy, 2012) and SRE's postmortem culture Contributing factors over a single root cause, first-person accounts without sanction, action items tracked to closure Postmortem (5), follow-through (6) ISO/IEC 27035 and SOC 2 CC7.3 to CC7.5 What an auditor expects to see evidenced: classification criteria, a documented process, a record per incident, and remediation tracked Severity table, scribe's timeline, action item close rate Sources NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3, Incident Response Recommendations, April 2025 Reference The four roles A SEV1 or SEV2 needs four jobs filled, by four different people where headcount allows. The most common failure is one senior engineer holding all four at once. Incident commander Owns coordination and decisions: what is being tried, in what order, who is doing it, when to escalate, and when the incident is over. Keeps the bridge focused. Does no debugging. Anti-pattern: the IC opens a terminal. The moment they do, nobody is running the incident. Operations lead Owns the technical investigation and the fix. Directs the responders, proposes actions to the IC, executes once approved. There may be several, one per affected system. Anti-pattern: three engineers making uncoordinated changes to production at once, each hoping theirs is the fix. Communications lead Owns every message leaving the bridge: status page, customer notices, executive updates, internal announcements. Keeps the cadence whether or not there is news. Anti-pattern: the IC is also writing customer updates, so both the updates and the response slow down. Scribe Keeps the live timeline: every action, decision, observation, and time, as it happens. This is the postmortem's raw material and the answer to any regulator's "when did you know." Anti-pattern: reconstructing the timeline from chat scrollback two days later, with the minutes that matter most missing. Under 30 engineers, the IC and comms lead are often the same person and the scribe is a bot capturing the channel. That works for SEV2. For SEV1 pull a second person in even if they are only writing updates; the cost of a confused communications thread during an outage is higher than one interrupted evening. 1 Detection & triage The first few minutes determine whether the rest of the response is calm or chaotic. Practice A single, unambiguous entry point for declaring an incident: one command or one button that opens the channel, pages the on-call, and starts the timeline, so nobody debates which Slack channel to post in while the outage continues. Whoever notices first declares. Severity gets assigned or corrected within minutes rather than negotiated at length before response starts. The first three questions on the bridge, in order: what is the customer impact, what changed recently, and what is the fastest way to stop the bleeding even if it isn't the fix. Common failure mode Multiple people independently investigating the same issue in different channels, duplicating effort and fragmenting the picture, because there was no single place established ahead of time to converge on. The second failure is the opposite: an engineer who is fairly sure something is wrong waits for certainty before declaring, and the incident is twenty minutes old before anyone is coordinating it. Mitigate before you diagnose. Rolling back the last deploy, failing over to the standby, or shedding load restores service in most incidents long before the cause is understood. The investigation continues afterward, on a running system, with the timeline intact. 2 Incident command One person owns the incident's coordination. They are explicitly not the person fixing it. Practice The incident commander's job is coordination and communication; someone else does the debugging. They track the timeline, decide when to escalate, approve any change to production during the incident, and are the single point deciding when the incident is resolved. The role rotates through a trained pool and is staffed from a rota rather than improvised by whoever happens to be senior and available. A good IC runs the bridge with a loop: current impact, current theory, current action, next check-in time. Common failure mode The most senior engineer in the room becomes both incident commander and lead debugger simultaneously. Both jobs suffer: the fix takes longer because they're context-switching to answer status questions, and communication suffers because they're heads-down in logs. The second failure is an executive joining the bridge and starting to direct it. The IC's authority during the incident has to be explicit and has to include the CTO. 3 Communication cadence What gets said, to whom, and how often, especially while the cause is still unknown. Practice A fixed cadence (every 15 to 30 minutes for a SEV1, hourly for a SEV2) with an update even when the update is "still investigating, no new information, next update at 14:30." Silence is worse than an uninformative update, since stakeholders fill silence with worse assumptions than reality usually warrants. Each audience gets a different message from the same facts: customers get impact, workaround, and next update time; executives get impact in business terms, what is being tried, and whether a decision is needed from them; the internal company gets enough to answer customer calls. Common failure mode Going quiet while "working the problem," which is defensible engineering instinct and terrible stakeholder management. The absence of updates reads as either incompetence or a bigger problem than what's happening. The other failure is over-sharing theories: a customer update that says "we believe the database is corrupted" is remembered long after it turns out to be a full disk. Audience Cadence (SEV1) What goes in it What stays out Status page and customers Within 30 minutes of declaration, then every 30 to 60 minutes What is affected, in product terms; any workaround; the time of the next update Cause theories, internal system names, blame, promises of a fix time you cannot keep Executives Every 30 minutes, or immediately on a change in impact Customer and revenue impact, current action, decisions needed, notification clocks that may be running Technical detail beyond one sentence; anything the comms lead has not said to customers first Internal company At declaration, at resolution, and on any major change What to tell customers who call, what not to promise The bridge link; the incident channel stays responders-only Regulators and counsel As soon as data or a reportable category is plausibly involved Facts and times, from the scribe's timeline Speculation; anything not yet in the timeline 4 Resolution & recovery Declaring an incident over is a decision. It does not happen automatically when the graphs look normal again. Practice Resolution requires the incident commander's explicit call, against a bar defined before the incident: customer-facing metrics back within SLO for a sustained window (30 minutes is common for a SEV1), any backlog or queue drained, a documented mitigation in place with a named owner for the permanent fix, and the timeline complete. Resolution and recovery are separate states: resolved means customers are no longer affected; recovered means the system is back to its pre-incident posture, with the failover reversed, the shed load restored, and the standby rebuilt. Common failure mode Calling it resolved the moment the immediate symptom disappears, then having it recur an hour later because the underlying cause was never addressed, only its most visible symptom. The recurrence is worse than the original: the responders have gone home, the customers who were told it was fixed are now angrier, and the second timeline starts from cold. 5 Blameless postmortem The written record that turns an incident into an organizational asset instead of a bad memory. Held within five working days, while the timeline is still fresh and before the action items get negotiated down. Practice A timeline of what happened, what was known at each decision point (as opposed to what's known now in hindsight), contributing factors framed as systemic rather than individual, and concrete action items with owners and due dates. "Blameless" means analyzing the system that allowed the error; it never means avoiding naming what happened. The person who ran the command that caused the outage is in the room and describes it in the first person, because the interesting question is why a reasonable engineer with the information available at the time made that call, and only they can answer it. Common failure mode A postmortem that either assigns individual blame (which teaches people to hide problems rather than surface them next time) or is so carefully blame-free it avoids naming any specific decision point, producing generic action items nobody's accountable for finishing. The third failure is stopping at a single root cause. Serious incidents almost always have several contributing conditions, and a postmortem that finds one and stops leaves the others in place for the next one. Section What it should contain What a weak one looks like Summary Three sentences: what broke, who was affected and for how long, how it was resolved A paragraph of context before the impact is stated Impact Customers affected, duration of customer-visible impact, revenue or SLA consequence, notifications made "Some customers experienced errors" Timeline Detection, declaration, each action and decision, mitigation, resolution, in minutes, from the scribe's record Times reconstructed from memory; a gap where the critical forty minutes were Contributing factors The triggering change, the condition that let it cause impact, and why detection or recovery took as long as it did. Usually three to five One root cause, typically the last thing anyone touched What went well Specific things that limited the damage, so they get reinforced Left blank, or filled with platitudes Action items Each with an owner, a date, and a category: prevent recurrence, detect faster, recover faster, or reduce impact "Improve monitoring" with no owner Five Whys is a fine facilitation technique and a poor model of

title: Innovation Portfolio Management
description: Structuring innovation as a managed portfolio across the same three horizons as the broader technology strategy.
body: 1 Portfolio structure follows the same three horizons Innovation is Horizon 2 and 3 of the same investment split covered on the Technology Strategy page, made explicit as a managed portfolio rather than a handful of side projects. It is never a separate budget line floating outside the strategy. Horizon 2 bets Adjacent opportunities with a clearer, though not yet proven, path to value. Roughly 20 to 30 percent of technology investment. These get funding and a named owner. A hackathon slot doesn't count. Horizon 3 bets Unknowns: unproven, high-uncertainty, high-potential-payoff exploration. Roughly 5 to 10 percent. Most of these fail, and that's the design. Picking better bets doesn't change it. The most common portfolio failure is disguising Horizon 1 optimization work as innovation because it's safer to fund and easier to report on, which quietly starves the two horizons that produce new capability. 2 Funding model: separate from core rather than carved out of it A dedicated innovation fund, protected from quarterly delivery pressure, is what keeps Horizon 2 and 3 bets alive past the first bad quarter. Why separation matters A bet funded out of a product team's normal budget gets cannibalized the moment that team hits a delivery crunch, which is often, since crunches are common and bets are inherently deferrable. A separate fund with its own governance is what survives that pressure. Sizing Sized against the same 20 to 30 percent Horizon 2 and 5 to 10 percent Horizon 3 split, rather than against whatever's left over after core delivery is funded. If the fund is sized residually, it will trend toward zero the first time the core business needs the money. 3 Stage-gate versus continuous discovery The mechanism by which a bet gets more funding, or doesn't, and the single biggest determinant of whether a portfolio learns anything from its failures. Stage-gate A big upfront business case, built for something inherently uncertain, followed by a large funding decision at a small number of gates. Produces confident-sounding plans for things nobody can forecast, and makes killing a bet feel like admitting the original business case was wrong. Continuous discovery Small funded experiments with a defined evidence bar for the next increment of funding. Each increment is small enough that killing it reads as the model working as designed rather than as an admission of failure. This is the harder model to run administratively and the one that produces learning. 4 Kill criteria, set before the bet starts The single most skipped discipline in innovation portfolios, and the reason most of them accumulate zombie projects that never officially die. What works Success and failure criteria named in writing before a bet is funded: what result, by when, would justify the next round of funding, and what result would justify killing it. Set before anyone's emotionally invested, when the criteria can still be objective. What happens without it Kill decisions get made, or more often don't get made, based on who's willing to have the uncomfortable conversation rather than the evidence. A bet with no named end condition never dies; it quietly stops being discussed while still consuming a line item. A portfolio without a visible kill rate is a portfolio that hasn't yet had the hard conversation. Zero kills in a year is a bigger red flag than a high kill rate. 5 Portfolio balance, measured What gets tracked to know whether the portfolio is working or theater. Metrics worth tracking Split of active investment across the three horizons, against the 60-70/20-30/5-10 target Bet velocity: how long from initial funding to a kill-or-scale decision Kill rate: bets stopped versus bets scaled, over a rolling period Diversity of bet type: adjacent-market bets versus new-capability bets versus new-business-model bets, so the portfolio isn't quietly all one type What it's for These are signals to act on rather than a vanity dashboard. If Horizon 3 investment has quietly drifted to zero, or the kill rate is zero, or every active bet is the same type of bet, something has to change. 6 Common failure modes Patterns specific to innovation portfolios, distinct from general project failure. Innovation theater A lab, an incubator, or a hackathon with plenty of energy and no connection to funding or authority to ship. Produces enthusiasm and demos, and no capability. The tell: ask what happened to last year's winning hackathon project. If nobody knows, it's theater. Portfolio capture by Horizon 1 Improvements to the existing product get relabeled as innovation because that's where the safe, fundable work already is. The portfolio looks balanced on a slide and is 90 percent Horizon 1 wearing a Horizon 2 label. Both failure modes are easier to prevent than to fix after the fact. A portfolio review that asks 'what did we kill this quarter, and what did that free up' catches both early. 7 Innovation tournaments: sourcing the portfolio Christian Terwiesch and Karl Ulrich, Innovation Tournaments (Harvard Business Press, 2009). Stage-gate versus continuous discovery, above, governs how a bet gets more funding once it exists. A tournament is the separate mechanism for deciding which bets enter the portfolio in the first place. See Transformation and Innovation for how this fits alongside the adoption side of the same problem. How it works A periodic open call, quarterly is typical, where anyone in engineering can pitch a bet against a short, consistent rubric: horizon fit, a proposed kill criterion, and a funding ask. Pitches are evaluated by a small panel that includes people outside the pitcher's own reporting line, and winners get seeded into the portfolio with funding rather than applause. Where it goes wrong Run as a one-time event, a hackathon, rather than a standing cadence, or winners get praise with no funding attached. Both produce the innovation-theater failure mode named above: energy with no connection to authority or budget. A standing forum with an empty docket is a natural home for this. See Architecture Review Board for turning an unscheduled review slot into an informal salon where early-stage ideas get tested before they're ready for a formal tournament pitch. Evidence Where the allocation percentages come from The best-known split is empirical, not theoretical, and the numbers in the source are averages rather than targets. Source Finding How to use it Nagji and Tuff, Harvard Business Review, 2012 Firms that outperformed in their sample allocated roughly 70 percent to core, 20 percent to adjacent, and 10 percent to transformational initiatives [1] A starting point, adjusted for industry and stage Same study Returns ran roughly in reverse: about 70 percent of long-term return came from the transformational 10 percent [1] The reason the small bucket must be protected from being raided in a bad quarter Same study Technology firms tended to put more into transformational bets; consumer goods firms less Your right split depends on how fast your market moves Sources Nagji and Tuff, Managing Your Innovation Portfolio, HBR, May 2012 Diagram Where the money goes, and where the return comes from The 70/20/10 split, mirrored against the return each bucket produced. Innovation allocation compared with where long-term returns came from Share of investment Share of long-term return 70% 10% Core 20% 20% Adjacent 10% 70% Transformational In the firms Nagji and Tuff studied, the smallest bucket produced most of the long-term return. That is why the 10 percent must be protected when a bad quarter makes it the easiest money to take. Averages from Nagji and Tuff, Harvard Business Review, 2012, as in the table above. They describe outperforming firms in that study, not a target for yours. Worked example Metered funding for one bet A $1.2M ceiling released in tranches, each tied to evidence rather than to calendar time. Tranche Funding Question it must answer Kill if 1 $150K Do target customers have the problem, and will they pay to solve it? Fewer than 5 of 20 interviewed customers rank it a top-three problem 2 $350K Can we build it at a cost that leaves margin? Unit cost in the prototype exceeds 60 percent of the price customers named 3 $700K Will customers adopt it in their real workflow? Fewer than 3 of 10 pilot customers use it weekly after 60 days Interactive Portfolio health check Keep a register of the bets you are funding. The tool works out the actual horizon split from the register, counts kills and scales, and checks the portfolio against the target bands and failure modes on this page. If you do not keep a register, type the split and counts directly instead. Runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere. Horizon 1 allocation (%) Horizon 2 allocation (%) Horizon 3 allocation (%) Bets killed this year Bets scaled this year Distinct bet types currently active 1 (all the same type) 2 3 (adjacent-market, new-capability, new-business-model) Check the portfolio

title: Legacy Modernization Execution
description: How a migration gets run once the decision to modernize has been made. Deciding what to modernize is the Application Portfolio Management question; this page is about the execution mechanics that determine whether the migration succeeds or stalls: choosing the seam, the strangler fig and the routing layer that makes it work, cutover and rollback, parallel-run validation, data migration sequencing, the program structure that keeps a two-year effort honest, sunsetting, and the two ways it usually goes wrong. Two worked cases, one that worked and one that was rescued.
body: Framework Which kind of migration this is "Modernize" covers six different projects with different risk profiles. Naming which one you are running is the first execution decision, and the one most often skipped, because a program that starts as a rehost drifts into a refactor without anyone approving the change. Strategy What changes Typical duration Where the risk sits Use when Rehost The infrastructure; the application is moved as-is Weeks to a few months per system Network, latency, licensing, and everything that assumed the old data center The application is fine and the platform is the problem, or a data center lease is ending Replatform Runtime components (managed database, container packaging) with the code largely intact Months Behavioral differences in the managed service; the cutover Operational cost and reliability are the drivers and the code is sound Refactor or rearchitect The code and its structure, usually toward services and a new data model One to three years Everywhere; this is where the strangler fig and everything below applies The application blocks the business and buying is not an option Repurchase The application is replaced with a commercial product Six to eighteen months Data migration and the processes the old system quietly encoded The capability is commodity; see Build vs Buy Retire The application is switched off Weeks, plus the time to find who still uses it The user nobody knew about The TIME map says Eliminate; often a third of an estate qualifies Retain Nothing, deliberately, with a date to revisit None Drift; the system ages while attention is elsewhere Low value, low risk, and the migration cost exceeds the carry cost Most of this page is about the third row, because that is the one that fails. Rehost and replatform fail on cutover mechanics, covered in section 2. Repurchase fails on data migration, covered in section 4. Retire fails on the sunset discipline in section 6, which is why estates carry so many systems that were "retired" years ago. Framework The strangler fig pattern, and the layer that makes it work The dominant strategy for modernizing a live system without a high-risk, high-visibility cutover: grow the new system around the edges of the old one until the old one can be safely retired. The mechanism New functionality is built in the new system and routed to it, while remaining functionality continues running in the old system, with a routing layer (a proxy, an API gateway, a facade, a feature flag) directing each request to whichever system currently owns it. Over time, more capability migrates to the new system until the old system handles nothing and can be decommissioned. The old system shrinks gradually instead of being replaced in a single event, which is what makes this the lower-risk default over a full rewrite and cutover. Two supporting pieces are load-bearing: the routing layer has to exist before the first capability moves, and an anti-corruption layer translates between the old model and the new domain model so the new services never inherit the old shape. Choosing the seam The strangler works capability by capability, and the order matters. Start with a capability that is valuable enough to prove the approach, self-contained enough that it does not drag the whole data model with it, and low enough in blast radius that a failure is recoverable. Candidates ranked by seam quality: a read-only capability (reporting, search) first, because it can be shadowed and compared at no risk; then a capability with its own data (notifications, a document store); then transactional capabilities in order of decreasing isolation; the shared core (accounts, orders, the ledger) last. Cutting by customer segment or by traffic percentage is the alternative axis, useful when the capabilities cannot be separated but the customers can. The first capability moved should take a quarter, produce visible value, and exercise every mechanism on this page (routing, parallel run, cutover, rollback, and a small data migration) at small scale. Programs that start with the hardest capability because it is the most valuable discover the mechanics under maximum pressure. 1 Cutover planning and rollback criteria Every cutover, whether a full system swap or a single capability moving to the new system, needs a defined rollback trigger decided before the cutover happens rather than improvised during it. Practice Specific, pre-agreed rollback criteria (error rate above X percent, latency above Y, a defined list of critical functions that must work correctly) checked immediately after cutover, with the rollback mechanism tested in advance rather than assumed to work when it's needed under pressure. The cutover itself is run as an incident, with an incident commander, a timeline, and the roles from Incident Response , because it is a planned incident and the same discipline applies. The go/no-go decision has a named owner and a checklist, and the checklist includes the rollback rehearsal date. Common failure mode "We'll roll back if it looks bad" as the entire rollback plan, which under pressure becomes a debate about whether it's bad enough yet, while customer impact accumulates during the debate. The second failure is a rollback that was never rehearsed and turns out to require a data step nobody scripted, so the team is now writing a migration backward at 2am. Cutover pattern How it works Rollback cost Fits when Canary Route a small share of traffic (1 percent, then 5, then 25) to the new path, watch, widen Trivial: route back Stateless or read paths; anything where a small blast radius is acceptable Blue/green Two complete environments; switch the router, keep the old one warm Low, until data diverges; then the data step from section 4 applies Whole-service cutovers where a fast switch matters and data can be reconciled Dark launch The new path runs on live traffic with its output discarded; only its telemetry is used None; nothing customer-visible changed Validating a new implementation before any customer sees it; the first step of a parallel run Segment cutover Move a customer cohort (internal users, then a friendly segment, then all) rather than a traffic percentage Moderate; the cohort's data is now on the new system Where behavior differs by customer and a percentage would split one customer's experience Big bang Everything switches at once, usually over a weekend High, and usually untested Almost never by choice; occasionally forced by a contract end or a regulatory date, in which case it gets rehearsed at least twice in full 2 Parallel-run validation Before fully trusting the new system, run it alongside the old one and compare outputs on live traffic. Practice Shadow traffic sent to both systems, with outputs compared automatically and discrepancies flagged, for long enough to build confidence: weeks for a low-volume system, potentially longer for something with meaningful seasonal or cyclical variation in the data it processes. The comparison needs a defined tolerance (exact match for a ledger, a rounding tolerance for a pricing engine, a semantic match for search results) and a defined exit criterion (discrepancy rate below X for Y consecutive days including a period end) agreed before the run starts. Every discrepancy is triaged into one of three buckets: new system wrong, old system wrong, or both acceptable. The second bucket is more common than anyone expects and is one of the quiet benefits of the exercise. Common failure mode A parallel run cut short because it's "looking fine so far," which misses the edge case that only shows up during month-end processing, a holiday traffic spike, or some other pattern the shortened window never covered. The second failure is a parallel run with no tolerance defined, so the team argues about whether a discrepancy matters instead of whether it exists, and the run never has an end condition it can meet. 3 Data migration sequencing Moving the data is usually harder and riskier than moving the code, and it's where migrations most often go over budget and over timeline. The sequence below is the one that survives contact with a live system. Step What happens The check before moving on 1. Backfill Historical data copied into the new store in batches, transformed through the anti-corruption layer, with the old system still the system of record Row counts and checksums reconcile per batch; a sample of records compared field by field 2. Change data capture Ongoing changes in the old system streamed to the new store, so the copy stays current while validation runs Replication lag measured and bounded; a reconciliation job runs nightly and reports drift 3. Dual-read validation The new system serves reads in shadow, compared against the old, per the parallel run above Discrepancy rate under the agreed tolerance across a full business cycle 4. Dual-write, old system primary Writes go to both; the old system remains the source of truth and the new one is checked against it Write reconciliation clean; the rollback path (stop writing to new) rehearsed 5. Cutover, new system primary Writes go to the new system first; the old system receives them via reverse replication so it remains a valid rollback target Reverse replication verified; the rollback (flip primary back) rehearsed once in a lower environment and once for real on a low-risk segment 6. Stop reverse replication The old system is now stale by design. This is the point of no return and is a dated, signed decision Rollback window declared closed; the decommission clock in section 6 starts Keep the old system's data as the system of record until the new system has been validated against it. Dual-write without a reconciliation job is the most common way a migration silently corrupts data: both stores accept writes, they diverge, and nobody notices until a customer does. The reconciliation job is the migration's most important piece of code and is usually the last one written. 4 The program structure that keeps a two-year effort honest A refactor of a core system outlasts most executives' attention span and at least one budget cycle. The mechanics above handle risk per cutover; this handles the risk that the program itself drifts. What works A migration tracker with one row per capability, showing its strategy, its seam, its percentage of traffic on the new path, its cutover date, and its decommission date, reviewed monthly by the sponsor. Value delivered at each step: every capability moved either retires something, unblocks a feature, or removes a cost, and the tracker records which. A fixed cadence for the go/no-go decisions, with the same checklist each time. A named business sponsor who is not the CTO, because a migration with only an engineering sponsor gets cut in the first downturn per Technology Strategy During a Downturn . And an explicit budget line for the double-running cost, which peaks in the middle of the program and surprises every CFO who was not told about it in year one. What backfires A program reported as percent complete, which is a number nobody can verify and which sits at 80 percent for a year. A scope that grows because the new system is where every new feature wants to be built, so the team modernizing the old system is also the team shipping the roadmap, and the migration becomes the thing that happens when there is time. And a sponsor change: the executive who approved the program leaves, the replacement did not choose it, and the program has no artifact that shows what it has already delivered. Measure What it tells the sponsor Share of traffic (or transactions) served by the new path, per capability Real progress, as opposed to percent complete; it can only be gamed by moving traffic Capabilities decommissioned, and run cost removed Whether the old system is shrinking or the estate is growing Double-run cost this month, against the plan Whether the program is on its cost curve; this number should start falling by the midpoint Defect and incident rate on migrated capabilities versus the old path Whether the new system is better, and whether the parallel run was long enough Features unblocked or delivered because of the migration The value story for the board, in the terms of Board Reporting 5 The big-bang trap The single decision that most reliably turns a modernization effort into a multi-year, over-budget program. What works Incremental migration, capability by capability or customer segment by customer segment, with value delivered and risk retired at each step, so a stalled migration still leaves something usable rather than two half-finished systems and no working whole. The routing layer is what makes incremental possible; the tracker is what makes it visible. What backfires A full rewrite planned as a single release after 18 months of development, betting the entire program on one cutover event. If it fails, there's no partial progress to fall back on, only a large sunk cost and a system still run

title: Org Design
description: How to structure an engineering organization so the structure helps rather than fights the work: the four team types and three interaction modes, the constraint that should drive every boundary decision, how big a team and a manager's span should be, which top-level shape fits which stage, when to split a team, and how to run a reorg without paying for it twice. Two worked cases, one growth and one repair.
body: Framework The constraint that drives everything: cognitive load Most org design conversations start with the org chart. The better starting point is a question about each team: can the people on it hold everything they are responsible for in their heads at once. When the answer is no, the boundary is wrong, whatever the chart says. What the constraint means in practice A team's cognitive load is the sum of the domains, systems, and tools it has to understand to do its normal work. Team Topologies splits it into intrinsic load (the skill itself), extraneous load (the tooling and process friction), and germane load (the business domain, where you want the attention to go). Org design's job is to shrink the first two so the third has room. A team that owns a product, its database, its Kubernetes config, its CI pipeline, its compliance evidence, and its on-call is over capacity before a single feature is planned. The platform and enabling team types exist to take the first two kinds of load off it. Conway's law, and the maneuver Systems end up mirroring the communication structure of the organization that builds them. Four teams building a compiler produce a four-pass compiler. The practical consequence: decide the architecture you want, then shape the teams to match, because the reverse will happen by default. That deliberate version is the inverse Conway maneuver, and it is why Integration & API Patterns and this page have to be read together. A team boundary is a future API boundary whether or not anyone intended it. Framework Four team types Most organizational dysfunction traces back to a team playing a type it wasn't set up to play rather than to the people in it. In a healthy organization the large majority of teams are stream-aligned; the other three exist to keep it that way. Stream-aligned Owns a full slice of a business capability end to end, from code to production, with minimal dependency on other teams for a normal change. Aligned to a product, a customer journey, a segment, or a user persona. Anti-pattern: a "stream-aligned" team that still needs three other teams' sign-off to ship, which means it isn't stream-aligned yet. Platform Provides internal services (infrastructure, deployment tooling, shared data platforms) that stream-aligned teams consume as a product, reducing their cognitive load. Success is measured by adoption and by how rarely anyone needs to talk to them. Anti-pattern: a platform team that requires a ticket and a two-week wait for anything, which relocates the bottleneck instead of removing it. Enabling Temporary, specialist expertise (security, a new technology adoption, test automation) that works itself out of a job by teaching stream-aligned teams the skill, then moves on. Anti-pattern: an enabling team that becomes a permanent dependency because it never transfers the capability and keeps doing the work itself. Complicated subsystem Owns a piece of the system that requires deep specialist knowledge (a pricing engine, a matching algorithm, a codec) that most stream-aligned engineers shouldn't need to hold in their heads. Rare by design. Anti-pattern: labeling a team "complicated subsystem" to justify a silo that formed for organizational-politics reasons rather than technical complexity. A sanity check for any org chart: count the teams of each type. A 200-engineer organization with twelve platform teams and eight stream-aligned ones has inverted the model and will feel it as every feature needing six handoffs. Roughly one platform engineer per eight to twelve product engineers is a common working ratio; past one in five, ask what the platform is for. Framework Three interaction modes The team type tells you what a team owns. The interaction mode tells you how two teams should work together, and mismatched modes are where coordination breaks down. Every pair of teams that touch should be able to name which mode they are in. Mode What it is When it fits How it goes wrong Collaboration Two teams working closely together for a bounded period, typically to discover something neither could figure out alone Early in a new platform capability, or when the interface between two systems has not been designed yet It becomes permanent. Collaboration has high communication overhead by design and should have a defined end date X-as-a-Service One team consumes another's output through a clean, documented interface with minimal ongoing communication, the way you'd consume a well-run internal API The default target for a platform team's relationship with stream-aligned teams, and for any mature internal dependency The interface was never built, so the relationship is collaboration wearing a service label, with the platform team fielding questions all day Facilitating One team temporarily helps another improve a specific capability (test automation discipline, incident response practice) without doing the work for them A narrow skill gap, weeks rather than months, that does not justify an enabling team It gets left out. Most summaries name two modes, and the gap between collaboration and pure service then has no name, so it gets filled with tickets A team stuck permanently in collaboration mode with another team it should be consuming as a service is a strong signal the interface between them was never built. That's usually a platform maturity gap rather than a people problem. Reference Team size and span of control Two numbers that come up in every reorg conversation, with the reasoning behind them rather than a single right answer. Team size Five to nine people is the range that holds up across Amazon's two-pizza rule, Team Topologies, and the small-group research it draws on. Below five, a single departure or vacation breaks the on-call rota and the team loses the ability to review its own work. Above nine, communication paths grow faster than headcount (36 pairs at nine, 66 at twelve) and the team starts forming sub-teams informally, usually along the lines of whatever it will eventually be split into anyway. Long-lived teams matter more than the exact number: a stable eight outperforms a rotating five. Span of control Six to eight direct reports is a reasonable default for a working manager who still does some individual contribution; eight to ten for a manager who doesn't. Adjust down for teams with junior engineers needing more development time, up for a team of senior staff who mostly need to be unblocked rather than developed. Past twelve, one-on-ones, career development, and performance calibration become triage. Below three for an extended period, the manager layer is adding latency without adding support, and the chart was probably built around a person rather than a function. Manager-to-engineer ratio is a different number from span of control and worth tracking separately. Around one manager per seven to nine engineers is typical; when it drifts toward one in four, the organization has usually been promoting into management to solve retention, which creates a layer of managers with nobody to manage. Reference Which top-level shape fits which stage The team types describe the leaves of the chart. The trunk, how engineering is grouped at the top, changes with size, and each shape has a characteristic failure that signals it is time for the next one. Stage Typical shape Why it works there The signal it has been outgrown Under 15 engineers One team, or two, reporting to the CTO or a single lead Everyone knows everything; structure would add cost and remove nothing Two people are arguing about who owns a decision and there is no answer 15 to 50 Three to six stream-aligned teams, each with a lead, reporting to the CTO or a head of engineering; infrastructure owned by one of them or a single platform engineer Product areas are distinct enough to own; a full platform team is not yet justified Every team has built its own deploy pipeline, and an outage traced to drift between them 50 to 150 Product-aligned groups of two to four teams under a director or senior manager, one platform team, an architecture function starting Groups match product lines or customer segments, so priority conflicts are resolved one level down from the CTO The CTO has more than eight reports and is the escalation path for every cross-group dependency 150 to 500 Product divisions or tribes, each with its own stream-aligned teams and an embedded platform or enablement presence; a central platform organization; a reliability function Divisions can plan and staff semi-independently; the center owns the shared foundation and standards Divisions have diverged on tooling and architecture far enough that moving an engineer between them is a re-onboarding 500 plus Business-unit engineering with a central platform, architecture, and security organization; matrixed specialists where the business units are unequal in size Local speed with a shared foundation; the classic trade the operating model example on Understanding the System Before Changing It works through The center becomes a bottleneck or the units become separate companies; the correction is a deliberate rebalancing of what is central, per Enterprise Architecture Functional grouping (all backend engineers under one manager, all front-end under another) is the one shape on no row of this table. It optimizes for skill development and against delivery, and every organization that runs it eventually reorganizes to product alignment once cross-team handoffs become the dominant cost. Matrixing a small guild structure across product teams keeps the skill development without the handoffs. Method When to split a team, and along what line Splitting too early creates coordination cost for no reason; splitting too late means the split happens informally first and formally later, with the friction of both. These are the signals and the seams.
