Signals it is time Headcount past nine, or a hiring plan that will get there within two quarters Two distinct backlogs sharing one board, with different stakeholders asking for each Standups where half the team has no reason to listen to the other half Code review consistently routed to the same three people because only they know that part On-call pages that half the rota cannot act on without escalating to the other half Where to cut Along a seam that already exists in the system or the customer base: a bounded context in the domain model, a customer segment with distinct needs, a user journey with its own entry point. The wrong seams are by technical layer (front-end and back-end) or by seniority. The test for a proposed boundary: after the split, can each team ship a normal change to production without a ticket to the other. If the answer requires a shared database that both will write to, the seam is wrong or the data needs an owner first, per Data Strategy . The mirror of a split is a merge, and it is neglected. Two three-person teams that share a backlog and page each other are one team with two managers. Merging is cheaper than splitting and almost never proposed, because it costs someone a title. Method Running the reorg Reorg cost is easy to underestimate: lost context, relationships rebuilt from scratch, a temporary productivity dip that shows up on every team, well beyond the ones directly restructured. The sequence below keeps the cost to one payment. Step What happens What it prevents 1. Name the structural problem One sentence, written down: the specific coordination failure or overload the new structure fixes, with evidence (handoff counts, lead time, the dependency map) A reorg justified after the fact, or one that is really about a person 2. Run the systems diagnostic The ten questions on Understanding the System Before Changing It , with particular weight on actors, incentives, and delays The indirect effect nobody modeled, discovered in month four 3. Design teams before boxes Team types, boundaries, and interaction modes first; reporting lines and titles second; names last An org chart drawn around the current people rather than the work 4. Pressure-test with the affected leads Every manager whose team changes sees the design before it is final and is asked what breaks The dependency only the team lead knew about 5. Announce once, completely The problem, the design, who reports where, what changes on Monday, what does not change, and the review date. Same day for everyone affected; individual conversations for anyone whose role narrows, before the announcement Rumor filling the gap between a partial announcement and the details; people learning about their own change in a group meeting 6. Hold structure for a cycle No further changes for two quarters barring a structural failure. Track the metric from step 1 Reorg fatigue: people disengaging from wherever they are placed because it won't last 7. Review at the stated date Did the metric move; what did the design get wrong; what is the next smallest correction The structure calcifying past its usefulness because

title: Platform Engineering
description: The team and system that make good delivery metrics achievable, treating internal infrastructure as a product with users.
body: Goals What this is for The central goal, and the ones downstream of it. Self-service, golden paths, and everything else on this page are the means; these are the ends. Goal What it means Reduce cognitive load on product engineering teams The central goal everything else serves. A team building a product shouldn't also have to be expert in Kubernetes, network policy, database operations, and compliance tagging just to ship; the platform absorbs that complexity. Increase delivery velocity Getting from "I need X" to "I have X" in minutes or hours instead of days or weeks. Enforce standards consistently Security, compliance, cost tagging, and network policy encoded once, in a template or golden path, rather than re-implemented, and inevitably re-implemented inconsistently, by every team on its own. Eliminate duplicated effort across teams Without a shared platform, every team quietly builds its own version of the same deployment pipeline, the same provisioning process, the same monitoring setup. Make scarce expertise available broadly A platform team's depth in networking, security, or database operations gets embedded into the platform itself, so every product team benefits without needing to hire for it directly. Improve developer experience in its own right A goal on its own terms, beyond being a side effect of the goals above. A platform can be technically capable and still fail if the people using it actively dislike it. Framework Platform as a product rather than a shared utility The distinction that determines whether a platform team gets adopted voluntarily or gets worked around. A platform built as a product has users (product engineering teams), a roadmap shaped by what those users need, and success measured by adoption and satisfaction, the same discipline applied to any external-facing product. A platform built as a shared utility gets whatever capacity is left over after feature work, has no user research behind its priorities, and gets adopted only where teams have no other choice. The first approach produces a platform teams want to use; the second produces one they route around the moment they're allowed to. Reference Cloud versus on-prem: what changes The self-service and golden path guidance below was written cloud-first, since that's the more mature case. Here's what's different if some or all of the estate is on-prem or bare metal. Dimension Cloud On-prem / bare metal Provisioning speed Minutes, via API Hours if capacity is already racked; weeks or months if new hardware has to be ordered Scaling Elastic; spin up and tear down on demand Bounded by physical capacity already on hand; scaling means ordering and racking more of it Self-service ceiling Effectively unlimited from the requester's point of view Self-service against a pre-provisioned capacity pool; a request past available headroom has to queue or escalate Cost model Opex, pay-per-use, elastic Largely fixed capex already spent; utilization efficiency matters more than avoiding waste, since the hardware cost is sunk either way Tooling maturity Mature; every major IaC tool has first-class cloud provider support Less mature; bare metal is still commonly flagged in current platform engineering discussion as "artisanal infrastructure," provisioned manually and outside the platform's own tooling, even at organizations that are otherwise fully API-driven everywhere else Most platform teams in 2026 run both. A common pattern: steady-state, predictable workloads (databases, core services) run on-prem or on bare metal where it's cheaper at scale or required for latency and compliance reasons, while variable and spiky workloads scale in the cloud. A small number of providers now offer "bare metal cloud," single-tenant physical performance with the same API-driven provisioning cloud users expect, narrowing this gap further, but it remains the less mature option and needs to be evaluated as such rather than assumed equivalent to a mainstream cloud provider's tooling. 1 Self-service versus ticket-driven infrastructure Whether provisioning something new takes minutes or a multi-day queue determines how much of the platform's value reaches engineering teams. Practice Common infrastructure needs, a new service, a database, a deployment pipeline, provisioned through self-service tooling with sane defaults, no ticket or human approval required for the standard case. Reserve human review for unusual requests; the routine ones that make up the bulk of demand should never see a human. Common failure mode Every infrastructure request routed through a ticket queue regardless of how routine it is, which caps how fast product teams can move at the platform team's ticket-processing capacity rather than at the complexity of the request. Worked example Self-service provisioning, concretely What "self-service tooling with sane defaults" looks like, rather than left as an abstraction. A developer needs a new PostgreSQL database for a service. Through a developer portal (Backstage is the common open-source choice; Port is a common commercial alternative) or an internal CLI, they select a pre-approved "new database" template and fill in a short form: service name, environment, expected scale tier. Submitting the form triggers an infrastructure-as-code pipeline, often a Terraform module or a Crossplane composition, that provisions the database with the organization's standards already baked in: encryption at rest, standard tagging for cost allocation, automated backups, and network policy applied without the developer having to know or configure any of it themselves. The database is ready in minutes, registered automatically in the service catalog, with ownership and cost attribution wired in from the start. No ticket, no human approval, for the standard case. The template itself is where governance lives. Security, compliance, and tagging requirements get encoded once, in the template, rather than re-checked by a human on every request. An unusual request, a non-standard database engine, an exception to the network policy, is exactly the case that should still route to a human, because it's the case the template wasn't built to handle safely on its own. On-prem, the same template pattern applies, provisioning still runs through a pipeline with standards baked in, but the pipeline also has to check available capacity before it commits, and route to a human when the request would exceed it. That capacity check has no equivalent in the cloud version of this example above. The database example above is self-service at the resource level, inside an environment that already exists. The same discipline applies one level up: issuing an entire new, pre-governed subscription or account to a team, Azure calls this subscription vending, AWS calls it Account Factory, GCP typically calls it a project factory. See the landing zone reference on Cloud Service Mapper for how each provider's version works. 2 Golden path design A golden path is the supported, well-paved way to accomplish a common task, deliberately easier than any alternative. Practice Design the golden path around the most common use case, make it the fastest option available, and keep it optional rather than mandatory. Teams with unusual requirements should be able to deviate, just without platform-team support for the parts they've customized away from the standard. Common failure mode A golden path built for an idealized use case that doesn't match what most teams need, so adoption stays low and everyone keeps building their own version, defeating the purpose of standardizing in the first place. 3 Team funding and organizational placement Platform teams funded as pure overhead get cut first when budget tightens, regardless of the value they're delivering. Practice Frame and track platform investment against a measurable outcome, deployment frequency, lead time, incident rate, so its value is visible in the same terms leadership already uses to evaluate engineering effectiveness. A cost center whose contribution is assumed rather than shown gets cut. Common failure mode A platform team that can't articulate its impact in outcomes anyone outside engineering tracks, which makes it the easiest line item to cut in a downturn, even when its removal would slow every other engineering team down. 4 Developer experience as a deliberate metric What a platform team optimizes for shapes what it builds; measuring the experience alongside uptime keeps the incentives pointed at the right outcome. Regular, structured feedback from the engineers using the platform, time-to-first-deploy for a new service, satisfaction survey results, support ticket volume and resolution time, treated as seriously as uptime and reliability metrics. A platform can be technically reliable and still be actively disliked by the people forced to use it, and that dissatisfaction shows up eventually as workarounds and shadow infrastructure. 5 The overbuilt platform trap Platform teams, left to their own judgment about priorities, tend toward building for imagined future scale rather than the problems product teams have today. What works Prioritization driven by direct input from the teams the platform serves, with roadmap decisions traceable to a specific request or a specific measured friction point, the same product discipline applied to any customer-facing roadmap. What backfires An elaborate multi-cluster, multi-region abstraction layer built for a scale the company is nowhere near, while product teams struggle with a basic deployment step nobody prioritized fixing because it wasn't as technically interesting to build. Interactive Score your own platform Score the five practices now and at target, then add three adoption facts. The tool ties the scores to the adoption numbers and flags the warning signs from the checklist below. Runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere. Calculate Checklist Signs the platform isn't earning its adoption Patterns that show up when a platform team exists but isn't delivering the leverage it's meant to. Product teams maintain workarounds or shadow infrastructure instead of using the platform's supported path Common provisioning tasks require a ticket and a multi-day wait rather than self-service The platform roadmap isn't traceable to specific requests or friction reported by the teams it serves Platform investment can't be tied to any measurable engineering outcome when leadership asks what it's delivering Developer satisfaction with the platform has never been measured, only assumed

title: Reliability as an Economic Decision
description: How much reliability the business can afford, and how much unreliability it's implicitly willing to sell, framed as an investment decision rather than a purely engineering one.
body: Reference Availability tiers, illustrative Each additional nine of availability costs disproportionately more than the last one, which is exactly why the target should be chosen deliberately rather than defaulted to the highest available. Availability Approx. annual downtime budget Relative cost to achieve 99% About 3.65 days per year Baseline 99.9% About 8.7 hours per year Meaningfully higher 99.95% About 4.4 hours per year Materially higher again 99.99% About 53 minutes per year Disproportionately higher; usually justified only for revenue-critical systems 1 The cost of downtime has to be a number A specific figure, or the investment decision that follows from it can't be evaluated at all. Practice Quantify what an hour of downtime costs this specific system: lost revenue, SLA penalties, support load, reputational cost where it can be estimated. Only then decide what reliability tier is worth paying for, working backward from that number. Common failure mode "Downtime is unacceptable" applied as an unexamined default to every system regardless of whether the math supports the investment that belief implies, which is how reliability spending ends up disconnected from business impact. 2 Error budgets make the tradeoff explicit A number both engineering and the business can agree on, replacing an unstated and unlimited expectation of perfection. Practice An error budget is the amount of unreliability your target explicitly allows, a 99.9% uptime target allows roughly 43 minutes of downtime a month. While that budget isn't exhausted, engineering has explicit permission to ship faster. Once it is, that's a non-personal signal to slow down and stabilize. Common failure mode Treating reliability as an unlimited, unstated expectation, where every incident is judged a failure regardless of whether the system was still within a sane, previously agreed tolerance. 3 Overengineering is a cost Redundancy protects against downtime, and it also carries an ongoing operational tax of its own. Practice Match redundancy investment to the tier a system needs rather than the highest tier available. A system that doesn't need five nines shouldn't be built to that standard just because the pattern exists elsewhere in the estate. Common failure mode Applying multi-region, high-availability architecture uniformly across the estate as the safe default, which quietly taxes every team's velocity for protection most of those systems never needed in the first place. Interactive Is the next nine worth it? List the systems whose availability target is in question. For each, the tool converts the current and target tier into hours of downtime a year, prices the difference, and compares it with the annual cost of reaching the target. The defaults are the two worked examples below plus one more. Runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere. Cost of downtime, per hour ($) Current availability tier 99% 99.9% 99.95% 99.99% Target availability tier 99% 99.9% 99.95% 99.99% Annual cost to reach target tier ($) Calculate Method Tiering the estate The calculator above evaluates one system. The decision that saves money is made once, across the estate: which systems get which tier, and why. Tier Typical target What qualifies What the tier buys Tier 1: revenue and safety critical 99.95% to 99.99% Checkout, order capture, clinical or safety systems, anything where an hour of outage is a board-level event Multi-zone or multi-region, automated failover tested quarterly, 24x7 on-call at least six deep, error budget policy signed by the product executive Tier 2: business critical 99.9% Internal systems that stop work when down: identity, CI, core data pipelines, customer support tooling Multi-zone, tested restore, business-hours on-call with escalation, an SLO with a dashboard Tier 3: important 99.5% Reporting, internal tools, anything with a manual workaround Single region with backups, restore tested annually, best-effort response Tier 4: everything else No commitment Experiments, sandboxes, deprecated systems awaiting retirement Backups if the data matters; otherwise nothing The assignment is a product decision with an engineering cost attached, made by the business owner of each system against the cost-of-downtime number rather than by engineering against what feels safe. Most estates that do this exercise find they have been paying Tier 1 costs on Tier 3 systems and running a Tier 1 system on Tier 3 infrastructure, at the same time. Worked example A checkout service, from 99.9% to 99.99% The arithmetic is simple. What matters is that it gets done before the architecture is chosen. The numbers An hour of checkout downtime costs $40,000 in lost orders and recovery effort. At 99.9% the annual downtime budget is about 8.7 hours, or roughly $350,000 of expected loss. At 99.99% it is about 53 minutes, roughly $35,000. The next nine is worth about $315,000 a year in avoided loss. Reaching it means a second region, automated failover, and a deeper on-call rota: about $220,000 a year in infrastructure and people. The investment clears by roughly $95,000 a year, and it is approved. The same arithmetic on the reporting system An hour of downtime on the internal reporting platform costs about $2,000 in delayed work. At 99.9% that is $17,000 a year of expected loss. The proposed multi-region rebuild costs $180,000 a year. It fails by an order of magnitude and is declined, and the team that proposed it is asked what a tested nightly restore would cost instead. That number is $15,000, and it gets funded. The two decisions together are the point: reliability spending moves toward where downtime costs money and away from where it does not. Diagram The two decisions side by side Moving from 99.9 to 99.99 percent availability, priced for both systems in the worked examples above. Loss avoided versus cost for the two reliability decisions Checkout $315K loss avoided per year $220K cost per year Approved: clears by about $95K a year Reporting platform under $17K loss avoided $180K cost per year Declined: a $15K tested restore funded instead Same arithmetic, opposite answers: reliability money moves toward where downtime costs money. Figures from the worked examples on this page. The calculator lets you run the same comparison across your own systems. Method Measuring availability from where the customer stands A tier target means nothing if it is measured at the wrong place. Most organizations measure where it is convenient and report a number the customer would not recognize. Measured at What it tells you What it hides The infrastructure (host up, container running) Whether the platform is alive Every failure above the platform: a deployed bug, a dependency timeout, a full disk that returns errors from a running process The load balancer (HTTP 200 rate) Whether requests are being answered Slow responses that time out on the client, correct-looking errors, and the customers who could not reach the load balancer at all A synthetic transaction (a scripted checkout every minute from outside) Whether the journey works end to end from the outside Real user diversity: regions, devices, the edge case only real traffic hits Real user monitoring (success rate of customer journeys as experienced) What customers experienced Nothing that matters, at the cost of more instrumentation; this is the number an SLO should be built on A defensible availability claim states the measurement point and the window. Five nines at the load balancer over a good quarter is not the same claim as four nines on real customer journeys over three years, and anyone doing diligence will ask which one you mean. Common pitfall The availability number that measures the wrong thing The most common failure in reliability economics is doing the arithmetic on a number that does not reflect the customer's experience. The arithmetic itself is rarely the problem. What it looks like The board deck reports 99.98% availability, measured as the percentage of minutes the load balancer returned a 200. Customer churn analysis shows that a meaningful share of cancellations cite reliability. Both are true: the checkout took nine seconds to respond for two weeks after a database change, every request returned 200, and no alert fired. The reliability investment case, built on the 99.98%, concluded no further spending was needed. The counter-move Define availability for each Tier 1 and Tier 2 system as the success rate of a named customer journey within a latency bound, measured from the client side. Rebuild the cost-of-downtime number against that definition. The number usually gets worse and the investment case usually gets clearer. See Observability & SRE Operating Model for how the measurement is built and who owns it. Checklist Signs reliability spend isn't tied to economics Patterns that show up when reliability investment is driven by instinct rather than a stated cost-benefit basis. No system has a stated availability target tied to a cost-of-downtime calculation Error budgets don't exist, so every incident is treated with the same severity regardless of whether targets were met Redundancy investment is uniform across the estate rather than tiered to criticality The cost of the current reliability posture has never been compared to the cost of the downtime it prevents "We need to be more reliable" gets stated with no number attached to what that would cost or save The next nine gets pursued because it's technically achievable rather than because the math above says it's worth it

title: Role Boundaries: CTO, CIO, CISO, CPO
description: Where these roles typically split, why the boundaries move by company type, how to write them down so the same decision doesn't get fought over by two people who each assumed it was theirs, and what to do with the newer titles (CDO, CAIO, CDAO) that keep arriving. Includes a decision-by-decision split, the CISO reporting question with its tradeoffs, a one-page charter template, and two worked disagreements.
body: Reference Typical scope by role Illustrative rather than universal. Many organizations don't have all four roles distinctly, and that's often the right call at their size. What each role is optimizing for matters more than the list of things it owns, because that is what predicts where two of them will collide. Role Typical scope Optimizes for Collides most often with CTO Technology strategy, engineering, architecture, technology-enabled competitive advantage Capability the business can sell or defend with CPO on sequencing, CIO on platform ownership CIO Internal technology estate, enterprise systems, business technology, IT operations, often the technology budget process Reliability and cost of the systems that run the business CTO on shared infrastructure and cloud, CISO on control friction CISO Security risk, cyber controls, security governance, incident response, compliance evidence Risk reduced per dollar and per unit of friction Everyone whose bonus depends on shipping; the board on what is material CPO Product strategy, roadmap, discovery, product outcomes Customer and market outcomes per engineering hour CTO on how much capacity goes to platform and debt versus features The last column is the useful one. Each pair collides on a predictable category of decision, which means the collision can be settled in advance by writing down who is Accountable for that category. That is the whole method on this page. Reference The decisions that fall between roles The org chart names the roles. It rarely names who owns the fifteen or so decisions that sit on the seams. This table is the one to fill in for your own organization; the entries are common defaults, and every one of them moves by company type. Decision Common owner Consulted Why it is contested Cloud platform and account structure CTO where the product runs on it; CIO where it is mostly enterprise workloads CISO, CFO Both product and internal systems land on it; whoever owns it owns the landing zone and the bill Identity provider and access policy CISO for policy; CIO or platform team for the directory CTO The control every other control depends on, and the source of most user friction complaints Security tooling budget CISO CTO, CIO, CFO Spent on other people's systems; friction lands on teams the CISO does not manage Security risk acceptance CISO recommends; the executive whose system carries the risk accepts, per Technology Risk Appetite CTO, counsel The CISO can name the risk but should not be the only one who can accept it, or every acceptance becomes their liability Product roadmap sequencing CPO CTO on feasibility and technical consequence Platform and debt work has no product sponsor and loses every trade unless a capacity floor is agreed Engineering capacity split (features, platform, debt) CTO, against the allocation on Technology Capital Allocation CPO, CFO The CPO experiences the platform floor as capacity taken away Enterprise applications (ERP, CRM, HR systems) CIO CTO on integration, CISO on access Product engineers build integrations against them and inherit their constraints Data platform and data ownership CDO or CDAO where one exists; otherwise CTO CIO, CISO, CPO Analytics, product features, and AI all want the same data with different quality bars; see Data Strategy AI use cases and governance Whoever owns the AI portfolio, usually CTO or CDO; a CAIO where one exists CISO, counsel, CPO Newest seam; the one most likely to have no owner today Vendor selection for shared platforms The role that will operate it CISO, procurement, CFO The buyer and the operator are often different people Technology budget process CIO in enterprises; CTO in product companies CFO, all of the above Whoever runs the process controls the framing of every other decision here Incident command for a security incident CISO as operations lead; the IC pool per Incident Response CTO, counsel Availability incidents and security incidents share a process and diverge on who leads 1 Why these lines move by company type The same role name can mean different jobs depending on what the business is. Where the split makes sense A hardware or deep-tech company often has the CTO own product direction fully, with no separate CPO, because the product and the technology are close to the same thing. A SaaS company usually splits CTO (how it's built) from CPO (what gets built) cleanly, because those really are separable questions there. A bank or insurer usually has a CIO running the estate and a CTO who is closer to a chief architect, because the technology is an operating cost rather than the product. The mistake Importing a role-boundary model from a different kind of company without checking whether the underlying business maps onto it, which produces two people with overlapping mandates and neither fully accountable for the outcome. The most common version is a newly hired executive bringing the structure from their last company, which was a different kind of company. Reference Role structure by company archetype What the boundaries above look like assembled into an org, at six points. The archetypes are common patterns rather than prescriptions; the useful exercise is finding the row closest to yours and noting where you differ, and why. Archetype CTO CPO CIO CISO Data and AI Early-stage startup (under 50 engineers) Owns strategy, engineering, and product direction together Doesn't exist yet; folded into the CTO role Doesn't exist; IT handled by a generalist or outsourced Doesn't exist; security owned by the CTO directly, with a fractional advisor Owned by the CTO; a first data hire around 30 engineers Mid-scale SaaS (200 to 1,000 engineers) Owns how the product is built: architecture, engineering, platform Owns what gets built: roadmap, discovery, customer research A light IT function, often still reporting through the CTO or COO Dedicated hire, reporting per the guidance below A head of data under the CTO or CPO; AI portfolio owned by the CTO Hardware or deep-tech Owns both product and technology direction; no separate CPO Doesn't exist; folded into the CTO role, sometimes a VP Product Management under the CTO May exist for internal systems, separate from the product itself Often folded into engineering leadership until the company reaches scale or a customer demands it Usually inside engineering Enterprise, non-tech (bank, insurer, manufacturer) Chief architect in practice: standards, platform direction, modernization; reports to the CIO or alongside Product leadership sits in the business units Owns the estate, the budget process, operations, and vendor management; the largest technology role Reports to the CIO, the COO, or the CEO; regulators increasingly want a line to the board A CDO or CDAO, often reporting to the COO or CFO rather than technology Regulated healthcare (provider or payer) Product and platform engineering where there is a digital product; otherwise architecture Digital product lead, if any Owns clinical and administrative systems, the EHR relationship, and integration; usually the senior technology role Dedicated, with a privacy officer as a peer; HIPAA makes the security officer role a named requirement A clinical informatics or CDO role; AI governance heavily shared with clinical leadership and compliance PE-backed portfolio company Often the only technology executive, wearing all four hats with the operating partner as the fifth Sometimes; often the CEO Rarely separate Fractional or shared across the portfolio, with a hard line to the deal team on diligence findings Owned by the CTO; value-creation plan usually names a data or AI workstream 2 The CTO / CIO split specifically The pairing most likely to exist on paper without a clear real-world distinction behind it. When it's earned At scale, the CTO owns what makes the product differentiated and the CIO owns what makes the business run: ERP, internal tools, IT operations, the employee technology experience. The split lets each focus without the other's priorities crowding it out, and both jobs are full-time at that size. The working agreement that makes it hold is a written answer to who owns shared infrastructure (cloud, identity, network), because both need it and each will assume the other is paying for it. When it isn't Most companies below a certain size never need both roles. Forcing the split prematurely creates two half-empowered leaders instead of one fully accountable one, and the resulting turf questions cost more than the specialization is worth at that stage. The tell: two executives each with a cloud budget, two identity providers, or a product team that files tickets to an IT team for infrastructure it could self-serve. 3 The CTO / CPO split The pairing this page's title implies gets equal treatment, so here it is. When it's earned Once "how to build it" and "what to build" are full-time, separate cognitive loads, with enough product surface area that no single person can hold both the technical architecture and the full market and customer picture in their head at once. The working agreement that makes it hold: the CPO is Accountable for roadmap priority, the CTO is Accountable for the capacity split, and both sign the capacity floor for platform and debt work at the annual allocation so it is never relitigated feature by feature. When it isn't Hiring a CPO before there's enough product complexity to justify it adds a translation layer between what customers need and what gets built, a layer a single technically fluent, product-minded CTO could have held directly, and often held better, with no handoff loss. The tell: the CPO's roadmap and the CTO's roadmap are two documents, and engineers are asked which one is real. 4 The CISO reporting line The most consequential structural decision in this group. Security reporting into a role whose other incentives directly compete with security priorities creates a structural conflict every time a security requirement would slow a release. There is no clean answer, only tradeoffs, and the trend in regulation is toward the board seeing the CISO directly regardless of the solid line. CISO reports to What it buys What it costs Fits when CEO Independence; security is visibly a business risk rather than a technology sub-function The CEO rarely has the context to arbitrate technical tradeoffs; the CISO can become isolated from engineering Regulated industries, public companies post-incident, anywhere the board has asked for it CTO Closest to the systems and the engineers; security controls get built into the platform rather than bolted on The structural conflict: the CTO's delivery incentives can override security when the two collide, and the CISO knows it Product companies where the product is the attack surface, with a written escalation path to the CEO or audit committee for disagreements CIO Natural fit for enterprise IT security; controls and operations sit together Product security can be an afterthought; same delivery-versus-control conflict as the CTO line Enterprises where most risk is in the internal estate General counsel or chief risk officer Aligns security with legal and regulatory risk; strong for privacy-heavy businesses Distance from engineering; controls can become paper-first Financial services and healthcare, often paired with a dotted line to the CTO COO Operational independence from both technology executives Depends entirely on the COO's appetite for the subject Companies where operations is the dominant risk surface (logistics, manufacturing) Whatever the solid line, three things should be true: the CISO presents to the board or its audit or risk committee at least twice a year without the CTO or CIO in the chair; the CISO can escalate a risk acceptance they disagree with to the CEO without asking permission; and the CISO's compensation is not tied to the delivery metrics of the function they report into. NYDFS Part 500 and the SEC's 2023 disclosure rules both push toward the first of these in regulated and public companies. See Building a Security Program for the rest of the argument. 5 The newer titles: CDO, CDAO, CAIO Chief data, chief data and analytics, chief AI. Each arrived to fill a gap the four classic roles left, and each creates a new seam if its boundary is not written down on the day it is created. What they own when they work A CDO or CDAO owns data governance, the data platform's product direction, data quality, and analytics enablement, and is the named owner the Data Governance and Data Strategy pages keep asking for. A CAIO owns the AI portfolio, the intake and risk-tiering process on the AI Governance Map , and the model inventory. In both cases the platform engineering underneath usually stays with the CTO, and the role is a product owner and governor of the capability rather than its builder. Where they fail Created as a reaction (a board asked about AI; a data breach embarrassed someone) with a title and no decision rights, so the new executive own

title: Security & Compliance Maturity
description: A maturity ladder across the six NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 functions, including Govern, scored on evidence rather than stated policy.
body: Framework Maturity ladder, mapped to NIST CSF 2.0 functions Five levels across the six NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 functions. Score each function separately; most organizations are unevenly mature across them, which is itself useful information. Govern provides the organizational context and direction for the other five, added in CSF 2.0 because a technically mature program with no executive-level ownership or risk strategy is a common gap. Function Level 1: Ad hoc Level 3: Defined Level 5: Optimized Govern No documented cybersecurity risk strategy at the leadership level; security reports up as a technical status update rather than a business risk Named executive accountability, a documented risk management strategy, and defined reporting cadence to leadership or the board Cybersecurity risk is a standing item in enterprise risk management, with roles, policy, and supply chain risk expectations reviewed on a defined schedule rather than only after an incident forces it Identify No current asset inventory; risk assessment happens reactively after an incident Documented asset inventory, periodic risk assessments on a defined schedule Continuous, automated asset discovery feeding a live risk register tied to business impact Protect Access controls inconsistent across systems; no formal least-privilege policy Documented access control policy, applied through a defined onboarding and offboarding process Least-privilege enforced automatically, access reviewed continuously rather than only at audit time Detect Reliant on external reports or customer complaints to learn about a problem Centralized logging and defined alerting rules for known threat patterns Behavioral anomaly detection running alongside signature-based rules, catching a wider range of patterns than either alone, though no detection approach guarantees catching a novel attack Respond No defined incident process; response improvised each time Documented incident response plan with defined roles, tested annually at minimum Response plan tested quarterly via tabletop or live drill, refined from each real incident's postmortem Recover Backups exist but restoration has never been tested Documented recovery procedures, restoration tested annually Recovery time objectives defined per system criticality and verified against actual tested restoration times How to use this Scoring on evidence, and what to do with the result The assessment only has value if the scoring holds up, which is harder than it sounds when the person scoring it is also accountable for the result. How to score it Score against evidence rather than intention. "We have a policy" is evidence of intent, and it does not reach Level 3 unless the policy is followed. Ask for the artifact, the access review log, the tested restore record, the tabletop exercise notes, before accepting a self-reported level. What to do with a low score A Level 1 or 2 in any function is a prioritization input rather than an emergency in itself. Rank functions by business impact if that function fails, rather than by how uncomfortable the low score is, and fund the highest-impact gap first rather than the easiest one to fix. Reference Framework status, September 2026 Dates that change what an auditor, customer, or acquirer will ask for this year. Framework Current state What it means NIST CSF 2.0 Published February 2024; added a sixth function, Govern [1] Maturity scoring should cover governance, roles, and supply chain risk, not only technical controls ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Certificates against the 2013 edition expired on October 31, 2025 [2] Any 2013 certificate still cited by a vendor or target is no longer valid PCI DSS 4.0.1 Requirements that were future-dated became mandatory on March 31, 2025 [3] Targeted risk analyses, authenticated internal scanning, and payment page script controls are now assessed CMMC 2.0 Phase 1 of the DoD rollout began November 10, 2025 [4] Defense contractors see assessment requirements appear in new solicitations and contracts CIS Controls v8.1 18 controls and 153 safeguards, with a Govern function added to match CSF 2.0 [5] A practical control baseline for organizations without a mandated framework SOC 2 AICPA Trust Services Criteria; points of focus revised in 2022 A Type II report covers a period of operation, so a new report says nothing about controls before its period began Sources NIST, release of Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, February 2024 IAF MD 26:2022, transition requirements for ISO/IEC 27001:2022 PCI Security Standards Council, future-dated requirements of PCI DSS v4.x DFARS final rule on CMMC, Federal Register, September 10, 2025 Center for Internet Security, CIS Controls v8.1 Worked example Scoring one function on evidence The Protect function for a 400-person SaaS company. The claimed score came from the security team's self-assessment; the evidence score came from artifacts. Practice Claimed Evidence found Evidence score Phishing-resistant MFA for all staff 4 Enforced for employees; 38 service accounts and contractors exempt 3 Quarterly privileged access review 4 Two of the last four reviews completed; no record of revocations 2 Encryption at rest for customer data 5 Default provider encryption on all stores; keys customer-managed for two regulated tenants 4 Patch critical vulnerabilities within 15 days 4 Median 22 days; 11 criticals older than 60 days 2 Function score 4.3 Gap of 1.5 points driven by process controls, not technology 2.8 Common pitfall Compliance certification as a false signal of maturity A frequent gap between what a certification confirms and what an organization assumes it confirms. What a certification confirms SOC 2 or ISO 27001 provides assurance over a defined scope and a defined audit period: that the specific controls in that scope existed and operated as described during that window. That's a narrower, bounded claim than "maturity" as this page uses the term. This ladder describes an ongoing, evolving posture across an entire function, whereas a certification is a point-in-time assurance statement about a control set the organization itself proposed for audit. What it doesn't confirm That the scope covered every system that matters, that the posture is sustained after the audit period ends rather than a snapshot assembled for it, or that a novel attack pattern outside the certified controls would be caught. Treat certification as evidence for one point on the ladder; the rest of it still has to be scored. Interactive Score your own organization Score each CSF 2.0 function three ways: what the team claims, what the evidence supports, and the target. The tool scores on evidence, shows the claimed-versus-evidence gap this page warns about, and ranks what to fund. Runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere. Calculate maturity score 1 Why NIST CSF functions as a crosswalk The practical reason to run this assessment at all, beyond the framework being well known. What it enables Many regulatory frameworks, industry standards, and customer security questionnaires reference or heavily overlap with CSF 2.0's six functions, Govern especially, since regulators and procurement teams increasingly ask the governance question directly: who owns this, and how is it reported to leadership. A single NIST CSF assessment gives a reasonable starting map for gap analysis against HIPAA, PCI DSS, or a customer security questionnaire, without redoing the assessment from scratch for each one. Where the crosswalk breaks down A healthcare or payments-specific regulation has requirements that don't map cleanly onto any single CSF function, a specific breach notification timeline, a specific cardholder data handling rule. The crosswalk gets you most of the way; the remaining gap has to be checked directly against the specific regulation's text. 2 How this differs from Zero-Trust Maturity Two maturity pages that look similar in structure but answer different questions, worth running both rather than picking one. This page scores a broad governance and lifecycle posture using a widely recognized standard, useful for board conversations, audit readiness, and mapping against specific regulatory obligations. Zero-Trust Maturity scores a specific architectural posture across six dimensions purpose-built around identity, segmentation, and blast radius, useful for engineering and security architecture decisions. The two should tell different stories about the same organization rather than duplicate the same story in different language. A team scoring well on this page's Protect function can still score poorly on zero-trust segmentation, and that gap is exactly the kind of thing worth knowing rather than averaging away.

title: Building a Security Program
description: How to stand up a security function from little or nothing, sequenced by what reduces risk first, as distinct from scoring a program that already exists.
body: Framework Sequencing: what to build first Security programs built in the wrong order spend budget on certifications before basics are solid, then fail an audit or a real incident on something the certification never checked. Stage Focus Why it sits here in the sequence Foundation MFA everywhere, least-privilege access, asset inventory, basic logging Everything else depends on this being in place rather than aspirational Visibility Centralized logging, vulnerability scanning, dependency tracking You can't manage what you can't see; this precedes any formal certification effort Process Incident response plan, vulnerability management SLA, access review cadence Turns visibility into action with defined ownership and timelines Certification SOC 2, ISO 27001, or industry-specific frameworks Documents what should already be true; pursuing it earlier produces a program built for the audit rather than for risk 1 Where security reports, and how it's funded Organizational placement determines whether security has authority or exists to be consulted and overruled. Practice Security leadership with a direct line to the CEO, CTO, or board, rather than buried three levels inside engineering where its priorities compete for the same budget and headcount as feature delivery and consistently lose. Funded as its own line item rather than a rounding error inside another team's budget. Common failure mode Security reporting to the VP of Engineering whose bonus is tied to shipping velocity, which creates a structural conflict every time a security requirement would slow a release. The person deciding the tradeoff has an incentive on only one side of it. 2 The certification trap Chasing SOC 2 or ISO 27001 before the underlying practice exists produces a certification that doesn't mean what it's supposed to mean. Practice Treat the certification as documentation of an existing, functioning program rather than the goal itself. If the auditor's checklist is the first time a control gets implemented, it'll be the first thing that lapses once attention moves elsewhere after the audit passes. Common failure mode A clean SOC 2 report sitting alongside weak day-to-day practice, because the control existed for exactly the audit window and nowhere else. This is discoverable, and it's the kind of gap a technology diligence process is built to find. 3 DevSecOps: where security enters the pipeline Security that only reviews code after it's written catches less and creates more friction than security embedded earlier. Practice Automated scanning (SAST, dependency checking, secret detection) running in CI on every commit, with findings surfaced to the engineer who wrote the code within minutes rather than batched into a security review weeks later when context is gone and the fix costs more. Common failure mode A security team that reviews finished features right before release, which makes every finding an emergency, teaches engineers to see security as an obstacle rather than a partner, and pushes fixes to be rushed under deadline pressure. 4 Building without headcount Early-stage companies rarely get a security team on day one. The sequencing still matters even with one part-time person or none. Start with the foundation-stage items above; they cost discipline more than headcount: enforce MFA, remove standing admin access, keep a current inventory of what systems exist and who owns them. A fractional security advisor or a well-scoped external assessment can substitute for a full-time hire through the visibility stage; process and certification need dedicated ownership once the company is large enough that a security incident would be existential. 5 Third-party and vendor risk as part of the program Verizon's 2025 Data Breach Investigations Report found a third party involved in 30 percent of breaches, double the year before. [1] A security program that stops at the company's own systems is scoped to the wrong boundary. Practice Every vendor with access to production systems or sensitive data gets a security review before signing, using the same evidence-over-policy discipline covered in the certification trap above. Track which vendors hold what data, and get notification obligations for a vendor's own breach written into the contract. Common failure mode Security review happens for major platform vendors and gets skipped for the small SaaS tool a team signed up for with a credit card, which is exactly the kind of vendor least likely to have a mature security program and most likely to be the entry point when something goes wrong. Sources Verizon, 2025 Data Breach Investigations Report (release, April 2025) 6 The human element Most incidents start with a person rather than a zero-day. Awareness training exists to address this and usually doesn't. What changes behavior Short, frequent, specific training tied to real incidents the company or its industry has seen, plus simulated phishing that's used to identify where more support is needed rather than to publicly shame whoever clicked. The goal is a workforce that reports a suspicious email in minutes instead of hiding a mistake. The checkbox version An annual training video nobody remembers a week later, run once for compliance purposes and never referenced again. It satisfies an audit requirement and does close to nothing for risk, which is the same gap the certification trap describes, applied to people instead of controls. 7 What the program looks like at different stages The sequencing above holds at every size. What changes is how much of it is a dedicated person versus a shared responsibility. Stage What's realistic Under 50 engineers Foundation stage owned by engineering leadership directly, no dedicated headcount yet. A fractional advisor for anything requiring specialized judgment. 50 to 200 engineers First dedicated security hire, typically a generalist covering foundation and visibility stages. Certification work, if customer-driven, usually needs external audit support. 200 to 1,000 engineers A small team with a named leader reporting per the authority guidance above, specialization beginning (application security separate from infrastructure security). 1,000-plus engineers A full function with dedicated roles across the domains this page and Security & Compliance Maturity describe, and enough scale that the vendor risk program above needs its own owner. 8 What attackers are actually doing Sequence the program against how breaches happen, not against a framework's table of contents. Figures are from Verizon's 2025 Data Breach Investigations Report, based on more than 12,000 confirmed breaches. [1] Finding What it means for sequencing Credential abuse was the leading initial access vector, at about 22 percent of breaches Phishing-resistant MFA and removing standing admin access belong in the first 30 days Exploitation of vulnerabilities was about 20 percent, up roughly a third on the prior year, with edge devices and VPNs heavily targeted An enforced patch deadline for known-exploited vulnerabilities on internet-facing systems, measured weekly Third-party involvement doubled to 30 percent Vendor inventory and access review before, not after, the certification effort Ransomware was present in 44 percent of breaches, and in the large majority of breaches at smaller organizations Offline or immutable backups with a tested restore are foundation-stage work, not resilience polish Sources Verizon, 2025 Data Breach Investigations Report (release, April 2025) 9 The first 180 days, sequenced A concrete plan that follows the stages above. Days are guides; the order matters more than the pace. Window Deliverables Days 0 to 30 Phishing-resistant MFA for administrators, email, and remote access; standing admin rights removed; asset and SaaS inventory started; endpoint detection deployed; backups verified offline or immutable, with one real restore Days 31 to 90 Central logging with at least 12 months retention for security-relevant sources; external attack surface scanning; a 14-day deadline for known-exploited vulnerabilities on internet-facing systems; an incident response plan and one tabletop exercise; vendor inventory with data access mapped Days 91 to 180 Secret scanning, dependency scanning, and static analysis in CI; quarterly access reviews with evidence; phishing simulation used for coaching; a risk register tied to the risk appetite ; a gap assessment against NIST CSF 2.0 or CIS Controls IG1 After 180 days Certification if customers require it, now documenting controls that already run; specialization of the team as described in section 7 Diagram The 180 days at a glance The plan above as a sequence. Days are guides; the order matters more than the pace. The first 180 days of a security program Days 0 to 30 Stop the common breach Phishing-resistant MFA for admins Standing admin rights removed Endpoint detection deployed Backups offline, one real restore Days 31 to 90 See and respond Central logging, 12 months kept Attack surface scanning 14-day deadline for known exploits IR plan and one tabletop Days 91 to 180 Build it into delivery Secret, dependency, static scans in CI Quarterly access reviews Risk register tied to appetite Gap assessment: CSF 2.0 or CIS IG1 After 180 Prove it Certification if customers need it, documenting controls that already run The order follows how breaches actually happen: credential abuse and exploited vulnerabilities first, then the ability to notice and respond, then prevention built into how software ships. Certification comes last because it should document controls that already run, not create them. Each phase assumes the one before it. MFA and admin rights come first because credential abuse was the leading initial access vector in the breach data this page cites. 10 Frameworks, and what each one is for Choosing a framework is choosing an audience. Most organizations use one as the internal backbone and map the others to it, as described on Governance, Risk & Compliance . Framework What it is Use it when NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 (2024) Outcome-based framework with six functions; 2.0 added Govern [2] You need a program backbone and a common language with the board CIS Critical Security Controls v8.1 18 controls and 153 safeguards, grouped into three implementation groups; IG1 is essential cyber hygiene You need a concrete, prioritized first-year checklist ISO/IEC 27001:2022 A certifiable information security management system with 93 Annex A controls; 2013-version certificates expired on October 31, 2025 [3] International or enterprise customers ask for certification SOC 2 (AICPA Trust Services Criteria) An auditor's report; Type II covers how controls operated over a period, commonly 6 to 12 months US B2B customers ask for an attestation HITRUST CSF A healthcare-oriented harmonized framework with e1, i1, and r2 assessment levels Health systems or payers are your customers PCI DSS v4.0.1 Card data security standard; the future-dated requirements became mandatory on March 31, 2025 [4] You store, process, or transmit card data CMMC 2.0 US Department of Defense requirement, phased into contracts from November 10, 2025 [5] You hold defense contracts involving controlled unclassified information Sources NIST, release of Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, February 2024 IAF MD 26:2022, transition requirements for ISO/IEC 27001:2022 PCI Security Standards Council, future-dated requirements of PCI DSS v4.x DFARS final rule on CMMC, Federal Register, September 10, 2025 Checklist Signs the program is theater Patterns that show up when a security program looks complete in documentation and isn't reflected in daily operation. Policies exist and are current, but engineers can't describe what they do differently because of them A clean audit report alongside known unpatched vulnerabilities or unreviewed access grants Security reviews happen only at release time, never earlier in the development process No one can say when the last access review happened or produce evidence it occurred Security funding and headcount decisions are made by the same leader whose other priorities compete directly with security requirements Vendor security review happens for large platform contracts and gets skipped for anything signed up with a credit card Administrator and email access use SMS or app codes rather than phishing-resistant MFA No written deadline exists for patching known-exploited vulnerabilities on internet-facing systems, or nobody measures it

title: Understanding the System Before Changing It
description: A ten-question diagnostic for understanding a system, team, process, or technology, well enough to anticipate how it will respond before you intervene.
body: Phase 1 · Understand the system : what it is, and what's inside it 1 Define the system What you're changing, stated at the level where the behavior lives rather than the level where the budget line sits. The question Name the system being changed, and go beyond the artifact being removed or added. The artifact is the visible trigger. The system is everything whose behavior depends on it. Operating model The artifact is four reporting lines. The system being changed is every business unit president's direct influence over what used to be their own technology priorities, and the speed that came from a technology leader who sat in that president's own staff meeting every week. System of systems The artifact is an event bus. The system being changed is every point-to-point contract between the five systems, the implicit timing and ordering assumptions baked into each one, and every downstream report or reconciliation process that quietly depends on those assumptions holding. The technique for finding the system instead of stopping at the artifact is root cause analysis: ask why the artifact is the proposed fix, then why that answer is true, and repeat until the answer isn't itself caused by something further upstream. Toyota's 5 Whys is the simplest version of this. Stop after one round and you've defined the artifact and missed the system. 2 Define the boundary What you're excluding, and whether that exclusion makes the analysis easier or makes it wrong. The question Every analysis draws a boundary around what counts as "in scope." The boundary is usually drawn to make the planning tractable, which means it's drawn to exclude exactly the inconvenient parts. Operating model The boundary drawn for planning was "reporting lines and the org chart." Excluded: the commitments each business unit president already made to their own board or customers based on having direct control over technology, and the unwritten, unit-specific prioritization logic no one ever documented centrally. System of systems The boundary drawn for planning was "the integration layer." Excluded: the five system owners' own roadmaps, each of which assumed continued control over their point-to-point contracts, and the data warehouse's nightly batch jobs, which rely on a delivery order the event bus doesn't guarantee. The technique for drawing a boundary that doesn't quietly exclude the inconvenient part is MECE, mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive, a McKinsey problem-structuring principle: break what's potentially in scope into pieces that don't overlap and, together, cover the whole system, then test each piece against the boundary question directly. An issue tree is the same technique on paper, one big question broken into an exhaustive, non-overlapping set of smaller ones, instead of a boundary drawn once by instinct and never checked for what it left out. 3 Identify actors Who behaves differently because of the intervention, beyond who signs off on it. The question Approval lists and stakeholder lists are not the same thing as the list of people whose day-to-day behavior changes. The second list is usually longer and less obvious. Operating model The four technology leaders now reporting to the CTO are the obvious actors. Beyond them: every business unit president who loses direct authority over what used to be their own roadmap. Every business stakeholder who now routes a request through a shared enterprise queue instead of a direct relationship with an embedded technology leader. System of systems The team building the event bus is the obvious actor. Beyond it: every system owner who now has to instrument their system to publish events instead of just responding to direct calls. Every analyst whose report assumed CRM updates arrive before billing updates, an order the bus doesn't guarantee. Phase 2 · Understand the behavior : what drives it, and what it's already doing 4 Identify incentives What behavior the current system rewards, which is usually not the same thing as what the org chart says it rewards. The question Every system rewards something whether anyone designed it to or not. Find the reward structure that operates in practice before assuming the intervention only changes what it was aimed at. Operating model The current system rewards each business unit's technology leader for being maximally responsive to their own president, since that's who evaluates them and controls their budget. Centralizing removes that direct incentive and replaces it with enterprise-level prioritization no single president controls, so responsiveness to any one unit necessarily drops even as total enterprise throughput rises. System of systems The current system rewards each system owner for shipping their own roadmap fast, since integrations are point-to-point and entirely theirs to manage. An event bus rewards owners for publishing stable, well-documented event contracts, a different skill than shipping features quickly. 5 Identify feedback loops What gets amplified, what gets suppressed, once the change is live. The question An intervention rarely adds a new behavior in isolation. It usually strengthens one existing loop and weakens another, and the weakened loop was often doing quiet, unglamorous work. Operating model Amplified: standardization pressure, since a centralized CTO is rewarded for reducing duplicate platforms and enforcing common tooling across units. Suppressed: the fast, informal channel that let a business unit president get an urgent fix bumped to the front of the queue without a formal enterprise-wide justification. System of systems Amplified: how freely owners add new integrations, since publishing an event is cheaper than negotiating a new point-to-point contract with another team. Suppressed: the friction that used to force two teams to talk before building a new dependency between their systems. 6 Identify delays What consequences won't appear immediately, and how long the gap plausibly runs before they do. The question A delay is what lets a bad intervention look successful for a while. The longer the delay, the more confidently people will point to the wrong evidence when asked if it worked. Operating model For the first two quarters, the four technology leaders keep making the same calls they always did out of habit and relationship, so almost nothing visibly changes. The effect that matters, roadmap decisions increasingly reflecting enterprise tradeoffs instead of any one unit's priorities, shows up nine to twelve months later, once the centralized budget cycle runs its first full round. System of systems The event bus goes live and every system publishes correctly on day one. The cost shows up months later, when the warehouse's nightly reports start silently running on stale data during any week event delivery lags by even a few minutes, a failure mode the old synchronous calls never had. Phase 3 · Understand the consequences : what an intervention would disturb 7 Identify indirect effects What emerges from the intervention beyond the thing it was aimed at, whether that shows up nearby, elsewhere, or later. The question The intended effect gets modeled because it's the point of the change. Indirect effects get missed because nobody's job was to look for them, and they don't always arrive as a single, traceable step. Sometimes it's a feedback loop producing a result much later. Sometimes it's simultaneous, showing up somewhere nobody thought to check. Operating model The goal was reducing duplicate technology spend across units. One indirect effect: business unit presidents who used to treat their technology leader as part of their own leadership team start making major business decisions with no technology input in the room, because that seat physically moved to a different reporting line and stopped showing up to their staff meeting. System of systems The goal was reducing integration maintenance burden. One indirect effect: the customer-facing app starts showing intermittent, hard-to-reproduce data inconsistencies, because two events that used to arrive in guaranteed order under a direct call now sometimes arrive out of order through the bus, a case nobody who built the original UI logic anticipated. 8 Identify constraints Which constraints are binding (physics, contract, regulation) and which are organizational habits nobody has re-examined lately. The question Every plan runs into "we can't do that because X." Half of those X's are load-bearing. The other half are how it's always been done, restated as if it were a law of physics. Operating model Binding constraint: one business unit operates under a regulatory requirement that mandates a separately governed technology function, so that unit can't be fully centralized without a compliance problem. Habit, never questioned: the assumption that every unit needs its own full technology leadership stack rather than shared platform capability with unit-specific product ownership. System of systems Binding constraint: billing's downstream finance reporting requires transactional consistency an eventually-consistent bus can't provide without extra work. Habit, never questioned: the assumption that every integration needs to be real-time, when several of the five systems only ever needed daily reconciliation. 9 Identify measures What you're optimizing, and what behavior that specific metric will produce once people start managing to it. The question Whatever gets measured gets managed to, including the parts of the metric you didn't intend. State the metric, then ask what the cheapest way to hit it looks like. Operating model If the measure is "total technology headcount reduced," the cuts land hardest on whichever unit documented its context the least rather than on duplication. The metric that matters is duplicate capability eliminated without loss of unit-specific delivery speed; headcount alone measures the wrong thing. System of systems If the measure is "point-to-point integrations removed," teams migrate the easy ones first and leave the fragile, high-risk ones for later, the opposite of where the risk lives. The metric that matters is risk-weighted fragility reduced; integration count measures the wrong thing. Phase 4 · Intervene : then close the loop 10 Design the intervention, then observe the response The intervention that changes the system behavior you want with the least unnecessary disruption, rather than the largest change that feels decisive. The question Everything above exists to inform this design choice. A sequenced intervention that respects the loops and delays you just found usually beats a bigger one that ignores them, though a structural problem sometimes needs a structural fix rather than a smaller version of the same mistake. Either way, the intervention is never the last step. Watch what the system does in response, and update the answers above if it's not what questions 4 through 9 predicted. Operating model Instead of centralizing all four units in one reorg announcement: a phased centralization starting with the shared services duplicated identically across all four units, common infrastructure, security, while each unit keeps a dedicated technology lead in their president's staff meeting for at least two more budget cycles. Afterward, check whether presidents still report technology as represented at their leadership table, rather than assuming the org chart change was fine because nobody complained in month one. System of systems Instead of cutting all five systems over in one release: a phased migration starting with the two systems least sensitive to ordering, with the old point-to-point path kept running in parallel until event delivery is proven reliable under production load. Afterward, the warehouse's report accuracy gets checked against the old baseline rather than assumed fine because the bus is technically delivering events. This is where the loop closes back into the rest of the toolkit: ADRs & Roadmapping records the decision, and whatever gets measured afterward feeds back into the Measurement stage of Decision Architecture , which feeds back into Strategy. This diagnostic continues past the decision. Checklist Before you sign off on the intervention Run this against any change crossing more than one team's boundary, a shared platform, or a standing risk control. You can name at least two actors, beyond the team proposing the change, who will behave differently once it ships You can name the current incentive the change removes or reverses, as well as the goal it's meant to achieve You've written down an indirect effect you expect, alongside the intended one the proposal is optimized for The success metric measures the outcome you want rather than the easiest thing to measure by the deadline You've stated which constraints are binding and which are how it's always been done, out loud, in the room

title: We're Introducing AI
description: A situational entry point for a technology leader being asked to bring AI into the enterprise: the decisions with dates, the questions that separate viable initiatives from demos, the pilot-sprawl trap, and what should exist at 30, 90, and 180 days.
body: Reading order Where to start Portfolio and data first, because they decide what is feasible. Governance and architecture next, because they decide what is safe and repeatable. Cost throughout. AI Portfolio Management Gate on feasibility and data readiness first, then classify every initiative as Scale, Incubate, Watch, or Kill. This is the page that turns a wishlist into a portfolio. Data Strategy Data quality, lineage, and ownership are the prerequisite most AI programs discover after the pilot. Read this before committing to anything that depends on your own data. AI Governance Map Risk tiering, intake, human oversight, and the standards landscape: ISO/IEC 42001, NIST AI RMF, and when certification is worth it. Regulatory Map The EU AI Act timeline after the 2026 deferral, the US state picture, and who owns each obligation. AI Architecture Map RAG, document intelligence, agent orchestration, PHI and PII protection, and observability, with provider choices at every stage. Identity & Access Architecture Agents act with whatever identity they are given; scope it before the first one reaches production. AI FinOps Map Token economics, reserved capacity, caching and batch discounts, and the break-even for self-hosting. Model this before the bill teaches you. AI and the Engineering Operating Model What changes in how engineers work when AI tooling is in the loop, and what does not. Technology Risk Appetite State explicitly what the organization will not accept from an AI system before someone ships it. Build vs Buy Most AI capability should be bought or composed. The page for deciding where the exceptions are. Decisions with a date What has to be decided, and by when The organization is already using AI whether or not a decision has been made. These decisions replace drift with structure without slowing the work down. By when Decision Who owns it What it looks like when it goes wrong Day 7 Who owns AI in the organization: one accountable executive, a portfolio, and an intake path, so that requests have somewhere to go CEO, on the CTO's recommendation Every function starts its own initiative, nobody can say what the company is doing with AI, and the board finds out from a vendor Day 14 What is already in use, sanctioned or not, and which of it handles customer, employee, or regulated data CTO with the CISO A shadow tool with an open data-retention policy has been receiving customer records for six months Day 30 The risk tiers and the intake criteria, published, with the uses that are prohibited outright named CTO with legal and the CISO Governance arrives after the first initiative ships and is experienced as a brake rather than a lane Day 45 The first portfolio classification: which initiatives Scale, Incubate, Watch, or Kill, and what each one costs CTO with the business owners Fifteen pilots, no kills, and a budget line that nobody can trace to an outcome Day 60 The platform decision: which model providers, which hosting posture, which guardrails and observability are mandatory for anything in production CTO with the architecture function Each team picks a provider, builds its own retrieval stack, and none of it is monitorable or portable Day 90 The unit economics of the first production initiative, measured, and whether it justifies scaling CTO with the CFO The pilot's demo cost is used as the production estimate and the bill arrives at ten times the model Questions to ask Questions that separate initiatives from demos Ask these of every proposed initiative before it gets a budget line, and again before it goes to production. For each proposed initiative, what data does it need, does it exist, who owns it, and what is its quality today Which initiatives would be valuable if they worked, and which are being proposed because they are visible What is the organization's tolerance for a wrong answer in this use case, and who has said so Which of the current AI tools in use retain or train on the data sent to them, and what has been sent Where does a human review the output, and is that review substantive or a checkbox What does the first initiative cost per transaction at production volume rather than demo volume Which regulations already apply to the decisions the AI will influence, regardless of the fact that it is AI If the model provider changed pricing, terms, or availability tomorrow, what would break and how fast could it be swapped What would the organization stop doing if this initiative succeeded, and does anyone want to stop doing it The trap Pilot sprawl The most common state of an enterprise AI program at month nine is a dozen pilots, each with a champion, none with a kill criterion, and no way to say which of them the company is betting on. What it looks like Every function got a pilot approved because saying no felt like being against AI. Each one used a different provider, built its own prompt library, and stored its own copy of the data. Six are technically working, none are in production, the cost is now visible on the cloud bill, and the board asks what the company got for it. The answer is a set of demos. The counter-move Run it as a portfolio from day one, with the gating in AI Portfolio Management : feasibility and data readiness before anything else, an explicit Kill classification that is used, and a cap on concurrent incubations. Pay for the platform layer once, centrally: guardrails, observability, retrieval, and cost attribution. Measure unit economics on the first production initiative before scaling anything, and report the portfolio to the board as a portfolio, including the kills. Outputs What should exist at 30, 90, and 180 days A program that can show these artifacts is a program the board can fund with confidence. One that cannot is a set of pilots. Checkpoint What exists Day 30 One accountable owner and a published intake path. An inventory of AI tools already in use, with data exposure classified. Risk tiers and prohibited uses published. The first version of the risk appetite statement covering AI systems. Day 90 A classified portfolio with costs, owners, and kill criteria. A platform decision recorded as an ADR: providers, hosting posture, mandatory guardrails and observability. The data readiness gaps for the Scale and Incubate initiatives named with owners. At least one initiative killed, publicly, so the organization learns the classification has teeth. Day 180 The first production initiative live, with measured unit economics and a monitored error rate, reported to the board. Cost attribution by initiative on the bill. A governance process that has processed real intake and can show its decisions. A one-page AI narrative for the board that describes a portfolio rather than a pile of pilots.

title: We're Cutting Costs
description: A situational entry point for a technology cost reduction mandate: the decisions with dates, the questions that separate real savings from deferred cost, the across-the-board trap, and what should exist at 30, 60, and 90 days.
body: Reading order Where to start Framing first, then the ranked list, then the CFO. The mechanics of cloud and vendor savings come after the decisions about what is protected. Technology Strategy During a Downturn The framing for the whole exercise: what to protect, what to pause, and what to kill, decided before the spreadsheet opens. Technology Capital Allocation The pre-ranked cut list this moment demands. If it does not exist yet, this page is how to build it in a week. Working with the CFO Numbers with visible derivation, and the conversation that has to happen before the budget meeting rather than in it.
