The transposition deadline was June 7, 2026; only a handful of member states met it [2] Treat the directive's requirements as the working standard across the EU even where local law is late NYC Local Law 144 An independent bias audit and candidate notice before using an automated employment decision tool Any AI resume screener or ranking tool used for New York City roles needs an annual audit Colorado SB 26-189 From January 1, 2027, notice, explanation of adverse decisions, appeal, and human review for automated decisions affecting employment [3] The same obligations reach any AI-assisted hiring step for Colorado candidates EU AI Act AI used in recruitment and worker management is high-risk; after the 2026 AI Omnibus those obligations apply from December 2, 2027 [4] Vendors and deployers of hiring AI need conformity work planned now Sources Directive (EU) 2023/970, Pay Transparency Seyfarth Shaw, Colorado enacts AI replacement law (SB 26-189), May 2026 European Commission, AI Omnibus enters into force, July 2026 Checklist Signs the hiring and leveling process isn't working Patterns that show up when hiring feels rigorous but the underlying signal is weaker than the process implies. Leveling is anchored to years of experience rather than documented scope and ambiguity handled Interviewers ask overlapping questions, leaving signal gaps (design, collaboration) untested Interviewers discuss impressions with each other before submitting independent scores The interview process screens for culture fit (similarity) rather than culture add (what's missing) No standing calibration mechanism exists to check whether "senior" means the same thing across different hiring managers or teams Interview questions have no written, anchored rubric, so scores reflect each interviewer's personal bar Postings go out without pay ranges in places that require them, or leveling bands do not exist to support the ranges An AI screening or ranking tool is in use without the audit, notice, and human review that apply where you hire

title: Running the Technology Budget
description: The operational mechanics of managing a standing budget across a year: variance, showback versus chargeback, and the review cadence that catches drift before it becomes a surprise. Distinct from deciding how to allocate capital in the first place.
body: Reference Vocabulary worth having cold Terms that come up constantly in a budget conversation and are worth knowing precisely rather than only recognizing. Term What it means Run-rate What a cost annualizes to at its current pace, distinct from a one-time cost that won't repeat Variance The gap between forecast and actual; favorable if actual cost came in lower or actual value came in higher than planned, unfavorable the other way Accrual versus cash timing A cost gets recognized when it's incurred, which is often a different moment from when cash moves; a signed annual contract can show up as a full expense before a single payment has gone out Burn rate Net cash spent per month; the number that determines runway at an early-stage company more than total budget size does 1 Forecast versus actual: what triggers a reforecast Most gaps between plan and reality are noise. Knowing which gaps are normal and which are signal is the skill here. Normal drift Cloud costs fluctuating with real usage, a hire landing a month later than planned, ordinary seasonal patterns already built into the forecast. Small variance in either direction, within roughly 5 to 10 percent, is what a forecast is supposed to absorb. Red flags A category running more than 10 to 15 percent off forecast for two consecutive months, a single large unplanned commitment, or the same category missing in the same direction every quarter. The last pattern usually means the estimate method itself is wrong, whatever the noise in reality. 2 Showback versus chargeback Two different mechanisms for making technology cost visible to the teams generating it, with different requirements and different politics. Showback Each team sees what it costs; no money moves between budgets. Builds awareness and light peer pressure without the political fight over whose budget absorbs what. The right starting point almost everywhere. Chargeback Team budgets are directly debited for what they consume. Creates ownership and an incentive to optimize, but it requires trustworthy, granular cost attribution first. Chargeback built on shaky tagging produces disputed bills nobody believes, which is worse than not having it. 3 The review cadence itself See The CTO Operating System for where this sits in the broader monthly rhythm. This is what the review itself needs to contain. What a working review covers Actuals versus forecast by category, with the variance explained in one sentence per line item instead of a number sitting next to another number. Any category trending toward a reforecast gets flagged as it happens rather than discovered when the quarter closes. What a review that's just theater looks like A spreadsheet recited back without anyone asking why a variance happened. It produces the same conversation every month, and no decision ever comes out of it differently than it would have without the meeting. 4 Consolidating a budget across multiple business units Everything above describes running one budget. Once the technology function serves several BUs with separate P&Ls, possibly on different fiscal calendars or in different currencies, the review cadence still applies but a roll-up layer has to sit on top of it. What the roll-up needs A common chart of accounts across every BU, so "cloud infrastructure" means the same category everywhere rather than each BU tracking spend under its own local taxonomy. A consolidation date that accommodates the slowest BU's close, or a documented estimate-then-true-up process for the ones that close later. Currency conversion locked to a single rate source and a single date per period, since a roll-up recalculated at spot rates on different days never reconciles cleanly. The funding model decided on Technology Capital Allocation (corporate-funded core, chargeback, showback, or federal) applied consistently, since a roll-up mixing funding models across BUs produces a total that doesn't mean anything. Common failure mode Each BU's finance team builds its own version of the technology budget using its own categories and its own judgment calls about what counts as technology spend at all, and the group-level total is assembled by a spreadsheet that reconciles those differences by hand every quarter. The reconciliation effort scales with the number of BUs and the roll-up becomes less trustworthy exactly as it becomes more important, since a larger, more complex group is precisely when leadership most needs one true consolidated number. A newly acquired BU is the most common source of a broken roll-up: its categories, fiscal calendar, and currency rarely match on day one. Build the mapping into the acquisition's technology integration plan rather than discovering the mismatch at the first group-level close; see Technology & M&A Integration . Reference A year in the budget A technology budget has a shape across the year that is predictable, and most of the surprises come from treating it as twelve identical months. When What happens What the CTO does Month 1 Plan locked; actuals from last year still closing Baseline every category; confirm the reserve is recorded as reserve and not quietly pre-spent Months 2 to 3 First real actuals; early variance appears, usually in cloud and contractors Set the variance thresholds per category; fix any tagging or attribution gap now, because showback later depends on it Month 4 First quarterly review with the CFO One page: actuals, variance explained per line, categories trending to reforecast, decisions requested Months 5 to 6 Mid-year; the point at which a reforecast is still worth doing Reforecast any category more than 10 to 15 percent off for two months; reconcile the vendor renewal calendar against the second-half budget Month 7 Second quarterly review; budget planning for next year begins in finance Bring the pre-ranked priorities to the CFO one-on-one, per Working with the CFO , before the formal cycle Months 8 to 9 Next year's budget submission Build next year from this year's run-rate plus decisions rather than from this year's plan; every ask carries its derivation Month 10 Third quarterly review; year-end pressure begins Decide what the reserve funds, if anything; resist the year-end spend-it-or-lose-it instinct unless the item was already on the ranked list Months 11 to 12 Close; accruals and timing Confirm which contracts hit which year; a renewal signed in month 12 for next year can land in either, and the CFO cares which Worked example A variance that was signal, and one that was not Two categories drift in the same quarter. The skill is telling them apart quickly. Cloud, up 18 percent for two months The cloud category is 18 percent over forecast in months 3 and 4. The instinct is to escalate. The review asks why per line: a new analytics workload is running as designed, and a data pipeline was duplicated during a migration and both copies are still running. The first is a forecast error, corrected by reforecasting the category up and noting that the workload's business owner approved it. The second is waste, and the duplicate is turned off the same week. Net: one reforecast, one saving, no escalation, and the FinOps tagging gap that hid the duplicate becomes a fix with an owner. Contractors, up 12 percent every quarter The contractor line has been over forecast by roughly 12 percent in each of the last four quarters. Each quarter it was explained as a specific project overrun and absorbed. In the fourth review someone lays the four explanations side by side: the pattern is that the organization is running a permanent contractor bench it has never budgeted for. This is the finding. A reforecast would paper over it; the fix is a decision about whether those roles should be headcount, and it goes to the capital allocation conversation with a number attached. Method The one-page monthly review The review that produces decisions fits on a page. The one that produces a recitation does not. Section Content Rule Headline Total actual versus forecast, year to date, one sentence on trajectory If the sentence is the same as last month, say so; that is information Variance by category Each category off by more than the threshold, with the cause in one line and whether it is timing, forecast error, or a change in the underlying cost No number without a cause; no cause without a category of cause Reforecast candidates Categories trending toward a reforecast, flagged before they cross the line Flag early; a reforecast announced after the quarter closes is a surprise, and surprises are what the CFO remembers Commitments ahead Renewals, hires, and purchases landing in the next 90 days, with the budget line each hits This is the renewal calendar from SaaS Contract & Renewal Negotiation merged into the budget view Decisions requested What the CTO needs the CFO or CEO to decide this month, with the recommendation A review with nothing in this section for three months running is theater Common pitfall The reserve that becomes a slush fund A budget with no reserve blows through its total the first time reality diverges from plan. A budget whose reserve is spent quietly on whatever came up last has the same problem with a worse audit trail. What it looks like Reserve is set at 8 percent. By month 5 it has funded a conference, an overrun on a project that was never reforecast, and a tool a team wanted. None of the three went through a decision. When the unplanned event that matters arrives in month 9, an unsupported database that has to be migrated after a vulnerability disclosure, the reserve is gone and the CTO is asking the CFO for money that was supposed to already exist. The counter-move Reserve is spent only by a recorded decision, against the same ranked list the capital allocation page describes, and it is reported in the monthly review as a line with a balance. Overruns are reforecast rather than absorbed. Anything that would have been declined at planning time is declined from the reserve too. The test of a reserve is that in month 9 it is still there. Checklist Signs the budget is being tracked rather than managed Patterns that show up when a budget process exists on the calendar but isn't catching anything before it becomes a problem. Variance gets discovered at quarter-end review rather than flagged as it's happening No one can explain why a specific line item is off forecast, only that it is Chargeback exists on paper but nobody trusts the underlying cost attribution The same category misses in the same direction every quarter and the forecast method has never been revisited Budget review meetings recite the numbers without any decision changing afterward

title: Technology Capital AllocationThe technology portfolio as proportional bands, with what is protected and where cuts are drawn from
description: The standing discipline of allocating scarce capital across run, grow, and transform, security, technical debt, headcount, vendors, and reserve, and being able to answer what gets cut or funded first without re-deriving the answer from scratch each time.
body: Reference Allocation categories The buckets a technology budget breaks into, distinct enough that lumping them together hides tradeoffs that should be explicit. Category What it covers Run The operational cost of keeping existing systems working: hosting, licensing, on-call, routine maintenance Grow Proven initiatives extending existing capability into adjacent, validated opportunity Transform New bets with unresolved uncertainty; the Horizon 3 work from the technology strategy Security Dedicated investment, evaluated on its own terms rather than folded into run cost or treated as a rounding error Technical debt remediation A deliberate allocation rather than whatever capacity happens to be left over after everything else is funded Headcount People cost not already attributed to one of the purpose bands above, such as shared management and central functions. Engineers working on a Run system count in Run, not here, so nothing is counted twice Vendors Licensing and contracted services not already attributed to a purpose band, such as enterprise agreements shared across teams, reviewed against the criteria in Vendor Evaluation Reserve Unallocated buffer for the unplanned; a budget with none is a budget that will blow through its total the first time reality doesn't match the plan Diagram The portfolio shape The categories above, drawn as one portfolio rather than a list, with the two things a cut conversation needs to know before it starts: what is protected, and where the ranked list is drawn from. The technology portfolio as proportional bands, with what is protected and where cuts are drawn from ONE PORTFOLIO, ILLUSTRATIVE PROPORTIONS Run 44% Grow 16% Transform 12% Security 10% Debt 10% Reserve 8% Most people and vendor cost is how each band is spent, so it belongs inside the band. The Headcount and Vendors lines in the calculator and workbook hold only what cannot be attributed to a band, which keeps the total from counting anything twice. Percentages are placeholders. PROTECTED BEFORE ANY LINE-ITEM REVIEW Security baseline. Regulatory obligations. The run cost of systems that make revenue. The reserve, which is spent only by recorded decision and is still there in month nine. WHERE THE RANKED CUT LIST IS DRAWN FROM, IN ORDER 1 Transform: pause with a restart condition. 2 Grow: reduce scope. 3 Vendors and duplicates: renegotiate, consolidate, exit. 4 Debt: defer with a date and carry cost. 5 Run: retire whole systems. THE THREE QUESTIONS THE PORTFOLIO MUST ALREADY ANSWER $10M less: what goes first, second, third, with the consequence of each stated plainly. $10M more: what gets funded next, tied to the horizon split and an expected outcome. Deciding again: knowing what we know now, which active items would we not start today. The proportions are illustrative; the calculator below takes yours. The cut order is the one the Cutting Costs situation page follows and is deliberately the reverse of how most across-the-board cuts land, which take from every band equally and therefore from security and run first in effect. Interactive Run your own allocation Enter your total budget, current spend, and target percentage for each category. Attribute each cost to one line only: people and vendor cost goes in the band it serves, and the Headcount and Vendors lines hold only what is shared or unattributable. Runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere. The downloadable workbook below carries the same logic across seven linked tabs; this is the quick version. Total annual budget ($) Category Current spend ($) Target % Calculate 1 The "$10M less" test A question every CTO eventually gets asked, and the quality of the answer depends entirely on whether it was worked out in advance. How to answer it well Have a pre-ranked list, before the question is asked, of what gets cut first, second, third, with the consequence of each cut stated plainly. "We'll do more with less" is a slogan, and the list is what replaces it. This list should already exist; deriving it live under budget pressure produces worse decisions and reads as unprepared. How it goes wrong An across-the-board percentage cut applied uniformly to every team and category, which protects nothing that matters and reflects no prioritization; it avoids the discomfort of choosing. 2 The "$10M more" test The less common but equally revealing version of the same question. How to answer it well A similarly pre-ranked list of what gets funded next, tied to the three-horizon split and stated expected outcomes, so a windfall gets deployed deliberately instead of triggering a scramble of proposals assembled after the fact. How it goes wrong The money gets absorbed by whichever team made the loudest case that quarter, evaluated against no consistent criteria, and disconnected from whatever priorities the rest of the portfolio was supposedly organized around. 3 What we'd stop if deciding again The question almost no organization asks explicitly, and the one most likely to surface a reallocation opportunity. Why it matters Sunk cost is the most common distortion in capital allocation. An investment that made sense eighteen months ago, under assumptions that have since changed, doesn't automatically still make sense, and few organizations ever explicitly re-ask the question rather than continuing to fund what's already funded. How to run it Annually, as part of the operating cadence's yearly review, walk the active portfolio and ask of each item: knowing what we know now, would we start this today. Anything that gets a no needs a stated wind-down plan; an uncomfortable silence lets it keep running by default. 4 Zero-based versus incremental budgeting Two methodologies for building next year's number, with different effort and different discipline built in. Incremental Start from last year's number and adjust up or down by category. Fast, low-effort, and the default almost everywhere. The cost: an investment that stopped earning its place three years ago keeps getting funded because nobody re-examines the base, only the delta. Zero-based Every line starts at zero and has to be justified from scratch each cycle, the same discipline as "what we'd stop if deciding again" applied to the entire budget rather than only flagged items. More rigorous and more expensive in time; most organizations can't sustain it annually, but running it once every few years catches what incremental budgeting has been quietly protecting. 5 Allocating for uncertainty: options over full commitments Few Horizon 3 bets need a full-year commitment on day one. Staging the commitment is itself a capital allocation decision. Practice Fund the next decision point rather than the whole initiative. A small spike that answers "is this technically feasible" preserves the option to scale up without committing the full budget before the uncertainty is resolved. This is real-options thinking applied to technology investment: the cost of the option is small, and it buys the right, without the obligation, to invest further. Common failure mode Approving a full-year budget for an unproven bet because a partial commitment feels indecisive. A partial commitment is how you avoid discovering in month nine that the bet was wrong after spending twelve months of budget finding out. 6 A worked allocation, illustrative What the categories above look like assembled into a single year's number for a mid-size technology organization. Category Share What's in it this year Run 45% Hosting, licensing, on-call coverage, routine maintenance across the existing estate Grow 20% Two validated adjacent-market initiatives with a stated business case each Transform 8% One staged option: a spike to test technical feasibility rather than a full build Security 10% Evaluated on its own terms rather than benchmarked against Grow's ROI bar Technical debt 8% A dedicated allocation rather than whatever's left over after the categories above are funded Vendors 4% Reviewed against the criteria on Vendor Evaluation, renewal timing staggered deliberately Reserve 5% Untouched unless a specific, named trigger occurs The specific percentages are illustrative rather than a template to copy. What matters is that every category has a number and a reason, and the reserve line exists at all. 7 Allocating across multiple business units Everything above assumes one budget and one owner. Once technology spend is split across business units with separate P&Ls, the categories still apply but the allocation mechanism has to be chosen deliberately, because the wrong one for the organization's structure produces the same fights every cycle. Funding model How it works Where it fits Corporate-funded core Platform, security, and shared infrastructure are funded centrally and treated as a fixed cost of doing business; BUs are not billed for them A small number of BUs, or a company where the center wants to standardize the platform and is willing to eat the cost of doing so Chargeback BUs are billed for what they consume, at a defined rate per unit (compute, seats, transactions); the bill lands on the BU's own P&L Consumption varies a lot by BU and the center wants that variance to show up as a cost the BU owner manages directly Showback BUs see the same consumption-based cost figure as chargeback, but it is not billed; it stays informational Building the metering and cost-allocation muscle before making it binding, or a culture where a hard chargeback fight would cost more political capital than it's worth yet Federal (shared core, funded local) A small centrally funded platform layer plus BU-funded local spend on top of it, with an explicit split of what's core versus local Several BUs of meaningfully different size and maturity, where full centralization would slow the larger ones down and full chargeback would starve the smaller ones of the shared platform they can't yet afford alone This maps onto the governance archetypes in Weill and Ross's IT Governance (MIT CISR, 2004): a business monarchy or IT monarchy tends toward corporate-funded core, a federal arrangement tends toward the federal funding model, and a duopoly of business and IT leadership usually lands on chargeback or showback depending on how much friction the relationship can absorb. Picking the funding model without first agreeing on the governance archetype is why the same allocation fight recurs every cycle under a different name. See Technology Governance Across Business Units for the decision-rights layer this funding choice sits on top of. Question What a working multi-BU allocation answers Who funds the shared platform Named explicitly as corporate, a lead BU, or a pooled contribution formula, not left as an assumption each BU makes differently What happens when a BU wants a platform exception A standing exception-request path with a named approver, rather than a one-off negotiation each time How a new BU or an acquired company gets onboarded to the funding model A defined ramp, since a newly acquired BU rarely has metering or budget discipline in place on day one; see Technology & M&A Integration Who arbitrates when two BUs disagree on a shared cost allocation A named forum with a decision deadline, not an open-ended email thread that resolves by whoever has the most patience Download Capital allocation workbook Seven linked tabs: the allocation summary above made live, a pre-ranked cut list and funding list with running totals, a zero-based review tracker, a real-options tracker for Horizon 3 bets, and a three-year projection. Every formula recalculates when you change an input; nothing is hardcoded. Download .xlsx Checklist Signs allocation discipline is missing Patterns that show up when capital allocation is happening by inertia rather than by explicit decision. No standing, pre-ranked list exists for what gets cut first under a budget reduction. See Technology Portfolio Management for a way to build and maintain that list across categories. Technical debt remediation gets whatever capacity is left over rather than a dedicated allocation Security investment is evaluated against the same ROI bar as a feature, rather than as its own category with its own logic An unplanned budget increase gets absorbed by whoever asks first rather than evaluated against the standing portfolio No investment currently in the portfolio has been explicitly re-justified in the past twelve months Every budget cycle is built incrementally off last year's number with no zero-based review, ever

title: Technology Decision Rights
description: Making decision ownership explicit with a RACI-style model, because most executive conflict is an undefined decision right wearing a personality conflict's clothes.
body: Reference An illustrative RACI R: Responsible, does the work. A: Accountable, owns the outcome and has final say. C: Consulted before the decision. I: Informed after. Adapt the roles to your organization; not every company has a distinct CISO or a CIO separate from the CTO. Decision CTO CEO CISO Product Engineering Technology strategy A C C C R Architecture standards A I C I R Product roadmap priorities C I I A R Security risk acceptance C I A C R Engineering org design A C I I R Major vendor selection A C C C R Technical debt allocation A I I C R Technology budget A C I C I 1 Why explicit rights beat "we'll figure it out when it comes up" The alternative to a stated model is a fresh political negotiation every time the same category of decision recurs. What explicit rights do A decision made once, in advance, about who owns what. A live disagreement becomes a matter of checking the model rather than relitigating it from scratch with whoever happens to be in the room and how forcefully they argue. What ambiguity produces The same category of decision gets resolved differently every time depending on who's present, which erodes trust in whoever "won" and guarantees the losing side argues it again next time, since nothing was settled. 2 Accountable and Responsible are different roles The distinction most RACI exercises blur, which is exactly where they stop working. The distinction Responsible executes the work. Accountable owns the outcome and has final say when consulted input conflicts. Exactly one person should be Accountable per decision; if two people are both marked A, the model has documented the ambiguity without resolving it. The common mistake Marking multiple people Accountable to avoid conflict in the room where the RACI gets built. This moves the conflict to the moment the decision has to be made, when the stakes are higher and the room is smaller. 3 Building the table for your organization The example above is a starting shape rather than a template to adopt unchanged. Build it in a room with the stakeholders rather than alone. Force explicit disagreement about at least one row before finalizing; if nobody disagrees with anything, the exercise was probably too polite, since every organization has tension over at least a few of these decisions. Revisit it annually, or after any reorg, since org changes shift decision rights even when nobody remembers to update the document. 4 When a decision doesn't map to any existing row A gap in the RACI is information. Improvising quietly and moving on wastes it. What to do Decide deliberately whether this is new, add a row, on the record, with the same rigor as the original exercise, or a variant of an existing row whose language was too narrow. Either way, the document changes instead of the gap being patched over informally and forgotten. Common failure mode Treating each gap as a one-off exception handled quietly in the moment. The RACI slowly becomes less accurate than the day it was built, and by the second year it covers less of what's happening than it did on day one, without anyone deciding that should happen. 5 When Consulted input gets ignored The most common source of quiet resentment in a working RACI, and it's usually a misunderstanding of what Consulted promises. What Consulted means The Accountable party has to hear the input before deciding, and is free to decide against it. Consulted is never a veto, and treating it like one defeats the entire purpose of having a single accountable owner who can move a decision forward. When it's a problem The same Consulted party's input gets dismissed without explanation, repeatedly, on the same category of decision. The RACI is working as written; the signal is that the Accountable assignment itself may be wrong, or that the underlying relationship needs the direct conversation described on Working with the CEO or Working with the CFO . 6 A worked disagreement What the mechanics above look like resolving a live tension. Product wants to ship a new vendor integration fast, a competitor just launched something similar and the sales team is asking daily. Security flags a data residency concern with the vendor's hosting: customer data would leave the region a key enterprise contract requires it to stay in. Checking the table: major vendor selection has the CTO Accountable, CISO and Product both Consulted, Engineering Responsible. The CISO's flag carries no veto, but the CTO has to weigh it rather than note it and move on. In this case, the CTO goes back to the CISO for the specific requirement, then negotiates a contractual data residency clause with the vendor rather than blocking the integration outright. The integration ships two weeks later than Product wanted. Security's concern gets addressed rather than either overridden or allowed to stall the decision indefinitely. Nobody has to relitigate who had the final call, because the table already said so before the disagreement ever started. 7 RACI is one model among several; match the model to the decision RACI documents who does what. It is weakest at the moment of a contested decision, which is why several alternatives exist. Most organizations use more than one. Model Roles Best for Watch out for RACI Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed Standing, recurring decision categories and process ownership Blurs who actually decides when Consulted parties disagree RAPID (Bain) Recommend, Agree, Perform, Input, Decide High-stakes cross-functional decisions where one party holds a formal sign-off, such as legal or security The Agree role quietly becomes a veto if its scope is not written down DACI Driver, Approver, Contributors, Informed Project-level decisions with a clear driver and a deadline Approver creep, where several people each believe they approve Advice process Anyone may decide after seeking advice from those affected and those with expertise Architecture and team-level technical decisions in organizations with strong trust and a decision log Fails without a visible log and a norm that advice is genuinely sought, not collected after the fact 8 Classify by reversibility before assigning an owner The fastest way to cut executive decision load is to separate decisions that are expensive to undo from those that are not. Amazon popularized the one-way and two-way door framing; the idea is older and simpler than the label. Thresholds below are illustrative for a mid-size company. Decision Reversible (two-way door) Hard to reverse (one-way door) Default owner The team closest to the work A named senior owner, with the Consulted list honored in writing Process Decide, record in a line or two, move on Written options with tradeoffs, an ADR or decision memo, a review date Spend (illustrative) Under $50K a year within approved budget: team lead. Under $250K: director Over $1M or any multi-year commitment: CTO with CFO. Over $5M or a new strategic vendor: CEO, and the board if above its delegated limit Architecture Inside one team's boundary, following approved patterns New system of record, new shared platform, or a deviation from a principle: through the Architecture Review Board , CTO accountable Risk acceptance Monitor-tier items within stated tolerance Temporary acceptance or anything reaching board visibility, per Technology Risk Appetite 9 The decision log The artifact that turns a decision-rights model from a chart into a working system. A decision log is a single, searchable list of consequential decisions: what was decided, the date, who decided, which options were considered, who was consulted, the one-paragraph rationale, and when it will be revisited. Architecture decisions live as ADRs, described on ADRs and Roadmapping ; the log indexes them alongside commercial, organizational, and risk decisions. Two practices make it pay for itself. First, link to the log entry whenever a settled question comes up again; that alone ends most relitigation. Second, review the log quarterly for decisions that were reversed or quietly ignored. A reversal is not a failure, but a pattern of reversals in one category usually means the wrong person holds the decision right, or the right person decided without the input they needed. Checklist Signs decision rights are still effectively undefined Having a document and having working decision rights are different things. These patterns show up when the model exists on paper but isn't load-bearing. The same category of decision gets escalated differently depending on who's involved Two people both believe they're Accountable for the same decision The RACI was built once and never revisited despite a reorg since Decisions get made in hallway conversations that bypass the stated model entirely No one can locate the document when a live disagreement happens A Consulted party's input has been dismissed without explanation on the same category of decision more than once No distinction is made between reversible and hard-to-reverse decisions, so both get the same slow process or the same casual one Spend approval limits are not written down, so the same purchase is approved at different levels depending on who asks

title: Technology Diligence
description: What's diagnosable in a compressed M&A diligence window, previewing a much larger diligence and post-merger integration toolkit built specifically for CTOs, PE operating partners, and integration management offices.
body: In the full toolkit What exists behind this preview Sixteen named tools and templates covering both sides of a transaction, buy-side and sell-side, and the full lifecycle from first data request through the first 100 days post-close. 16 tools and templates · 6 categories · buy-side, sell-side, and post-close Buy-side diligence The core engagement: structure, scope, and score a technology assessment end to end. M&A Technology Due Diligence Playbook , the umbrella process across seven evaluation domains, from engagement structuring to report construction Technology DD Process Map , the end-to-end engagement visualized: planning, deep assessment, synthesis, with deliverables and timing at each phase Technology DD Scoring Workbook , an eight-domain weighted instrument with a red-flag pattern library and a scoring-to-cost/timeline translation Diligence Question Bank , over 300 questions across architecture, security, compliance, data, operations, organization, IP, and healthcare-specific domains Diligence Response Tracker , logging target-company answers and following up on incomplete or concerning ones Sell-side preparation The other side of the table: positioning a technology organization for sale rather than evaluating one. Sell-Side Technology Preparation Guide , pre-diligence cleanup, data room construction, management presentation prep, and post-LOI execution through earnout negotiation Data Room Organization Template , a staged access model usable from either side of a transaction Technical debt economics Converting engineering debt into a defensible business artifact with dollar figures a CFO will trust. Technical Debt Assessment Framework , a seven-domain, five-level severity model with effort bands and a dollar overlay, adapted for pre-deal diligence, 100-day assessment, and ongoing portfolio health Technical Debt, Risk & Application Portfolio Simulator , classifying a portfolio using the Gartner TIME framework, plus a separate M&A-specific variant Technical Debt Carry Cost Optimizer , a multi-year remediation plan minimizing total cost within budget and capacity constraints, built so every sequencing decision can be explained rather than treated as a black box Integration & post-close What happens after signature: architecture decisions, the first 100 days, and the 12-18 months after that. The conceptual version of this, free, is Technology M&A Integration elsewhere on this site; what's below is the working-artifact layer beyond it. Integration Architecture Decision Tree , choosing merge, integrate, or coexist per system category based on the specifics of the deal, beyond the free page's system-category table Post-Merger Integration Playbook , the full 12-18 month framework: day-one readiness, stabilization and discovery, then integration execution 100-Day Integration Timeline , phased workstream milestones across the critical first 100 days, a scheduled artifact rather than the free page's phase-by-phase reasoning PMI Tracker , a working dashboard for key-person retention and synergy realization Healthcare & regulated industries Depth for the domains general frameworks skip over. Healthcare M&A Technology Reference , covering HIPAA, HITRUST, BAAs, and state licensure across the diligence and integration lifecycle ML-augmented Where the toolkit moves past static templates into inspectable models trained on engagement patterns. Diligence Prioritization Engine , turning a completed scoring workbook into a sequenced, rationale-backed 100-day remediation plan, using an inspectable classifier by design 1 Technical debt and code health signals What's diagnosable in a compressed diligence timeline, versus what requires the seller's own candor. What's diagnosable externally Test coverage trend over time (not a single snapshot), dependency freshness and known vulnerability count, build and deploy frequency as a proxy for how painful shipping is, and the ratio of time spent on new feature work versus maintenance in recent sprint history if available. What requires asking directly Which systems the engineering team itself is afraid to touch, and why. This question, asked plainly to individual engineers rather than through the seller's leadership, surfaces more risk than most automated code analysis. 2 Key-person risk The single most common surprise that surfaces after close rather than during diligence, because it's uncomfortable to investigate thoroughly before a deal is signed. How to assess it Map named individuals against system ownership: which systems have exactly one person who understands them deeply, and what's that person's stated intent post-acquisition. Check git history or equivalent for the bus factor as it stands rather than org-chart assumptions about who owns what. The trap Assuming a documented ownership chart reflects reality. Documentation frequently lags reorgs and attrition; the org chart says one thing, the person who gets paged at 2am says another, and the second one is the answer. 3 Security posture specific to acquisition context Different from an ongoing vendor security review, since the diligence question is about accumulated, possibly undisclosed history as well as the current-state snapshot. What to check Whether a breach or significant incident occurred in the last 24 to 36 months and whether it was disclosed proactively versus discovered through diligence. Current access control hygiene, specifically whether departed employees' access was revoked, checked directly rather than taken on the seller's word. The red flag Any hesitation or vagueness answering the incident history question directly. A clean answer given confidently and a vague answer given confidently look identical in a single meeting; press for specifics (dates, what happened, what changed afterward) rather than accepting a general reassurance. 4 Regulatory and compliance exposure inherited at close Certifications and audit history transfer with the deal whether or not the buying organization has fully absorbed what they mean. What to check Current certification status against the renewal calendar, beyond whether a certification exists; an attestation eight months from lapsing with no remediation plan is a different risk than a freshly renewed one. Whether certifications were scoped to match current operations, or scoped years ago and never re-baselined. The red flag A compliance program that reads as a once-a-year attestation exercise rather than something embedded in day-to-day operations. Ask how a policy change reaches an engineer's day-to-day work; a vague answer here usually means the paperwork and the practice have drifted apart. 5 Integration complexity assessment Estimating the cost and timeline of combining systems post-close, which drives the economics of the deal far more than the initial purchase price. What to model Data model compatibility between the two organizations' core systems, authentication and identity system overlap or conflict, and which systems are redundant (safe to sunset) versus which have diverged enough that a migration rather than a simple consolidation is required. The estimation trap Integration timelines estimated by the acquiring team's own engineers, who are systematically optimistic about unfamiliar systems they haven't worked inside. Weight their estimate down, or better, get a few hours of hands-on access during diligence rather than relying on an outside-in guess. 6 IP and third-party exposure A separate domain from security or compliance, and one of the most common ways a clean-looking deal turns expensive after signature. What to check Whether every current and former employee and contractor who touched the codebase has a signed, complete IP assignment agreement on file, beyond a policy that says they should. An open-source inventory checked against the license terms themselves, specifically anything copyleft (GPL and similar) that could obligate source disclosure if triggered by the deal structure. The red flag A core dependency, commercial or open-source, whose license doesn't survive a change of control, or a contractor engagement from early in the company's history with no IP assignment paperwork at all. Both are cheap to check and expensive to discover after close. 7 Engineering organization and talent, beyond one or two named people Key-person risk is the sharpest version of this question; the fuller version is whether the organization as a whole can execute the roadmap the deal assumes. What to check Voluntary attrition over the trailing 24 months against a reasonable industry benchmark, alongside the current headcount. Compensation positioning relative to market, since a team paid meaningfully under market carries retention risk the org chart won't show. Whether there's a bench below the CTO or VP Engineering, or whether departure of one or two people at the top empties the leadership layer. The red flag Attrition trending up over the trailing year rather than flat or down, especially concentrated among senior engineers, paired with exit interview themes that repeat. One departure is a data point; a pattern across several is the organization telling you something the management deck won't. Structure Where findings go A finding without a deal-structure destination is an observation rather than a diligence output. Every material item from the sections above lands in one of these. Purchase price adjustment , for findings that warrant a quantified reduction in consideration Representation and warranty requirement , for findings where a specific seller commitment protects the buyer Indemnification requirement , for findings creating potential future liability the buyer needs covered Escrow requirement , for findings where holding back part of consideration is warranted pending resolution Post-close investment requirement , for findings that need spending after close to achieve the deal thesis, tracked rather than absorbed silently into "integration cost" Integration planning input , for findings that inform how systems get combined without changing deal terms at all Interactive Integration complexity scorer Score seven dimensions from 1 (clean, compatible) to 5 (deeply divergent, high-effort) and note the finding behind each score. Tick any red flags from the checklist below and label each one stop, reprice, or integration cost. The tool gives the complexity band, the three biggest drivers, and a findings memo you can print. Runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere. The full toolkit's version weights each dimension by deal thesis and layers on a dollar overlay; this tool uses an even weighting to keep the mechanics visible. Score it Checklist Red flags that should stop or reprice a deal Not exhaustive, but the items that most consistently turn out to matter more than they appeared to during a compressed diligence window. No test coverage on the systems that generate the majority of revenue, discovered rather than disclosed A single named individual who is the only person capable of deploying or debugging a core system, with no stated transition plan An undisclosed prior security incident surfacing during diligence rather than in the seller's initial disclosure Customer contracts with data residency or security commitments the acquiring organization's own infrastructure can't currently meet A certification or attestation presented as current that has lapsed, or was never re-scoped to match how the business operates today A core dependency whose license doesn't survive a change of control, or a contractor engagement with no IP assignment on file Senior-engineer attrition trending up over the trailing year with no bench below the departing leaders

title: Technology M&A Integration
description: What happens after the deal closes. Diligence tells you what you're buying; this is the discipline of combining it, sequenced across the first day, the first 100 days, and the first year.
body: Reference The five phases Each phase has a different job, and doing a later phase's work during an earlier one is one of the most common ways integrations go wrong. Phase Job Focus Day 0 Don't break anything Identity, access, security continuity, communications, critical systems kept running exactly as they were First 30 days Understand what you have Technology inventory, people, vendors, contracts, architecture, security gaps, dependencies 100 days Decide rather than default Converge, coexist, or replace decisions per system, made and assigned an owner, with execution still ahead 100 days to Year 1 Execute the decisions The migration, consolidation, and platform convergence work, sequenced and tracked against what was decided at day 100; this is most of the calendar and most of the effort Year 1 Test the thesis Measure realized synergies and convergence against what diligence promised, technical debt remediation, target architecture, operating model Diagram The phases, with the TSA running underneath Integration work and transition services run in parallel. The phases decide; the TSA exits are when the decisions become real. Integration phases from Day 0 to Year 1, with transition services running alongside Day 0: keep it running. First 30 days: understand. 100 days decide Execute the decisions most of the effort Test the thesis synergies vs promise Integration Transition services Email and collaboration exits month 4 HR and payroll exits month 9 Finance and ERP exits month 15 Data center hosting exits month 12 close month 3 month 6 month 12 month 18 Every transition service needs a dated exit plan from Day 0. The longest one, usually ERP, sets the real length of the TSA, and a 6-month term on a 15-month separation is where carve-out cost overruns come from. Phase lengths follow the table above; the TSA services and exit months are illustrative. See the TSA card further down for how to structure them. 1 Day 0 is about keeping everything running The most common integration mistake happens in the first week rather than the first year. Practice Identity and access continuity, security posture held exactly where it was, communications sent as planned, critical systems left untouched. The goal on day 0 is invisibility to customers and continuity for employees, nothing more ambitious than that. Common failure mode Attempting a quick consolidation win, merging two identity systems, migrating a customer-facing tool, before the estate is even fully understood. This creates a new outage layered on top of the transition itself, at the exact moment trust is most fragile. 2 The 100-day converge, coexist, or replace decision Every inherited system needs an explicit call. The absence of a decision is itself a decision, and usually the worst one. Practice Score the combined estate the same way any application portfolio gets scored, then assign each system a named owner and an explicit converge, coexist, or replace call within the 100-day window, in place of a default assumption that everything eventually merges. Common failure mode Systems left in undecided limbo well past 100 days, with no owner for the call, while both organizations quietly keep maintaining duplicate infrastructure indefinitely because deciding felt harder than deferring. 3 Days 100 to 365: executing the decisions The phase this framework most commonly loses, a decision made at day 100 with no visible forcing function behind it for the next nine months. Practice Each converge, coexist, or replace decision made at day 100 gets a named owner, a sequenced execution plan, and a specific target date within the year, tracked on the same standing cadence as everything else in this phase. Migration and consolidation work starts immediately after the decision rather than months later once someone remembers it was made. Common failure mode The decision gets made and recorded at the 100-day mark, then nobody schedules or resources the execution work. Six months later the system is still officially "decided to converge," with nothing having moved, which in practice is indistinguishable from never having decided at all. 4 The call, worked across common system categories What the decision looks like against specific, common systems, rather than as an abstract framework. System Typical call Why CRM Converge onto the acquirer's system Sales process consistency and pipeline visibility matter more than any feature gap the acquired system might have had Identity & access Converge immediately, within Day 0 to 30 Security and access control can't safely run on two separate systems for long; this is the one category that shouldn't wait for the 100-day window Core product data warehouse Coexist initially, converge during Year 1 Migration risk is high; premature convergence risks corrupting the acquired product's own operational data before it's understood Internal ticketing or ITSM Replace both with a new standard, or converge onto whichever is stronger Internal and lower stakes, which is why it often gets deferred the longest despite being one of the easiest calls to make 5 The diligence-to-integration handoff Where institutional knowledge most commonly gets lost, right at the moment the deal closes and attention shifts. What works The people who ran diligence stay involved through at least the first 100 days, so findings, the security gap, the key-person risk, the technical debt hotspot, translate directly into the integration plan rather than getting rediscovered from scratch by a different team. Common failure mode Diligence findings live in a report that gets filed away once the deal closes, and the integration team, often entirely different people, rediscovers the same risks weeks into the process that diligence had already flagged in detail. 6 Cultural integration, in this specific window See Engineering Culture for the general argument about whose culture wins in a merger. This is that argument, compressed into a much higher-stakes, much shorter timeframe. Practice Decide deliberately, before Day 0, what's worth preserving from the acquired team's culture and practices, and build that preservation explicitly into the integration plan, rather than assuming the acquirer's culture automatically and correctly wins by default. Common failure mode The acquired team's good practices and institutional knowledge get silently discarded as "not how we do things here," the same credibility-erosion pattern described on Engineering Culture, just compressed into a much shorter and higher-stakes window where the damage happens faster and is harder to reverse. 7 Year 1 is where the deal thesis gets tested The numbers used to justify the deal don't disappear once it closes, even though attention usually does. This is the measurement point for the execution work from Stage 3 rather than a separate deliverable that appears on its own. Practice Track cost synergies and platform convergence against the specific figures used to justify the deal, on a standing cadence, with a named owner accountable for the gap between promised and realized. Common failure mode The synergies promised during diligence quietly stop being tracked once the deal has closed and organizational attention has moved to the next priority, so no one ever finds out whether the thesis was right. Interactive PMI tracker: synergy realization and key-person retention The working dashboard Stage 3 and Stage 7 both argue you need. Runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere. Synergy realization The specific figures used to justify the deal, tracked against what's been realized. Synergy Promised ($) Realized ($) Add Clear synergies Key-person retention The people the deal thesis quietly depends on staying. Name Role / why they matter Status Retained At risk Departed Add Clear people 8 Before close: clean teams and Day 1 readiness Most Day 0 problems are decided in the weeks before signing, while the two companies still cannot share competitively sensitive information freely. Practice Use a clean team, a small group bound by a clean-team agreement and advised by counsel, to review sensitive items such as customer contracts, pricing, and detailed architecture before close. Build the Day 1 plan from its findings: identity bridging, email and collaboration access, finance system cutoffs, and the systems that must not be touched. Common failure mode Gun-jumping in reverse: teams avoid all joint planning out of caution, then discover on Day 1 that nobody has admin access to the target's identity provider and the only person who does has already resigned. 9 Transition service agreements (TSAs) In a carve-out, the buyer usually depends on the seller's systems for months after close. The TSA is where most carve-out cost overruns come from. TSA element What good looks like Common mistake Service schedule Every service listed with scope, service levels, and a named owner on each side Vague descriptions such as IT support that nobody can hold to a standard Duration Sized to the realistic exit plan, commonly 6 to 18 months, with extension terms priced in advance A 6-month term for an ERP separation that takes 15 Pricing Cost-based, with step-ups that reward an early exit Flat monthly fees that remove any incentive to move faster Exit plan A dated migration plan per service, reviewed monthly by a joint steering group Treating the TSA as the plan rather than as the bridge to one Data and security Access boundaries, logging, and data segregation defined per service Buyer staff left with broad access to the seller's environment for months Checklist Signs integration is drifting Patterns that show up when an integration has good intentions but no forcing function behind them. No named owner exists for the converge, coexist, or replace decision on a given inherited system Cost synergies promised during diligence aren't being tracked against actuals a year later Identity and access consolidation is still incomplete well past the 100-day mark with no active plan Key people from the acquired company have left without the succession plan that was supposed to prevent it The acquired company's application portfolio has never been scored on the same terms as the acquirer's own The diligence team's findings never made it into the integration plan in any traceable way A carve-out closed with TSA services that have no dated exit plan

title: Technology Portfolio Management
description: Ranking and sequencing competing initiatives across categories rather than within one, plus a WSJF calculator that ranks your own list.
body: Reference How this relates to the other four portfolio pages Four different lenses on four different things rather than four competing answers to the same question. Page What it scores What it doesn't do Application Portfolio Management The existing application estate: Tolerate, Invest, Migrate, Eliminate Doesn't rank new initiatives against each other, or against running applications AI Portfolio Management AI initiatives specifically, gated on feasibility and data readiness first Doesn't compare an AI initiative's priority against a non-AI one competing for the same sprint capacity Innovation Portfolio Management Exploratory bets specifically, across the three horizons Doesn't cover run-the-business work, which is most of the portfolio at most companies Technology Capital Allocation The dollars, split across Run, Grow, Transform, Security, Debt, and Reserve as one portfolio Allocates budget to buckets; doesn't rank individual competing initiatives within or across those buckets This page Every competing initiative, any category, ranked and sequenced on one list against the same capacity constraint Doesn't replace the category-specific scoring above; a project still needs its AI-readiness or innovation-stage evaluation before it lands here 1 The default is a de facto portfolio rather than a deliberate one Most organizations never decide their portfolio. It accumulates. What a deliberate portfolio looks like Every active initiative sits on one list, ranked against every other active initiative, regardless of which team or category proposed it. The list is re-ranked on a fixed cadence, whether or not something new has shown up. Items get removed as well as added. The tell that it accumulated The roadmap has never had an item removed, only added. Nobody can say, without checking three different documents, what the fourth-highest-priority initiative in the company is right now. Prioritization happens by whoever escalates loudest rather than by a comparable score. 2 WSJF: ranking across categories on one scale Weighted Shortest Job First, from SAFe's Lean Portfolio Management, built on Don Reinertsen's Cost of Delay economics. The reason it works here: it doesn't care what type of work an item is. WSJF = Cost of Delay ÷ Job Size. Cost of Delay is the sum of three components, each scored on a relative Fibonacci scale (1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 20): User-Business Value (the direct economic or customer benefit), Time Criticality (does the value decay if this waits), and Risk Reduction / Opportunity Enablement (does this unlock or de-risk other work). Divide that sum by relative Job Size , and the result ranks a moderately valuable two-week job above a highly valuable six-month one, because value delivered sooner compounds and value delayed decays. An AI pilot, a compliance mandate, and a technical debt paydown all get scored on the same four inputs, which is exactly what makes this usable across categories where the other four portfolio pages can't reach. The scores are relative rather than precise measurements. Anchor the smallest, most obvious item on your list at 1 for each component, then size everything else against it. The ranking is the useful output; the individual numbers are scaffolding. Interactive Rank your own portfolio List every initiative competing for capacity, regardless of category, and set the capacity you have in job-size points. The tool ranks by WSJF, draws the cut line where capacity runs out, and totals the cost of delay deferred below it. Runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere. Initiative Business value 1 2 3 5 8 13 20 Time criticality 1 2 3 5 8 13 20 Risk reduction / opportunity 1 2 3 5 8 13 20 Job size 1 2 3 5 8 13 20 Add Clear all Worked example WSJF with three competing items Cost of delay is the sum of business value, time criticality, and risk reduction or opportunity enablement, each scored on the modified Fibonacci scale. WSJF divides it by job size. Item Business value Time criticality Risk reduction Cost of delay Job size WSJF Rank A. New pricing engine 8 5 3 16 8 2.0 2 B. Certificate automation before mass expiry 5 8 2 15 3 5.0 1 C. Data platform re-architecture 13 2 5 20 13 1.5 3 Reading it Why the smallest item wins C has the highest cost of delay but ranks last, because it takes four times as long as B. What the ranking says Do B first; it is urgent and small. Then A. Split C into increments so the first slice can compete on its own size rather than waiting behind everything. What it does not say WSJF ranks within available capacity. It does not tell you whether C should be funded at all; that is the capital allocation decision, made before this ranking runs. 3 Category-blind ranking vs. reserved capacity An unresolved tension. Pure WSJF ranking can starve categories that never win on pure economic score. Pure ranking Every initiative competes on the same list, highest WSJF wins the next slot regardless of category. Simple, defensible, and explicit about tradeoffs. The risk: technical debt and security work, which rarely score high on Time Criticality until something breaks, permanently lose to visible, revenue-attached features. Reserved capacity by category A fixed share of capacity, say the debt and reserve percentages from Technology Capital Allocation , is set aside before ranking begins, then WSJF ranks within each reserved share. Protects categories that would otherwise never win, at the cost of a less pure, harder-to-defend prioritization story. Most functioning portfolios use both: a capacity floor for the categories that lose on pure economics, WSJF ranking inside and above that floor for everything else. 4 Sequencing and dependencies A ranked list is a different thing from a schedule. Value-order ignores what blocks what. A high-WSJF initiative that depends on a lower-ranked one still has to wait; running it first produces rework or a stalled effort waiting on its own dependency. Before finalizing sequence, check the top ten items against each other for blocking relationships, in addition to checking them against the full backlog. The common failure: nobody maps this until two teams have already started conflicting work, which is a coordination cost the ranking itself was supposed to prevent. 5 Killing something already in flight The hardest and most avoided move in portfolio management, and the one that matters most. The failure mode An initiative that scored well six months ago keeps running on inertia. Re-scoring it against today's list would rank it below several things that didn't exist when it started, but nobody re-runs the comparison because it's already funded and staffed. The discipline Every re-ranking cycle scores in-flight work against new proposals on the same list, with no separate "already committed" list exempt from comparison. Money and time already spent are gone regardless of the decision now; the only question is whether finishing beats every current alternative for the capacity remaining. 6 Cadence A portfolio ranked once a year is a portfolio managed by whoever spoke last in December. Quarterly re-ranking of the full list is the common floor, monthly for organizations moving fast enough that a quarter is a long time. Between formal cycles, a time-critical item can force an out-of-cycle re-rank, but that path should be visibly rare; if it's common, the formal cadence is too slow for the business it's serving.

title: Technology Risk Appetite
description: Explicitly defining which risks the organization won't accept, will accept temporarily, will monitor, and what crosses the threshold for board visibility.
body: Reference The five tiers The same tiers apply regardless of category, security, resilience, architecture, technical debt, vendors, AI, regulatory exposure, or concentration risk. Tier Definition Who can accept it Will not accept Downside unacceptable regardless of likelihood: unencrypted regulated data at rest, no tested recovery plan for a revenue-critical system No one; this is a standing prohibition rather than a judgment call Will accept temporarily Known, tracked, with a remediation date and a named owner The accountable owner from the decision-rights model, with the remediation plan documented Will monitor Acceptable at current severity, tracked in case that changes The team or function closest to the risk, without escalation, as long as it stays within stated bounds Requires board visibility Severity or category crosses a stated materiality threshold Surfaced regardless of whether it's currently being actively managed well Requires CEO approval Acceptance could affect company viability or a public commitment The CEO specifically, never delegated downward regardless of technical familiarity 1 Why implicit risk tolerance is worse than a strict written one A conservative appetite stated clearly beats a permissive one left unstated, because the unstated version is an accident waiting to be discovered rather than a tolerance. What an explicit appetite does Gives engineers and managers a standing answer to "is this acceptable" without escalating every individual judgment call, and gives the CTO a defensible basis for a decision rather than an after-the-fact justification assembled once something has already gone wrong. What implicit tolerance produces Risk tolerance gets set retroactively, by whoever made the loudest case for or against a specific risk at the time, and the same category of risk gets treated inconsistently across teams depending entirely on who happened to be asking. 2 The board-visibility threshold The line that determines whether a risk stays a team-level judgment call or becomes something the board has to know about. What crosses it A materiality standard stated in advance: dollar exposure above a specific threshold, any risk with potential regulatory or public-disclosure consequence, anything that could affect a stated company commitment. The threshold has to be a number or a specific condition. A feeling is what the threshold exists to replace. The trap Defining materiality vaguely enough ("significant risk") that it becomes a judgment call made under pressure in the moment, right when the incentive to under-report is highest and the person making the call has the least distance from the situation. 3 A worked example, applying the tiers What the five-tier model looks like against a common scenario rather than an abstract description. The finding: a known vulnerability in a legacy authentication library, requiring a multi-month migration to remediate properly, discovered during a routine dependency audit. Will not accept? No. Exploiting it requires a specific, unlikely combination of internal network access and a second, unrelated compromise; it doesn't meet the "unacceptable regardless of likelihood" bar on its own. Will accept temporarily. Yes, with a remediation date tied to the migration timeline, a named owner (head of security), and interim compensating controls (additional network segmentation around the affected service) documented alongside the acceptance itself. Board visibility? Depends on whether the affected system handles regulated data. If it does, the materiality threshold is crossed regardless of how contained the practical exploit path looks, because the threshold is about data category rather than the CTO's confidence in the mitigation. 4 When the remediation date passes The moment that reveals whether "will accept temporarily" was a tier with teeth or a way to defer a hard conversation indefinitely. What should happen The accepted risk gets reviewed again with the same rigor as the original acceptance. If the date passes without remediation and without a re-justified new date, it escalates automatically to the next tier up, board visibility, rather than quietly receiving a new date stamped on it by the same person who missed the last one. Common failure mode A risk accepted a year ago, now on its third quietly extended remediation date, still sitting in the same tier with no escalation and no accountability for the pattern of missed dates itself, which is a worse signal than the original risk. 5 Revisiting the appetite as the company changes The appetite itself has a shelf life, distinct from any individual risk decision made under it. Practice What was reasonable to tolerate at a five-person startup with no customers often becomes "will not accept" the moment the company signs its first enterprise customer with a security addendum, or crosses into handling regulated data for the first time. Revisit the appetite itself, and beyond it the individual risk decisions made under it, on the same annual cadence as the strategy reset. Common failure mode The appetite document was written once, early, by whoever was CTO at the time, and nobody revisits the thresholds as the company's regulatory exposure, customer base, or public profile changes around it, so the document quietly stops matching the business it's supposed to govern. 6 Capacity, appetite, and tolerance are three different numbers Most appetite documents blur these, which is why they read well and decide nothing. The distinction comes from ISO 31000 and the COSO ERM framework, and NIST uses the same vocabulary for cybersecurity risk. Term What it means How it shows up in practice Risk capacity The most loss the organization could absorb before its viability, license to operate, or major commitments are threatened Set by the CFO and board, not by technology. A ceiling the appetite must sit well below Risk appetite The amount and type of risk the organization is willing to pursue or retain to meet its objectives Qualitative statements per category, the five tiers above, approved by the executive team Risk tolerance The acceptable variation around the appetite, stated as a measurable threshold on a specific indicator Key risk indicators (KRIs) with a green, amber, and red line, owned by a named person and reported on a cadence Materiality The point at which a risk or incident must be disclosed to the board, a regulator, or investors For US public companies, tied to the SEC disclosure process; the board-visibility tier above should map onto it explicitly Diagram The four terms on one scale The table above, drawn as levels, with the tier that decides at each one. Risk capacity, materiality, tolerance, and appetite as levels on one scale more risk Risk capacity the most loss the company could absorb; set by the CFO and board Materiality must be disclosed to the board, regulators, or investors Tolerance (KRI red and amber lines) measurable variation around the appetite, owned by a named person Appetite the risk the company chooses to take to meet its objectives, written as statements per category CEO approval could affect viability Board visibility crosses materiality Accountable owner accept temporarily, dated fix The team monitor within bounds Who decides An appetite document that states only the green zone decides nothing. The lines above it are where the decisions are. Terms follow ISO 31000, COSO ERM, and NIST, as the table above explains; the decision-makers are this page's five tiers. 7 Statements people can act on An appetite statement is usable when an engineer can check a situation against it without asking anyone. Each row pairs a statement that sounds fine with one that works. Thresholds are illustrative; set yours from your own exposure. Category Sounds fine, decides nothing Usable statement and KRI Vulnerabilities We take vulnerabilities seriously Vulnerabilities on the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list are fixed or mitigated on internet-facing systems within 14 days. Any overdue item goes to the CISO weekly; more than three overdue goes to the board risk report Resilience Critical systems are highly available Every tier-1 system has passed a restore test within its stated RTO in the last 12 months. An untested tier-1 system is a temporary acceptance with a date, never a monitor item Third parties We manage vendor risk No vendor gets production or regulated-data access without a completed security review. More than five reviews overdue moves the category to amber Data Customer data is protected Regulated data never sits unmasked in non-production environments. Any exception is will-not-accept, with no approver End of life We keep our stack current No internet-facing component runs more than 90 days past its vendor end-of-support date without a compensating control and a named exception AI We use AI responsibly No customer-facing generative AI feature ships without a documented evaluation, a human escalation path, and logging sufficient to reconstruct a decision Concentration We avoid lock-in No single vendor supports more than two of our five most critical capabilities without a tested exit plan 8 The standards this sits on None of this is invented here. Anchoring the appetite to a recognized standard is also what makes it defensible to auditors, acquirers, and a board committee. Source What to take from it ISO 31000:2018, Risk management guidelines The general vocabulary and process: establish context, assess, treat, monitor, and communicate risk as a continuous cycle COSO ERM, Integrating with Strategy and Performance (2017) Appetite set in the context of strategy, and tolerance as variation in performance, which is the framing most CFOs and audit committees already use NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 (2024), Govern function Risk management strategy as a governed outcome: appetite and tolerance statements established, communicated, and maintained, which CSF 1.1 did not ask for explicitly [1] NIST IR 8286 series How to roll cybersecurity risk registers up into the enterprise risk register, so technology risk and business risk are ranked on the same terms FAIR (Open Group Risk Taxonomy and Risk Analysis standards) A method for expressing a risk as a range of annual loss in dollars, useful when a decision turns on whether a control is worth its cost SEC Form 8-K Item 1.05 and Regulation S-K Item 106 (US public companies) A material cybersecurity incident is disclosed within four business days of the materiality determination, and the annual report describes risk management and board oversight. The board-visibility tier should feed the materiality process directly [2] Sources NIST, release of Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, February 2024 SEC press release 2023-139, cybersecurity disclosure rules, July 2023 9 Quantify the risks where the number changes the decision Putting a dollar range on every risk is expensive and invites false precision. Reserve it for the few decisions where the choice actually depends on the size of the exposure. Practice For a contested control or a large acceptance, estimate how often the loss event could happen and how large it could be, as ranges with a stated confidence, then compare the annualized exposure to the cost of the control. A range such as $0.4M to $2.5M a year is a far better input to a budget debate than the word high. The trap Producing a single precise figure from guessed inputs and presenting it as a measurement. The first person to ask where the probability came from ends the conversation, and the credibility of every other number in the risk report goes with it. Checklist Signs risk appetite is undefined despite feeling settled An organization can feel like it has a consistent approach to risk while having none written down anywhere. Risk acceptance decisions aren't documented anywhere, so no one can show why a given risk was judged acceptable six months later The same category of risk gets treated differently by different teams with no stated reason No materiality threshold exists for what triggers board visibility "We'll accept this for now" risks have no remediation date or owner attached The CTO has never stated, in writing, what the organization will not accept regardless of cost or convenience A remediation date has slipped more than once on the same accepted risk with no automatic escalation No key risk indicator with a numeric threshold exists for each risk category, so tolerance is a feeling rather than a line For a public company, the board-visibility tier and the SEC materiality process are run by different people with different criteria

title: Technology Strategy
description: What a technology strategy is, as distinct from a roadmap or a tech stack decision, the three-horizon investment split, the test that ties an initiative to a business outcome, and why a strategy is only usable once it states its tradeoffs.
body: 1 What a technology strategy is A frequent source of confusion worth resolving before anything else, because a roadmap, a list of tools, and a tech stack decision each get mistaken for it. What it is An explicit, prioritized set of choices about where to invest scarce engineering capacity, what capabilities to build versus buy, and what technical risk to knowingly accept versus what to remediate. A strategy is defined as much by what it says no to as what it says yes to. What it gets confused with A roadmap is the sequenced execution of a strategy, one level below it. A tech stack decision is an implementation detail below the strategy. A wish list of every capability engineering would like to build, with nothing prioritized against anything else, fails the definition entirely. Framework Three horizons Adapted from McKinsey's Three Horizons model, applied to technology investment specifically. Most technology strategies fail by spending everything on Horizon 1 and nothing on Horizon 3, then getting blindsided by a competitor who didn't. See Innovation Portfolio Management for how Horizon 2 and 3 get run as a managed portfolio rather than a handful of side projects.
