Horizon Focus Typical investment share Horizon 1 Optimize and defend the core: keep what's working reliable, fast, and cheap to run Roughly 60 to 70 percent Horizon 2 Extend into adjacent, emerging opportunities with a clearer but not yet proven path to value Roughly 20 to 30 percent Horizon 3 Bets: unproven, high-uncertainty, high-potential-payoff exploration Roughly 5 to 10 percent 2 The "so that" test The single question that separates a strategy tied to business outcomes from a list of things engineering finds interesting. How it works Every strategic initiative should complete the sentence: "we will invest in X, so that Y business outcome becomes possible, measured by Z." If an initiative can't complete that sentence with a specific business outcome and a way to measure it, it doesn't belong in the strategy document, whatever its technical merit. Where it gets skipped Infrastructure and platform investments are the most common place this test gets waived, on the assumption that their value is self-evident. It rarely is to a non-technical stakeholder, and skipping the test here is exactly why platform investment is often the hardest thing to get funded. 3 Tradeoffs are the strategy What separates a document leadership uses from one that gets written once and never referenced again. A strategy document that gets used States explicit tradeoffs: we are prioritizing reliability over feature velocity this year, we are building this capability in-house rather than buying because it's a differentiator, we are accepting this specific technical risk rather than remediating it now because the cost of remediation exceeds its near-term impact. A document that gets ignored Lists initiatives with no stated tradeoff, which means every initiative reads as equally important, which means nobody can use the document to make a prioritization call when two initiatives compete for the same engineers. 4 A worked example A compressed scenario showing the method end to end: strategic priority through horizon allocation through a stated tradeoff. Situation: a mid-market SaaS company, $60M ARR, engineering team of 90, competing against two larger incumbents on feature breadth and one well-funded startup on price. The CEO wants to know what the technology organization is going to do about it this year. Strategic priority: defend gross margin while shipping the two integrations sales says are costing the most deals, without adding headcount. Horizon What's in it this year The "so that" test applied Horizon 1 (65%) Infrastructure cost reduction, on-call load reduction, the two highest-defect legacy modules stabilized "We will invest in cost reduction, so that gross margin improves 4 points without a price increase, measured monthly" Horizon 2 (25%) The two integrations sales has flagged, built on a shared integration platform rather than one-off connectors "We will invest in a shared integration layer, so that the next five integration requests ship in weeks rather than quarters, measured by integration lead time" Horizon 3 (10%) A single exploratory bet: whether usage-based pricing is technically feasible on the current billing system "We will invest in a pricing model spike, so that the leadership team has an answer before the next pricing conversation, measured by a working prototype rather than a slide deck" The stated tradeoff: no new customer-facing features outside the two flagged integrations ship this year. That line is what makes the document usable; it's the sentence a product manager points to when a stakeholder asks for a third integration in March. 5 One strategy, two audiences The same mistake covered on ADRs & Roadmapping for the roadmap itself shows up one layer up, at the strategy document. The board and executive version Three to five priorities, each with the business outcome and the tradeoff stated in one sentence, no architecture detail, no technology names unless the technology itself is the competitive story. This is the version that goes in the board deck alongside the content on Board Reporting . The engineering version The same priorities, expanded with the technical approach, sequencing dependencies, and named owners. Engineers need to know how as well as why; a strategy document that stays at board-level abstraction throughout gives a team nothing to plan against. Maintain one underlying document and generate both views from it, the same discipline as the roadmap split, rather than maintaining two documents that drift out of sync within a quarter. 6 Revisiting and sunsetting a strategy A strategy document has a shelf life, and most organizations never explicitly declare when it's expired. Practice Revisit formally on the annual cadence described in The CTO Operating System , and out of cycle the moment a stated assumption breaks: a competitor ships the thing Horizon 3 was betting against, a key hire who owned a priority leaves, the market shifts underneath the plan. A strategy that hasn't been checked against reality in six months is being followed on faith. Common failure mode Last year's strategy document quietly stays the reference point because writing a new one feels like admitting the old one failed. Circumstances changed, which is what strategies are supposed to respond to, and revising it is the strategy working. An unrevised strategy is a bigger tell than a revised one. Download Technology strategy template The three-horizon investment table and a dedicated tradeoffs section above, in a fillable format, plus strategic pillars, success metrics, risks, and a governance cadence. Markdown for pasting into your own docs system, or a formatted Word doc. Download .md Download .docx

title: Technology Strategy During a Downturn
description: What to do when the CEO says cut technology spend twenty percent by next quarter. The distinction between a cut that costs the business less than it saves and one that doesn't.
body: Reference Bad cuts versus better cuts Reductions in spend differ in kind. Some remove cost with almost no value loss; others remove cost by removing value. Bad cuts Better cuts Across-the-board headcount reductions Low-value initiatives already flagged as candidates before the pressure arrived Security budget Duplicate tooling and licensing Reliability investment Unused cloud capacity Critical infrastructure Premature platform work built for scale the company isn't at yet Necessary architectural remediation Low-value vendor relationships Across-the-board innovation freeze Innovation bets that already failed their own kill criteria and hadn't been stopped yet 1 Reducing spend and reducing value are different things The best cuts are the ones where the two diverge most. Execute these first Cloud rightsizing, duplicate SaaS tooling consolidation, and unused capacity elimination reduce spend with close to zero value loss. These should always be executed before anything with value attached, and they're usually available in weeks rather than quarters. The trap An across-the-board percentage cut applied uniformly treats a duplicate analytics tool and a security control as equally expendable, which they are not, and guarantees the cut removes value somewhere it didn't need to. 2 Communicating the cut without destroying morale How the reduction is explained matters almost as much as what's cut. Practice Be specific about what's being cut and why, tied to the pre-ranked priority list, so the team understands this was a deliberate choice made against known criteria rather than a panicked reaction to a number that arrived from finance. Common failure mode Vague, repeated "doing more with less" messaging with no specifics, which reads as either incompetence or dishonesty to the people doing the work, and erodes trust well beyond whatever the cut itself cost. 3 What not to cut even under heavy pressure Some categories aren't discretionary line items, whatever the topline number demands. Cutting security, reliability, or necessary architectural remediation defers cost at compounding interest rather than reducing it. A downturn is exactly the moment the organization can least afford a preventable incident stacked on top of everything else already under pressure. If these categories appear on a cut list, the list needs to be rebuilt rather than defended. 4 Sequencing the cuts, in order Each step down this list is harder to reverse and costlier to trust than the one before it. Skipping ahead means paying the hardest cost first. Reversible, near-zero value loss: cloud rightsizing, duplicate tooling consolidation, unused capacity elimination Hiring freeze on non-critical roles: cheap, fully reversible, buys time to assess whether deeper cuts are needed Discretionary spend: travel, non-essential contractor engagements, training budgets not tied to a specific delivery commitment Innovation kill-criteria enforcement: stop bets that already failed the criteria set for them and hadn't been formally killed yet Structural headcount reduction: the last resort, the hardest to reverse, and the one that costs the most trust and future hiring ability 5 A worked example What the sequencing above looks like against a concrete target. Target: an 18 percent reduction in a $12M engineering budget, roughly $2.16M. Step What it produces Running total Rightsizing and tooling consolidation $400,000, reversible, near-zero value loss $400,000 Hiring freeze on three open non-critical reqs $450,000 annualized $850,000 Discretionary spend reduction $300,000 (travel, training, non-essential contractors) $1,150,000 Kill two innovation bets past their own criteria $350,000 $1,500,000 Remaining gap $660,000, requiring structural headcount reduction $2,160,000 The headcount reduction still happens, but it's sized to $660,000 rather than the full $2.16M. Skipping straight to headcount to hit the number in one step would have meant a layoff roughly 3.3 times larger than what was necessary once the reversible options were exhausted first. 6 Rebuilding after the downturn ends The moment most organizations handle almost as badly as the cut itself. Practice Revisit the cut list in the same order it was built. Some items, duplicate tooling, unused capacity, should stay cut permanently, since they never carried value to begin with. Reinstate only the categories that were value-reducing when cut. Common failure mode Automatically restoring every cut the moment budget allows, without asking whether the cut item was ever needed, which quietly re-inflates spend the organization had already proven it could operate without. 7 Constraints that bind the cut list Some cuts that look available on a spreadsheet are not, on the timeline finance expects. Check these before committing a number. Constraint What it does What to do Cloud commitments Reserved instances, savings plans, and committed-spend agreements are paid whether or not the capacity is used Move workloads onto committed capacity first; cut on-demand spend before touching anything committed SaaS contract terms Annual and multi-year contracts often cannot be reduced mid-term, and renewal notice windows can be 60 to 90 days Pull the renewal calendar from SaaS Contract & Renewal Negotiation before promising license savings Layoff notice rules In the US, the federal WARN Act generally requires 60 days [1] ' notice for mass layoffs and plant closings at employers with 100 or more employees, and several states require more. Other countries require consultation periods Involve HR and employment counsel before the headcount number is fixed, and account for notice-period cost Compliance obligations Certifications, audits, and regulatory controls carry dates that do not move with the budget Treat them as protected, alongside the security baseline Capitalized projects Cancelling a project with capitalized costs can trigger a write-off Tell the CFO before the cut list is final, per Working with the CFO Sources US Department of Labor, Plant Closings and Layoffs (WARN) Checklist Signs the cut was done badly Patterns that show up when a budget reduction was executed under pressure without the discipline this page describes. Cuts were applied as a uniform percentage rather than against a pre-ranked priority list Security or reliability budget was reduced specifically to hit a topline number The team was told to do more with less without specifics on what was deprioritized Innovation bets were cut without applying the kill criteria that should have already existed for them No one has revisited the cuts to confirm they didn't quietly become permanent once the downturn ended Headcount reduction happened before reversible options one through four were exhausted

title: Transformation and Innovation
description: Two different problems that get called the same thing. Innovation is a selection problem, transformation is an adoption problem, and most failed initiatives are solving the wrong one.
body: 1 · Reference Two different problems, one blurred word The distinction that most conversations about "driving change" skip past. Innovation Transformation Core question What should exist that doesn't yet? How does the whole organization work differently? Fundamentally a problem of Selection, generating enough options and killing the weak ones early Adoption, getting people and systems to change behavior and keep it changed Where it fails Too few alternatives, or nothing ever gets killed The kickoff gets funded, reinforcement six months later doesn't Symptom when it's missing The org executes reliably but keeps optimizing the same things the same way The org has good pilots that never make it past the flagship site Innovation without transformation produces pilots that never scale. Transformation without innovation produces the same organization, just faster and more expensive to run. Neither failure looks like the other, which is why treating them as one problem usually means solving neither. 2 Diagnose which one you have Before fixing anything, find out which problem you have, because the fixes don't transfer. You have an innovation problem if The org executes reliably, ships on schedule, runs a tight operation, and keeps optimizing the same processes the same way. Nobody's proposing anything different, or the ideas that do surface never get evaluated against a kill criterion. More change management won't fix this. The gap is upstream: too few options ever reach a decision. You have a transformation problem if The org has plenty of good ideas, pilots that work, proofs of concept that prove the concept, and none of them make it past the team or facility that built them. More AI pilots won't fix this. The gap is downstream: adoption, incentives, and the operating model never got built to carry a working idea past its origin point. 3 The innovation stack: generating and selecting Three citable pieces for the selection problem. Concept What it does CTO example Jobs to Be Done Clayton Christensen, Competing Against Luck , 2016 Before generating options, name the job the user is hiring a solution to do. Prevents building impressive things nobody needed. A platform team ships a slicker internal dashboard nobody asked for, while the job engineers were hiring the old one to do, tell me fast whether my deploy is safe, went unaddressed Innovation Tournaments Terwiesch & Ulrich, Innovation Tournaments , 2009 Treat innovation as a funnel: generate far more ideas than you need, then kill most of them fast and cheap, before they're expensive. The discipline is in the killing far more than the generating. See Innovation Portfolio for how this runs as a standing quarterly mechanism. A quarterly open call where any engineer pitches against a fixed rubric, horizon fit, a kill criterion, a funding ask, judged by a panel outside the pitcher's own chain Ten Types of Innovation Keeley et al. (Doblin/Deloitte), 2013 Innovation covers far more than new product features. It spans configuration (how you're organized, your business model), the offering itself, and experience (how people interact with it). A hospital IT org whose entire "innovation" pipeline is AI features misses that a new referral or scheduling workflow can be just as innovative, and often ships faster 4 The transformation stack: adoption at scale Three citable pieces for the adoption problem, which is the one most technical leaders have the least formal training in. Concept What it does CTO example Kotter's 8-Step Model John Kotter, Leading Change , 1996 The sequence: urgency, coalition, vision, communication, removing obstacles, short-term wins, consolidating gains, anchoring in culture. Most failed transformations skip straight to communicating the vision and never build the coalition or clear the obstacles. A platform migration gets a company-wide announcement and a town hall, but no coalition of respected engineers vouching for it inside each team, and adoption stalls exactly where the announcement didn't reach Dual Operating System John Kotter, Accelerate , 2014 Restructuring the org chart transforms nothing. Run a second, network-like structure alongside the hierarchy, specifically for the change effort, because the hierarchy is built for reliable operations rather than for change. Staffing a transformation initiative with the same reporting lines and cadence as steady-state IT operations, then wondering why it moves at steady-state speed ADKAR Jeff Hiatt / Prosci, 2006 The individual mechanics of adoption: Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability, Reinforcement. Explains exactly where adoption dies, usually Desire or Reinforcement, rarely Awareness, since most initiatives over-invest in the kickoff announcement and under-invest in what happens six months later. A new clinical documentation tool gets a full rollout announcement (Awareness, done well) and training (Knowledge, done well), but no reinforcement once the project team disbands, so usage quietly reverts within two quarters Awareness and Knowledge are the easy, visible parts of a rollout, an announcement and a training session. Desire and Reinforcement are the parts that determine whether the change survives contact with a busy person's existing habits, and they're the parts almost every initiative underfunds. 5 Where this fits in the toolkit This page is the adoption layer the rest of the toolkit didn't have a name for. Page What it answers Systems Thinking for CTOs What structure is producing the behavior you're trying to change Understanding the System Before Changing It What a specific intervention would disturb before you make it Decision Architecture How the decision to act gets made Transformation and Innovation, this page Whether what you're trying to do is generate the right option or get an organization to adopt one Innovation Portfolio Where a sourced, tournament-selected bet gets funded, staged, and killed if it doesn't earn the next stage Checklist Before you call it a transformation Run this before staffing an initiative as a transformation. If most of these are unanswered, it's still an innovation effort, and that's fine, just don't fund or staff it like the bigger thing. You can name the coalition, the specific people whose credibility will carry this past their own team, beyond the executive sponsor who announced it You have a reinforcement plan for six months after launch, as well as a training plan for week one The initiative is staffed and run differently from steady-state operations rather than folded into the normal reporting cadence You know which ADKAR stage past pilots have died at, and it has moved past Awareness You've distinguished whether the gap is generating better options or getting existing good ones adopted, and you're applying the matching fix

title: Vendor Evaluation
description: A preview of the Vendor Evaluation Scorecard: weighted, multi-evaluator scoring across functional fit, security posture, financial stability.
body: Mechanic Why multi-evaluator rather than single-decision-maker The scorecard's value is in forcing the score itself to survive more than one perspective before it becomes a decision. The criteria list is the smaller part. How it works Each stakeholder category (technical, security, finance, the end users) scores the vendor independently against the same criteria before anyone compares notes. Independent scoring first prevents the most senior or most vocal evaluator's opinion from anchoring everyone else's. Where it earns its keep The interesting result is usually the variance rather than the average score. A vendor scored a 2 by security and a 5 by the business sponsor is a conversation the scorecard forces to happen explicitly, before a contract is signed, rather than as a surprise after go-live. Framework Weighted scoring criteria The categories that belong in every vendor evaluation, regardless of what's being bought, with the weighting varying by how critical and how sticky the vendor relationship will be. Category What to check Common mistake Functional fit Score against your own top ten requirements rather than the vendor's feature list Scoring against the demo instead of a trial with your own data Security & compliance posture A current SOC 2 or ISO certification rather than an expired one; the pen test summary if available Accepting a security questionnaire response at face value with no artifact requested Financial stability Funding stage or profitability, customer concentration risk, runway if it's an early-stage vendor Skipping this for anything that isn't a large, obviously stable vendor Integration complexity API quality and documentation, tested in an integration spike rather than taken from a sales engineer's assurance Estimating integration effort from a slide deck instead of a technical spike Support & SLA Historical response time from reference customers rather than the SLA document's stated target Trusting the SLA document without checking whether it's ever enforced against the vendor Exit & data portability Can you export your data in a usable format, and what does contract termination require Leaving this question until the relationship is already ending Interactive Score a vendor Compare up to four vendors side by side on the six weighted dimensions, scored by one evaluator. Weights are editable. A vendor with any dimension at 1 is knocked out whatever its average, and the tool checks whether the winner survives a switch to equal weights. The full workbook supports multiple evaluators scoring independently and surfacing the variance between them, which is where this framework earns its keep; this tool is a single evaluator's pass. Runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere. Score it 1 Reference calls that surface something The single highest-value, most consistently skipped step in vendor evaluation. What works Asking the vendor for a reference in a similar situation to yours (similar scale, similar use case), then asking that reference one specific question: "what would you do differently if you were choosing again today." That question surfaces friction far more reliably than "are you happy with them." What backfires Accepting only the references the vendor's sales team hand-picked, and asking only satisfaction questions that have an obvious socially expected positive answer. This step becomes a formality that confirms nothing. 2 The lock-in question, asked before signing Exit cost is far easier to evaluate before a contract exists than after switching costs have already accumulated. Questions to answer now What format can data be exported in, is there a contractual data portability clause, what's the notice period and any early termination penalty, and how much custom integration work exists that would need to be rebuilt for a different vendor. The cost of skipping this Discovering the exit cost during a renewal negotiation, at exactly the moment the vendor has the least incentive to make leaving easy and the most leverage to raise price, since they know switching now looks expensive. 3 Contract terms that matter beyond price The number in the proposal is the easiest thing to negotiate. The clauses nobody reads carefully are usually what costs money later. Auto-renewal terms. How much notice is required to opt out, and does the notice window open before or after the price for the next term is disclosed. A short window that closes before the new price is revealed is a structural risk to you regardless of the vendor's intent, and worth negotiating out of the contract either way. Liability caps. What the vendor is on the hook for if their product causes a breach or an outage, often capped at fees paid, which can be a small fraction of the damage. SLA penalty structure. Whether missing the SLA produces an automatic credit or requires the customer to notice, document, and formally claim it, which most SLAs quietly rely on nobody doing. Most-favored-nation and price-lock clauses. Whether the contract protects against a price increase at renewal, and whether it's enforceable or only a stated intention. 4 Negotiation leverage, and when to use it Leverage in a vendor negotiation exists but is time-bound. Knowing when it exists changes what's worth pushing for. Where leverage exists The vendor's fiscal quarter-end or year-end, when a sales rep needs the deal to close on their timeline rather than yours. A competitive alternative already evaluated rather than bluffed. A multi-year commitment offered in exchange for a meaningful discount, since the vendor values the certainty more than the marginal revenue from staying month-to-month. Where it doesn't Threatening to walk with no alternative lined up gets tested and lost quickly. A vendor negotiation team that's dealt with the bluff before will call it, and the next negotiation starts from a weaker position because the threat is no longer credible. 5 After signing: performance management A vendor evaluation that stops at the signature misses the half of the relationship that determines whether the choice was right. Practice A standing quarterly business review for any vendor above a materiality threshold, tracking the same dimensions scored during evaluation, support responsiveness, uptime against the SLA, whether the integration is still fit for purpose. This is what turns the next renewal negotiation from a cold restart into a conversation grounded in a track record. Common failure mode The scorecard gets built once, before signing, and never revisited. By renewal, eighteen months of drift in support quality or product direction is invisible, and the renewal decision gets made on inertia rather than on evidence, exactly the failure mode this whole page exists to prevent at the front end. 6 The vendor risk register Above a materiality threshold, a vendor is a standing risk that outlives the purchase decision that created it. Enterprise risk management treats it that way; a vendor scorecard that ends at signing does not. Field What it tracks Criticality tier Whether the vendor is on the critical path for revenue or compliance, important but replaceable, or low-impact; sets the review cadence below Concentration Share of category spend, share of total technology spend, and whether the vendor sits behind more than one internal system, so the real blast radius is visible rather than assumed Financial health Last checked date and source (funding round, public filings, a credit check for a private vendor); refreshed at each renewal at minimum, sooner for an early-stage vendor Security posture drift Current SOC 2 or ISO status against what was true at signing; certifications lapse and breach histories accumulate after the initial evaluation Named exit path The migration plan and its estimated cost and duration, reviewed rather than assumed still valid as the vendor's product and your integration with it both keep changing Owner A named individual accountable for the vendor relationship, not a team or a function; see the same pattern in SaaS Contract & Renewal Negotiation This is the same register discipline that underlies third-party risk management frameworks such as NIST SP 800-161 and ISO 27036; a formal certification against either is unnecessary for most organizations, but the register they describe, one row per material vendor, reviewed on a fixed cadence rather than only at renewal, is worth running regardless of whether the paperwork ever gets audited. Feed the criticality tier and concentration fields from here directly into the vendor concentration checklist on SaaS Contract & Renewal Negotiation ; the two pages track the same underlying risk from different angles and should use the same numbers. 7 Worked example: three vendors, one knockout The six weighted dimensions from the table above: functional fit 30, security and compliance 20, financial stability 15, integration complexity 15, support and SLA 10, exit and data portability 10. Scores are 1 to 5. These are the default values in the tool above. Vendor Functional Security Financial Integration Support Exit Weighted Outcome Vendor A 5 3 4 3 3 2 3.65 Viable; negotiate data export and termination assistance Vendor B 4 4 3 4 4 4 3.85 Selected Vendor C 4 1 4 5 4 4 3.55 Knocked out: a 1 on security disqualifies, whatever the average says 8 Third-party risk is now a regulated topic Vendor evaluation used to be a procurement exercise. For many sectors it is now an examined control. What changed The EU Digital Operational Resilience Act has applied since January 17, 2025 and requires financial entities to keep a register of information on ICT third-party arrangements. [1] Verizon's 2025 Data Breach Investigations Report found third-party involvement in about 30 percent of breaches, double the prior year. [2] What to do Record for each critical vendor the services it supports, the data it holds, the exit plan, and the subcontractors it relies on. Re-score critical vendors annually, not only at renewal. Sources Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 (Digital Operational Resilience Act) Verizon, 2025 Data Breach Investigations Report (release, April 2025) Download Vendor evaluation scorecard The six weighted dimensions above in a fillable format, with per-dimension guidance and a place to log key risks and mitigations. Markdown for pasting into your own docs system, or a formatted Word doc. Download .md Download .docx

title: Zero-Trust Maturity PreviewSix zero-trust dimensions with identity as the foundation the others assume
description: A preview of the six-dimension Security & Zero-Trust Maturity Model, scored on evidence rather than stated policy: identity and access, segmentation and blast radius, detection and response, vulnerability management, third-party risk, and governance and culture.
body: Framework Six dimensions, scored independently Most organizations are unevenly mature across these six; that unevenness is itself the most useful output of the assessment. Dimension Level 1: Ad hoc Level 3: Defined Level 5: Optimized Identity & access Standing broad access, no consistent least-privilege policy across systems Documented access policy applied through a defined onboarding/offboarding process Just-in-time, continuously verified access with no standing privilege by default Segmentation & blast radius Flat network, one compromised credential reaches most of the environment Defined network segments with controlled points between them Micro-segmented to the workload level; a single compromise is contained by design rather than by luck Detection & response Reliant on external reports to learn about a problem Centralized logging and defined alerting on known threat patterns Behavioral anomaly detection catching novel patterns, with a tested response plan behind it Vulnerability management Scanning inconsistent, patching reactive and undocumented Regular scanning cadence, patching SLA defined and mostly met Continuous scanning integrated into deployment, patching SLA consistently met with evidence Third-party risk Vendor access granted with no ongoing review Vendor risk assessed at onboarding, reviewed periodically Continuous vendor risk monitoring, access scoped and reviewed on the same cadence as internal identity Governance & culture Security treated as a separate team's job, outside delivery Defined security requirements built into the delivery process Security ownership distributed to delivery teams, with a lightweight central function rather than a gate Interactive Score your own environment Score each dimension today and where it needs to be, with a line of evidence for each score. The tool applies this page's identity-first rule, ranks the gaps, and gives the sequence to close them. Runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere. Calculate maturity score Diagram Why identity is scored first The six dimensions are scored independently above, but they are not independent in practice. Five of them rest on one. Six zero-trust dimensions with identity as the foundation the others assume Identity and access who is asking FIRST MOVE Segmentation limits where a trusted identity can go Detection and response notices when trust was misplaced Vulnerability management closes the doors identity guards Third-party risk extends the boundary outward Governance and culture keeps all of it from decaying Every outer dimension assumes the request came from who it says it did. Micro-segmentation on top of standing broad access is complexity around a weak foundation. Arrows show what each outer dimension takes for granted. The sequencing card below follows from the picture: concentrate on the hub until it holds, then move outward. Sequencing Where to start, since you can't do all six at once Treating six dimensions as equally urgent is how effort gets spread thin everywhere and deep nowhere. The highest-leverage starting point Identity and access almost always comes first. Segmentation, detection, and even third-party risk all assume you can trust who's making a request in the first place; building micro-segmentation on top of standing broad access adds complexity around a foundation that's still weak. The trap Spreading effort evenly across all six dimensions produces slow, shallow progress everywhere and leaves the foundational dimension exactly as weak as it started, which is worse than concentrating effort where it compounds. Worked example Reading a score pattern instead of the average What the six-dimension breakdown reveals when it's uneven, which it almost always is. Scores: Identity & access 2, Segmentation & blast radius 2, Detection & response 4, Vulnerability management 3, Third-party risk 2, Governance & culture 3. Average: 2.7. The diagnosis the average hides: strong detection sitting on top of weak identity and segmentation is a specific, dangerous pattern. This organization can see an attacker after they're already in, but the foundational controls that would have made getting in hard, or limited what they could reach once inside, are still weak. The instinct this score pattern usually triggers, buy more detection tooling since it's already the strongest area, is exactly backwards. More visibility into a wide-open environment doesn't reduce how wide open it is. Identity and segmentation need the next dollar; detection can wait. Reference The standards behind the six dimensions Map the scores to a published model so auditors and customers recognize the vocabulary. Source Date What it contributes NIST SP 800-207, Zero Trust Architecture August 2020 The core definition: no implicit trust based on network location; per-request access decisions [1] CISA Zero Trust Maturity Model 2.0 April 2023 Five pillars (identity, devices, networks, applications and workloads, data) across four stages: traditional, initial, advanced, optimal [2] NIST SP 800-207A September 2023 Zero trust for cloud-native applications across multiple locations [3] NIST SP 1800-35, Implementing a Zero Trust Architecture June 2025 Nineteen example implementations built with commercial products at the National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence [4] OMB M-22-09 January 2022 US federal agency targets, useful as a public benchmark for sequencing [5] Sources NIST SP 800-207, Zero Trust Architecture, August 2020 CISA, Zero Trust Maturity Model Version 2.0, April 2023 NIST SP 800-207A, September 2023 NIST NCCoE, final SP 1800-35, June 2025 OMB Memorandum M-22-09, January 2022 How to use this Scoring on evidence, and what to do with the result The assessment only has value if the scoring holds up, which is harder than it sounds when the person scoring it is also accountable for the result. How to score it Score against evidence rather than intention. "We have a policy" is evidence of intent, and it does not reach Level 3 unless the policy is followed. Ask for the artifact (the access review log, the segmentation diagram, the vendor review record) before accepting a self-reported level. What to do with a low score A Level 1 or 2 in any dimension is a prioritization input rather than an emergency in itself. Rank dimensions by business impact if that dimension fails, rather than by how uncomfortable the low score is, and fund the highest-impact gap first rather than the easiest one to fix. Common pitfall Compliance certification as a false signal of maturity A frequent gap between what a certification confirms and what an organization assumes it confirms. What a certification confirms SOC 2 or ISO 27001 confirms that defined controls existed and were followed during the specific audit period the certification covers, evaluated against a scope the organization itself proposed. What it doesn't confirm That the scope covered every system that matters, that the maturity level is sustained rather than a point-in-time snapshot assembled for the audit, or that a novel attack pattern outside the certified controls would be caught. Treat certification as a floor. See Security & Compliance Maturity for the broader NIST CSF-based governance ladder this architecture-specific model complements; the two are meant to disagree sometimes rather than tell the same story twice.

title: Integration & API PatternsCommand in, events out: the integration combination most estates should converge on
description: A selection guide and catalog for integration patterns: the three questions that narrow the choice, synchronous, asynchronous, and data integration patterns with the rule that keeps each healthy, the combinations that recur in healthy estates, the rules an architecture review should enforce, and the enterprise service bus mistake that keeps returning under new names.
body: Framework Three questions before any pattern Integration patterns are chosen by habit: whatever the last project used, or whatever the vendor's platform makes easy. Three questions narrow the field to one or two patterns almost every time. Question If the answer is It points toward Does the caller need the answer to proceed Yes, right now, and it changes what the caller does next Synchronous: REST, gRPC, GraphQL No, the caller only needs to know it will happen Asynchronous: message queue, event stream, or a command with a callback What happens if the other side is down The caller must fail too, visibly Synchronous, with a circuit breaker and a clear error The work should wait and complete later Queue with durable storage and retry; the caller is decoupled from the consumer's availability How many consumers, and do they know each other One known consumer Point-to-point call or queue Many, changing, not all known to the producer Event stream with a published schema; producers do not know who listens Is this a request, a fact, or a bulk movement of data A request to do something API call or command message A fact that something happened Domain event A large dataset moving on a schedule Batch, ELT into a warehouse or lakehouse, or change data capture. An API is the wrong tool here Pattern catalog Synchronous patterns Use when the caller needs the answer to proceed. The cost is coupling to the callee's availability and latency; the benefit is simplicity and immediate consistency. Pattern Use it for Do not use it for The rule that keeps it healthy REST over HTTP Resource-oriented APIs consumed by many clients, public or partner APIs, anything a browser calls High-frequency internal service-to-service calls where payload overhead matters, streaming Version in the URL or header from day one; never break a published contract, add a new version gRPC Internal service-to-service calls with strict contracts, low latency, polyglot teams, streaming Browser clients without a gateway, partner APIs where the consumer will not adopt protobuf The proto file is the contract; it lives in one repository and is reviewed like code GraphQL A single front-end aggregating many back-end sources, mobile clients that need to control payload size A general replacement for REST between services, anything where callers can craft arbitrarily expensive queries unchecked Depth and complexity limits enforced at the gateway; persisted queries for production clients API gateway One entry point for authentication, rate limiting, routing, and observability across many services A place to put business logic; a gateway with transformations nobody can find is the next legacy system Cross-cutting concerns only; if a rule references a specific business entity, it belongs in a service Backend for frontend Each client type (web, mobile, partner) gets its own thin aggregation layer Sharing one BFF across clients with different needs, which recreates the problem it solves Owned by the client team that needs it rather than by a central integration team Pattern catalog Asynchronous patterns Use when the caller does not need the answer now, when the other side may be down, or when many consumers should react to one fact. The cost is eventual consistency and harder debugging; the benefit is resilience and decoupling. Pattern Use it for Do not use it for The rule that keeps it healthy Message queue (point-to-point) Work that must be done exactly once by one consumer: order fulfillment, email sending, background jobs Broadcasting a fact to many consumers Dead-letter queue with an owner and an alert; idempotent consumers, because at-least-once delivery is the reality Publish and subscribe One fact, many independent reactions, consumers added without touching the producer Request-reply disguised as events, where the producer secretly waits for a specific subscriber The producer never knows or cares who listens; if it does, the pattern is wrong Event streaming (log) High-volume ordered event history, replayable by new consumers, the backbone of event-driven architecture Simple job queues where a stream's operational cost is unjustified Schema registry with compatibility rules enforced at publish time; retention decided by the business need to replay rather than left at the default Change data capture Getting data out of a database into analytics, search, or another system without touching the application A substitute for a domain event, because a row change is not a business fact Treat the captured change as an internal feed; translate to a domain event before other teams consume it Saga (choreography or orchestration) A business transaction spanning several services where a distributed transaction is not available Anything that could be a single service with a local transaction Every step has a compensating action written and tested before the saga goes live Outbox Publishing an event reliably in the same transaction as the database write Nothing; it is the correct way to do this and the alternative is lost events The relay that reads the outbox is monitored for lag like any other consumer Pattern catalog Data integration patterns Moving data in bulk is not an integration problem to solve with APIs. Most systems that try end up with a nightly job that calls an endpoint a million times. Pattern Use it for Trade-off Scheduled batch, file or bulk export Large periodic movements between systems that tolerate hours of latency: finance close, regulatory extracts, partner feeds Simple and cheap; latency and the operational fragility of schedules and file formats ELT into a warehouse or lakehouse Analytics, reporting, and anything that needs a joined view across many sources Decouples producers from consumers entirely; the platform becomes a dependency and the data has an owner problem, covered in Data Strategy Streaming ingestion Near-real-time analytics and operational dashboards Cost and complexity are much higher than batch; justify the latency requirement with a business decision that changes at that latency Data virtualization or federation Querying across sources without moving data, for low-volume exploratory use Performance and the illusion of a single system; it cannot stand in for an integration layer Managed file transfer Regulated B2B exchange where the counterparty will only do SFTP Old, boring, and still correct for that case; wrap it with monitoring and a retention policy Reference Common combinations that work Working architectures combine patterns. These are the combinations that recur in healthy estates. Command in, events out A service accepts synchronous commands over REST or gRPC, writes to its own database, and publishes domain events through an outbox. Consumers subscribe. The service never calls other services synchronously to complete a write. Gateway plus BFF plus internal gRPC Public traffic enters through a gateway that handles auth and rate limits, hits a client-specific BFF, which calls internal services over gRPC. Nothing internal is reachable from outside. Event stream plus CDC plus lakehouse Operational events flow through a stream; CDC captures the database changes that predate the event design; both land in the lakehouse for analytics. The lakehouse never feeds an operational decision back synchronously. Queue plus saga for long-running business processes An order, a claim, a loan application: a saga orchestrator steps through services via queues, each step idempotent, each with a compensating action, with the state of every in-flight process visible in one place. Strangler with an anti-corruption layer New services sit behind the same gateway as the legacy system; an anti-corruption layer translates between the legacy model and the new domain model so the new services never inherit the old shape. See Legacy Modernization Execution . Diagram Command in, events out The first combination in the list above, drawn. It is the shape most estates should converge on, and the dashed brown line is the rule that is broken most often. Command in, events out: the integration combination most estates should converge on Client web, mobile, partner Gateway auth, rate limit, routing REST Service A accepts commands command Own database plus an outbox table one local transaction Outbox relay monitored for lag Event stream published schema domain event Service B reacts, idempotent Service C reacts, idempotent Dead-letter queue owned, alerted Lakehouse analytics only, never back into operations failed after retries Service C never reads Service A's database; the contract is the only path. Service A never calls B or C synchronously to finish a write. THE RULE Synchronous in for the answer the caller needs now. Asynchronous out for every fact others react to. Consumers are added without touching the producer, and every consumer is idempotent. The outbox is what makes the event reliable: it is written in the same transaction as the data, and the relay publishes it afterwards. The lakehouse consumes the same stream but never feeds an operational decision back synchronously. Governance The rules an architecture review should enforce Pattern choice is a team decision. These rules are the small set an Architecture Review Board should hold across teams, because violating them is expensive for everyone else. Every published contract (OpenAPI, proto, event schema) is versioned, in a repository, reviewed, and never broken in place No service reads another service's database; the only path is the contract Every asynchronous consumer is idempotent and has a dead-letter path with an owner Every synchronous call across a network boundary has a timeout, a retry policy with backoff, and a circuit breaker Every integration is observable end to end: a correlation identifier propagates through calls and messages, and a trace exists for a single business transaction Domain events describe business facts in business language rather than table changes Internal integration does not go through a vendor iPaaS unless the vendor owns both ends; iPaaS is for SaaS-to-SaaS Any integration that runs on a schedule has an alert when it does not run, in addition to one when it fails Reference Specifications to standardize on, September 2026 Pick these as defaults in the integration standards so teams only argue about the exceptions. Specification Current version or status Use it for OpenAPI 3.2, released September 2025 [1] Synchronous HTTP APIs: contract first, generated clients, linting in CI AsyncAPI 3.0, released December 2023 [2] Event-driven interfaces: channels, messages, and bindings for Kafka, AMQP, MQTT, and others CloudEvents (CNCF) 1.0; the project graduated in CNCF in January 2024 [3] A common envelope for events so routing and tracing work across brokers and clouds RFC 9457, Problem Details for HTTP APIs IETF standard, July 2023; replaces RFC 7807 [4] One machine-readable error format across every API OWASP API Security Top 10 2023 edition The review checklist; broken object-level authorization is still the top risk [5] Model Context Protocol (MCP) Contributed to the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation in December 2025 [6] Exposing tools and data to AI agents; treat each MCP server as an API with its own authentication, authorization, and rate limits Sources OpenAPI Initiative, Announcing OpenAPI v3.2, September 2025 AsyncAPI Initiative, AsyncAPI 3.0.0 release notes, December 2023 CNCF, graduation of CloudEvents, January 2024 IETF, RFC 9457, Problem Details for HTTP APIs, July 2023 OWASP, API Security Top 10, 2023 edition Linux Foundation, formation of the Agentic AI Foundation, December 2025 Worked example Choosing a pattern for three real integrations The same selection questions applied three times: who needs to know, how fast, and what happens if the other side is down. Integration Pattern chosen Why Checkout calls tax calculation Synchronous API with a timeout and a cached fallback rate The answer is needed before the order completes; an outage cannot be allowed to stop sales Order placed, notify fulfilment, billing, and analytics Published event, one topic, three subscribers The producer should not know or wait for its consumers; each can fail and replay independently Nightly load of 40 million rows to the warehouse Batch file or change data capture, not an API Volume and latency tolerance make request-response the wrong tool Retries on any of the above Idempotency keys on every write At-least-once delivery is the realistic guarantee, so duplicates must be harmless Diagram The selection questions as a flow The same three questions from the worked example above, in the order to ask them. Choosing an integration pattern with three questions Does the caller need the answer to continue? Should several consumers react without the producer waiting? Large volume and latency tolerant? Synchronous API with a timeout and a fallback e.g. checkout calls tax calculation Publish an event one topic, many subscribers e.g. order

title: Technical Debt Economics
description: Technical debt gets discussed in adjectives and funded by whoever argues best. This page replaces that with three numbers per item and a sequencing method simple enough to defend to a CFO: what it costs each year to leave it, what it costs once to fix it, and therefore which items to fund first within a fixed budget.
body: Framework Three numbers per item, or it is a complaint rather than a debt conversation Technical debt discussions fail because they are conducted in adjectives. An item becomes fundable once it has a carry cost, a remediation cost, and a risk exposure, each stated in dollars per year. Rough is fine. Absent is the problem. Number What it is How to estimate it in an hour Carry cost What the debt costs every year it stays: slower delivery, extra operational toil, licensing for the thing you should have retired, the workaround everyone maintains Engineering hours per month spent working around it, times a loaded hourly rate, times twelve, plus any hard costs (licenses, hosting, support contracts) that exist only because of it Risk exposure The expected annual cost of the incident, breach, or outage the debt makes more likely Probability of a material event in a year, times the cost of that event (revenue, recovery, credits, regulatory). A 20 percent chance of a $500k event is $100k a year. The order of magnitude is what matters, well ahead of precision Remediation cost What it costs to make it go away, once Engineering hours to fix, migrate, or retire, times the loaded rate, plus any one-time hard costs. Include the cost of the parallel run or cutover if there is one Carry cost plus risk exposure is the annual cost of doing nothing. Divided into remediation cost it gives the payback period. Items with a payback under a year are operating decisions that have been avoided rather than debt decisions. Items with a payback over five years are usually not worth doing unless the risk exposure is dominated by a tail event that the organization has said it will not accept, which is what Technology Risk Appetite is for. The one-paragraph CFO test. Before an item goes on the list, write the case for it in one paragraph a CFO would accept: what it costs to leave, what it costs to fix, what goes wrong if nobody does. If that paragraph cannot be written, the severity is overstated or the numbers are missing, and either way the item is not ready to compete for budget. Diagram From three numbers to a decision The three numbers above are enough to put every item in one of three places, and each place has a different conversation with finance. Accepted items are not failures. Reporting them as deliberately carried cost is what stops them resurfacing as surprises. Interactive Carry-cost calculator and multi-year sequencer Enter up to eight debt items and an annual remediation budget. The tool computes annual cost of doing nothing, payback, and a ranking, then sequences the items across years within the budget. Runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere. Loaded engineering cost per hour ($) Annual remediation budget ($) Planning horizon (years) Item Hours / month lost to it Hard carry cost / yr ($) Event probability / yr (%) Event cost ($) Remediation hours Remediation hard cost ($) Rank and sequence Load sample portfolio Clear Method How the sequencer decides The logic is deliberately simple enough to explain to a CFO in one sentence: fund the items that remove the most annual cost per remediation dollar, within the budget, and carry the rest. Annual cost of doing nothing Carry cost plus risk exposure, for each item. Ratio Annual cost of doing nothing divided by remediation cost. This is the return on the remediation dollar. Items are ranked by it. Greedy allocation by year Walk the ranked list. If an item fits in the current year's remaining budget, fund it that year. If it does not fit, carry it to the next year and keep walking so smaller items can use the remaining capacity. Repeat for the horizon. Payback gate An item is only funded in a year where the cost it avoids over the rest of the horizon exceeds its remediation cost. An item that would not pay back even if funded in year one is marked Accept: carry it knowingly, or take it to the capital allocation conversation as an investment in its own right. Items that pay back but do not fit the budget are shown as unfunded, which is a budget question rather than a merit question. Carry cost paid meanwhile Every year an item is not yet remediated, its annual cost of doing nothing is paid. The total across the horizon is reported so the sequence can be compared against a different budget. What it does not do It does not model dependencies between items, capacity constraints per team, or the option of partial remediation. The private version does; this is the transparent core. A sequencing decision that cannot be explained is one the CFO will not fund twice. Worked example Reading a ranked portfolio Load the sample portfolio above. The ranking usually surprises people in the same way. What the ranking shows The item everyone talks about, the large monolith rewrite, ranks last: a large remediation cost against a carry cost that is substantial but diffuse. The item nobody talks about, a nightly retry workaround that costs one engineer a week a month, ranks first because it is nearly free to fix. The unsupported database with a meaningful breach probability sits in the top four with a payback under three months, because its risk exposure dominates its carry cost. Three of the top four items cost less than $15k to fix. What to do with it Fund the top of the list this quarter without a further business case; the numbers are the case. Take the monolith to the capital allocation conversation as a transform investment rather than a debt item, because that is what it is. Report the annual cost of doing nothing for the unfunded remainder to the board as a number, once a year, so nobody can later say the risk was hidden. Reference Where debt hides and how to find it The backlog in Application Portfolio Management and the signals in Technology Diligence are the inputs. These are the places that reliably produce items with high ratios. Source What to look for Typical carry cost driver Unsupported or end-of-life versions Runtimes, databases, operating systems, and frameworks past vendor support Risk exposure; also extended support contracts and the inability to patch Manual operational toil Deployments, restores, certificate renewals, and data fixes done by hand Hours per month, plus the outage each one eventually causes Duplicated capability Two or more systems doing the same job because a migration stopped halfway Double licensing, double integration, double on-call Undocumented single-person systems Anything only one engineer can change Key-person risk expressed as a probability times the cost of losing them Missing tests on critical paths Change failure rate concentrated in a few services Incident cost and the slowdown of every change to those services Deferred security findings Pen test and scan findings older than one quarter Almost pure risk exposure; usually cheap to remediate relative to it Cloud spend outpacing usage Cost per transaction or per customer rising while volume is flat Architecture debt surfacing in the bill first: chatty services, oversized data movement, capacity bought to paper over contention Workarounds in the integration layer Transformations and retries that exist because a contract was never fixed Hours per month and the incidents when the workaround meets an edge case Download Carry-cost workbook and a sample remediation plan The workbook runs the three-number method above on a portfolio of up to forty items: NPV cost of doing nothing, NPV savings for each candidate year, best year, savings ratio, priority class, and a ranked list, with the discount rate and horizon as inputs. It ships loaded with a twelve-item sample portfolio. The second file is the output the full optimizer produced for that same portfolio: a five-year plan with per-item rationale. Download carry-cost workbook (.xlsx) Download sample remediation plan (.xlsx) The workbook stops at the ranking. The full optimizer adds the constrained multi-year sequencer (annual budget, engineer-day capacity, dependency chains, deferred items reported as accepted risk), a rationale per item, and in the production version a learned priority scorer, skill-mix capacity, and sensitivity analysis. Available through direct engagement. Common pitfall The debt budget that funds nothing in particular Allocating twenty percent of capacity to debt without a ranked list produces twenty percent of capacity spent on whatever each team finds annoying. What it looks like Every sprint has a debt allocation. Engineers use it to refactor code they touch anyway. The unsupported database, which nobody enjoys working on, is untouched for three years. The allocation is visible in the roadmap, so leadership believes debt is being managed. The breach, when it comes, is on the database. The counter-move The debt allocation funds the ranked list, top down, and nothing else. Local refactoring is part of normal delivery and stays out of the debt budget. The list is reviewed quarterly, new items need the three numbers to get on it, and the annual cost of doing nothing for the unfunded tail is reported alongside the items funded. See Engineering Metrics for the delivery signals that tell you whether the carry cost estimates were right.

title: Identity & Access ArchitectureIdentity reference architecture: layers, populations, and supporting services
description: The identity layer as a control plane: workforce, privileged, workload, and customer populations, a reference architecture mapped across Entra, AWS, Google Cloud, and independent platforms, joiner-mover-leaver lifecycle, non-human and agent identity, sequencing by risk reduced, and the one export that reveals how seriously identity has been taken.
body: Framework Identity is the control plane Every other security control assumes the request came from who it says it did. If that assumption is weak, segmentation, detection, and encryption are all decorating an open door. Most estates have at least four identity populations, and most identity programs are built for only the first. The others are where the breaches happen. Population What it covers Where it usually is Where it needs to be Workforce Employees and contractors signing in to SaaS, VPN, and internal apps SSO for the big apps, local accounts for everything else, MFA on the VPN only One directory, every app federated, phishing-resistant MFA everywhere, no local accounts left standing Privileged Admins of cloud tenants, directories, databases, network, and the identity platform itself Standing global admin held by six people, shared break-glass account in a password manager No standing privilege. Just-in-time elevation with approval, time-bound, logged, and reviewed. Break-glass accounts monitored, tested quarterly Workload Service principals, managed identities, IAM roles, API keys, CI runners, agents Long-lived secrets in config, keys created by whoever needed one, nobody knows how many exist Managed identities or short-lived federated tokens wherever the platform supports them, secrets in a vault with rotation, an inventory with owners Customer and partner External users of your products and B2B partners reaching internal systems Built into each product separately, partner access through a shared VPN account A dedicated customer identity platform with its own risk policy, partners federated to their own directory with scoped, expiring access Diagram The identity estate at a glance The four layers are what the table below maps to each provider. The four populations are who those layers serve, and the row beneath is the supporting service each population depends on most, which is where most estates are weakest. Identity reference architecture: layers, populations, and supporting services LAYERS, IN ORDER OF DEPENDENCY Authoritative source HR: who exists, in what role Directory and federation one identity, every app Authentication policy allow, step up, block Governance reviews, packages, SoD joiner, mover, leaver SAML and OIDC, no local accounts risk, device, session signals default on no response: removal per-request decisions, every population POPULATIONS Workforce employees, contractors Privileged admins: no standing rights Workload services, CI runners, agents Customer and partner external users, B2B Device and session trust the device as well as the user Just-in-time elevation time-bound, approved, logged Federated identity and vault no long-lived credentials Own identity platform own policy, scoped partner access THE WEEK-ONE EXPORT Every account holding a privileged role: permanent or eligible, last used, phishing-resistant MFA registered. Then every service principal with owner-level rights and a non-expiring secret. More than a handful of permanent admins, any shared or departed, any without strong MFA, any tenant-wide service principal with a non-expiring secret: the identity layer has been administered rather than architected. That reading shapes the first quarter. Dashed arrows lead from each population to the supporting service it depends on most. Authentication policy sits in the middle of the layer chain but applies to every population; the horizontal line makes that explicit. The privileged population is the smallest and the one where the week-one export tells you the most. Reference architecture The layers a mature identity estate has Provider names differ; the structure does not. The table maps each layer to what it looks like on the major platforms so an architecture review can ask whether each layer exists rather than which product it uses. Layer Purpose Microsoft Entra AWS Google Cloud Independent Authoritative source One system of record for who exists, in what role, reporting to whom HR system feeding Entra ID via provisioning HR system feeding IAM Identity Center via an external IdP HR system feeding Cloud Identity via an external IdP Workday, SAP SuccessFactors, or similar as source; Okta or Entra as the directory Directory and federation Single identity, federated to every application Entra ID with SAML and OIDC apps, Enterprise Apps gallery IAM Identity Center for AWS accounts, external IdP for everything else Cloud Identity plus an external IdP Okta, Ping Authentication policy Decide per request whether to allow, step up, or block, based on risk Conditional Access with sign-in and user risk from Identity Protection IdP-side policy; AWS does not own workforce authentication policy IdP-side policy; Context-Aware Access for Google resources Okta Adaptive MFA, Ping policy engine Privileged access Time-bound elevation with approval and audit Privileged Identity Management for roles and groups, Administrative Units for scope Permission sets in IAM Identity Center with short session durations; no standing admin in the management account IAM Conditions with time bounds, Privileged Access Manager CyberArk, BeyondTrust, or the IdP's own JIT feature Workload identity Services authenticate without long-lived secrets Managed identities, workload identity federation for GitHub and Kubernetes IAM roles, IRSA and Pod Identity for EKS, OIDC federation for CI Service accounts with workload identity federation, no downloaded keys SPIFFE and SPIRE for cross-platform workloads Secrets The credentials that cannot be eliminated, held once, rotated, audited Key Vault Secrets Manager, Parameter Store Secret Manager HashiCorp Vault Governance Access reviews, entitlement packages, separation of duties, certifications Entra ID Governance: access packages, access reviews, lifecycle workflows IAM Access Analyzer for unused access, external IGA for reviews Policy Analyzer, external IGA for reviews SailPoint, Saviynt Device and session Trust the device as well as the user Intune compliance signal into Conditional Access IdP device trust signal Endpoint Verification into Context-Aware Access Jamf, CrowdStrike, or the IdP device trust integration Lifecycle Joiner, mover, leaver: the process that decides whether the architecture works The most sophisticated Conditional Access policy in the world does nothing about the contractor who left eight months ago and still has a working account. Where it fails Access is granted by ticket, on request, by whoever is asked. Nobody removes access when someone changes role, so tenure equals entitlement. Offboarding disables the directory account but not the twelve SaaS apps with local accounts, the shared service credential the person knew, or the API key they created. The access review is an annual spreadsheet that every manager approves in full because rejecting anything means explaining it. What good looks like Birthright access is defined per role and granted automatically from the HR event. Anything beyond birthright is requested through an access package with a named approver and an expiry. A mover event triggers removal of the old role's entitlements as well as addition of the new. A leaver event is a single action that cascades to every federated app within minutes, and there is a report of what could not be cascaded, which is the list of local accounts still to be eliminated. Access reviews are quarterly, scoped to privileged and sensitive entitlements, and the default on no response is removal. Non-human identity The population that is now larger than the workforce In most cloud estates service principals, roles, keys, and automation identities outnumber people three to one and nobody owns the inventory. AI agents are adding to this fast, and they act with whatever identity they are given. The questions to ask, in order: How many exist Pull the full list of service principals, IAM roles, service accounts, and API keys from every cloud tenant and the CI system. If the number is a surprise, that is the finding. Which have an owner Every non-human identity needs a named human owner and a purpose. Anything without one is a candidate for disablement after a quarantine period. Which use long-lived secrets A client secret or access key that does not expire is a credential that will eventually be in a repository, a log, or a former employee's laptop. Migrate to managed identity or federated tokens; where impossible, vault and rotate. Which are over-privileged Most workload identities were granted Contributor or PowerUser because it worked. Use the platform's unused-access analysis to shrink them to what they call. Which can reach production from outside it CI runners and developer tooling that hold production credentials are the standard path from a compromised laptop to a production breach. What identity do agents act with An AI agent that calls tools does so as something. If that something is a broadly-scoped service principal, the agent's judgment is now a security control. Give agents their own scoped identities, short-lived, with the same review cadence as privileged humans. Sequencing Where to start when everything is weak Identity programs fail by trying to do all of this at once and finishing none of it. The order below is by risk reduced per unit of effort. Order Move Why first Evidence it is done 1 Phishing-resistant MFA for all privileged accounts, then everyone Credential theft is the entry point in most breaches; this closes it for the accounts that matter most Sign-in logs show no privileged authentication without FIDO2, passkey, or certificate 2 Eliminate standing privileged access Turns a stolen admin credential from a catastrophe into a logged, time-bound event Zero permanent assignments to global or account-level admin roles; PIM or equivalent activation history exists 3 Federate every application, kill local accounts Offboarding cannot work while apps hold their own passwords Application inventory with a federation status per app and a shrinking count of exceptions 4 Automate joiner, mover, leaver from the HR source Removes the human step that fails, and makes the directory trustworthy as an inventory of people Leaver-to-disabled time measured in minutes; mover events remove old entitlements 5 Inventory and shrink non-human identities The largest and least-governed population An owned inventory, no non-expiring secrets for new identities, a rotation report 6 Risk-based authentication policy and device trust Moves from static rules to per-request decisions Policies in report-only mode first, then enforced, with an exception register 7 Governance: reviews, packages, separation of duties Keeps the estate clean after the cleanup Quarterly review completion with a non-zero removal rate Week one The single artifact that tells you the most For a new CTO, an acquirer, or an auditor, one export answers most of the question of how seriously identity has been taken. What to pull The list of every account holding a privileged role in each cloud tenant and the directory, with whether the assignment is permanent or eligible, when it was last used, and whether the account has phishing-resistant MFA registered. Then the same for service principals with owner-level rights. It takes an hour and requires no tooling beyond what the platform provides. How to read it More than a handful of permanent global admins, any of them shared or belonging to people who have left, any without strong MFA, or any service principal with tenant-wide write access and a non-expiring secret: each is a finding in its own right, and together they say the identity layer has been administered rather than architected. That reading should shape the first quarter's security priorities regardless of what the security roadmap deck says. Common pitfall Buying the identity platform and calling it done Most organizations that fail on identity already own the right products. The failure is in the process, the scope, and the exceptions. MFA is enforced, but the legacy authentication protocols that bypass it are still enabled Conditional Access exists, but the policy has forty exclusions and the exclusion group is the one everyone ends up in PIM is deployed for global admin, but the subscription and resource-group owners are still permanent The HR feed is connected, but contractors are not in HR, so the largest leaver risk is unmanaged Access reviews run, but the approval rate is 100 percent, which means nobody is reviewing The break-glass account exists and has never been tested, or has been tested and used routinely because it is convenient Secrets are in a vault, but the application also has a copy in an environment variable that was never removed

title: Observability & SRE Operating ModelObservability signal flow from instrumentation to its three consumers
description: How a reliability function is run rather than how much reliability to buy: four operating models and the one most organizations end up running, what the function owns (SLOs, error budget policy, observability standards, alert hygiene, production readiness, toil), an observability architecture that survives scale and cost, an on-call design people will keep doing, a sequence for standing the function up, and the rename-the-ops-team pitfall.
body: Framework Four models, and the one most organizations end up running Reliability as an Economic Decision answers how much reliability to buy. This page answers how the function that delivers it is organized, because the same reliability budget produces very different outcomes under different operating models. Model Who is on call Who owns reliability work Fits when Fails when Ops team owns production A central operations team The ops team, reactively Small estates, few changes, a product team that cannot be paged Change volume rises; the ops team cannot understand what it is paging on, and the product team has no incentive to build operable software You build it, you run it Each product team, for its own services Each product team Autonomous teams with the platform support to be self-sufficient Teams lack observability tooling, on-call is unfunded, and reliability work loses every prioritization to features Embedded SRE Product team, with an SRE embedded in it Shared; the SRE drives standards and the team executes Critical services that justify a dedicated reliability engineer The SRE becomes the team's ops person and the standards work never happens Central SRE with a platform Product teams for their services; SRE for the platform and for a defined set of critical services SRE owns the platform, the standards, the tooling, and error budget policy; teams own their services within it Ten or more teams and a shared platform, which is most enterprises The SRE team is treated as a rename of the ops team and is paged for everything Most organizations claiming the second model are running the first with extra steps: product teams are nominally on call, but escalate to a central team that does the restoration and owns none of the fixes. Naming the model that is running is the first step. Diagram Where the signals go, and where the money goes The architecture list further down describes this in words. The picture makes the two boundaries visible: what reaches a pager, and where the cost owner sits. Observability signal flow from instrumentation to its three consumers PRODUCE Services vendor-neutral instrumentation Platform and infra same standard AI layer tokens, latency, cost, quality Synthetic and real user the customer's view COLLECT Collector correlation id propagated sampling, retention tiers, cardinality limits STORE Metrics state over time Traces request flow Logs forensic detail CONSUME SLO alerts, to the pager symptoms only: error rate, latency Dashboards causes: CPU, queues, saturation Incident investigation one trace per business transaction COST OWNER LIVES HERE ingest volume by service, a budget per service, an alert when exceeded TWO RULES Only symptoms page a human; causes go to dashboards and the investigation. Standardize the instrumentation rather than the backend, so the backend stays a renewal decision rather than a hostage. The producers on the left include the AI layer and the customer's own view, which most estates leave uninstrumented. The collector is the one place cost is controlled; if there is no owner there, the bill grows with coverage. Reference What the function owns An SRE or reliability function that owns only incident response is an operations team. The list below is what distinguishes a reliability function from a rename. Responsibility What it looks like when owned What it looks like when nobody owns it Service level objectives Every customer-facing service has an SLO agreed with its product owner, measured from the user's perspective, reviewed quarterly A 99.9 percent target inherited from a contract, measured at the load balancer, that nobody can explain Error budget policy A written rule for what happens when a service exhausts its budget: feature work pauses, reliability work is prioritized, the product owner signs off The budget is reported and ignored Observability standards A required minimum for any service in production: structured logs, metrics with defined names, traces with propagated correlation, dashboards from a template, alerts tied to SLOs Each team instruments what it thinks of; the incident reveals the gap Alert hygiene Every page maps to a user-visible symptom and has a runbook; pages per shift are measured and capped Hundreds of alerts, most ignored, the important one lost among them Incident management A defined severity scale, an incident commander role that rotates, a communications role, a timeline kept live, and postmortem follow-through tracked as in Incident Response Whoever is loudest runs the bridge;
